finders.domain: TRNG entropy source, health tests, conditioning and output path (rtl/modules/crypto_trng/rtl/*, rtl/modules/crypto_top/rtl/trng.sv)
finders.coverage_notes:
COVERED (read end-to-end): rng_top.v (142 lines), digitalization.v (146), healthtest.v (55), data_buf.v (104), lfsr129.v (134), postprocess.v (208), ctr_aes.v (217), aes_update.v (67), and rtl/modules/crypto_top/rtl/trng.sv (540) including the embedded apb_shfin/apb_buf modules. I traced every output of the TRNG forward: rngcore_dataout -> scedma_chnl chnlo -> ramreq[14] -> SCERAM SEG_RNGA/RNGB, and every control input backward to its APB SFR and its reset value (verified apb_cr/apb_sfr2 default IV='0 at rtl/modules/amba/rtl/apb_sfr.sv:81,308,339, and `theregrn` reset semantics at rtl/modules/common/rtl/template.sv:82-91). I grepped the whole rtl/ tree for consumers of healthtest_err/sr_hlthtest_err and confirmed there are none outside the status counter. I verified the TRNG's APB slot (sce.sv:537 apbs[6], apb_mux PAW=15/DECAW=3 at sce.sv:179 -> 0x4002_E000) and that trng is reset by the SCE's system `resetn`, not `sceresetn` (sce.sv:533, soc_coresub.sv:532), and that the SCERAM wipe explicitly excludes the RNG pool (sce.sv:417 `.clrend (scedma_pkg::SEGADDR_RNGA-1)`) while RNGA/RNGB are bus-readable (scedma_pkg.sv:308-309 accessrule 8'b10_11_10_10).

COULD NOT COVER / LIMITS:
1. RNG_CELL, OSC_32M, RNGCELL_BUF and ICG are analog/foundry black boxes with no RTL in this repo (grep finds only the instantiations at trng.sv:194-233). The actual jitter/min-entropy per sample is therefore unmeasurable from source; my finding on the LFSR's 1:1 entropy ratio states the consequence as a function of the unknown per-sample min-entropy rather than asserting a specific number.
2. No entropy characterization report, SP 800-90B min-entropy estimate, or health-test threshold justification exists anywhere in the repo (grep for startup/known-answer/adaptive-proportion tests returns nothing).
3. docs/src/*.md contains essentially NO TRNG documentation — the only hits for "trng/rng/random/entropy" are a pin name (ch01-00-electrical-specifications.md:33), a bullet list entry (README.md:38) and a power-rail note (pmu.md:56). I therefore could not do a documented-guarantee vs. RTL comparison for this block; there is no stated guarantee to violate. That absence is itself notable for a security chip.
4. aes_cipher_top.v / aes_sbox.v were read only enough to confirm the CTR_DRBG datapath shape; I did not audit them for correctness of the AES round function or for timing/power side channels, since the AES-based postprocess_opt values (1 and 2) are not the reset default and the LFSR path dominates the risk.
5. I did not simulate. All claims are from static reading of combinational/sequential expressions; I have stated the sequencing arguments explicitly so they can be checked against the vendor's own regressions.
6. Exploit reachability of the TRNG APB window depends on sce_sec.ahben, which I verified is unconditionally 1 while scemode==0 (sce_sec.sv:72) — the reset state. Post-mode-lock reachability is another reviewer's domain.

findings.title: Health-test failure never stops TRNG output: healthtest_err has zero consumers in the datapath, no startup test, no adaptive-proportion test, non-sticky error, and the test is disabled at reset
findings.cwe: CWE-1241 Use of Predictable Algorithm in Random Number Generator (SP 800-90B health-test enforcement missing); see also CWE-330
findings.description: healthtest.v implements only a repetition-count test (RCT) and its result is a pure status bit. `healthtest_err` leaves healthtest.v, passes straight through rng_top.v as a top-level output, and in trng.sv is consumed ONLY by a rising-edge counter and a flag register. A repo-wide grep for consumers of healthtest_err/sr_hlthtest_err finds nothing else. Nothing in the path digi_data_out -> data_buf -> lfsr129/ctr_aes -> rngcore_dataout -> scedma_chnl -> SCERAM RNGA/RNGB is gated by it: rng_top.v:89-140 wires digi_data_out/digi_data_vld into data_buf and postprocess unconditionally, and trng.sv:357 `assign chnlo_start = rngcore_en & rngcore_dataout_vld & ~chnlo_busy ;` does not reference it. Four compounding defects: (a) the test is DISABLED at reset — `healthtest_en` is `cr_hlthtest_en` from `cr_postproc`, an apb_cr whose default IV is '0 (apb_sfr.sv:81,308; theregfull reset at template.sv:82), so healthtest_cnt is forced to 0 and no test runs until software opts in; (b) the threshold `healthtest_length` is a 6-bit software register, also 0 at reset, and there is no minimum — software may set a cutoff of 0 or 63 at will; (c) `healthtest_err` is non-sticky — line 39 clears it on the very first differing bit, so a source that alternates 0/1 (a stuck oscillator being pulled by an injected clock) clears the alarm continuously; (d) there is no SP 800-90B startup test, no known-answer test, and no adaptive-proportion test anywhere in the block (grep for startup/known-answer/adaptive over crypto_trng/ and trng.sv returns nothing). Escalation to the SoC is also dead: trng.sv:283-284 hardwires the module's interrupt and error buses to zero, and the only flag, fr[2], requires 4095 separate error rising-edges to accumulate before it asserts.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker (T2/T4) attacks the noise source physically: EM/clock injection on the OSC_32M ring, or holding the die at a temperature/supply corner that locks the eight RNG_CELL ring oscillators to the sampled HF phase, so `data_samp` becomes constant or periodic. 2. `digi_data_vld` continues to pulse normally — digitalization.v:83-84 derives validity from clk_ana_pos[0], i.e. from the LF ring still oscillating, never from data quality — so buf_cnt still reaches 256 and buf_ready still asserts (data_buf.v:64,100-101). 3. healthtest.v raises healthtest_err (only if firmware happened to enable it; at reset it does not). 4. Nothing happens: rngcore_dataout continues to be produced, chnlo_start (trng.sv:357) continues to fire, and 128-bit words continue to be written into SCERAM SEG_RNGA/RNGB (trng.sv:366). 5. Victim firmware calls its key-generation routine, which reads RNGA/RNGB and derives an AES/ECC/RSA private key from output that has no entropy. 6. Because the default conditioner is a bare LFSR (see the separate lfsr129 finding), the attacker recovers the generator state from one observed 128-bit word — RNGA/RNGB are bus-readable by design (scedma_pkg.sv:308-309 accessrule 8'b10_11_10_10) and are excluded from the SCERAM wipe (sce.sv:417 `.clrend (scedma_pkg::SEGADDR_RNGA-1)`), so a leftover word from the victim's draw is still sitting in the pool. The generated key is then computable offline. Even a purely passive T2 attacker who merely cools the chip gets the same result, because there is no boot-time startup test to refuse to run.
findings.preconditions: Attacker can perturb the analog noise source (T2 EM/clock/temperature/voltage injection) or the source degrades/dies in the field. No software access required for the degradation path; reading the residual RNG pool afterwards requires T1 bus access to 0x4002_1F00-0x4002_26FF, which is unrestricted while scemode==0 (sce_sec.sv:72 `assign ahben =  mode_non ? 1'b1 :`).
findings.mitigation: RTL: gate the output path on health-test status — qualify digi_data_vld into data_buf/postprocess with (~healthtest_err), and force rngcore_dataout_vld low and chnlo_start low while an error is latched. Make healthtest_err STICKY until an explicit software clear, add an SP 800-90B adaptive-proportion test (window 512/1024, cutoff from the estimated min-entropy) alongside the RCT, add a mandatory startup test (at least 1024 consecutive samples passing both tests) that must complete before buf_ready may assert for the first time after reset, enforce a hardware minimum on healthtest_length, and route the error to `err`/`intr` (currently tied to '0 at trng.sv:283-284) so the SCE and the CPU see it. Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: (1) always write cr_postproc with cr_hlthtest_en=1 and a justified healthtest_len before ar_start; (2) never consume RNGA/RNGB directly — after every draw, read sr_rng (0x4002_E010) and discard the entire batch if sr_hlthtest_errcnt moved; (3) implement the SP 800-90B RCT and APT in software over the raw stream read from sfr_buf and refuse to key on failure; (4) always run the raw output through a software SHA-2/SHA-3 extractor at >=2:1 compression before use as key material, and never use TRNG output directly as a key.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (physical: EM/clock/temperature/voltage injection on the noise source), T4 (supply/clock manipulation); T1 to read the residual pool afterwards

findings.title: Default post-processing (postprocess_opt=0, the reset value) is a bare 129-bit LFSR that publishes its entire internal state as the random output, with a 1:1 raw-bit-to-output-bit ratio and no entropy compression
findings.cwe: CWE-338 Use of Cryptographically Weak Pseudo-Random Number Generator (PRNG)
findings.description: `cr_postproc` is an apb_cr with default IV='0 (apb_sfr.sv:81,308,339), so at reset postprocess_opt==2'd0 and postprocess.v:156 selects `lfsr_dataout[127:0]` as the SoC's random output. lfsr_dataout is literally the LFSR state: `assign lfsr_dataout = lfsr_chain[127:0];` — 128 of the 129 state bits are emitted verbatim. Three consequences follow directly from the RTL. (1) FULL STATE DISCLOSURE. After the first 128-bit word the attacker knows lfsr_chain[127:0]; after the second word he also knows lfsr_chain[128], because the shift at line 90/91 moves old bit[127] into bit[128], i.e. bit[128] of the state at output N+1 is bit[0] of output N. Two consecutive words therefore reveal the complete 129-bit state. (2) NO ENTROPY COMPRESSION. lfsr_cnt (lines 96-98) advances one step per digi_data_vld and the word is declared valid at lfsr_cnt==128 (line 102), so exactly 128 raw digitized bits are absorbed per 128 output bits. The mixing at line 91 is `{lfsr_chain[127:0], lfsr_out^digi_data_out}` — a bijective GF(2)-affine map. A conditioner that is invertible and 1:1 cannot increase entropy density: the min-entropy of a 128-bit 'random' word equals the min-entropy of 128 raw ring-oscillator samples. For a directly-sampled jittery oscillator that is typically well under 1 bit/sample, so a 128-bit word intended to carry 128 bits of security carries far less. SP 800-90B requires a vetted conditioning function with compression; there is none here. (3) INVERTIBILITY. Because the state is public and the feedback is a known linear function, the attacker computes lfsr_out at every step and recovers each raw entropy bit exactly as e_k = f_k XOR lfsr_out_k — the output stream is a transparent window onto the unconditioned noise source, so any bias, correlation or injected periodicity in the source translates one-for-one into predictability of the key material. (4) NO RESEED IN THE DEFAULT CONFIG. reseed_interval is 2'd0 at reset, and line 106 gates the reseed counter on `(reseed_interval!=2'h0)`, so reseed_cnt never leaves 0 and never equals generate_value*reseed_value (1*1024); lfsr_stable (line 85) stays 1 forever. The LFSR is seeded once from buf_data[255:127] and never re-seeded, so every word after the first has the degenerate 1:1 ratio with no re-conditioning.
findings.evidence:
rtl/modules/crypto_trng/rtl/lfsr129.v:100:
assign lfsr_dataout     = lfsr_chain[127:0];		  

rtl/modules/crypto_trng/rtl/lfsr129.v:88-94 (invertible 1:1 mixing; only one raw bit absorbed per shift):
assign lfsr_chain_pre   = (|lfsr_chain==1'b0) ? 129'h1_A39A8864_5DF3BECE_074EC5D3_BAF39D18:
	                  (rngcore_en_lfsr& (~lfsr_stable) &  buf_ready & post_read_lfsr) ? buf_data[255:127]:
                          (rngcore_en_lfsr&   lfsr_stable  &  (~lfsr_dataout_vld) &   trng_drng_sel)                  ? {lfsr_chain[127:0],lfsr_out}: 
                          (rngcore_en_lfsr&   lfsr_stable  &  (~lfsr_dataout_vld) & (~trng_drng_sel) & digi_data_vld) ? {lfsr_chain[127:0],lfsr_out^digi_data_out}: 
               		  lfsr_chain;
	
assign lfsr_out         = lfsr_chain[128]^lfsr_chain[114]^lfsr_chain[110]^lfsr_chain[100]^lfsr_chain[43]^lfsr_chain[41];

rtl/modules/crypto_trng/rtl/lfsr129.v:96-98,102 (128 raw bits per 128 output bits):
assign lfsr_cnt_pre     = (~rngcore_en_lfsr| ~lfsr_stable |rngcore_rddone) ? 8'h0 :
                          ((lfsr_cnt<8'd129)&trng_drng_sel) |
			  ((lfsr_cnt<8'd129)&(~trng_drng_sel)&digi_data_vld) ? (lfsr_cnt +1'b1):lfsr_cnt;
assign lfsr_dataout_vld_pre = (lfsr_cnt_pre==8'd128)&&(lfsr_cnt==8'd127) ? 1'b1 :

rtl/modules/crypto_trng/rtl/lfsr129.v:105-107 (reseed disabled when reseed_interval==0, its reset value):
assign reseed_cnt_pre       = (~rngcore_en_lfsr)|(buf_ready & post_read_lfsr) ? 14'd0 : 
	                      (lfsr_dataout_vld & ~lfsr_dataout_vld_pre & (reseed_interval!=2'h0)&
			                     (reseed_cnt < (generate_value*reseed_value))) ? (reseed_cnt+1'b1):reseed_cnt;

rtl/modules/crypto_trng/rtl/postprocess.v:156 (default selection):
assign rngcore_dataout    =(postprocess_opt==2'd0)? lfsr_dataout[127:0]  :

rtl/modules/crypto_top/rtl/trng.sv:110,257-264 (cr_postproc is an apb_cr with default IV='0, so postprocess_opt=0 and reseed_interval=0 at reset):
    apb_cr #(.A('h08), .DW(17) )      sfr_pp          (.cr(cr_postproc), .prdata32(),.*);
    assign { cr_reseed_sel,
            cr_reseed_intval[1:0],
             cr_gen_intval[1:0],
             cr_healthtest_len[5:0],
             cr_postproc_opt[1:0],
             cr_drng_en,
             cr_hlthtest_en,
             cr_pfilter_en, cr_gen_en } = cr_postproc;
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Firmware leaves cr_postproc at its reset value (or writes it without setting postprocess_opt) and issues ar_start (0x4002_E014 <= 0x5a). The RNG runs in bare-LFSR mode. 2. The generated 128-bit words are DMA'd by chnlo into SCERAM SEG_RNGA/RNGB at 0x4002_1F00-0x4002_26FF (trng.sv:366), which per scedma_pkg.sv:308-309 carry accessrule 8'b10_11_10_10 — AHB read is permitted — and which sce.sv:417 explicitly excludes from the crypto-RAM wipe (`.clrend (scedma_pkg::SEGADDR_RNGA-1)`). 3. An unprivileged T1 attacker reads two consecutive 128-bit words from that pool. From word N he obtains lfsr_chain[127:0]; from word N+1 he obtains the remaining bit — the full 129-bit state is now known. 4. He now knows the exact linear evolution of the generator. Every subsequent output word differs from the predicted pure-LFSR word only by the 128 raw entropy bits absorbed, which he can enumerate: if the source has, say, 0.1 bit/sample of min-entropy, the next word has ~12.8 bits of entropy and is brute-forceable in ~10^4 tries. 5. The victim's next draw is used to generate an ECC/RSA/AES key. The attacker enumerates the candidate 128-bit words offline, derives each candidate key, and tests it against any public artifact signed or encrypted with it. 6. If the attacker additionally stalls the noise source (see the health-test finding), the raw bits are constant, the residual is zero, and the next key is computed deterministically with a single guess.
findings.preconditions: Firmware uses the reset default postprocess_opt=0 (bare LFSR), which is what an uninitialised or partially-initialised boot path produces. Reading the RNG pool needs T1 bus access to SCERAM, unrestricted while scemode==0 (sce_sec.sv:72). Even without any read access, the 1:1 no-compression property alone caps every generated key's real entropy at the raw min-entropy of 128 oscillator samples.
findings.mitigation: RTL: never emit the raw LFSR state — postprocess_opt=0 should be removed entirely, or lfsr_dataout must be the output of a one-way compression (e.g. SHA-256 or an AES-CBC-MAC over >=2x as many raw bits as output bits) rather than `lfsr_chain[127:0]`. Make CTR_DRBG (postprocess_opt=2) the reset default and the only non-debug mode, hardwire a minimum compression ratio of 2:1 between raw bits absorbed and bits emitted, and force a re-seed from a freshly filled 256-bit buf_data before every output word rather than gating the reseed counter on a software-selectable reseed_interval that defaults to 'disabled'. Software/firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: (1) the boot ROM must write cr_postproc with cr_postproc_opt=2'd2 (CTR_DRBG) and a non-zero cr_reseed_intval BEFORE the first ar_start, and must re-verify the register read-back; (2) treat every 128-bit word read from RNGA/RNGB as raw entropy worth far less than 128 bits — collect at least 8 words and compress them through a software SHA-256/SHA-3 before using any of it as key material; (3) zeroize RNGA/RNGB in software after every draw, since the hardware wipe skips them.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software on either CPU, to read the RNG pool); the entropy-density defect degrades security even with no attacker present

findings.title: LFSR zero-state guard reloads a hard-coded compile-time constant, converting a dead or software-zeroed entropy source into a fixed, publicly computable random sequence; the entropy tap-enable register that can force this resets to zero
findings.cwe: CWE-1241 Use of Predictable Algorithm in Random Number Generator
findings.description: lfsr129.v line 88 handles the all-zero LFSR state by reloading a constant that is also the reset value at line 66: 129'h1_A39A8864_5DF3BECE_074EC5D3_BAF39D18. This is a silent known-answer fallback, not an error. It is reachable in normal operation because the seed at line 89 is `buf_data[255:127]`, and buf_data is all zeros whenever the digitized bit stream is stuck at 0 — data_buf.v:79 shifts digi_data_out in, so 256 zero bits produce a zero seed, buf_cnt still reaches 256 (data_buf.v:64) and buf_ready still asserts (data_buf.v:101). The sampled datum is trivially forced to 0: trng.sv:228 ANDs the 128 buffer-chain taps with `rngchainen`, which is `sfr_chain`, an apb_cr at offset 0x40 whose default IV is '0 (apb_sfr.sv:81,308) and whose sfrlock is hardwired to '0 (trng.sv:52). With rngchainen==0 the XOR reduction is over an all-zero vector, so rngclkhfxor is constant 0, every t_rngsrc_dat bit latched at trng.sv:237-244 is 0, and digi_data_out is constant 0. The result is: seed=0 -> zero-state guard fires -> lfsr_chain = the hard-coded constant -> 128 shifts of `lfsr_out^digi_data_out` with digi_data_out==0 -> a pure, unmodified LFSR sequence from a publicly known initial state -> a 128-bit 'random' word that is identical on every chip and every boot and can be computed offline from this source file. Because rngchainen is a plain unlocked register, this is not only a misconfiguration hazard but an active denial-of-entropy primitive.
findings.attack_scenario: Active variant (T1): 1. An unprivileged task on either CPU writes 0x0000_0000 to 0x4002_E040/44/48/.../5C (sfr_chain, four 32-bit words), which is permitted because trng.sv:52 hardwires sfrlock to 0 and, while scemode==0, sce_sec.sv:72 leaves the SCE AHB slave ungated for every bus master. 2. rngclkhfxor is now constant 0; all eight sampling flops latch 0; digi_data_out is constant 0. 3. The victim (boot ROM or a secure task) issues ar_start and generates keys. data_buf fills with 256 zeros, buf_ready asserts, the LFSR is seeded with 0, the zero-state guard at line 88 reloads 129'h1_A39A8864_5DF3BECE_074EC5D3_BAF39D18, and 128 shifts with a constant-0 entropy input produce a word the attacker computed offline from this file. 4. Every key the victim derives is known to the attacker before the victim generates it. Passive variant (T2, no software access): the ring oscillators fail or are pulled/frozen by EM or thermal attack; digi_data_out goes constant; the identical fixed sequence is produced, and the only alarm — healthtest_err — gates nothing (see separate finding). Misconfiguration variant (no attacker): firmware that enables the oscillators via cr_src but never writes sfr_chain gets the identical fixed sequence, silently.
findings.preconditions: For the active variant: any bus write access to 0x4002_E040 (T1). Unrestricted while scemode==0 (`assign ahben =  mode_non ? 1'b1 :`, sce_sec.sv:72). For the passive/misconfiguration variants: none — a dead source or an unwritten sfr_chain suffices.
findings.mitigation: RTL: an all-zero LFSR state must be a fatal error, not a reload. Replace the line-88 fallback with an error latch that forces rngcore_dataout_vld and chnlo_start low and asserts `err`. Refuse to seed at all if buf_data is all-zeros or all-ones, and require the startup health test to have passed before buf_ready may assert. rngchainen must not be able to zero the source: hardware-force a minimum number of enabled taps (e.g. OR the register with a non-zero constant mask), and add a real sfrlock to the TRNG SFR block — trng.sv:52 currently ties it to '0 — so that boot code can lock the entropy configuration before untrusted code runs. Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: the boot ROM must (1) program sfr_chain with a validated non-zero tap mask, (2) read back and verify sfr_chain, cr_src and cr_ana before every key generation, (3) compare the first generated word against the known constant sequence derived from 129'h1_A39A8864_5DF3BECE_074EC5D3_BAF39D18 and hard-fault if it matches, (4) since the registers cannot be locked, re-verify them immediately before and after each draw and discard the batch if they changed.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software write to 0x4002_E040) for the active attack; T2 (physical noise-source attack) or plain firmware error for the passive path

findings.title: Raw pre-conditioning entropy and the live DRBG seed are directly readable over an unlocked APB register at 0x4002_E030
findings.cwe: CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor (raw noise-source output exposed; SP 800-90B forbids outputting raw entropy from a validated source)
findings.description: data_buf.v's `buf_data` register is simultaneously (a) the shift register into which every unconditioned digitized entropy bit is clocked (data_buf.v:79) and (b) the seed material for all three post-processing modes: it is loaded into the LFSR state (lfsr129.v:89 `buf_data[255:127]`), used directly as the AES key and plaintext in mode 1 (postprocess.v:179,182), and XORed into the CTR_DRBG's initial key and counter in mode 2 (ctr_aes.v:163,171 `K0 ^buf_data[255:128]^personalization_string[255:128]` and `(M0 ^buf_data[127:0] ^personalization_string[127:0])+1'b1`). trng.sv:278 exposes this register through `apb_buf` at offset 0x30, and trng.sv:58 ORs its read data into the module's prdata, so eight reads of 0x4002_E030..0x4002_E03C return the full 256 bits. The apb_buf read path has no privilege or lock check: trng.sv:434 computes apbrd from psel/penable alone (sfrlock is hardwired 0 at trng.sv:52) and trng.sv:443 drives the data out. There is no separation between a 'raw entropy debug tap' and normal operation — the window is live at all times, in USER mode, with no CMS/lifecycle gate. Reading also lets the attacker profile the raw source directly (bias, autocorrelation, response to injected clock/EM), which is exactly the measurement he needs to make the 1:1 LFSR conditioner exploitable.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. An unprivileged task (T1) polls 0x4002_E030 while a victim task is generating a key. While scemode==0 the SCE AHB slave is ungated for every master (sce_sec.sv:72 `assign ahben =  mode_non ? 1'b1 :`), and trng.sv:52 ties sfrlock to 0, so the reads succeed. 2. buf_addr auto-increments on each read (trng.sv:439), so seven consecutive reads yield 224 of the 256 seed bits without ever touching buf_addr==3'd7 (the only value that clears buf_ready/buf_cnt at data_buf.v:64,100), i.e. the attacker can harvest the seed without perturbing the RNG's ready handshake. 3. In postprocess_opt=2 the attacker now knows buf_data, and K0/M0 are compile-time constants in this file (ctr_aes.v:59-60); personalization_string and additional_input_* are themselves software registers (trng.sv:275-277) that the attacker can read back or has written. He therefore reconstructs the CTR_DRBG's initial key and counter exactly and computes every subsequent output word offline. 4. In postprocess_opt=1 the exposure is total in one step: the output is AES(key=buf_data[255:128], pt=buf_data[127:0]) (postprocess.v:179,182), so knowing buf_data gives the output directly. 5. In the default postprocess_opt=0 the seed is buf_data[255:127] (lfsr129.v:89), giving the attacker the complete initial LFSR state and hence, combined with the 1:1 non-compressing mixing, the entire output stream. In all three cases the keys derived from RNGA/RNGB become computable. 6. Independently, the attacker uses the same window as a raw-entropy oscilloscope to characterise the noise source's bias and its response to injected EM/clock, which is the calibration step for the physical attacks described in the other findings.
findings.preconditions: Any bus read access to 0x4002_E030 (T1). Unrestricted while scemode==0 (sce_sec.sv:72). No lifecycle/CMS gate exists on this window in any mode.
findings.mitigation: RTL: remove the raw-entropy read-back entirely from production silicon, or gate apb_buf's read path on a test-mode lifecycle signal (cmstest/cmsbist) so it is dead in USER mode, and separate the raw-entropy accumulator from the seed register so that the seed is never software-visible. At minimum, give the TRNG a real sfrlock (trng.sv:52 currently ties it to '0) that boot code can set to make the whole 0x4002_E000 page read-and-write protected before untrusted code runs. Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: none is fully effective, because the window has no lock. Partial mitigations: (1) never leave scemode==0 once boot has finished — enter a non-zero scemode as early as possible so sce_sec's ahben restricts the SCE APB page to the owning core's coreuser; (2) generate all key material inside a window in which no untrusted code is scheduled on either CPU; (3) treat the TRNG output as public and derive keys by hashing TRNG output together with a ReRAM-resident device secret, so that knowledge of buf_data alone does not yield the key.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software on either CPU)

findings.title: Every TRNG control register is permanently unlocked (sfrlock tied to zero), letting unprivileged software switch the generator into deterministic DRNG mode with an attacker-chosen 256-bit seed at any time
findings.cwe: CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection
findings.description: trng.sv:52 hardwires the module's sfrlock to '0. Because apb_cr/apb_sfr2 derive their write strobe as `assign apbwr = ~sfrlock & apbslave.psel & apbslave.penable & apbslave.pwrite;` (apb_sfr.sv:333) and apb_buf does the same at trng.sv:433, EVERY TRNG register is writable by any master that reaches the SCE APB page, at any time, including while a key generation is in flight. The reachable controls include: sfr_pp (0x4002_E008) carrying cr_drng_en, cr_postproc_opt, cr_hlthtest_en, cr_healthtest_len and cr_pfilter_en; sfr_crsrc (0x4002_E000) carrying the oscillator enables, the HF configuration and chaincut; sfr_crana (0x4002_E004) carrying the per-channel ana_en/ana_vld; sfr_chain (0x4002_E040) carrying the 128 entropy tap enables; and sfr_buf (0x4002_E030), which in DRNG mode writes buf_data directly (data_buf.v:68-77). Setting cr_drng_en=1 and writing eight words to sfr_buf therefore installs a fully attacker-chosen 256-bit seed and asserts buf_ready (data_buf.v:101 `(trng_drng_sel & buf_write & (buf_addr==3'd7))`), after which the generator is a pure deterministic function of that seed — in postprocess_opt=1 the output is literally AES(buf_data[255:128], buf_data[127:0]), and in opt=0 the LFSR is loaded with buf_data[255:127] and then shifted with no entropy at all (lfsr129.v:90, the trng_drng_sel branch, has no digi_data_out term). There is no lock bit, no write-once behaviour, no requirement that these registers be frozen while rngcore_en is asserted, and no coreuser/privilege check anywhere in this module. Compare with aes.sv:135 and combohasha.sv:159 in the same subsystem, which do implement an operational sfrlock — the TRNG is the outlier.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. An unprivileged task (T1) on either CPU writes 0x4002_E008 with cr_drng_en=1 and cr_postproc_opt=2'd1 (or 2'd0). While scemode==0 the SCE AHB slave is ungated for every bus master (sce_sec.sv:72), and trng.sv:52 means there is no lock to defeat. 2. It writes eight words of its own choosing to 0x4002_E030 (auto-incrementing buf_addr, trng.sv:439); on the write that lands at buf_addr==3'd7 data_buf.v:101 sets buf_ready. buf_data is now entirely attacker-chosen and no entropy is being mixed in — data_buf.v:78 gates the entropy shift on `(~trng_drng_sel)`, so it is disabled. 3. It writes 0x5a to 0x4002_E014 (ar_start) or simply lets the victim's own ar_start proceed. 4. The victim's key-generation routine reads SEG_RNGA/RNGB and obtains, in mode 1, exactly AES(attacker_key, attacker_plaintext) — a value the attacker computed before the victim ran; in mode 0, the LFSR sequence from the attacker's seed. 5. The victim's private key is fully known to the attacker. The same primitive also works in reverse for a covert channel or for downgrading a victim mid-operation: because the registers are not frozen while rngcore_en is asserted, the attacker can flip cr_drng_en between the victim's ar_start and the victim's read of the pool.
findings.preconditions: Bus write access to 0x4002_E000-0x4002_E05C (T1). Unrestricted while scemode==0 (sce_sec.sv:72 `assign ahben =  mode_non ? 1'b1 :`); after mode lock the page is restricted to the owning core's coreuser, but note sce_sec.sv:62/73 only recognise AMBAID4_CM7P and AMBAID4_VEXD, while the Vex peripheral port drives AMBAID4_VEXP.
findings.mitigation: RTL: drive sfrlock properly — either an operational lock in the style already used at aes.sv:135 (`sfrlock <= optlock ? 1'b1 : mfsm_done ? '0 : sfrlock;`) so the configuration freezes while rngcore_en is asserted, or a boot-set one-way lock bit that boot code sets before releasing control to application firmware. In addition, DRNG mode (cr_drng_en) and the software seed-write path should be gated on a lifecycle/test-mode signal (cmstest/devmode) so they cannot be reached in a production USER-mode part at all, and switching postprocess_opt or trng_drng_sel should force a full re-seed and invalidate any pending output rather than being accepted mid-flight. Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: (1) leave scemode==0 for the shortest possible window — enter a non-zero scemode immediately after boot so sce_sec's ahben restricts this page; (2) before every key draw, read back sfr_crsrc, sfr_crana, sfr_pp, sfr_opt and sfr_chain and verify them against the expected values, and read them back again after the draw, discarding the batch if anything changed; (3) do not schedule untrusted code on either CPU across a key-generation window; (4) derive keys by hashing TRNG output together with a device secret so a forced-DRNG output alone does not determine the key.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software on either CPU)

findings.title: Parity-filter mode forces digi_data_vld high regardless of the per-channel enable/valid bits, so the digitizer emits a stream of 'valid' constant bits from disabled, frozen entropy channels
findings.cwe: CWE-1241 Use of Predictable Algorithm in Random Number Generator
findings.description: digitalization.v produces two signals for the downstream conditioner: digi_data_out (the entropy bit) and digi_data_vld (the 'this bit is real' qualifier). When partityfilter_en is set, line 83-84 replaces the per-channel qualifier ana_vld_sys[0] with a literal 1'b1, so validity is asserted purely because the LF ring oscillator produced an edge (clk_ana_pos[0]) — with no reference to ana_en or ana_vld at all. Simultaneously line 81 forms the data bit as `^data_samp[ANA_NUM-1:0]`, the XOR of ALL eight channels, again ignoring ana_en, so channels the software believes it disabled still contribute. And line 61 makes a channel with ana_vld[i]==0 hold its previous sample forever: `assign data_samp_pre[i]=ana_vld[i]?ana_data[i]:data_samp[i];`. Combining these: with cr_ana at its reset value (an apb_cr with default IV='0, trng.sv:109, so ana_en=8'h00 and ana_vld=8'h00) and cr_pfilter_en set, all eight data_samp bits are frozen at their reset value 0, the XOR is constant 0, yet digi_data_vld pulses once per LF oscillator period. The downstream logic cannot tell the difference: data_buf.v:64-65 increments buf_cnt on digi_data_vld and data_buf.v:101 asserts buf_ready at 256, so the conditioner is handed a 256-bit all-zero 'seed' and the LFSR falls through to its hard-coded constant (lfsr129.v:88). The failure is silent and produces a fixed, publicly computable output rather than stalling. Note the asymmetry: with partityfilter_en cleared the same misconfiguration fails SAFE (digi_data_vld stays low, buf_cnt never reaches 256, the RNG simply never produces output) — so the parity path specifically converts a safe stall into a catastrophic silent success.
findings.attack_scenario: Attack variant (T1): 1. An unprivileged task writes 0x4002_E004 (sfr_crana) with 0x0000, clearing every channel's ana_en and ana_vld. This is permitted because trng.sv:52 hardwires sfrlock to 0 and, while scemode==0, sce_sec.sv:72 leaves the SCE APB page ungated. 2. It ensures cr_pfilter_en is set in sfr_pp (0x4002_E008) — or simply waits, if firmware already set it, which is the configuration a designer would choose since the parity filter is the intended de-biasing mode. 3. Every data_samp[i] now freezes (digitalization.v:61) while digi_data_vld keeps pulsing (line 84), so the digitizer emits a constant bit stream that the rest of the block accepts as valid. 4. The victim's key generation proceeds normally: buf_cnt reaches 256 (data_buf.v:64), buf_ready asserts, the LFSR is seeded with the constant, the zero-state guard reloads 129'h1_A39A8864_5DF3BECE_074EC5D3_BAF39D18, and the output word is the fixed sequence the attacker computed offline. 5. The victim's key is known. Firmware-error variant (no attacker): boot code writes cr_src to start the oscillators and writes cr_postproc with cr_pfilter_en=1, but omits or mis-orders the cr_crana write; the part ships and every unit generates the same key material, with no error indication anywhere — healthtest_err would flag it but gates nothing, and `err`/`intr` are tied to 0 at trng.sv:283-284.
findings.preconditions: cr_pfilter_en set (the intended de-biasing configuration) together with cr_ana at or driven to zero. For the active variant, bus write access to 0x4002_E004 (T1), unrestricted while scemode==0.
findings.mitigation: RTL: qualify the parity path with the channel enables — the XOR must be `^(data_samp & ana_en)` and digi_data_vld in parity mode must be `clk_ana_pos[0] & (|(ana_en & ana_vld))` rather than a literal 1'b1, so a fully disabled source produces no valid bits and the pipeline stalls safely instead of emitting constants. Additionally, refuse to assert buf_ready on an all-zero or all-ones 256-bit accumulation, and require the startup health test to pass before the first buf_ready. Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: (1) boot code must write sfr_crana (0x4002_E004) with all eight ana_en and ana_vld bits set BEFORE writing cr_pfilter_en, and must read the register back to confirm; (2) re-verify sfr_crana immediately before and after every key draw, since the register has no lock; (3) enable the health test and check sr_hlthtest_errcnt in sr_rng (0x4002_E010) across each draw; (4) as a defence in depth, compare the first generated word against the known constant sequence and hard-fault on a match.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software write to 0x4002_E004); also reachable with no attacker at all as a silent firmware-initialisation error

finders.domain: JTAG TAP, DFT/scan and memory BIST — debug and test access
finders.coverage_notes:
COVERED (read end-to-end): rtl/modules/dft/rtl/tap_top.sv (all 567 lines), jtagtap.sv, jtagreg.sv, jtag_sync.sv, bscell.sv, rtl/modules/rbist/rtl/rbist_wrp.sv (all 461 lines), rtl/asic_top/include/jtagtap_inc.sv. Traced every DFT signal outward to its integration points and verified each by direct read: rtl/asic_top/rtl/soc_top.sv:376-400 and :890-1010 (cms instance, cmsbist, iptap_en, jtagtap iptdap, rbist_wrp instance, iptregin/iptregout fan-out), rtl/asic_top/rtl/pad_frame_arm.sv:214-281 (WMS/XRSTn/JTAG pad gating, atpgse/atpgrst/clkatpg buffers, pbtestpo test-output mux), rtl/modules/sysctrl/rtl/cms.sv:20-160 (mode decode), rtl/modules/sysctrl/rtl/sysctrl.sv:250-330 (cmstest register, ipt_socreg overrides), rtl/modules/bio_bdma/rtl/ram_1rw_s.sv:26-140 (rbif interface + rbspmux), rtl/modules/crypto_top/rtl/cryptoram.sv:100-260 and cryptoram_verilate.sv:21-40 (ramtrm->macro EMA/WABL/RAWL mapping), rtl/modules/rrc/rtl/rrc.sv:392-424 and :860-1000 (ACRAM rbspmux, ReRAM macro JTAG TAPs, bist_enable), rtl/modules/core/rtl/vexsys.sv:120-160,335-355 (Vex debug TAP gating), rtl/modules/ao/rtl/ao_top.sv:138-150 + ao_sysctrl.sv:280-290,418-435 (aocmsuser sticky latch, POR source), rtl/modules/amba/rtl/apb_sfr.sv:317-380 (sfrlock semantics), rtl/asic_top/rtl/daric_cfg_pkg.sv:44-60 (APB map), rtl/scripts/headergen/output/doc/rbist_wrp.rst and bao1x_peri.h (confirmed 0x40045000 base).

CHECKED AND CLEARED (no finding): the Vex debug TAP is correctly gated — vexsys.sv:136 `assign jtagtck0 = jtags.tck & vexcfg_dev;` gates TCK, plus tdi/tms at :347,349, so an ungated PAD_JTRST (vexsys.sv:146) cannot advance the TAP. The IPT/rbist/ReRAM TAPs are held in TRST when cmstest=0 (pad_frame_arm.sv:233-246,249-250). `atpgse` is gated by cmsatpg (pad_frame_arm.sv:281). tap_top's IR decode has no undocumented opcode reaching internal state — undecoded IRs fall to BYPASS (tap_top.sv:507) and scan_sel_o (:515) only matches REG1..REG1+4.

COULD NOT COVER: (a) the `rbist rbcore` engine itself is a black box (rbist_wrp.sv:408 `rbist rbcore(.*);`) — its TAP instruction set, whether it exposes a raw read-out instruction versus only pass/fail signatures, and whether it drives rbif ramtrm from trmdat, are all outside this repo. I verified the trim bit-field mapping matches exactly (t_trm struct vs. the vendored `rf_sp_hde_inst_bio` macro) but the final wire is inside the black box. (b) `trbcx1r32_daric_wrapper` (ReRAM macro + its two JTAG TAPs) is a black box — I can show the TAP pins are wired raw (rrc.sv:970-976) but not what commands they accept. (c) Scan chains are inserted at synthesis; no scan chain exists in this RTL, so I cannot evaluate chain stitching, scan-chain compression, or whether secret-holding flops are excluded from the chains. (d) `nic400_1`, `CM7AAB`, `cm7top` (CoreSight/SWD DAP) are black boxes, so SWD-side debug authentication could not be assessed. (e) I did not audit the FPGA-only branches (`ifdef FPGA`) as attack surface since they are not in the taped-out netlist.

findings.title: DFT/BIST JTAG access is authorised solely by two external pads — all four ReRAM chip-mode patterns are the same constant 128'h0
findings.cwe: CWE-1191 On-Chip Debug and Test Interface With Improper Access Control
findings.description: The chip-mode-select (CMS) block is the only lifecycle gate on the entire DFT infrastructure. It is supposed to combine two sources: the three WMS pads and a 128-bit 'CMS data' word read out of ReRAM. However all four mode patterns are declared as the same value, '0. Every `cmsdatareg == CMSDAT_*` comparison in the decode at cms.sv:119-137 therefore reduces to the identical test 'is the ReRAM CMS word zero?', and the first matching branch (VRGN) always wins. The ReRAM default is also zero (nvrcfgs.sv:102-105). Mode selection collapses to a pure function of the WMS pads, which are pulled DOWN in the pad frame (pad_frame_arm.sv:214-216) — i.e. the secure USER state is the state where the attacker does nothing, and driving the pads high is all that is required to select a test mode. There is no fuse, no one-way counter, no challenge/response, and no authentication anywhere on any TAP: `cmstest` directly ungates the ReRAM-macro TAPs, the RAM-BIST TAP, the IPT TAP and the test-output pins (pad_frame_arm.sv:232-250, 262-269), and `assign cmsbist = cmstest;` (soc_top.sv:397) ungates the memory BIST port of every RAM in the SoC. The only backstop is a sticky always-on latch `aocmsuser` (ao_top.sv:144) that forces CMS_USER once user mode has been seen — but that latch is cleared by `porresetn_undft`, which is derived from the external PAD_XRSTn pin (`assign por = ~pmu_POR & padresetn ;`, ao_sysctrl.sv:422), so a reset pulse on an external pin re-arms mode selection without a power cycle.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker with physical access to a deployed board decapsulates nothing and probes nothing — they simply tie PAD_WMS0 and PAD_WMS1 high (both are pulled down by default, so no contention with any on-board net is likely) and pulse PAD_XRSTn low. 2. PAD_XRSTn low drives `por` low (ao_sysctrl.sv:422), clearing the sticky `aocmsuser` latch (ao_top.sv:144), so the AO override no longer forces CMS_USER. 3. On release, the CMS block samples the pads for 128 cycles (cms.sv:93-95) and evaluates cms.sv:124-134. Because `cmsdatareg` equals CMSDAT_VRGNMODE (= 0) for every possible ReRAM content that is zero — and every one of the four patterns is zero, so the VRGN branch is taken unconditionally — and cmspadout[1] is 1, the chip enters CMS_VRGN. 4. `cmstestreg` is set (cms.sv:157), so `cmstest = 1`, which sets `cmsbist = 1` (soc_top.sv:397) and `iptap_en = 1` (soc_top.sv:907). 5. The JTAG TRST/TMS/TDI AND-gates at pad_frame_arm.sv:233-250 now pass through, releasing the RAM-BIST TAP, both ReRAM-macro TAPs, and the IPT TAP; the corresponding TDOs are routed to package pins by pad_frame_arm.sv:262-269. 6. The attacker now has the full DFT surface of a production part with no credential of any kind.
findings.preconditions: Physical access to the package pins PAD_WMS0, PAD_WMS1, PAD_XRSTn and the PA0/PA1/PA2/PA4/PA7/PB0..PB15 test pins (T2). No decapsulation, no glitching, no knowledge of any secret. The ReRAM CMS word must be zero, which is both its erased state and its declared default (nvrcfgs.sv:102-105).
findings.mitigation: RTL: give the four CMS patterns distinct, high-Hamming-distance 128-bit constants so that the ReRAM word actually authorises the mode, and require a non-zero, correctly-matched word before any test mode is entered (fail closed to CMS_USER on a mismatch, not to CMS_SCDE). Make the USER latch one-way in a non-volatile element (fuse/OTP/ReRAM one-way counter) rather than an AO flop cleared by an external reset pin. Silicon workaround: none from firmware — `cmscode` is evaluated before software runs. Board-level mitigation only: permanently tie PAD_WMS0/WMS1 to ground under the package (e.g. via-in-pad to a ground plane) and provision the ReRAM CMS word with a non-zero USER pattern if a future metal revision gives the patterns distinct values.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (physical access to package pins); T4 (reset control) for the aocmsuser clear

findings.title: Memory-BIST port hands full read/write control of every SRAM — including the ReRAM access-control RAM and AO SRAM — to the JTAG BIST controller, with no zeroization on test-mode entry
findings.cwe: CWE-1244 Internal Asset Exposed to Unsafe Debug Access Level or State
findings.description: `rbspmux` is instantiated in front of every RAM macro in the SoC (cryptoram.sv:146-164 for SCERAM/HRAM/ARAM/PRAM/ALURAM, rrc.sv:405-422 for the ACRAM, aoram.sv, ifram.sv, tcmram.sv, core_srambank, bioram, udcmem). When `cmsbist` is asserted it multiplexes the *entire* macro control set — clock, chip-enable, global write-enable, per-bit write-enable, address and write data — from the `rbif` bus, and returns the macro's read data on `rbs.ramrdata`. This is not a signature-only BIST wrapper: it is unrestricted random-access read and write. `cmsbist` is `cmstest` (soc_top.sv:397), which per Finding 1 is selected by two external pads, and the BIST TAP is released by the same signal (pad_frame_arm.sv:244-246). Critically, entering BIST/TEST mode triggers no zeroization of any kind. The only wipe machinery in the design is the SCE's `sceramclr` (sce_sec.sv:87), and it (a) is confined to the SCE's own RAMs, (b) skips the RNGA/RNGB pools (sce.sv:417 `.clrend(scedma_pkg::SEGADDR_RNGA-1)`), and (c) is not connected to `cmstest`, `cmsbist` or any tamper input. Nothing at all clears the ReRAM ACRAM (which holds the per-key-slot owner/permission descriptors that rrc.sv:712-726 uses to gate ReRAM key reads), the CM7 ITCM/DTCM, the core SRAM banks, IFRAM0/1, the BIO RAM, or the always-on SRAM — and the AO SRAM contents survive every reset short of a battery removal (ao_top.sv:248-266, `.ret1n(1'b1)`). No memory in the SoC is scrambled (cryptoram.sv:112-113 `.scmben('0), .scmbkey('0)`), so what BIST reads back is plaintext.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker obtains a running device that has just performed a secure operation, so software copies of key material, unwrapped secrets and the ReRAM ACRAM image are resident in core SRAM / TCM / AO SRAM / ACRAM. 2. Attacker pulses PAD_XRSTn with WMS0=WMS1=1 (Finding 1) to enter CMS_VRGN. SRAM contents are not destroyed by reset — no RTL path clears core_srambank, ITCM, DTCM, IFRAM, aoram, bioram, udcmem or the RRC ACRAM on any reset, and none of them is scrambled. 3. `cmsbist` is now 1, so for every RAM in the SoC, rbspmux lines 125-132 route the macro's clock, cen, gwen, wen, address and write data from the `rbif` bus, and line 140 returns the macro read data to the BIST controller. 4. The attacker drives the released BIST TAP (jtagrb, pad_frame_arm.sv:243-246, TDO on PB3 via pad_frame_arm.sv:263) with a read-address sequence and shifts out the contents of rbif_ram32kx72 / rbif_ram8kx72 / rbif_dtcm8kx36 / rbif_itcm32kx18 / rbif_aoram1kx36 / rbif_acram2kx64, recovering plaintext secrets that were never zeroized. 5. Alternatively the attacker WRITES the ACRAM through the same port: setting a key slot's `userid_k[7:4]` field to 0 makes rrc.sv:717's trailing `& (userid_k[7:4] != 4'h0)` term false, disabling the key-slot access check entirely for that slot, after which normal software can read the ReRAM key slot over the ordinary bus.
findings.preconditions: Physical pin access (T2) plus the ability to reset the part (T4). Requires Finding 1 (or any other route to cmstest=1). Exploiting step 4/5 additionally requires the raw-access instruction set of the closed-source `rbist` core; the RTL guarantees the datapath is present and unrestricted, but the command encoding is not in this repo.
findings.mitigation: RTL: qualify `cmsbist` with a non-volatile lifecycle bit rather than a pad-derived mode, and force a hardware zeroization sweep of every RAM (not just SCE RAMs) as an unconditional precondition of asserting cmsbist/cmsatpg — hold the BIST enable off until a wipe-done flag from every RAM's clear FSM is asserted. Wire the tamper/mesh/sensor outputs into `sceramclr` and into an equivalent clear for the ACRAM, TCM and AO RAM. Enable the memory scrambler that is already plumbed but tied off (`.scmben('0), .scmbkey('0)` at cryptoram.sv:112-113, aoram.sv:95, ifram.sv:82, cm7sys_tcm.sv:116-117, soc_coresub.sv:721,739). Silicon workaround: firmware must explicitly overwrite every buffer that has held key material — including stack and heap in SRAM/TCM, the AO SRAM and aobureg — immediately after use, and must not rely on reset to clear them; there is no firmware action that can prevent the BIST port itself from being enabled.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (physical), T4 (reset/power control)

findings.title: RAM margin-trim registers at 0x40045000 are unlocked and unprivileged, giving unprivileged software a fault-injection primitive against the SCE key RAM and the ReRAM access-control RAM
findings.cwe: CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection
findings.description: `rbist_wrp` exposes a 24-bit APB control register that selects one of the 28 RAM groups and writes its 16-bit timing-margin trim word. The module hard-ties its own lock signal to zero, so `apb_sfr`'s write gate (`assign apbwr = ~sfrlock & apbslave.psel & apbslave.penable & apbslave.pwrite;`, apb_sfr.sv:333) is permanently open. The register sits on apbsys[5] (soc_top.sv:968) i.e. 0x40045000 (confirmed by the generated header, bao1x_peri.h:3259 and doc/rbist_wrp.rst), which is in the apb1-system window 0x40040000-0x4004FFFF. No slave in this SoC consumes `pprot`/`hprot`, and there is no coreuser check anywhere on this path, so any bus master that can reach the peripheral bus — CM7 AHB-P (hauser=0x8), Vex AHB-P (0xD), the MDMA (0x7) and the BIO/BDMA peripheral master (0x0) — can write it from unprivileged code. The trim word is not cosmetic: the packed `t_trm` struct is {ema[15:13], emab[12:10], emaw[9:8], emas[7], wabl[6], wablm[5:3], rawl[2], rawlm[1:0]} and the vendored macro-instantiation macro maps exactly those bit ranges onto the Artisan macro's extra-margin-adjustment, write-assist and read-assist pins. Group 9 is the SCE unified crypto RAM (sce_sceram_10k, which holds SKEY/SCRT/AKEY/PKB), group 26 is the RRC ACRAM that holds the ReRAM key-slot access-control descriptors, and group 27 is the always-on SRAM. Detuning EMA/WABL/RAWL on a live macro is a standard, well-characterised way to induce read and write failures without any physical apparatus.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Unprivileged software running on either CPU writes 0x40045000 with {sfrtrmsel=26, sfrtrmdat=<aggressive margin>} to select the RRC ACRAM group and set an EMA/RAWL combination outside the qualified window; a write to 0x40045008 with 0x5a fires `sfrar_trm`, which the sync_pulse at rbist_wrp.sv:187 converts into `sfrtrmset`, latching the new trim into trmdat[26] (rbist_wrp.sv:194-198). There is no lock bit to stop this (line 161) and no privilege check on the APB. 2. Software then performs a ReRAM key-slot access at 0x603Fxxxx. The RRC reads the slot's access-control descriptor out of the now-detuned ACRAM (rrc.sv:404-424, rrc.sv:684-697). 3. A read failure that returns zeros for the descriptor makes `userid_k[7:4] == 4'h0`, and the whole key-access check in rrc.sv:712-717 is multiplied by the trailing term `& (userid_k[7:4] != 4'h0)` — so `key_access_error` becomes 0 and the read is permitted. rrc.sv:583 returns HRESP=OKAY and rrc.sv:555-558 delivers the key word instead of zeros. 4. The same primitive aimed at group 9 (sce_sceram_10k) or group 27 (aoram) corrupts SCE key/state words or AO-domain secrets, and aimed at group 7/6 (ITCM/DTCM) corrupts instruction memory of the other CPU — all from unprivileged software, with no physical access and no glitch equipment.
findings.preconditions: Any code execution that can issue a store to 0x40045000/0x40045008 — i.e. unprivileged software on either CPU, or the BIO/BDMA peripheral master (which presents hauser=0). Confirmation of the final trm->ramtrm wire requires the closed-source `rbist` core (rbist_wrp.sv:408 `rbist rbcore(.*);`); the bit-field mapping between t_trm and the vendored macro-instantiation macro is exact, and the same trmdat path is fed by the production ReRAM IFR trim load (nvrtrmset/nvrtrmdat, rbist_wrp.sv:197), which establishes it as the real trim mechanism.
findings.mitigation: RTL: drive `sfrlock` from a sticky, boot-set lock bit (the pattern already used in aes.sv:135 and combohasha.sv:159, `theregrn( sfrlock ) <= optlock ? 1'b1 : mfsm_done ? '0 : sfrlock;`) so that the trim registers become read-only once the ReRAM IFR trim load completes; alternatively gate the register with a coreuser/boot-region check as the RRC CFG region is, and exclude the security-critical groups (9, 26, 27) from software-writable trim entirely. Silicon workaround: the earliest boot stage must relocate this peripheral out of reach — since no lock exists, the only firmware mitigation is to configure the CM7 MPU / Vex PMP to make 0x40045000-0x4004500C inaccessible to all non-boot code, and to keep the region blocked for the life of the boot. Note that the CM7 MPU configuration in daric_cfg_pkg.sv:117-127 is currently commented out, so this workaround requires firmware to program the MPU itself.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software on either CPU) — no physical access required

findings.title: BIST read-data port is driven with live functional RAM read data at all times, not only when BIST is enabled
findings.cwe: CWE-1272 Sensitive Information Uncleared Before Debug/Power State Transition
findings.description: In `rbspmux`, every control input to the RAM macro is multiplexed on `cmsbist` (lines 128-132: `undft_cen = cmsbist ? rbs.ramcen : cen`, etc.), but the read-data *output* back to the BIST interface is not. Line 140 unconditionally exports whatever the macro just read to `rbs.ramrdata`, with the only mux being the ATPG placeholder. This means that during entirely normal USER-mode operation — SCE key scheduling, HMAC key-store fetches, AES round-key reads, ACRAM descriptor lookups — every word read from every RAM macro in the SoC is continuously presented on the `rbif` bus that fans out to `rbist_wrp` (soc_top.sv:990-1008) and from there into the JTAG-attached `rbist` core. The correct structure, matching lines 128-132, would be `assign rbs.ramrdata = cmsbist ? rb_q : '0;`. As written, the secret is already inside the BIST/repair logic before any mode check is made, so the security of the crypto RAM contents depends entirely on the closed-source BIST core never capturing or shifting out data it was not asked for, and on every one of the eight AND-gates in pad_frame_arm.sv:243-246 holding — there is no defence in depth.
findings.attack_scenario: An attacker who obtains any partial or transient enable of the BIST TAP — a laser or EM fault on the single `cmstest & jtagtrst` AND-gate at pad_frame_arm.sv:244, a glitch on the `cmstestreg` flop in cms.sv:157, or a scan-shift of the BIST core's own capture registers during ATPG — observes crypto-RAM read data that the design intended to be visible only in BIST mode, because line 140 has been feeding it into the BIST core continuously. Concretely: firmware performs an HMAC over a ReRAM key slot; the SCE reads AKEY/SKEY words out of sce_sceram_10k; each of those words appears on rbif_sce_sceram_10k.ramrdata in the same cycle. A single successful glitch on the TAP-release gate at the right moment captures a live key word, where a properly gated design would have required the attacker to also win control of address and enable.
findings.preconditions: Requires a fault or partial enable on the cmstest/cmsbist path, or a BIST core that samples ramrdata outside its enabled window. On its own this is an information-flow defect rather than a directly exploitable path; it removes the second layer of defence that lines 128-132 provide on the control side.
findings.mitigation: RTL one-liner: `assign rbs.ramrdata = cmsatpg ? undft_q : (cmsbist ? rb_q : '0);` — mirror the cmsbist gating already applied to cen/gwen/wen/a/d. Apply the same to `rbs.ramrdatab` in the dual-port variant `rbdpmux`. Silicon workaround: none — this is a pure combinational path inside every RAM wrapper with no software-visible control.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (physical/fault injection), amplifying Finding 1 and Finding 2

findings.title: The DFT TAP enable is a single non-redundant AND gate used only as an asynchronous reset, while the TAP clock runs free from an ungated pad
findings.cwe: CWE-1319 Improper Protection against Electromagnetic Fault Injection (EM-FI)
findings.description: The IPT TAP — which owns the PMU/oscillator trim register set (ipt_aoreg), the SoC PLL/OSC/RNG configuration (ipt_socreg, consumed at sysctrl.sv:258,317-326 and as ipt_rngcfg at soc_top.sv:646), the ATPG mode-setup bits (iptregout[4], decoded at soc_top.sv:934-940), the 64-bit direct pad drive/output-enable (soc_top.sv:929-930) and the RAM-trim write port (iptregout[2] -> rbist_wrp) — is protected by exactly one two-input AND term. `jtags_resetn = enable & resetn & jtags.trst` is the only thing standing between the attacker and the whole DFT register file, and it acts purely as an asynchronous reset on the TAP flops. Meanwhile the TAP's clock is NOT gated at all: pad_frame_arm.sv:248 wires jtagipt.tck straight from the PA0 pad (`assign jtagipt.tck = jtagclk;`), unlike the RRC and rbist TAPs whose TMS/TDI are also gated but which still take an ungated clock. Consequences: (a) `enable` (= cmstest|cmsbist|cmsatpg, soc_top.sv:907) is a combinational signal from the clksys domain with no synchroniser into the TCK domain, so the asynchronous *release* of jtags_resetn is unsynchronised with respect to a clock that is already toggling — a classic reset-removal violation that can leave the tap_top FSM and jtagreg shift chains in an arbitrary state; (b) a single-bit fault (laser, EM, VCC glitch) on the AND gate, on the cmstestreg flop (cms.sv:157) or on the trst gate at pad_frame_arm.sv:249 releases the entire DFT register file with its clock already running and no re-authentication, re-check or redundant confirmation anywhere downstream. There is no second, independent copy of the mode decision, no error-detecting encoding on `enable`, and no periodic re-validation.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker in USER mode drives PA0 (jtagclk) with a continuous TCK, PA1 (jtagtrst) high and PA2 (jtagtdi) with a chosen bit pattern, and PA3 (jtagipt.tms, pad_frame_arm.sv:286) with the TMS sequence for Shift-IR/Shift-DR. Nothing is gated on PA0 or PA3, so the TAP's clock and TMS are already live; only the trst and tdi AND-gates at pad_frame_arm.sv:249-250 and the enable AND at jtagtap.sv:33 hold the flops in reset. 2. Attacker applies a localised EM or laser pulse to the small cone of logic driving `iptap_en`/`cmstestreg`/the trst AND-gate while continuously replaying the JTAG sequence. 3. A single successful fault deasserts the reset for a window during which the free-running TCK clocks the tap_top FSM out of Test-Logic-Reset and into Shift-DR with the attacker's data. Because there is no synchroniser on the reset release and no redundant confirmation of the mode anywhere downstream, the released state is not re-checked: `regset[i] = tap_updatedr & regsel[i]` (jtagtap.sv:78) fires and the value lands in iptregout, from which it propagates to the PMU/OSC trims (a voltage-glitch primitive against the crypto engines), the ATPG setup bits, and the RAM trim write port. 4. The captured/injected state persists until the next sysresetn, since nothing re-validates iptap_en after the fact.
findings.preconditions: Physical access with fault-injection capability (T2) and access to the PA0-PA3 pins. The attack does not need the WMS-pad route of Finding 1; it targets the enable logic directly.
findings.mitigation: RTL: (a) gate the TAP clock, not just its reset — insert an ICG on jtags.tck enabled by the (synchronised) DFT-enable, as vexsys.sv:136 already does for the Vex TAP (`assign jtagtck0 = jtags.tck & vexcfg_dev;`); (b) synchronise the reset release into the TCK domain with a reset-removal synchroniser instead of releasing an async reset against a free-running clock; (c) make the enable redundant — carry it as a multi-bit error-detecting code or duplicate the cms decode and require both copies to agree, and re-check the enable on every update_dr rather than only at reset; (d) hold the downstream consumers (ipt_socreg/ipt_aoreg/iptregout[4]) behind a second, independently-derived mode qualifier so that one fault is not sufficient. Silicon workaround: none — the path is entirely combinational from pads to TAP with no software-visible control.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (physical access + clock/voltage/EM/laser fault injection)

findings.title: RAM-trim write pulse crosses clock domains through a synchroniser declared on the wrong launch clock
findings.cwe: CWE-1298 Hardware Logic Contains Race Conditions
findings.description: `rbist_wrp` receives `iptregset` from the IPT JTAG TAP: soc_top.sv:966 connects `.iptregset(iptregset[2])`, and `iptregset[2]` is produced inside `jtagtap` as `assign regset[i] = tap_updatedr & regsel[i];` (jtagtap.sv:78), where every flop in that TAP is clocked by `jtags.tck` = `jtagipt.tck` = `jtagclk` (pad_frame_arm.sv:248). The synchroniser that carries this pulse into the clksys domain, however, declares its launch clock as `jtagrb.tck` — a different net, assigned `jtagclk_occ = cmsatpg ? clkocc : jtagclk` (pad_frame_arm.sv:229,243). In CMS_TEST/VRGN the two happen to alias to the same physical net (jtagclk), which is why this has not been caught; in CMS_ATPG they are genuinely different clocks (clkocc, the on-chip-clock-controller output, versus the JTAG pin), so the `iptregset` pulse is sampled asynchronously by a synchroniser that was never told about it. The compiler cannot flag it because both are named `.tck` on `jtagif` instances. The result is that a JTAG-issued RAM-trim write can be silently dropped, doubled, or latch a metastable `ipttrmsel`/`ipttrmdat` value into the trim flops at rbist_wrp.sv:194-198 — i.e. a RAM group other than the intended one can receive an out-of-window margin setting.
findings.attack_scenario: During ATPG/characterisation the clkocc and jtagclk domains are independent. An attacker (or, more likely, a mis-set production tester) issuing a JTAG trim write to a benign RAM group can have the `ipttrmsel` field sampled metastably by the su0 synchroniser, so that `ipttrmset & ( ipttrmsel == 128+i )` at rbist_wrp.sv:196 matches a different `i` than intended — landing an out-of-window margin word on, for example, group 9 (sce_sceram_10k) or group 26 (acram2kx64). The affected RAM then exhibits marginal read/write behaviour in the field with no error indication, since the trim registers persist until sysresetn (rbist_wrp.sv:194). This is the same corruption as Finding 4 but arrived at accidentally, and it can also cause a deliberately-issued trim write to be silently dropped, so a part shipped from test with the wrong margins believes it was programmed.
findings.preconditions: Chip in CMS_ATPG (or any future mode where jtagrb.tck and jtagipt.tck are not the same net). In CMS_TEST/VRGN the aliasing masks the bug. Requires JTAG access, i.e. Finding 1 or a legitimate tester.
findings.mitigation: RTL: change the launch clock to the domain in which the pulse is actually generated — `sync_pulse su0 ( .clka(jtagipt.tck), ... )` — matching the pattern already used correctly at soc_top.sv:947 and :951 for the sibling pulses iptregset[1] and iptregset[0]. Better still, pass the IPT TAP's clock into rbist_wrp explicitly rather than deriving it from an unrelated jtagif instance, so the connection is checkable. Silicon workaround: production test flow must read back the trim word through SFRSR_TRM (0x40045004) after every JTAG trim write and retry on mismatch; end-user firmware should read back and verify the trim values for the security-critical groups (9, 26, 27) at boot.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (JTAG access) — primarily a reliability/integrity defect rather than a direct attack path

finders.domain: Tamper detection: mesh, glue chain, sensors, security subsystem (rtl/modules/sec/rtl/*, rtl/asic_top/include/sec_inc.sv, and their integration in soc_top.sv / sysctrl.sv / evc.sv)
finders.coverage_notes:
COVERED (read end-to-end, all four files are small): rtl/modules/sec/rtl/mesh.sv (286 lines), sensorc.sv (140), gluechain.sv (88), secsub.sv (140), and rtl/asic_top/include/sec_inc.sv (a pure `include list, no logic). Traced every output of secsub forward: vdresetn -> soc_top.sv:712 secresetn -> sysctrl.sv:794 sysresetgen.resetnin; irq8 -> soc_top.sv:713 secirq -> soc_top.sv:473 ev[239:224] and soc_top.sv:480 err[3] -> evc.sv:71 cm7nmi. Traced every input backward: pclkmesh <- soc_top.sv:702 pclksub[7] <- sysctrl.sv:635 ICG gated by sysctrl.sv:867 sfr_pclkgr (unlocked APB CR @0x4004_006C); resetn <- soc_top.sv:703 coreresetn <- sysctrl.sv:799-804 coreresetgen (watchdog + sfr_rcurst1 @0x4004_0084); porresetn <- socresetn. Verified the APB path to 0x4005_xxxx (soc_top.sv:661-666 apb_bdg off coreahb_sec, then secsub.sv:46 apb_mux DECAW=4) carries NO hauser/coreuser/pprot check, so mesh=0x4005_2000, sensorc=0x4005_3000, gluechain=0x4005_4000 are writable by any AHB master that reaches core_ahb32. Verified apb_cr/apb_sr/apb_fr/apb_sfr2 semantics in rtl/modules/amba/rtl/apb_sfr.sv:74-124,126-231,304-360 (apb_cr default IV=32'h0; apbwr = ~sfrlock & ...). Verified parameter values in daric_cfg_pkg.sv:203-214 (MESHLC=64, MESHPC=32, SENSORVDC=6, SENSORLDC=2, GLCX=64, GLCY=32) and the pad wiring at soc_top.sv:688-690,717-729. Confirmed pclksub[7] feeds NOTHING except the mesh. Confirmed evc.sv:158 sfr_cm7errcr .IV(0) and sfrlock='0.

NOT COVERED / CANNOT BE VERIFIED:
- The analog tamper cells are black boxes or behavioral-only models: ip_gluecell (rtl/modules/model/rtl/gluecell.sv, real body only under `ifdef SIM`), ip_lightdet (rtl/modules/model/rtl/ld.sv, body only `ifndef SYN`, light_out is left undriven in the SYN build), and `meshlines` (mesh.sv:198-270 is an EMPTY module body for the non-SYN case; the SYN case binds a physical macro not present in this repo). I therefore cannot verify actual detector polarity, trip thresholds, response time, or the physical mesh routing. Findings 2/3 rest on the digital compare/arming logic, which is fully visible; where I depend on the behavioral model's polarity I say so.
- The VD09/VD25/VD33 voltage comparators are off-RTL analog IP (soc_top.sv:105-110 are top-level input pins). I could not determine what vd[] reads when vdena is deasserted, so I did not file a finding on sensorc.sv:78 sfr_vdip_ena (software power-down of the voltage detectors) even though it is an unlocked register at 0x4005_3040 — the exploitability depends on analog behaviour I cannot see.
- No documentation for the tamper subsystem exists under docs/src/ (only bio, adc, usb, io, pmu, clock-generation, system-control). There is therefore no documented guarantee to compare the RTL against for this domain; the "intended behaviour" had to be inferred from the RTL itself.
- Whether the sysctrl `sfrlock` input is tied to 0 in the synthesized netlist: soc_top.sv:217 declares `logic sfrlock;` with no driver anywhere in the file and passes it at soc_top.sv:361. Undriven nets normally optimize to 0 (writes enabled), but I cannot prove the netlist behaviour, so Finding 5's clock-gate vector is stated with that caveat; its watchdog/coreresetn vector does not depend on it.
- I did not attempt gate-level, timing, or formal analysis, and did not simulate.

findings.title: Voltage-tamper reset mask cr_vdmask1 is used as a scalar condition and resets to all-ones, so the only autonomous hardware tamper response in the chip is disabled by default and cannot be selectively armed
findings.cwe: CWE-1221 Incorrect Register Defaults or Module Parameters
findings.description:
sensorc has exactly one path that produces a hardware (non-software) reaction to a tamper event: `vdresetn`, which feeds soc_top.sv:712 `.vdresetn( secresetn )` and from there sysctrl.sv:794 `resetnin ( { socresetn, vdresetn, secresetn, ~sysreset_sw } )` of `sysresetgen`. That path is qualified by a 6-bit per-detector mask `cr_vdmask1`. Two defects compound:

(a) OPERATOR DEFECT. At line 93 the 6-bit vector `cr_vdmask1` is used as the *condition* of a ternary, not as a bitwise mask. SystemVerilog evaluates a multi-bit condition as `|cr_vdmask1`. So the expression reduces to `vdresetnreg <= (|cr_vdmask1) ? 6'b111111 : &(~vdflag)`, i.e. ANY single set bit in the 6-bit mask suppresses the tamper reset for ALL SIX voltage detectors (VD09L/H, VD25L/H, VD33L/H). Contrast the sibling IRQ mask two lines above, which is correctly bitwise: `assign sr_vdsr = vdflag & ~cr_vdmask0;`. The commented-out original at line 92 has the identical bug, so this is not a late typo.

(b) PERMISSIVE RESET DEFAULT. The mask register is instantiated with `.IV({VDC{1'b1}})` (all ones), so out of every reset `vdresetn` is stuck at 1 and no voltage-tamper event can ever assert a reset. `apb_cr` defaults elsewhere in this module use IV=0; this one deliberately resets to the fully-masked state. sensorc's `resetn` is `porresetn` = `socresetn` (secsub.sv:73, soc_top.sv:702), so brown-out or POR restores the all-masked value.

The register is at 0x4005_3004 with `sfrlock` hardwired to 0 (sensorc.sv:57 `` `theregrn( sfrlock ) <= '0; ``) and the 0x4005_xxxx APB is reached through soc_top.sv:661 `apb_bdg uapbsecbdg` with no hauser/coreuser/pprot check, so any bus master can re-mask it at any time with a single 32-bit store.
findings.attack_scenario:
Case 1 (no attacker action needed - the default). Chip powers up. cr_vdmask1 = 6'b111111, so `vdresetnreg` is unconditionally 1. Attacker (T2/T4) applies a voltage glitch on the 0.9 V core rail to fault an SCE key comparison or a secure-boot branch. VD09L trips, `vdflag[0]` goes high, `sr_vdsr` sets a status bit and pulses an IRQ - but `secresetn` never deasserts, `sysresetgen` never fires, the SCE is never reset, and the crypto RAM wipe (`sce_sec.sv:85-87 sceramclr = (initregs==4'h7)|ar_clrram`, which is triggered by SCE reset release) never runs. The glitch campaign proceeds unimpeded; the only consequence is a status bit the attacker's own fault may have already prevented firmware from reading.

Case 2 (T1, active bypass after firmware arms it). Suppose firmware correctly writes 0x0000_0000 to 0x4005_3004 during boot to enable the tamper reset. Unprivileged software on either CPU - or the BDMA peripheral AHB master, which drives hauser=0 and is subject to no coreuser check on this bus - stores 0x0000_0001 to 0x4005_3004. Setting one bit of a six-bit mask disables the reset response for all six detectors because the mask is consumed as a scalar. There is no lock bit (sfrlock is a constant 0) and no privilege check on the path, so this cannot be prevented and cannot be detected by the hardware. The attacker then glitches at leisure.
findings.preconditions: Case 1: none - this is the post-reset state of the fabricated part. Case 2: any write access to 0x4005_3004, i.e. unprivileged code on CM7 or Vex, or any AHB master reaching core_ahb32 (CM7-P, Vex-P, MDMA, BDMA-AHB).
findings.mitigation:
RTL fix: (1) make the mask bitwise, e.g. `vdresetnreg <= &( cr_vdmask1 | ~vdflag );` so each bit gates only its own detector; (2) change `.IV` to all-zeros so the reset response is armed out of reset and software must explicitly opt out; (3) make cr_vdmask1 write-once / lockable by driving a real sfrlock instead of `` `theregrn( sfrlock ) <= '0; ``, or gate writes on coreuser[5:4] (boot0/boot1) the way rrc.sv:815 gates its CFG region; (4) route the tamper condition to an asynchronous reset/zeroize path that does not require clksys.
Silicon workaround (partial, does not fix the scalar bug): immutable boot ROM/boot0 code must write 0x0000_0000 to 0x4005_3004 as one of its first stores, and must also program a plausible cr_vdcfg debounce at 0x4005_3020. Firmware should then periodically re-read 0x4005_3004 and 0x4005_3000 and treat any nonzero value as a tamper event itself. This is only a mitigation while the CPU is running and trusted; it cannot restore the per-detector granularity, and it is defeated by anything that gains a single 32-bit write.
findings.threat_actor: T2/T4 for the physical glitch; T1 alone is sufficient for the active-bypass variant

findings.title: Anti-tamper mesh integrity check is a static, software-chosen DC level compared against the same software-readable register that drives it - no challenge-response, and the reset default drives all 64 mesh lines to constant 0
findings.cwe: CWE-330 Use of Insufficiently Random Values
findings.description:
The mesh has 64 lines (MESHLC=64) each with 32 sense points (MESHPC=32). Each line is driven by one bit of the software register `cr_mldrv` (mesh.sv:62), the sense point is registered (mesh.sv:67), and the integrity test is a direct equality against that very same drive register (mesh.sv:68).

There is no LFSR, no counter, no per-cycle toggling, no random challenge and no timing/propagation-delay measurement anywhere in the module. `cr_mldrv` is a plain APB control register that changes only when software writes it; between writes each mesh line carries a constant DC level. Worse, `cr_mldrv` is in the read-back OR list (mesh.sv:48-51 `assign apbx.prdata = '0 | sfr_mldrv.prdata32 | ...`), so the exact static level of every one of the 64 lines is readable at 0x4005_2000-0x4005_2004 by any bus master, with sfrlock hardwired to 0 (mesh.sv:46) and no coreuser/privilege check on the 0x4005_xxxx APB.

And the reset default is the worst case: `apb_cr` has default `IV=32'h0` (apb_sfr.sv:81), and sfr_mldrv is instantiated without an IV override, so out of every core reset all 64 mesh lines are driven to constant logic 0 and every sense point is expected to read 0. `cr_mlie` also resets to 0, which zeroes `apterr` entirely (mesh.sv:68), so the mesh reports nothing at all until firmware arms it.

A mesh whose expected value is a constant that the adversary can either read out of a register or simply guess (all-zero at reset) provides no protection against the standard attack: cut/delaminate the mesh and tie the sense side of each line to the expected level.
findings.attack_scenario:
Attacker (T2) decapsulates the package and needs to reach the die under the active mesh. Step 1: before or during the attack, read 0x4005_2000 and 0x4005_2004 over the APB - either with T1 software (no privilege check exists on this path: soc_top.sv:661-666 bridges coreahb_sec straight to the secsub APB, and secsub.sv:46 is a bare apb_mux) or, if the part has just been reset, skip this step entirely because `cr_mldrv` resets to 0 and every line is at constant 0. Step 2: the 64-bit value read back is the exact DC level held on every mesh line, and it does not change unless firmware writes the register. Step 3: cut the mesh anywhere to open a hole for probing/FIB, and short each severed sense-side line to the level named in `cr_mldrv[i]` (ground for the reset default). Because mesh.sv:68 only tests `aptreg[i][j] != cr_mldrv[i]`, every sense point still matches, `apterr` stays 0, `sr_mlsr` stays 0, and `irq` stays 0. The mesh is now transparent while the die is fully exposed for microprobing of the SCE key RAM buses or laser fault injection. A rotating pseudo-random pattern with propagation-delay checking - the standard construction - would make this replay impossible; none is present anywhere in the module.

Variant requiring no physical mesh work at all: write 0 to `cr_mlie` at 0x4005_2010 (reset value is already 0). mesh.sv:68 ANDs every error term with `cr_mlie[i]`, so the entire 64x32 detector array reports clean. There is no lock bit to prevent this and no way for hardware to notice.
findings.preconditions: For the replay: physical access to the die (T2). Reading cr_mldrv additionally needs any APB read to 0x4005_2000 (T1), but is unnecessary against a freshly-reset part since the default pattern is all-zero. For the disarm variant: any write to 0x4005_2010 (T1, or any AHB master on core_ahb32).
findings.mitigation:
RTL fix: drive the mesh from a hardware LFSR/PRNG reseeded from the TRNG rather than from a software register, and compare the sense point against a delayed copy of the *driven* pattern rather than against a static CR; the driving pattern must not be readable over the bus (remove sfr_mldrv.prdata32 from the prdata OR list, or make it write-only). Add propagation-delay checking so that a shorted or re-routed line fails timing. Add a real lock: replace `` `theregrn( sfrlock ) <= '0; `` with a set-once lock bit, and default cr_mlie to all-ones so the mesh is armed out of reset rather than disarmed.
Silicon workaround: firmware must write a nonzero, ideally per-boot-random, pattern to cr_mldrv (0x4005_2000/4) and 0xFFFF_FFFF to cr_mlie (0x4005_2010/14) very early in boot0, and should rewrite cr_mldrv with a fresh random value frequently (each rewrite forces the attacker to re-short every line to a new level in real time). Firmware must also poll cr_mlie/cr_mldrv for unexpected changes. This raises the bar but cannot make the mesh unpredictable to an attacker who can read the register, so key material should not be treated as mesh-protected.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (physical) for the replay; T1 for the disarm variant

findings.title: Glue chain (anti-decap/laser detector) is held in reset out of reset, its stimulus is a software register, and software can clear the latched tamper state at will
findings.cwe: CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection
findings.description:
The glue chain is 64 chains (GLCX=64) of 32 series `ip_gluecell` tamper cells (GLCY=32). Three separate software registers control it, all instantiated as plain `apb_cr` with no IV override, i.e. reset value 0, and all with `sfrlock` hardwired to 0 (gluechain.sv:42):

1. `gluerst` (sfr_gcrst, offset 0x10 for GCX=64 -> 0x4005_4010/14) is ANDed into the per-chain reset at gluechain.sv:58. Reset value 0 means `glueresetn[i] = 0` for all 64 chains, i.e. every glue cell is held in reset out of every core reset. Per the only available cell model (rtl/modules/model/rtl/gluecell.sv:32-34) `always@(negedge d2a_nrst) thereg <= 0;` and `assign a2d_glue_out = thereg | d2a_glue_in;` - with nrst held low the cell can never latch a tamper event.
2. `gluetest` (sfr_gctest, 0x4005_4018/1C) is fed directly into the head of every chain at gluechain.sv:55. Reset value 0, so even if the chain were out of reset the propagated value is 0 and `gluereg` can never set.
3. `cr_gcmask` (sfr_gcmask, 0x4005_4000/04) ANDs off the alarm per chain at gluechain.sv:56.

So the glue chain is completely inert until firmware writes all of gluerst and (per the model) gluetest, and the *only* consequence when it does fire is `` `theregrn( irq ) <= |gluereg; `` (gluechain.sv:69) - a maskable interrupt (see the separate finding on evc erren).

Separately, because `gluerst` is a live read/write CR rather than a one-way arm bit, writing 0 then 1 to 0x4005_4010 pulses `d2a_nrst` low on every cell, clearing any latched tamper. The design provides an explicit, unlocked, unprivileged "erase the tamper evidence" control.

Finally the module's `resetn` is `coreresetn` (secsub.sv:93 `.resetn` bound to secsub's `resetn`, which soc_top.sv:703 drives with `coreresetn`), so a watchdog reset or a write of 0x55AA to sysctrl `sfr_rcurst1` at 0x4004_0084 returns gluerst/gluetest/cr_gcmask to 0 and disarms the whole chain again.
findings.attack_scenario:
Step 1 (T1, one store). Unprivileged code on either CPU - or the BIO/BDMA peripheral AHB master, which drives hauser=0 and hits no coreuser check on this bus - writes 0x0000_0000 to 0x4005_4010 and 0x4005_4014. `gluerst` goes to 0, `glueresetn[i]` (gluechain.sv:58) goes to 0 for all 64 chains, every `ip_gluecell` is held in its reset state and `a2d_glue_out` collapses to the chain input, which is `gluetest` = 0. `gluereg` can no longer set; `irq` can no longer assert. There is no lock bit (gluechain.sv:42 ties sfrlock to constant 0), no privilege check, and no hardware record that the detector was disarmed.
Step 2 (T2). Attacker decapsulates the package and applies laser fault injection or UV/optical probing over the die. The glue cells that would have latched the event are in reset. No interrupt, no status bit, no reset, no key erase.
