Every input to that decision is software-controlled and none are bound to each other: (a) which key is used is the software bit opt_ifskey (bit 6 of the plain APB CR sfr_opt2 at 0x4002_B014, combohasha.sv:218), selecting SEG_SKEY (unreadable) or SEG_KEY (freely bus-writable, ACRULEs 8'b01_01_01_01) at combohasha.sv:645; (b) where the expected digest comes from is the software bit tsmode (bit 5 of the same register), selecting the ReRAM key store (combohasha.sv:462) or bus-writable SEG_SCRT (combohasha.sv:477, 662-666); (c) which trust bit is set is the 10-bit software CR sfr_keyidx at 0x4002_B060 (combohasha.sv:221), forwarded verbatim as hmac_kid at combohasha.sv:490, with nothing correlating it to the key actually hashed; (d) sce_sec.sv:117 accepts hmac_pass identically regardless of tsmode/ifskey, and sce_ts is reset by the SYSTEM resetn (sce.sv:298) rather than sceresetn, so a forged bit survives sfr_arrst, sfr_arclr and mode-quit. The comparison itself is also one non-redundant bit initialised to PASS (combohasha.sv:480-482 seeds chkprepass to '1 and only clears it on cycles carrying a write strobe), with no re-check.
findings.attack_scenario:
Attacker = software that owns the SCE (T1). Goal: unlock a ReRAM key slot whose akeyid trust bit it is not entitled to.
1. Pick an arbitrary HMAC key K and message M in software; compute T = HMAC-SHA256_K(M) on the CPU.
2. Write K into SEG_KEY at 0x4002_0100 and T into SEG_SCRT at 0x4002_0300 (both AHB-writable per ACRULEs 8'b01_01_01_01).
3. Program SFR_OPT2 (0x4002_B014) with ifskey=0 (use SEG_KEY, not the unreadable SEG_SKEY), tsmode=0 (compare against SEG_SCRT, not against the ReRAM key store), scrtchk=1.
4. Write SFR_KEYIDX (0x4002_B060) = N, where N is the akeyid of the ReRAM key slot the attacker wants.
5. Run HF_HMAC256_PASS1 (cr_func=0x50) over M, then HF_HMAC256_PASS2 (cr_func=0x60). PASS2 reaches MFSM_LD_SECRET (combohasha.sv:415-417), XORs the computed tag against SEG_SCRT, finds all zero, so chkprepass stays 1 and chkpass asserts.
6. hmac_pass with hmac_kid=N propagates to sce_sec.sv:117 and sets tsreg[N]=1; confirm via sfr_ts (sce_glbsfra.sv:103) at 0x4002_80e0.
7. truststate[N] now feeds rrc.sv:717, removing the trustkey gate on every ReRAM key slot whose ACRAM descriptor carries akeyid==N. Read the slot at 0x603F_xxxx.
8. Because sce_ts is reset by the system resetn rather than sceresetn (sce.sv:298), the forged bit survives sfr_arrst / sfr_arclr / mode-quit - the attacker can drop the SCE back to a non-secure mode and the unlock persists.
A physical attacker (T2) has an even cheaper path: one glitch on the chkprepass/chkfail flop during the single cycle chkdone is high converts a genuine FAIL into a PASS, since the decision is one non-redundant bit with no re-check.
findings.preconditions: The attacker must be the SCE owner in mode_sec (scemode[1]=1). scemode is a write-once-from-zero CR reset to 0 (sce_glbsfra.sv:78) and the owning coreuser is latched from whichever master last did an AHB address phase before the transition (sce_sec.sv:58-64), so the first code to program scemode after any sysresetn wins. No physical access, no fault injection, and no knowledge of any real secret is required for the software path.
findings.mitigation:
RTL: (1) qualify hmac_pass with the mode that produced it - export tsmode/opt_ifskey alongside hmac_pass and have sce_sec.sv:117 set tsreg only when the compare was against the ReRAM key store (tsmode=1) AND the key came from SEG_SKEY (opt_ifskey=1); (2) derive hmac_kid from the same kid that generated schcrx.axstart rather than from a live CR, and lock sfr_keyidx for the operation; (3) make the comparison redundant - keep a complemented pass bit and a fail counter and require chkpass && ~chkfail && (words_compared == STSIZE); (4) move sce_ts onto sceresetn (sce.sv:298) so a forged bit cannot survive an SCE reset; (5) drop the hardwired 1'b1 MSB at sce_sec.sv:123.
Already-fabricated silicon: do not rely on truststate for any authorisation. In the ACRAM descriptors written at boot, give every sensitive ReRAM key slot a non-zero userid_k[7:4] and rely on the coreuser check (rrc.sv:712) rather than the trustkey term; choose akeyid values only from indices you can prove are never set - note akeyid 127 and 255 are permanently trusted by construction (sce_sec.sv:123, plus the unconnected truststate[255:128]), so never use those. The boot ROM must claim SCE ownership by writing scemode before any other code runs, and must never hand SCE ownership to code not already entitled to every ReRAM key slot.

findings.title: HF_INIT loads the entire hash constant table (SHA-2 IVs and round constants, SHA-3 rho offsets and round constants) from bus-writable crypto RAM, and that region is deliberately excluded from the SCE RAM wipe
findings.threat_actor: T1 (any software able to reach the SCE window before or while it is unlocked)
findings.cwe: CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Protection (attacker-writable algorithm constants, no lock, no zeroization)
findings.description: The hash engine holds no hard-coded constants. Every initialisation vector and round-constant table lives in the first INITSIZE = hash_pkg::RAMSEG_CHACHA20_H = 428 words of the private hash RAM (HRAM), and the only way to populate them is HF_INIT, which DMAs SCERAM words 0..427 verbatim into HRAM words 0..427 (combohasha.sv:78-87, SEG_INIT has segaddr:'0, segsize:INITSIZE; combohasha.sv:580-588, MFSM_LD_INIT). Per hash_pkg.sv:90-104 that region is exactly the SHA-256 IV (HRAM 0..7), SHA-256 K (8..71), SHA-512 IV (72..87), SHA-512 K (88..247), the BLAKE2/3 IVs and tables (248..313), the RIPEMD tables (314..369), the SHA-3 rho-offset table (370..379) and the 24 Keccak round constants (380..403). SCERAM words 0..427 span SEG_LKEY, SEG_KEY, SEG_SKEY, SEG_SCRT, SEG_MSG and part of SEG_HOUT, every one of which permits AHB writes (scedma_pkg.sv:250-255). So any master that can write the SCE crypto RAM chooses the arithmetic constants of every hash algorithm in the chip. Worse, the poisoning persists across the security boundary: the HRAM cryptoram is instantiated with .clrstart(INITSIZE) (combohasha.sv:857), so the sceramclr wipe FSM (cryptoram.sv:61-68) starts at word 428 and runs to WCNT-1=767 - HRAM words 0..427 are never cleared by sfr_arclr, sfr_arrst, mode-quit or any SCE reset. There is no integrity check, no lock bit, and no way for later, more-privileged code to detect tampering short of running its own known-answer test.
findings.attack_scenario:
Attacker = unprivileged software (T1) able to reach the SCE window at 0x4002_xxxx - which, per sce_sec.sv:72 ('assign ahben = mode_non ? 1'b1 : ...'), is every AHB master while scemode==0, i.e. from reset until some code claims the SCE.
1. Attacker writes a doctored 428-word constant image over 0x4002_0000..0x4002_06AF (SEG_LKEY/KEY/SKEY/SCRT/MSG/HOUT - all AHB-writable). For example it leaves the SHA-256 IV alone but replaces the 64-entry K table with one for which it has precomputed a collision pair, or simply zeroes K so the compression function becomes trivially collidable.
2. Attacker writes COMBOHASH_SFR_CRFUNC = 0xff (HF_INIT) and 0x5a to SFR_AR. MFSM_LD_INIT copies all 428 words into HRAM 0..427.
3. Attacker restores the SCERAM contents so nothing looks amiss, then yields to the next boot stage.
4. The next stage claims the SCE (writes scemode) and may issue sfr_arclr / sfr_arrst to 'wipe' the crypto RAM before use. Because the HRAM clear FSM starts at word 428, the poisoned constants survive intact.
5. Every subsequent SHA-256/SHA-512/SHA-3/BLAKE hash in the chip - including secure-boot image measurement and the HMAC that drives truststate - is computed with the attacker's constants. The attacker supplies a rogue image whose doctored-SHA-256 digest equals the reference digest, and secure boot accepts it.
Because these are the only constants the engine has, there is no known-good copy in silicon to fall back on.
findings.preconditions: Write access to 0x4002_0000..0x4002_06AF and to the COMBOHASH SFR page. Both are open to any AHB master while scemode==0 (the reset state), so the attacker only needs to run once, before whoever claims the SCE. If the attacker instead owns the SCE in mode_sec, all six of those segments still permit AHB writes under ACRULEs, so the same attack works.
findings.mitigation:
RTL: hold the IVs and round constants in ROM or hardwired constants rather than a bus-loadable RAM region; or at minimum make HF_INIT one-shot per SCE reset (latch a constants_loaded flag cleared only by sceresetn) and make sceramclr cover HRAM word 0 (.clrstart('0)) so entering or leaving a secure mode forces the new owner to reload the constants. Sourcing SEG_INIT from SCERAM address 0 - which aliases the key segments - should also be changed to a dedicated non-key segment.
Already-fabricated silicon: the boot ROM must (a) claim the SCE (write scemode) and load the constant table via HF_INIT itself, before any third-party code executes, and (b) re-run HF_INIT plus a known-answer test (e.g. SHA-256 of the empty string compared against a hardcoded digest) immediately before every security-critical hash, since nothing else can detect a poisoned table. Note re-running HF_INIT requires writing 428 words into the key segments, so the KAT must be done where clobbering SEG_LKEY/KEY/SKEY/SCRT/MSG is acceptable.

findings.title: BLAKE2 finalization flag is hardwired off - the last-block domain separation that makes BLAKE2 length-extension resistant is never applied
findings.threat_actor: T1 for the length-extension variant; the correctness defect is unconditional
findings.cwe: CWE-1240 Use of a Cryptographic Primitive with a Risky Implementation
findings.description: hashcore implements the BLAKE2 finalization flag f0 as an inversion of working-vector word v[14] on the last block: hashcore.sv:286 'assign vreg_mfsmin_blk[14] = cfg_finalhash ? ~vreg[14] : vreg[14];'. The only instantiation of hashcore, in combohash, ties that input to a constant zero (combohasha.sv:550 '.cfg_finalhash('0),'). No other driver of cfg_finalhash exists anywhere in the design (grep-verified). Consequently v[14] is never complemented, f0 is never set, and the latched copy finalrnd (hashcore.sv:75, 80) is dead logic nothing reads. Two consequences: (1) HT_BLK2s / HT_BLK2b digests do not match RFC 7693, so a hardware-computed BLAKE2 tag will never verify against any software implementation - a silent interoperability failure in a security path; (2) the finalization flag is precisely what makes BLAKE2, and the standard keyed-BLAKE2 MAC (a key block prepended to the message), resistant to length extension. Without it the emitted digest is a plain iterated chaining value, so anyone holding a tag can extend it. Related: the BLAKE2 message-length counter is also degenerate - hashcore.sv:739-746 increments only ST word 12 (t0) by the 8-bit software register cfg_blkt0 (COMBOHASH_SFR_BLKT0 at 0x4002_B01C, combohasha.sv:220, IV 0x40), and the t1 half of BLAKE2's 128-bit counter is never written at all.
findings.attack_scenario:
Case A (interoperability becomes a security failure): firmware uses HF_BLK2s (cr_func=0x03) to compute a BLAKE2s digest over a firmware image and compares it against a reference produced by a host-side BLAKE2s implementation. Because the hardware never sets f0, the two digests never match for any input, so either the check is silently disabled during bring-up or the reference is regenerated from the hardware - in which case the 'BLAKE2' digest being trusted is an unspecified non-standard function with no third-party analysis.
Case B (length extension against keyed BLAKE2): firmware uses keyed BLAKE2 (key block prepended, the RFC 7693 MAC mode) to authenticate message M and publishes tag T. Because f0 is never applied, T is exactly the chaining value h after the last block of M - the same value the engine loads as the state for a continuation (hashcore.sv:221-222, with cfg_firsthash=0 selecting RAMSEG_ST). An attacker who observes T writes T into SEG_HOUT, runs the same HF_BLK2s command with ifstart=0 and an appended block M', and obtains a valid tag for M||M' without knowing the key. Setting SFR_BLKT0 lets the attacker keep the byte counter consistent.
findings.preconditions: Any use of HT_BLK2s / HT_BLK2b / HT_BLK3 in a security role. For case B the attacker also needs access to the COMBOHASH SFR page and to SEG_HOUT - available to any AHB master while scemode==0 and to the SCE owner in mode_sec.
findings.mitigation:
RTL: drive cfg_finalhash from a real control bit - expose it as an SFR bit, or derive it from 'opt_cnt == hashcnt' in the MFSM_HF branch at combohasha.sv:288-295, which is exactly the last-block condition - and route it to hashcore.cfg_finalhash. Widen the block counter to the full 128-bit BLAKE2 t0/t1 pair rather than an 8-bit software CR that only touches ST word 12. Then re-validate against RFC 7693 test vectors.
Already-fabricated silicon: no register can set cfg_finalhash, so the BLAKE2 modes cannot be made spec-compliant. Firmware must not use HF_BLK2s (0x03), HF_BLK2b (0x04) or HF_BLK3 (0x05) for anything security-relevant - no MACs, no image measurement, no KDF. Use HF_SHA256/HF_SHA512 (whose padding is done in software and is correct, per deps/sha2-bao1x) or compute BLAKE2 in software. If a BLAKE2 tag has already been published by a fielded device, treat it as extendable and add an outer length-committing wrapper in software.

findings.title: A single write of an unrecognised cr_func permanently latches the COMBOHASH sfrlock, wedging the hash engine until an SCE reset
findings.threat_actor: T1 (any software able to write two words in the SCE APB window)
findings.cwe: CWE-1245 Improper Finite State Machines in Hardware Logic (unhandled encoding leaves a lock permanently asserted)
findings.description: sfrlock is set by optlock (a start write while mfsm==MFSM_IDLE) and is only ever cleared by mfsm_done, i.e. mfsm reaching MFSM_DONE (combohasha.sv:203, 225, 245). The main FSM's cr_func case statement (combohasha.sv:256-449) has a default branch that keeps the FSM in MFSM_IDLE and never asserts mfsmdone (combohasha.sv:443-448), so for any cr_func outside the enumerated hashfunc_e values the FSM cannot advance and mfsm_done can never become true. sfrlock therefore latches high forever. Because sfrlock gates apbwr for the whole block (apb_sfr.sv:333 'assign apbwr = ~sfrlock & apbslave.psel & apbslave.penable & apbslave.pwrite;'), software cannot even rewrite sfr_crfunc to a legal value to recover - the only exit is asserting sceresetn via the separate sce_glbsfr action register at 0x4002_801C. Note also that busy (combohasha.sv:237 'assign busy = |mfsm | ramclrbusy;') reads 0 in this state, so the wedge is invisible to a caller polling busy or SFR_FR.
findings.attack_scenario:
Attacker = unprivileged software (T1) with access to the COMBOHASH APB page, i.e. any AHB master while scemode==0, or the SCE owner in mode_sec.
1. Write COMBOHASH_SFR_CRFUNC (0x4002_B000) = 0x07, or any of the ~230 unassigned encodings (0x08-0x3F, 0x42-0x4F, 0x52-0x5F, 0x62-0xFE).
2. Write 0x5a to COMBOHASH_SFR_AR (0x4002_B004). optlock pulses, sfrlock latches to 1, and mfsm stays in MFSM_IDLE.
3. Every subsequent write to any COMBOHASH register is discarded by apb_sfr's 'apbwr = ~sfrlock & ...', including writes to SFR_CRFUNC and SFR_AR. SFR_SRMFSM still reads MFSM_IDLE and busy reads 0, so a victim driver sees a healthy, idle engine that silently ignores every command.
4. All hash-dependent services stall: secure-boot measurement, the HMAC path that drives truststate, and any software using the sha2-bao1x driver, which spins forever in 'while csr.rf(utra::combohash::SFR_FR_MFSM_DONE) == 0' (deps/sha2-bao1x/src/sha256.rs:78).
5. Recovery requires writing 0x5a to sce_glbsfr's sfr_arrst at 0x4002_801C, which asserts sceresetn for the whole SCE and triggers the crypto-RAM wipe, destroying any in-flight secure-session state.
findings.preconditions: Two APB writes, to 0x4002_B000 and 0x4002_B004. No physical access, no privilege beyond reaching the SCE APB window (unrestricted while scemode==0 per sce_sec.sv:72).
findings.mitigation:
RTL: make the default branch of the cr_func case set 'mfsmnext = MFSM_DONE; mfsmdone = '1;' so an illegal opcode completes with an error instead of parking, and/or gate optlock on cr_func being a recognised encoding. Add an unlock path (e.g. clear sfrlock when mfsm==MFSM_IDLE for N cycles with no start) and report the illegal opcode on the err bus (combohasha.sv:894 currently reports only RAM errors).
Already-fabricated silicon: firmware must validate cr_func against the hashfunc_e whitelist {0x00-0x06, 0x40, 0x41, 0x50, 0x51, 0x60, 0x61, 0xff} before writing SFR_CRFUNC, and must not expose the COMBOHASH page to code that has not been so validated. Hash drivers should add a timeout around the SFR_FR_MFSM_DONE poll and, on timeout, recover by issuing sfr_arrst (0x5a to 0x4002_801C), accepting the SCERAM wipe.

finders.domain: System control: clocks, PLL, reset, config/fuse straps, frequency monitor (rtl/modules/sysctrl/rtl/*)
finders.coverage_notes:
READ END-TO-END: rtl/modules/sysctrl/rtl/{sysctrl.sv (1070L), cms.sv, cgucore.sv, cgupll.sv, cgudyncswt.sv, cgufdsync.sv, freqmeter.sv, brc.sv, nvrcfgs.sv, evc.sv, apbsys_intf.sv, gearbox.sv}. Traced every security-relevant signal out of these files to its consumers: soc_top.sv (cms/brc/sysctrl/evc/secsub instantiation, clock sub-gate fan-out lines 329-336, 397, 438-505, 572-578, 690-730, 764-765, 907-968), pad_frame_arm.sv:214-216 (WMS straps), secsub.sv:51-58, mesh.sv (full), ao_top.sv:144, ao_sysctrl.sv:415-435, rrc.sv (boot-read FSM 111-235, brdatreg), soc_coresub.sv (devmode/coresel latches), amba/apb_sfr.sv (apb_cr/apb_ar/apb_sfr2 sfrlock semantics), common/insauth.v (drng_lfsr). Cross-checked docs/src/clock-generation.md (full CGU + IPC register tables) and docs/src/system-control.md (RCU/WDT sections).

VERIFIED NEGATIVES (things I checked and did NOT find a bug in): cgudyncswt.sv glitch-free mux handshake is correct (2-flop sync each way, one-hot enables, both enables low during transition); cgufdsync.sv divider counters are correct; cgupll.sv output ICG is properly gated off on reconfiguration (setcfgextlock cleared on setcfg&lock) — no unlocked-PLL clock escape found; resetgen's 2048-cycle extension and cmsatpg override are consistent with the rest of the design; brc.sv's 2-cycle pipeline alignment between bridx_pl2/brvld_pl2 and brdat is correct (brdat is the registered brdatreg output, so no off-by-two word mis-latch).

COULD NOT COVER / OUT OF REACH:
- INNO_FNPLL_TOP (cgupll.sv:83), OSC_32M, RNG_CELL, ICG/CLKCELL_MUX2/DATACELL_BUF are black boxes not in this repo. I cannot verify whether the PLL `lock` output has any frequency-range qualification, nor whether the ICG cells are glitch-free. My CLKSCREW finding therefore rests on the absence of any RTL-side limiter, not on a claim about the PLL analog behaviour.
- I could not determine whether the CM7's MPU is actually instantiated: cm7sys.sv:364 passes `.MPU(MPU)` but `MPU` is not declared as a parameter in cm7sys.sv, and daric_cfg_pkg.sv:117-127 (`MPU : 16`) is commented out. I therefore did NOT rely on "unprivileged user-mode code" anywhere; every finding is scoped to T1 = any code able to issue an APB write to 0x4004_0000, which includes the Vex AHB-P port and the BDMA AHB master (hauser=0x0), neither of which is subject to any coreuser check.
- NVR/ReRAM integrity: I confirmed there is NO ECC, parity, CRC or redundant copy anywhere on the boot-read config path (rrc.sv:156 `brdatreg[bridx_org] <= {trc_dout_s1,trc_dout_s0}` -> brc.sv:80,87 raw latch -> nvrcfgdata), and no "config valid" interlock beyond `brdone`. I did not report this as a standalone finding because the security-critical consumers (devmode magic compare, coreselcm7/vex magic compare) all fail *closed* on a corrupted word, and the ReRAM array itself is another reviewer's domain. Worth flagging to the vendor as a hardening item: a single fault injected at soc_coresub.sv:271 `corecfg_devreg` (one flop, one 32-bit compare, no redundancy) enables all five SCE security bypasses via sce.sv:131.
- docs/src/system-control.md documents RCUSRCFR[7] as "vdresetn — Voltage detector reset", but soc_top.sv:373 `assign vdresetn = 1'b1;` hardwires that resetgen input inactive, so bit 7 can never set. The real voltage-detector reset still reaches sysresetn via `secresetn` (soc_top.sv:712), so this is a dead/misleading status bit rather than a lost protection; not reported as a finding.
- I did not audit the WDT (cmsdk_apb_watchdog, ARM IP) or the AO PMU register file beyond the reset tree.

findings.title: Chip-Mode-Select lifecycle gate is decided entirely by two external pads: all four non-volatile CMS mode patterns are the identical constant 128'h0
findings.cwe: CWE-1191 On-Chip Debug and Test Interface With Improper Access Control
findings.description: The chip lifecycle mode (USER vs. TEST / VIRGIN / ATPG / SUICIDE) is intended to be a two-factor decision: three external strap pads AND a 128-bit pattern read out of ReRAM at boot. The ReRAM half of that decision is void. All four members of the `cmsdata_e` enum are defined as '0, so every comparison in the mode decode (`cmsdatareg == CMSDAT_VRGNMODE`, `== CMSDAT_TESTMODE`, `== CMSDAT_USERMODE`) is literally the same test, and the first branch always wins. The ReRAM default word is also all-zero (nvrcfgs.sv:102-105 `cmsdata0/1 : CMSDAT_USERMODE` = '0), so a part provisioned as USER MODE evaluates `cmsdatareg == CMSDAT_VRGNMODE` as TRUE. Additionally cms.sv:92 forces cmspadout[2] to 0, making the `3'bxx1` case unreachable, so only two of the three straps matter. Tracing the bit order (cmspadout[2]=cmspad[0]=PAD_WMS0, cmspadout[1]=cmspad[1]=PAD_WMS1, pad_frame_arm.sv:214-216, both pulled DOWN), the effective table is: WMS0=0 -> CMS_USER; WMS0=1,WMS1=1 -> CMS_VRGN; WMS0=1,WMS1=0 -> CMS_ATPG. CMS_TEST and CMS_SCDE are unreachable, and no value of the non-volatile word can prevent entry into VRGN or ATPG. CMS_VRGN sets cmstest, and soc_top.sv:397 `assign cmsbist = cmstest;` — which unlocks the ReRAM JTAG BIST TAPs (rrc.sv:884 `bist_enable = ((cmscode == CMS_VRGN) | (cmscode == CMS_TEST)) & (brfsm == 3'h5)`), the rbist RAM-readback path into every crypto RAM (ram_1rw_s.sv:124-131), the IPT TAP (soc_top.sv:907), and JTAG ownership of the PMU/OSC trims (ao_sysctrl.sv:285-286).
findings.preconditions: Physical access to the package/board to drive PAD_WMS0/PAD_WMS1 (T2). The only thing standing in the way is the sticky always-on latch `aocmsuser` (ao_top.sv:144 `theregfull( clksysao_undft, porresetn_undft, aocmsuser, '0) <= aocmsuser | cmsuser;`), which forces CMS_USER on subsequent evaluations (cms.sv:155). That latch is reset by `porresetn_undft`, which is derived from `por = ~pmu_POR & padresetn` (ao_sysctrl.sv:422) — i.e. it is cleared by asserting the external PAD_XRSTn pin, no power cycle required.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker gets the board/package (lost, stolen, or supply-chain intercept). 2. Strap PAD_WMS0 high and PAD_WMS1 high. 3. Pulse PAD_XRSTn low; this clears `aocmsuser` in the always-on domain (ao_sysctrl.sv:422 -> ao_top.sv:144) but does NOT clear any SRAM, TCM, IFRAM, AO SRAM, BIO RAM or the RRC ACRAM (no macro in the design has a power-on wipe). 4. After the 128-cycle strap-lock window, cms.sv:126 evaluates `cmsdatareg == CMSDAT_VRGNMODE` — TRUE regardless of what the vendor programmed into the ReRAM CMS word, because both sides are 128'h0 — and cmspadout[1]=1 selects CMS_VRGN. 5. cmstest and therefore cmsbist assert. The ReRAM BIST TAPs (rrc.sv:884,898-899, clocked directly by JTAG TCK) and the rbist RAM TAP are enabled at the pads (pad_frame_arm.sv:232-250), and the IPT TAP is enabled (soc_top.sv:907), giving raw ReRAM macro access that bypasses every coreuser/ACRAM check in rrc.sv, and read-back of the SCE key RAMs via ram_1rw_s.sv:127-131. 6. Attacker dumps ReRAM key slots and any secret still resident in SRAM from the previous boot.
findings.mitigation: RTL fix: give each mode a distinct, high-Hamming-distance 128-bit pattern (e.g. VRGN/TEST/ATPG each a different random constant, USER a fourth), and make the decode require an exact match on the corresponding constant with a default of CMS_USER — never fall through to a test mode when the pattern is unrecognised. Restore cmspadregs[1][2] instead of forcing it to 0 so all three straps participate. Make the `aocmsuser` sticky latch clearable only by a true cold power-on (pmu_POR) and not by PAD_XRSTn. On already-fabricated silicon there is no software workaround for the mode decode itself; the only field mitigations are (a) board-level: permanently tie PAD_WMS0 to ground under the package/with a buried via so it cannot be re-strapped, and (b) never leave key material in SRAM/TCM across a reset — have firmware explicitly overwrite all SRAM and the SCE crypto RAM before any reset it initiates, since no reset does it for you.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (physical access: strap pads + XRSTn + JTAG probing)

findings.title: sysctrl's write-protect input `sfrlock` is an undriven net in soc_top: every CGU, PLL, clock-gate and software-reset register is permanently unlocked
findings.cwe: CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection
findings.description: `sysctrl` exposes an `sfrlock` port that is threaded into every one of its SFRs via the `.*` connection, and apb_sfr2 uses it as the sole write-enable qualifier (`assign apbwr = ~sfrlock & apbslave.psel & apbslave.penable & apbslave.pwrite;`, apb_sfr.sv:333). In soc_top.sv the signal `sfrlock` is declared at line 217 and connected at line 361 — those are the only two occurrences of the identifier in the entire file. It has no assignment anywhere, so it is a floating net (synthesised as a constant 0, or X in simulation). The result is that there is no write-protection mechanism at all on the sysctrl register block at 0x4004_0000: the clock-cipher seed, CGUSEL0/1 source selects, all CGUFD_* dividers, the clock sub-gates CGUACLKGR/CGUHCLKGR/CGUICLKGR/CGUPCLKGR, the PLL M/N/F/Q registers, the internal-oscillator trim, and both software reset action registers RCURST0/RCURST1 are writable by any bus master that can reach the peripheral APB. There is no coreuser check on this path either (rrc.sv:666-671 is the only coreuser consumer on the bus, and it only covers ReRAM), and no APB slave in the design consumes `pprot`. That the design idiom exists elsewhere makes this clearly an omission: the WDT has a real unlock register (docs/src/system-control.md:590, WDT_LOCKCR write 0x1ACEE551), and other blocks drive sfrlock from real logic (e.g. aes.sv:135 `theregrn( sfrlock ) <= optlock ? 1'b1 : mfsm_done ? '0 : sfrlock;`). This single dangling net is the enabler for the two findings below.
findings.preconditions: Any bus master able to issue an APB write into the apb1-system block at 0x4004_0000. Per the address map (daric_cfg_pkg.sv:51, soc_top.sv:362) that is reachable from the CM7 AHB-P port (hauser 0x8), the Vex AHB-P port (hauser 0xD), the MDMA (0x7) and the BDMA/BIO peripheral AHB master (hauser 0x0) — none of which is subject to any privilege or coreuser filter on this path.
findings.attack_scenario: Attacker with code execution on either CPU (or with control of the BIO/BDMA, which any code that can write 0x5012_4000 has) issues a single 32-bit APB store into 0x4004_00xx. Because `sfrlock` is stuck at 0, apb_sfr.sv:333 unconditionally asserts apbwr and the register updates. There is no way for firmware to close this door after boot: the intended latch-and-lock mechanism exists in the port list but has no driver, so a hardened boot ROM cannot freeze the clock tree, the PLL, or the reset controller before handing control to less-trusted firmware. Concrete downstream consequences are the mesh-clock kill and the CLKSCREW primitive described in the next two findings.
findings.mitigation: RTL fix: drive `sfrlock` from a sticky, set-only flop in soc_top that is set by a write-once 'CGU lock' action register and cleared only by socresetn, e.g. the same pattern already used at aes.sv:135. Better still, split it so that the RCU action registers and the frequency-control registers have independent lock bits. On fabricated silicon there is no software workaround — the net has no driver — so the only mitigation is architectural: keep every bus master that must not be able to reprogram the clock tree off the peripheral AHB entirely (in practice this means not enabling the BDMA peripheral master, and treating any code that reaches the CM7-P/Vex-P port as fully trusted).
findings.threat_actor: T1 (software execution on either CPU, or control of the BIO/BDMA peripheral master)

findings.title: The anti-tamper mesh detector's only clock is behind an unlocked software clock gate: writing CGUPCLKGR[7]=0 silently and permanently freezes tamper detection
findings.cwe: CWE-1247 Improper Protection Against Voltage and Clock Glitches
findings.description: The mesh tamper detector (rtl/modules/sec/rtl/mesh.sv) is entirely synchronous: it samples the mesh aperture lines into `aptreg` on its clock, and registers the resulting alarm into `irq` on that same clock. Its clock port is driven from `pclkmesh` (secsub.sv:55), which soc_top.sv:702 wires to `pclksub[7]`. `pclksub[7]` is produced by an ICG whose enable is `pclken & pclksubgate[gvi]` (sysctrl.sv:635), and `pclksubgate` is nothing more than a plain APB control register at 0x4004_006C with reset value 0xFF and — because of the previous finding — no write protection whatsoever. Documented as 'CGUPCLKGR bit [7] = mesh clock enable' (docs/src/clock-generation.md). Clearing that one bit stops the mesh's clock: `aptreg` stops updating, `apterr` freezes at its last (all-zero) value, `sr_mlsr` freezes, and `irq` freezes at 0. There is no interlock anywhere in the design that detects the tamper block's clock has stopped — no heartbeat, no watchdog on the mesh, no comparison against the freqmeter, and no fail-safe that treats a stopped tamper clock as a tamper event. The identical construction applies to the SCE clock (CGUHCLKGR[0] -> hclksub[1] -> soc_top.sv:573 `.clksce ( hclksub[1] )`), which lets software freeze the crypto engine mid-operation while its RAMs remain on the ungated `clk`, and to the QFC (CGUACLKGR[4]) and BIO (CGUICLKGR[7]).
findings.preconditions: Ability to perform one APB write to 0x4004_006C. Reachable from the CM7 AHB-P port, the Vex AHB-P port, the MDMA, or the BDMA peripheral AHB master (hauser=0x0, which matches no check anywhere). Requires the `sfrlock` defect above, i.e. it is unconditional on this silicon.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker obtains code execution on either CPU, or programs the BIO to issue a peripheral write (bio_bdma peripheral AHB master, hauser=0). 2. Writes 0x0000007F to 0x4004_006C (CGUPCLKGR), clearing only bit 7. 3. The ICG at sysctrl.sv:635 stops pclksub[7]. mesh.sv's `aptreg` and `irq` flops stop clocking; the mesh alarm output is frozen low. Note that the mesh's own APB slave also runs on this clock, so a monitor task reading MESH_MLSR at 0x4005_2020 sees a stale all-zero status and cannot tell the block is dead — apbx.pready is combinational (`apbs_common`), so the read completes normally. 4. The attacker now decapsulates / drills / probes through the mesh with tamper detection disabled. This composes with the fact that mesh.sv:53-54's `cr_mldrv` and `cr_mlie` reset to 0 (mesh detection is OFF at reset until firmware enables it) and with the fact that the mesh IRQ is routed to `err[3] = |secirq` -> evc, whose NMI mask resets to 0 (see finding below), so even a working mesh raises nothing by default.
findings.mitigation: RTL fix: remove pclksub[7] from the software-writable gate — clock the mesh (and sensorc/gluechain) from an ungateable branch of pclk, or hard-tie pclksubgate[7] to 1. If a gate must exist, add a lock bit (see previous finding) and add a heartbeat: a counter in the always-on or sysctrl domain that asserts a tamper reset if the mesh clock has not toggled for N cycles. Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: (a) have the boot ROM / trusted firmware never hand off with the tamper block reachable — but the register is unlockable, so this is not enforceable; (b) periodically prove liveness from a different clock domain, e.g. set MESH_MLDRV to a known pattern with MESH_MLIE enabled and confirm MESH_MLSR changes as expected within a bounded time measured on clksys, treating a stale value as a tamper event; (c) additionally enable EVC_ERRCR bit 3 so |secirq escalates to NMI (see next finding), which at least removes the silent-failure mode for a live mesh.
findings.threat_actor: T1 to disable the detector, then T2 to exploit the disabled detector (decapsulation / probing)

findings.title: CLKSCREW: PLL ratio, oscillator trim and every clock divider are software-writable with no bound, no lock, and a frequency monitor that is advisory only
findings.cwe: CWE-1247 Improper Protection Against Voltage and Clock Glitches
findings.description: Every knob that sets the operating frequency of the crypto and security logic is a plain, unlocked APB control register in the sysctrl block: PLL feedback/pre-divider (`sfr_ipcpllmn`, 17 bits, 0x4004_00A0), PLL post-dividers (`sfr_ipcpllq`, 0x4004_00A8), PLL charge-pump/VCO bias (`sfr_ipccr`, 0x4004_00AC), the internal 32 MHz oscillator trim (`sfr_ipcosc`, 0x4004_009C), the clktop/clksys source selects (`sfr_cgusel0`/`sfr_cgusel1`), and the per-domain frequency dividers (`sfr_cgufd` for FCLK/ACLK/HCLK/ICLK/PCLK, plus PKE and PER). Nothing in the RTL bounds any of them. The design contains a frequency meter — `freqmeter` (freqmeter.sv), measuring FCLK, CLKPKE, CLKAO, CLKAORAM, OSC, XTAL, PLL0 and PLL1 — but its outputs `fsvld`/`fsfreq` are consumed by exactly two read-only status registers and by nothing else in the entire design (verified by grep across rtl/: the only consumers are sysctrl.sv:849-850). It gates no clock, triggers no reset, and raises no interrupt. It is purely advisory. Furthermore, the one structure that looks like a hardware frequency floor is dead: `cgufdsync` declares `parameter FD0 = 2**(FDW-1)-1` and cgucore.sv:177/210 instantiate it with `.FD0('h7F)`/`.FD0('hF)`, but the identifier `FD0` is never referenced in the module body — the only 'min cycle' limit that has any effect is the runtime `fd0` input, which comes from CGUFD_*[23:16] and resets to 0 (no limit) for FCLK/ACLK/HCLK/ICLK/PCLK. docs/src/clock-generation.md publishes hard maxima (FCLK 700 MHz, ACLK 350, HCLK 175, PCLK 43.75, PKECLK 175/300) that exist only as documentation.
findings.preconditions: One or more APB writes into 0x4004_0000-0x4004_00AF. Same reach as the previous findings (CM7-P, Vex-P, MDMA, BDMA-AHB), and unconditional because `sfrlock` has no driver. No coreuser, hauser or pprot check exists on this path.
findings.attack_scenario: CLKSCREW-style software-only fault injection against the SCE. 1. Attacker code (on either CPU, or via a BIO peripheral write) starts a victim crypto operation — e.g. an AES or an HMAC/trust-state check in the SCE, which is clocked from hclksub[1] derived from clktop. 2. Attacker writes an out-of-spec PLL ratio into 0x4004_00A0 / 0x4004_00A8, commits it with the action register (write 0x32 to 0x4004_0090), and/or writes CGUFD_HCLK at 0x4004_001C with normal-FD = 0xFF (CLKTOP x 1/1 per the documented encoding) and min-cycle = 0. Alternatively, and without touching the PLL at all, the attacker retunes the root 32 MHz oscillator by writing `sfr_ipcosc` at 0x4004_009C and committing with 0x57 to 0x4004_0090 (sysctrl.sv:257) — clksys feeds clktop by default (CGUSEL0 resets to 0), so this directly overclocks every synchronous block including the SCE. 3. The target domain now runs above its timing closure point; setup violations produce a faulted computation. Nothing intervenes: the freqmeter records the excursion in a read-only register that no logic reads, `cgufdsync`'s only floor (`fd0`) is 0, and there is no reset, interrupt or clock kill. 4. Classic exploitation follows — a faulted RSA-CRT signature in the PKE leaks the private factors; a faulted comparison in combohasha.sv:483-490 flips `chkprepass` and sets a trust-state bit (sce_sec.sv:117), which unlocks a ReRAM key slot (rrc.sv:717 `!trustkey[akeyid]`).
findings.mitigation: RTL fix: (1) clamp `pll_m`/`pll_n`/`pll_q*` and the CGUFD values in hardware to the documented maxima before they reach cgupll/cgufdsync, or at minimum bound the resulting fd0 min-cycle to a non-zero safe floor per domain (make the existing FD0 parameter actually drive the reset value of `fd0reg` instead of being dead); (2) close the freqmeter loop — compare fsfreq against per-domain hardware limits and assert `secresetn` (which already feeds sysresetgen at sysctrl.sv:794) on an over-frequency excursion, and separately on `fsvld` deasserting for a clock that is supposed to be running; (3) put the whole IPC/CGU register bank behind the (currently undriven) sfrlock. On fabricated silicon: firmware must treat 0x4004_0000-0x4004_00AF as a privileged region and prevent any less-trusted code from reaching the peripheral APB at all — but note there is no hardware enforcement available to do this, so the practical workaround is to never enable the BDMA peripheral master and to keep all code with peripheral-bus access inside the trusted boundary; additionally, software can poll CGUFSFREQ0-3 and CGUFSVLD before and after each sensitive crypto operation and discard the result if the measured frequency changed, which detects (but does not prevent) the attack.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (software on either CPU or control of the BIO/BDMA), giving a T2-class fault-injection capability without physical access

findings.title: The CGU 'clock cipher' side-channel countermeasure is a fixed-IV LFSR with one bit of software seed entropy, and the level field is inverted relative to the documentation so the documented 'slowest' setting disables it entirely
findings.cwe: CWE-1241 Use of Predictable Algorithm in Random Number Generator
findings.description: docs/src/clock-generation.md states: 'The clock cipher scrambles the system clock by skipping pulses according to the state of an LFSR configured by CGU_SEED. This feature can harden the system against side channel analysis.' Two RTL defects void that claim. (a) PREDICTABILITY: both cipher instances are `drng_lfsr` with compile-time-constant initial vectors ('h55aa_aa55_5a5a_a5a5 for clktop, 'hfedcba9876543210 for clkpke). The only reseed path is `swr`, and insauth.v:38 implements it as `sdin[LFSR_IW-1] ^ sdata` — a single bit (bit 31 of the 32-bit CGU_SEED word) XORed against a 59-bit state, which by Verilog width extension flips only bit 0. The entire 32-bit seed register therefore injects exactly ONE bit of entropy, so the pulse-skip sequence has only two possible trajectories, both derivable from the public RTL. Worse, `sen` is tied to the enable bit (`.sen(clkcipheren)`), so while the cipher is off the LFSR is frozen at its IV and the seed write is ignored — every enable event restarts from the identical state, making the skip pattern perfectly reproducible and trace-alignable across power cycles. CGU_SEED is also plainly bus-readable (sfr_seed.prdata32 is ORed into apbx.prdata at sysctrl.sv:820). (b) INVERTED SEMANTICS / FAIL-OPEN: the documented CGUSEC table says '[3:0] clkcipher level: 0xF = full speed, 0x0 = slowest'. The RTL computes `clkcipherdat >= clkcipherlevel * 16` over an 8-bit LFSR output, so level=0x0 gives threshold 0, the comparison is always true, and NO pulses are ever skipped — level 0 is full speed with the countermeasure silently doing nothing, while level 0xF skips ~94% of pulses. An integrator following the register documentation and writing level=0x0 to select 'slowest / maximum scrambling' gets zero mitigation, with the enable bit reading back as set.
findings.preconditions: For the fail-open case: firmware configures CGUSEC per the published register documentation. For the predictability case: the attacker has the (public, CERN-OHL licensed) RTL and can capture power/EM traces; no software access is needed at all since the IV is a compile-time constant.
findings.attack_scenario: Case (b), fail-open: firmware enabling the countermeasure for the PKE writes CGUSEC = 0x1000 (enable, level 0) intending 'slowest / most scrambling' per the documented table. sysctrl.sv:555 evaluates `clkpkecipherdat >= 0` which is always true, so `clkpketopenin` stays 1 and the ICG at sysctrl.sv:545 never gates a pulse. The RSA/ECC private-key operation runs with a perfectly regular clock while the status register reports the countermeasure as enabled. Case (a), predictability: even with a correct level, the attacker reads the LFSR polynomial and IV out of the published RTL, simulates 59 bits of state forward from the enable event, and knows exactly which clock cycles were skipped. He resamples/realigns his power traces to remove the skipping and recovers the same leakage he would have had with the countermeasure off. The bus-readable CGU_SEED at 0x4004_0008 removes even the need to guess which of the two possible trajectories is live. Note this composes with the PKE's other masking defect: pke.sv:788-805 uses the same `drng_lfsr` with `.LFSR_IV('h5a5a_a5a5)` and `sen(optsec)`, so the PKE's data masking is deterministic from reset too.
findings.mitigation: RTL fix: (1) reseed the LFSR properly — replace `sdin[LFSR_IW-1] ^ sdata` in insauth.v:38 with a full-width XOR (`{{(LFSR_W-LFSR_IW){1'b0}}, sdin} ^ sdata` or better, load the full seed) so the seed register actually carries 32 bits of entropy; (2) source the seed from the TRNG rather than from a bus-writable/bus-readable register, and make CGU_SEED write-only; (3) let the LFSR free-run (`sen` tied 1) so its state is not reproducible from the enable event; (4) fix the level polarity in sysctrl.sv:673/555 or fix the documentation — and in either case make level=0 the maximally-scrambled setting so the fail-safe direction is 'more mitigation', not 'none'. Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: treat the level field as inverted with respect to the documentation — write CGUSEC[3:0] = 0xF (and CGUSEC[11:8] = 0xF for PKE) to get maximum pulse skipping, never 0x0. Reseed CGU_SEED from the TRNG with bit 31 varied (only bit 31 has any effect) before every sensitive operation, and re-toggle CGUSEC[4]/[12] so the enable edge is at an unpredictable time. Understand that the countermeasure provides at best trace-misalignment against an attacker who does not have the RTL, and essentially nothing against one who does; do not rely on it as the sole DPA defence.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (power/EM side-channel measurement); the fail-open half needs only a documentation-following integrator

findings.title: Security-error escalation to NMI is disabled at reset and can be silently re-masked: evc's `erren` resets to 0 with sfrlock hardwired to 0
findings.cwe: CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection
findings.description: The event controller aggregates the SoC's hard error sources into a single non-maskable interrupt to the CM7: `assign cm7nmi = |(errin&erren);`. In soc_top.sv the `errin` bundle is the set of security-relevant fault indications — `err[0] = |coresuberr`, `err[1] = |sceerr`, `err[2] = |ifsuberr`, `err[3] = |secirq` (the OR of the mesh, voltage/light sensor and glue-chain tamper interrupts from secsub), `err[4] = |aoramerr`. The enable mask `erren` is a plain APB control register instantiated with `.IV(0)`, and evc drives its own write-protect to a constant: `assign sfrlock = '0;`. Consequently (a) out of reset, and after every coreresetn — including the software core reset via RCURST1 at 0x4004_0084 — no error source, including tamper, raises an NMI; and (b) any bus master able to write 0x4004_4084 can clear the mask again at any time with no lock and no privilege check. There is no redundant or non-maskable path: the tamper indications reach the CPU only through this register (and through the ordinary maskable IRQ vector at ev[239:224]). Combined with the previous finding — that the mesh's clock itself can be stopped from the same unprotected APB block — an attacker can render the tamper subsystem both clock-dead and interrupt-silent with two 32-bit stores.
findings.preconditions: For the reset-state exposure: none — this is the power-on and post-core-reset condition. For the active-masking case: one APB write to 0x4004_4084 (evc is apbsys[4], base 0x4004_4000), reachable from the CM7 AHB-P, Vex AHB-P, MDMA or BDMA peripheral AHB master, with no coreuser/pprot check.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker with code execution writes 0 to EVC_ERRCR at 0x4004_4084 (or simply relies on the reset value if he can force a core reset first — RCURST1 at 0x4004_0084 accepts 0x55AA from any master and, per sysctrl.sv:803, drives coreresetgen, which is evc's reset). 2. `erren` is now 0, so `cm7nmi` is stuck low regardless of what `errin` reports. 3. Any subsequent tamper event (mesh aperture break, voltage/light sensor trip, glue-chain break — all funnelled through `err[3] = |secirq`), SCE error, or AO RAM ECC error is no longer escalated. The flag register EVC_ERRFR at 0x4004_4080 still shows the event, but nothing forces the CPU to look. 4. Combined with the mesh clock-gate kill described above, the attacker has both removed the detector and removed the alarm. The window is also relevant on its own: between reset release and the first firmware write to EVC_ERRCR, any hard error — including a tamper trip during early boot, which is exactly when secrets are being loaded — is silently ignored.
findings.mitigation: RTL fix: make the security-critical error bits (at minimum err[3], the tamper OR) non-maskable — route them to cm7nmi unconditionally, or give `sfr_cm7errcr` a sticky set-only semantic (bits can be enabled but never disabled without a system reset) plus a real sfrlock driven from a write-once lock register, and set `.IV` so tamper escalation is ON out of reset rather than OFF. Route the tamper OR to `secresetn` as well so it does not depend on the CPU responding at all. Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: have the boot ROM write EVC_ERRCR = 0x1F as one of its very first actions, before any secret is loaded; and because the register cannot be locked, add a periodic integrity check that re-reads 0x4004_4084 and treats any cleared bit as a tamper event. Also enable the redundant maskable IRQ path (ev[239:224] via EVC_CM7EVSEL/EVC_CM7EVEN) so there are two independent notifications.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (software on either CPU or control of the BIO/BDMA peripheral master)

finders.domain: Always-on (AO) domain: ao_top3 / ao_sysctrl / aobureg / aoram / dkpc / ao_peri, plus their integration in daric_top.sv, soc_top.sv, soc_ifsub.sv, cms.sv, sysctrl.sv and pad_frame_arm.sv
finders.coverage_notes:
COVERED (read end-to-end): rtl/modules/ao/rtl/ao_top.sv (274 l), ao_sysctrl.sv (731 l), aobureg.sv (39 l), aoram.sv (238 l), dkpc.sv (578 l incl. its `ifdef SIM_DKPC testbench, which I used only for understanding), rtl/modules/sysctrl/rtl/aoperi.sv (118 l). Traced every AO output signal outward: ao_top3 instantiation in daric_top.sv:891-960; the AO APB path soc_coresub.sv:647 -> soc_top.sv:830-838 (ahbasync + apb_bdg + apb_thru, no identity filter); the AO SRAM path soc_top.sv:841-881 and its bus window soc_ifsub.sv:127-149; aocmsuser -> cms.sv:50,155; ipsleep <- sysctrl.sv:779-782, sfr_ipclpen (sysctrl.sv:879) and sfr_cgulp (sysctrl.sv:832); ipflow_set <- sysctrl.sv:877 sfr_ipcaripflow + soc_top.sv:948; wkupvld_async -> sysctrl.sv:772-773; the DFT/BIST readback path aoram.sv:148-166 -> ram_1rw_s.sv:94-138 (rbspmux) -> soc_top.sv:1008 -> rbist_wrp.sv:64 -> pad_frame_arm.sv:244-246; pad definitions pad_frame_arm.sv:214-218. Confirmed gnrl_sramc.sv:18-35 has no clear/zeroize port. Cross-checked against docs/src/pmu.md (lines 120-190, 254-420), docs/src/system-control.md (lines 7-30, 171-310) and docs/src/ch03-00-io-configuration.md:21.

NOT COVERED / LIMITATIONS: (1) The PMU itself, the OSC_32K/OSC_32M cells, and the aoram1kx36 macro are analog/foundry black boxes not present in this repo, so the *electrical* consequence of a given pmu_TRM_* code (Finding 3) is inferred from docs/src/pmu.md's own trim tables, not from RTL. (2) The `rbist` MBIST engine itself (rbist_wrp.sv instantiates a black-box `rbist rbcore`) is not in the repo; I verified the rbspmux datapath into the AO RAM macro and the cmstest pad gating, but the exact JTAG command sequence to read a word out cannot be shown from open RTL. (3) `Rtc`, `cmsdk_apb_watchdog` and `apb_timer_unit` in ao_peri.sv are third-party IP not in this repo; I did not audit their internals (e.g. whether WDOGLOCK is implemented), so ao_peri is effectively uncovered beyond its wiring. (4) I did not attempt to determine which AO addresses the shipping Xous firmware actually uses for key material; Findings 2 and 6 rest on the vendor's own documentation designating AORAM/BUREG as the retention store, not on observed firmware. (5) I deliberately did not report the unsynchronised combinational pad -> async-reset path (dkpc.sv:65,89 -> ao_sysctrl.sv:594-601 -> sysctrl.sv:772) because its reachable impact appears to be limited to power-management flops (pdreg, aopdreg), i.e. denial of service rather than asset disclosure.

findings.title: Sticky USER-mode lifecycle latch in the AO domain is cleared by the external XRSTn pad, allowing lifecycle downgrade into TEST/VRGN with all volatile memory contents intact
findings.cwe: CWE-1243 Sensitive Non-Volatile Information Not Protected During Debug / CWE-1244 Internal Asset Exposed to Unsafe Debug Access Level
findings.description: `aocmsuser` is the one and only latch that makes the chip's USER lifecycle state sticky. Once the CMS controller has resolved to CMS_USER, `aocmsuser` is set and forces every subsequent CMS evaluation to CMS_USER (cms.sv:155), which is what keeps the ReRAM BIST TAPs, the rbist/MBIST TAP, the IPT TAP and the PMU-trim JTAG path locked out. That latch lives in the AO domain and its only reset is `porresetn_undft`, which is derived from `por = ~pmu_POR & padresetn` — i.e. from the external PAD_XRSTn pin (pad_frame_arm.sv:218). Asserting XRSTn therefore clears the sticky USER latch WITHOUT removing power from the SoC domain: the regulator enables come from `pmucrreg`, which resets to `IV_PMUCR = 8'b01111100` (VR25ENA/VR85AENA/VR85DENA/IOUTENA/POCENA all still enabled), so VDD85D and VDDAO stay up and every SRAM in the chip (core SRAM banks, ITCM, DTCM, IFRAM, BIO RAM, the SCE crypto RAMs and the AO RAM) retains its contents across the event. On the way back up the CMS controller re-samples PAD_WMS0/1 and, with `aocmsuser` now 0, is free to resolve to CMS_TEST or CMS_VRGN, which asserts `cmstest` and (soc_top.sv:397) `cmsbist`. `cmsbist` hands the JTAG rbist master direct clock/address/enable control of every RAM macro through `rbspmux` (ram_1rw_s.sv:127-131), and `cmstest` un-gates the rbist and ReRAM JTAG TAP pins in the pad frame (pad_frame_arm.sv:244-246). The security state that gates debug is thus a single non-redundant flop whose reset is an attacker-controlled pin.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker owns the board (T2). Chip boots normally into CMS_USER (PAD_WMS0 pulled down by padcell_i #(.pu('0),.pd('1)) at pad_frame_arm.sv:214). `aocmsuser` latches to 1; JTAG BIST/ReRAM TAPs are dead. 2. Firmware runs, unwraps keys into the SCE crypto RAM / core SRAM / AO RAM. 3. Attacker drives PAD_WMS0=1 and PAD_WMS1=1 and pulses PAD_XRSTn low for >10 clk32k cycles (the genporreset EXTCNT), then releases. VDD, VDD25, VDD85A/D and VDDAO are never interrupted — only the reset pin moves — so no SRAM loses state. 4. `por` goes low, `porresetn_undft` goes low, `aocmsuser` clears to 0. 5. `sysresetn_undft` also drops, so `cmscodereg` re-evaluates; with `aocmsuser==0` line 155 now takes the `cmscodepre` branch, and cmspadout={1,1,0} resolves to CMS_VRGN (cms.sv:130-133). `cmstestreg` sets, hence `cmstest=1` and `cmsbist=1`. 6. The pad frame now feeds the real TMS/TDI/TRST pins to `jtagrb` (rbist) and to `jtagrrc[0:1]` (raw ReRAM macro TAPs). `rbspmux` (ram_1rw_s.sv:127-131) hands the rbist master the clock, address and enables of every RAM macro, and `assign rbs.ramrdata = cmsatpg ? undft_q : rb_q;` returns live macro read data. 7. Attacker walks the address space of rbif_sce_sceram_10k (SKEY/AKEY/PKB segments), rbif_aoram1kx36 and rbif_acram2kx64 over JTAG and reads the key material that step 2 left resident. Total cost: two pin holds and one reset pulse; no decapsulation, no glitching, no power cycle.
findings.preconditions: Physical access to PAD_XRSTn, PAD_WMS0, PAD_WMS1 and the JTAG pins (a 5-pin test header or probe pads). The ReRAM CMS word must be at its default all-zero value, which cms.sv:34-39 shows is the value of CMSDAT_VRGNMODE, CMSDAT_TESTMODE, CMSDAT_ATPGMODE and CMSDAT_USERMODE alike. The board must not gate XRSTn behind a power sequencer that also drops VDD85D.
findings.mitigation: RTL: `aocmsuser` must be reset only by a true power-on reset of the AO rail (pmu_POR alone), never by the external reset pin — change `assign por = ~pmu_POR & padresetn;` (ao_sysctrl.sv:422) so that the porresetn used for the lifecycle latch excludes padresetn, and give the latch its own dedicated reset. Additionally, make the latch redundant (multi-bit / dual-rail) rather than a single flop, and give the four CMSDAT_* patterns distinct non-zero values so the ReRAM half of the mode gate actually contributes. Independently, entry into any non-USER CMS mode should unconditionally trigger a wipe of all crypto RAMs, the AO RAM and the core SRAMs before the BIST/JTAG paths are enabled. Silicon workaround: none in hardware. Board-level only — do not bring PAD_WMS0/1 or the JTAG pins to accessible pads; tie PAD_WMS0 to ground in the package/substrate if possible; and have firmware scrub all key material from SRAM/AO RAM immediately after use so that the retention window is minimised, since firmware cannot observe or prevent the XRSTn event.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (physical access: pin control plus JTAG), optionally combined with T4

findings.title: AO SRAM is never zeroized by any reset, contradicting the documented guarantee that it is cleared on external reset, and its bus window has no access control
findings.cwe: CWE-1266 Improper Scrubbing of Sensitive Data from Decommissioned Device / CWE-226 Sensitive Information in Resource Not Removed Before Reuse
findings.description: docs/src/pmu.md instructs firmware to 'Store any important data to AO backup registers or AORAM before entry' to power-down (line 184) and then guarantees that 'Backup-registers, RTC and AORAM in the AO domain are preserved if the wake-up source is from the PF pins; if external reset is used, then these registers are cleared' (line 140). That guarantee holds for the backup registers (aobureg is a flop array reset by porresetn, ao_top.sv:237) and for the RTC (presetn=porresetn, aoperi.sv:54), but it is false for AORAM. The AORAM is two aoram1kx36 SRAM macros instantiated bare in the AO domain with no clear logic (ao_top.sv:243-270), driven by an aoram controller whose only backing block is `gnrl_sramc`, and gnrl_sramc has no ramclr/zeroize port at all (gnrl_sramc.sv:18-35). Nothing anywhere in the design writes zeros into these macros on any reset, on lifecycle change, or on tamper. Separately, the AORAM's bus window at 0x5030_0000-0x5030_1FFF sits behind `ahbsramc32` with no coreuser check, no hauser check and no hprot check, in the ifsub matrix reachable by the CM7 and Vex peripheral ports, by the BIO/BDMA AHB master (which drives hauser=0), by the uDMA and by the USB device controller.

findings.attack_scenario:
Path A (physical, T2): firmware follows docs/src/pmu.md:184 and stashes a session key or unwrapped PIN-derived secret in AORAM before deep sleep. The attacker asserts PAD_XRSTn, believing per docs/src/pmu.md:140 that this clears AORAM — it does not. The 8 KB of AO SRAM comes back with the secret intact, and it is now reachable either over the ordinary bus at 0x5030_0000 by whatever code runs first after reset, or, chained with Finding 1, through the JTAG rbist path (aoram.sv:148-166 wires rbif_aoram1kx36 straight into rbspmux, and soc_top.sv:869/1008 connect it to the BIST master). Because `scmben` is tied 1'b0 (aoram.sv:95) there is no address/data scrambling, so the readback is plaintext.
Path B (software/peripheral, T1/T3): the AORAM window has no privilege gate. Unprivileged code on either CPU, or the BIO/BDMA peripheral master (which drives hauser='0', bio_bdma.sv:1580/1670 — matching no identity check anywhere), or a DMA descriptor set up on the uDMA, or an attacker-controlled USB device transfer routed by the udc master, can read 0x5030_0000..0x5030_1FFF directly and recover whatever the secure firmware retained there.
findings.preconditions: Firmware uses AORAM to retain any secret across sleep/power-down, which is exactly what docs/src/pmu.md:184 and docs/src/system-control.md tell it to do. For path B, any of: unprivileged code execution, the ability to program a uDMA/BDMA descriptor, or control of the USB device endpoint.
findings.mitigation: RTL: add a clear/zeroize FSM to the AORAM path exactly as `cryptoram.sv` does for the crypto RAMs (a ramclr input on gnrl_sramc that walks the address space writing zeros), and trigger it from porresetn, from any CMS mode change out of CMS_USER, and from a tamper event. Enable the scrambler that is already present (`isSCMB:'1` in the aoram thecfg, aoram.sv:21-32) instead of tying `.scmben(1'b0)` at aoram.sv:95, and feed `scmbkey` from a per-boot random value rather than the `'0` passed at soc_top.sv:870. Add a coreuser/hauser filter in front of `ahbaoram` so the AO SRAM is not a general-purpose DMA target. Documentation must be corrected: pmu.md:140 currently states a guarantee the silicon does not provide. Silicon workaround: firmware must explicitly overwrite the whole 8 KB AORAM window before any sleep/reset it can anticipate, and must never rely on reset to scrub it; and firmware should treat 0x5030_0000 as world-readable and therefore unsuitable for any secret.
findings.threat_actor: T2 for the retention/readback path; T1 or T3 for the unprotected bus window

findings.title: PMU regulator enables and analog voltage trims are software-writable with no lock and no privilege check, while the regulator-ready reset sources are masked off by default — a pure-software undervoltage fault-injection primitive
findings.cwe: CWE-1247 Improper Protection Against Voltage and Clock Glitches / CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection
findings.description: Three defects compose. (a) Every SFR in ao_sysctrl is unlockable: `assign sfrlock = '0;` (line 362), and the whole 0x4006_0000 AO window arrives over an ahbasync+apb_bdg bridge (soc_top.sv:830-838) that carries no coreuser, hauser or pprot filtering — so any bus master, including unprivileged code on either CPU and the BIO/BDMA AHB master, can write it. (b) Those registers drive the analog PMU directly. `sfr_pmucr`/`sfr_pmutrm0`/`sfr_pmutrm1` (offsets 0x10/0x20/0x24) load `pmucrreg`/`pmutrmreg` whenever `ipflow_set` pulses, and `ipflow_set` is raised by writing 0x57 to sysctrl's `sfr_ipcaripflow` at 0x4004_0090 (sysctrl.sv:877 -> ipflowfsm_setipcr -> soc_top.sv:948 sync_pulse -> ao_sysctrl.sv:282,287). `pmu_trm` fans out to pmu_TRM_DP60_VDD85D (the 0.6 V reference for the 0.85 V *digital core* regulator) and pmu_VDDAO_VOLTAGE_CFG (ao_top.sv:192-200); `pmu_ctrl` fans out to pmu_VR85DENA/pmu_VR25ENA (ao_top.sv:176-185). Per the vendor's own table, PMU_TRM0[7:3] trims the core rail reference and PMU_CR[4] is the VR85D enable. There is a second, even shorter path: `pmu_trm` and `pmu_ctrl` are taken *directly* from the low-power shadow registers PMU_TRMLP0/1 (0x28/0x2C) and PMU_CRLP (0x14) whenever `ipsleep` or `aopdreg` is asserted (lines 245 and 251), and `ipsleep` is raised by two ordinary SFR writes (sysctrl.sv:832 sfr_cgulp bit 1, sysctrl.sv:879 sfr_ipclpen) followed by a WFI. (c) The safety net that should catch the resulting brown-out is disabled at reset: `cr_rstcrmask` has `.IV(5'h1f)`, and `rstsrc` ORs that mask over the five PMU status bits, so `&rstsrc` is permanently 1 and `socresetnin` never de-asserts because a regulator dropped out. The chip therefore keeps running through a software-induced undervoltage instead of resetting.
findings.attack_scenario: Unprivileged code on either CPU (T1) does the following, with no privilege escalation required because nothing between the CPU peripheral port and 0x4006_0000 checks coreuser, hauser or hprot: 1. Leave AO_RSTCR_MASK (0x4006_000C) at its reset value 0x1F — all five PMU brown-out/ready reset sources are already masked, so a collapsing core rail will not reset the chip. 2. Write PMU_TRMLP0 (0x4006_0028) with an out-of-range value in bits [7:3] (VR85D bias trim) so that the 0.85 V digital core reference is driven far below its 5'h10 nominal, and write PMU_CRLP (0x4006_0014) to keep VR85D enabled at the low trim. 3. Write CGULP (0x4004_0004) bit 1 = 1 and IPCLPEN (0x4004_0098) bit 3 = 1, then execute WFI. `ipsleep[3]` asserts, and ao_sysctrl.sv:251 immediately switches `pmu_trm` from `pmutrmreg` to the attacker's `sfrpmutrmlp` — the core supply reference changes on the fly. Per docs/src/pmu.md:124, 'Crypto engines, peripherals, and memories remain operational' in sleep, so the SCE keeps executing while the rail is out of spec. 4. The attacker tunes the trim to the marginal point where the AES/PKE datapath produces faulty results but the machine does not crash, and harvests faulty ciphertexts for a differential fault analysis key recovery. The whole primitive is software: no probe, no injection needle, no clock manipulation. The same registers also permit a permanent denial of service (write PMU_CR with VR85D disabled, then pulse 0x4004_0090 with 0x57), and the mask at step 1 guarantees the chip does not reset itself out of the condition.
findings.preconditions: Any code execution that can issue bus transactions to 0x4006_0000-0x4006_0FFF and 0x4004_0000-0x4004_0FFF. There is no coreuser check, no hauser check, no pprot/hprot consumer, and no sfrlock on either window (ao_sysctrl.sv:362; and in sysctrl the sfrlock port is fed by the undriven net soc_top.sv:217/361). The BIO/BDMA AHB master, which drives hauser='0', also reaches this window.
findings.mitigation: RTL: (1) Drive `sfrlock` in ao_sysctrl from a write-once lock bit rather than `assign sfrlock = '0;`, and make the PMU_TRM*/PMU_CR*/PMU_TRMLP* group lockable independently so that boot firmware can seal the analog trims before handing control to application code. (2) Bound the trim: clamp pmu_TRM_DP60_VDD85D / VDD85A / VDD25 and pmu_VDDAO_VOLTAGE_CFG to a hardware-defined safe window rather than passing the raw register bits to the analog macro. (3) Change `cr_rstcrmask`'s `.IV(5'h1f)` to `.IV(5'h00)` so the regulator-ready and POR reset sources are armed out of reset — a security-relevant default must be the restrictive one — and make the mask itself lockable. (4) Put a coreuser/hauser filter in front of the AO APB bridge at soc_top.sv:830-838 so that only the boot/secure identity can reach the PMU. Silicon workaround: the earliest boot stage must write AO_RSTCR_MASK=0 to arm the brown-out reset, program the intended PMU_CR/PMU_TRM/PMU_CRLP/PMU_TRMLP values, and then permanently prevent later code from reaching 0x4006_0000 — but since neither CPU has a working MPU configuration in this build (the CM7 MPU config in daric_cfg_pkg.sv:117-127 is commented out) and no bus-level filter exists, this is only enforceable if the OS never maps the AO page into any untrusted address space, which is a software-only, bypassable control.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software on either CPU), amplified by T4

findings.title: AO power-domain isolation is incomplete and is enabled by an unlocked software register: only cen/gwen are clamped, while clock, address and write data from the powered-off SoC domain reach the AO SRAM unisolated
findings.cwe: CWE-1263 Improper Physical Access Control / CWE-1220 Insufficient Granularity of Access Control (power-domain isolation)
findings.description: The AO SRAM macros physically sit in the always-on domain but every one of their control pins is driven from the aoram controller, which lives in the switched SoC domain (soc_top.sv:864-881, clocked by clkaoram and reset by coreresetn). The only isolation applied at the domain crossing is a two-signal OR clamp inside ao_top: `.cen(aoram_bcen[i]|ao_iso_enable)` and `.gwen(aoram_bwen[i]|ao_iso_enable)`. The macro's clock `aoram_clkb[i]`, its address `aoram_ba` and its write data `aoram_bd` are passed straight through with no isolation cell at all, so when the SoC domain is powered off those nets are driven by unpowered gates and float. Worse, the clamp itself is under software control: `ao_iso_enable` comes from `pdisoreg`, which is only set during the power-down flow if the plain APB config bit `pdisoen` is 1 — and `pdisoen` is bit [1] of AO_CLK32K_SEL at 0x4006_0000, an unlocked `apb_cr` (sfrlock is hard-tied 0 at ao_sysctrl.sv:362). docs/src/pmu.md:291 documents this bit as user-settable: '0 = isolation disabled, 1 = isolation enabled'. A design that lets software turn off the isolation between a powered-off domain and the always-on secret store has made a physical-integrity guarantee optional.

docs/src/pmu.md:291
| \[1\] | pdisoen | Isolation control on power-down entry: `0` = isolation disabled, `1` = isolation enabled |
findings.attack_scenario: Unprivileged code (T1) writes 0x4006_0000 clearing bit [1] (pdisoen -> 0), then writes 0x5A to PMU_PDAR at 0x4006_0044 to enter power-down (ao_sysctrl.sv:404 `apb_ar #(.A('h44), .AR(32'h5a)) sfr_pmupdar`, also unlocked). The pdflow FSM runs with `pdisoreg` stuck at 0, so `ao_iso_enable` stays 0 and the AO SRAM's cen/gwen are left connected to the collapsing SoC domain. As VDD85D decays, `aoram_bcen`/`aoram_bwen`/`aoram_ba`/`aoram_bd`/`aoram_clkb` pass through the indeterminate region: a spurious low on cen coincident with a low on gwen and any edge on the unisolated clock writes garbage into the macro at the floating address. The attacker thereby corrupts the retained AO SRAM contents (integrity attack on whatever the secure firmware retained there per docs/src/pmu.md:184) without ever having read access to it, and can repeat the cycle to bias the corruption. Even with pdisoen left at its default 1, the clock/address/data pins remain unisolated on every power-down, so this is a latent reliability-and-integrity exposure on the normal path as well; a T4 attacker who browns out the SoC rail without a clean power-down sequence gets the same effect with no software involvement, because the pdflow FSM never runs.
findings.preconditions: For the software-driven variant: any bus master able to write 0x4006_0000 and 0x4006_0044 (no lock, no privilege check). For the T4 variant: the ability to collapse the switched-domain supply while VDDAO stays up, which docs/src/pmu.md:234 confirms is a distinct rail. The severity depends on analog behaviour of unpowered driver outputs that cannot be confirmed from RTL alone.
findings.mitigation: RTL: isolate the full set of signals crossing from the switched domain into the AO domain — clock, address and write data as well as cen/gwen — using proper isolation cells clamped to the inactive value (clock clamped low, cen/gwen clamped high). Remove software control of the clamp: `ao_iso_enable` should be generated unconditionally by the power-down sequencer from `aopdreg`/pdflowfsm state, not gated by the `pdisoen` config bit; if the bit must remain for debug, gate it behind devmode and behind a write-once lock. Silicon workaround: firmware must never clear AO_CLK32K_SEL[1], must verify it reads back as 1 immediately before writing PMU_PDAR, and must treat AO SRAM contents as untrusted after any power-down by storing a MAC alongside the retained data and verifying it on resume.
findings.threat_actor: T1 for the software-defeat variant; T4 for the unsequenced brown-out variant

findings.title: Keypad (PIN entry) pad inputs are unconditionally mirrored into the main-domain GPIO input path, and the keypad/GPIO mux plus the full keystroke event FIFO are exposed through unlocked registers with no privilege check
findings.cwe: CWE-1274 Improper Access Control for Volatile Memory Containing Boot Code / CWE-1189 Improper Isolation of Shared Resources on System-on-a-Chip
findings.description: On this device lineage the 4x4 keypad on PF9-PF2 is the user's PIN/passphrase entry channel. The AO pinmux is asymmetric: the direction that matters for confidentiality is not gated. Line 563 correctly gates the keypad controller's view of the pads on `kpiosel` (`assign kpio[i-2].pi = kpiosel ? socpad[i].pi : 1'b1;`), but line 562 routes the raw pad input into the SoC-domain pinmux with no gate at all (`assign socpad[i].pi = aopad[i].pi;`). Those pads are iopad_F -> iopad[80:89] in the main pinmux (soc_top.sv:806), so while the user is typing a PIN the raw column/row lines are simultaneously readable through the ordinary GPIO input registers by any code in the main domain. Compounding this: `kpiosel` itself is AO_IOX at 0x4006_0060, a plain unlocked `apb_cr` with reset 0, so any master can also take the pads away from the keypad controller and drive them from the SoC pinmux (line 559/561 select socpad's po/oe when kpiosel=0). And the keypad controller's own registers are equally open — `assign sfrlock = '0;` (dkpc.sv:182) — exposing the live 16-node matrix plus the four raw KPI pins in KPC_SR0 at 0x4006_4010 and a FIFO of {16-bit timestamp, node index} press/release events at KPC_FF 0x4006_4020. Nothing in the AO APB path applies a coreuser, hauser or pprot check, so there is no notion of a privileged owner of the keypad.
findings.attack_scenario: 1. A compromised unprivileged process on either CPU (T1), or the BIO/BDMA AHB master (hauser='0', matching no identity check anywhere in the design), configures the PF9-PF2 pads as GPIO inputs in the main-domain pinmux. Because ao_sysctrl.sv:562 mirrors `aopad[i].pi` into `socpad[i].pi` unconditionally, this works even while `kpiosel=1` and the keypad controller believes it owns the pins. 2. The attacker polls the GPIO input register while the user enters a PIN, observing the scan pattern: the keypad drives one KPO row at a time (dkpc.sv:100-105) and the pressed key pulls the corresponding KPI column, so the row/column pair is directly recoverable from the raw pad samples. 3. Alternatively, and more cheaply, the attacker just reads KPC_SR0 at 0x4006_4010 for the decoded 16-node matrix state, or pops KPC_FF at 0x4006_4020 for a stream of {16-bit tikcnt timestamp, node index} press and release events — giving both the digits and the inter-keystroke timing, which is itself usable for a timing-based guessing advantage. 4. As an active variant, the attacker writes 0 to AO_IOX (0x4006_0060); lines 559/561 then hand po/oe of the keypad pads to the SoC pinmux, letting the attacker drive the rows and columns directly and forge keypresses to the real keypad controller, or hold a column asserted to mask the user's real input.
findings.preconditions: Any code execution able to reach the AO APB window (0x4006_0000-0x4006_0FFF) or the main-domain GPIO input registers. Requires the device to use the PF keypad as its trusted PIN/passphrase entry path, which docs/src/system-control.md:171-198 and docs/src/ch03-00-io-configuration.md:21 describe.
findings.mitigation: RTL: gate the pad-to-SoC input path on the mux select exactly as the reverse path is gated — change ao_sysctrl.sv:562 to `assign socpad[i].pi = kpiosel ? 1'b0 : aopad[i].pi;` so the keypad lines are not visible to the general-purpose GPIO block while the keypad function is selected. Make `kpiosel` (AO_IOX) a lockable register so that boot firmware can pin the keypad to the AO controller. Drive `sfrlock` in dkpc from a real lock, and put a coreuser/hauser filter in front of the AO APB so that only the identity that owns the secure input path can read KPC_SR0/KPC_FF. Silicon workaround: partial only. Firmware must keep the PF9-PF2 GPIO input registers and the whole 0x4006_4000 page out of every untrusted address space, must never map the AO page to application code, and should treat any concurrent GPIO configuration of iopad[80:89] as a compromise indicator — but with no MPU configuration active in this build and no bus-level filter, this is a software-only control that anything with bus access can bypass.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software on either CPU, or a BIO/BDMA program); T3 for the pad-drive variant

findings.title: AO backup registers — the documented cross-power-down secret store — have sfrlock hard-tied to zero, no privilege check, and no tamper-triggered erase
findings.cwe: CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection / CWE-1272 Sensitive Information Uncleared Before Debug/Power State Transition
findings.description: aobureg is 8 x 32 bits (256 bits) of always-on, battery-backed storage at 0x4006_5000-0x4006_501F. The vendor documentation explicitly designates it as the place to keep secrets across power-down: docs/src/pmu.md:184 says 'Store any important data to AO backup registers or AORAM before entry' and docs/src/system-control.md:16 says 'BUREG — Backup registers in AO domain. Contents are retained during SoC power-down.' The module implements no access control whatsoever: `sfrlock` is hard-tied to zero, the register file is a plain read/write `apb_cr`, and the AO APB path it hangs off (soc_top.sv:830-838 -> ao_top.sv:127) carries no coreuser tag, no hauser check and no pprot consumer. This is a notable asymmetry with the rest of the SoC, which does implement a coreuser/ACRAM ownership scheme for the ReRAM key slots and an owner-lock for the SCE. In addition, nothing clears these registers on a tamper event: grepping the tamper/mesh/sensor subsystem shows no path from any tamper detector into the AO domain, so a detected intrusion leaves the retained secret in place.
findings.attack_scenario: Secure firmware follows docs/src/pmu.md:184 and stores a wrapped-key handle, a resume authentication token, or a PIN-attempt counter in BUREG before entering power-down. On resume, before or concurrently with the secure resume path, unprivileged application code (T1) — or the BIO/BDMA AHB master, whose hauser='0' matches no identity check anywhere in the design — simply reads 0x4006_5000..0x4006_501C and recovers all 256 bits, because there is no ownership tag, no lock bit, and no privilege gate on the path. The same access is a write: an attacker who cannot read a value can still overwrite it, so a PIN-attempt or anti-rollback counter kept in BUREG can be rewound to zero by any code that can issue a bus write, defeating lockout/throttling. Because there is no tamper input to this block, a physical attacker (T2) who trips the mesh or a sensor also does not cause the secret to be erased; combined with the fact that only PAD_XRSTn/POR clears these flops, the retained value survives every reset an attacker might trigger short of pulling the reset pin.
findings.preconditions: Firmware uses BUREG for anything security-relevant, which the vendor documentation directs it to do. Attacker needs only the ability to issue bus reads/writes to 0x4006_5000 — no privilege escalation, since neither the AO bridge nor the module performs any check.
findings.mitigation: RTL: give aobureg a real `sfrlock` driven by a write-once lock bit (following the pattern in aes.sv:135 / combohasha.sv:159 rather than the `assign sfrlock = '0;` used here), and add an owner tag so that only the coreuser identity that wrote a slot can read it back — the mechanism already exists for the ReRAM key slots in rrc.sv and should be extended to the AO domain. Add a coreuser/hauser filter in front of the AO APB bridge at soc_top.sv:830-838. Route the tamper/mesh/sensor event into the AO domain and clear `cr_buregs` (and the AO SRAM) on it. Silicon workaround: firmware must not store plaintext secrets in BUREG. Store only a ciphertext blob whose key never leaves the SCE, and derive that key from something not resident in the AO domain, so that a BUREG read yields nothing usable; and store any monotonic counter in the ReRAM one-way counters at 0x603D_A000/B000 rather than in BUREG, since BUREG offers no rollback protection.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software or a BIO/BDMA program); T2 for the no-tamper-erase aspect

finders.domain: ReRAM controller (RRC) and non-volatile memory protection — rtl/modules/rrc/rtl/
finders.coverage_notes:
COVERED (read end-to-end): rtl/modules/rrc/rtl/rrc.sv (all 1282 lines, including the appended ahb_cr_ECO / ahb_sfr2_ECO modules), rrc_pkg.sv, rerammacro.sv, rrc_emu.sv, trbcx1r32_daric_wrapper.sv, rtl/asic_top/include/reram_inc.sv. Traced integration outward: rrc instantiation in soc_coresub.sv:809-850 (both ahbs and ahbx bound to coreahbmux[0] = 0x4000_0000, axis = rrc_axi64), master routing in bmxcore.sv:100-300 (confirmed bdma_axi32 -> axi_mux_dma -> axi_mux -> nic_s2 -> nic400 .m0 = rrc_axi64, i.e. BDMA reaches ReRAM while MDMA is address-excluded), AxUSER->HAUSER propagation in aab_intf.sv:54,67,116, BDMA master-ID in bio_bdma.sv:122,1360,1373 + soc_ifsub.sv:344, ahb_ar semantics in ahb_sfr.sv:286-344, and evc.sv:85-90,160-161 for the one-way-counter event source. Compared against docs: rtl/scripts/headergen/output/doc/rrc.rst (register map, confirms RRC_SFR_RRCAR @ 0x400000f0 is a plainly documented, unlocked register).

VERIFIED-AND-DISMISSED (so the vendor does not waste time): the shared recon's lead #14 ("data_access_error_pre compares against userid_k instead of userid_d") is NOT a defect — rrc.sv:688 and rrc.sv:689 are literally identical expressions (`haddr_reg[5] ? acram_rdata[63:32] : acram_rdata[31:0]`), so userid_k and userid_d are the same net and the check is functionally correct. Likewise rrc.sv:663's stray double `&` (`axis.awvalid & & axis.awready`) parses as a unary reduction of a 1-bit signal and is benign.

NOT COVERED / CANNOT BE COVERED:
- trbcx1r32_daric_wrapper.sv is a thin port-mapping shell only. The actual ReRAM controller (u_trc_top = trcx1r32_..._trc_top) and the JTAG BIST engine (u_bist_top_mux) live in asic_top/lib/trbcx1r32_.../rtl/ which is NOT present in this repository. Therefore I could NOT verify: the program/erase (SET/RESET) sequencing, whether an interrupted write leaves a word half-programmed, the ECC encode/decode correctness, the internal IFR1 lock (`OPT_IFR1_LOCK` is not defined so trc_info_lock_err_o is left unconnected at rrc.sv:1005/1091 while rrc.sv:289 reports trc_info_lock_err into rrcsr — that status bit is therefore likely reading an undriven net, but I cannot confirm without the IP), or what the JTAG BIST TAP can actually do to the array once bist_enable is granted. The write-abort/suspend/resume inputs are all tied to 'h0 (rrc.sv:958,961-963), so there is no software-visible write-abort primitive in the open RTL.
- rrc_emu.sv defines a competing `module rrc` used only under `ifdef FPGA` / `ifdef SIM` / `ifdef SYN` (rrc_emu.sv:93-119) and is instantiated only in the soc_coresub `ifdef FPGA` branch (soc_coresub.sv:772-798). It ties its AHB SFR port off with ahbs_null and replaces the array with a plain SRAM.
