It is NOT reachable in the ASIC build, so it is not an attack surface — I confirmed this and am reporting no finding on it.
- I did not attempt to assess ReRAM cell-level retention/laser sensitivity (physics, not RTL). Finding 5 is limited to the RTL-visible fact that the macro's ecc_err_o/trc_err_o outputs are never consumed by any decision logic.
- rrccr bit semantics beyond [0],[1],[12],[15],[31:16] are undocumented in both the RTL comments and rrc.rst (which describes the whole register as "sfr_rrccr read/write control register"); I only report on bits whose use I could trace in the RTL.

findings.title: Live access-control table (ACRAM) is rewritten by an unprivileged bus master even when the RRC's own cfg_access_error denies the write — full ReRAM key-slot access-control bypass
findings.cwe: CWE-1220 Insufficient Granularity of Access Control (access-control configuration writable by the subject it constrains)
findings.description: The RRC keeps the per-slot access-control descriptors for all 2048 ReRAM key/data slots in a volatile SRAM shadow (`acram2kx64`, rrc.sv:424), loaded at boot from the ReRAM CFG region and re-writable at runtime by writing 0x603D_C000-0x603D_FFFF. The runtime update path is triggered by `rram_write_run & rramcfg_vld` (rrc.sv:361,365) with NO reference to `cmd_user_write_dis`. The corresponding non-volatile programming of the same CFG words IS gated (`( rrcfsm == 0 ) & rram_write_run & (!cmd_user_write_dis) ? 4`, rrc.sv:853). So when `cfg_access_error` fires — e.g. because the requester's coreuser is not boot0/boot1 (`cfg_prev_dis`, rrc.sv:815-816) — the ReRAM itself is protected but the SRAM table that actually enforces key/data slot access control is overwritten with attacker data anyway. The write address `{haddr_reg[13:5],acram_idx}` (rrc.sv:393) is attacker-chosen and spans the entire 2048-entry ACRAM (512 CFG lines x 4 words), i.e. every key and data slot descriptor: `core_rd_dis_k`, `core_wr_dis_k`, `sce_rd_dis_k`, `sce_wr_dis_k`, `keytype_k`, `userid_k`, `akeyid` (rrc.sv:691-697). Because every key/data check is qualified by `& (userid_k[7:4] != 4'h0)` (rrc.sv:717) / `& (userid_d[7:4] != 4'h0)` (rrc.sv:726), writing a descriptor with a zero owner nibble disables that slot's access control entirely. The buffer that supplies the data, `ahb_wr_buf`, is filled with no privilege check at all (rrc.sv:568-571 has only `ahb_array_write_reg & !rrccr[1]`).
findings.attack_scenario:
Attacker is unprivileged/late-stage code on the CM7 (coreuser = fw1, i.e. coreuser_in[5:4] == 2'b00), which is exactly the identity `cfg_prev_dis` is designed to keep out of the CFG region.
1. Write 0x0000_0002 to RRC_SFR_RRCCR at 0x4000_0000 to clear rrccr[1]. This SFR is on ahbx = coreahbmux[0] (soc_coresub.sv:823-824) and is instantiated `.sfrlock(1'b0)` (rrc.sv:274) with no coreuser/hauser filter anywhere on that port.
2. Issue eight 32-bit (or four 64-bit) writes to 0x603D_Cnnn (the CFG line that backs the ACRAM entry for the target key slot), carrying the forged descriptor: userid_k[7:4] = 4'h0, core_rd_dis_k = 0. With rrccr[1]==0 these land in `ahb_wr_buf` (rrc.sv:568-571) and go no further.
3. Write 0x0000_0003 to 0x4000_0000 to set rrccr[1].
4. Write the magic 0x0000_9528 (PM_RRAM_WRITE) to the same 0x603D_Cnnn address. `cfg_prev_dis` -> `cfg_access_error` -> `cmd_user_write_dis` = 1, so rrcfsm never enters state 4 and the ReRAM CFG word is correctly NOT programmed. But rrc.sv:361/365 fire regardless: `acram_wrbuf <= ahb_wr_buf`, `acram_wrbusy` asserts, and over the next four clktop cycles acram_idx 0->3 writes the forged 4x64-bit descriptor into ACRAM at {haddr_reg[13:5],idx}.
5. Read the ReRAM key slot at 0x603F_xxxx over the AXI slave. `keycfg`/`userid_k` now come from the forged ACRAM entry; `key_access_error_pre & ... & (userid_k[7:4] != 4'h0)` evaluates to 0, `cmd_user_read_dis` is 0, and `ahbarray.hrdata` returns the raw key material instead of 64'h0 (rrc.sv:555-558).
The hardware reports success on the write (rrc.sv:583 `assign ahbarray.hresp = 2'h0;` — denials are silent) and, because `rrccr[15]` resets to 0 (rrc.sv:292), no NMI is raised. Repeating step 2-4 for other CFG lines unlocks every key and data slot in the device. Note the desynchronisation also survives in the other direction: the volatile table now disagrees with the NV backing store, so the compromise persists until the next sysresetn re-runs the boot read.
findings.preconditions: Attacker needs (a) write access to the RRC SFR window at 0x4000_0000 — available to CM7 AHB-P (hauser 0x8), Vex AHB-P (0xD), BDMA AHB (0x0) and MDMA (0x7), none of which are filtered on that port — and (b) write access to the ReRAM AXI slave 0x603D_C000-0x603D_FFFF, which the CM7/Vex have by construction. No coreuser/boot-stage privilege is required; in fact the bug is only interesting precisely when the attacker LACKS boot0/boot1 coreuser. The trustkey term `(!trustkey[akeyid] & (haddr_reg[15:6] != 10'h0))` still applies, but the attacker also controls `akeyid` in the same forged descriptor, and sce_sec.sv:123 (`assign ts = { 1'b1, tsreg };`) hardwires trustkey[127] to 1; key slots 0 and 1 are exempt from the trustkey term outright.
findings.mitigation:
RTL fix: gate the ACRAM shadow update with the same term as the NV write, i.e. change rrc.sv:361 and rrc.sv:365 to `rram_write_run & rramcfg_vld & (!cmd_user_write_dis)`. Better still, make the ACRAM update strictly a consequence of a successful NV program completing (drive it from the rrcfsm==4 -> 0 transition) so the volatile table can never diverge from the non-volatile backing store. Also give the RRC SFR port at 0x4000_0000 a coreuser/hauser filter, or at minimum a real `sfrlock` instead of the hardwired `.sfrlock(1'b0)` at rrc.sv:274-286.
Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon (partial only): boot0/boot1 must never leave rrccr[1] clearable by later stages — but rrccr has no lock, so this cannot actually be enforced from software. The only effective mitigation is to prevent any code that is not boot0/boot1 from reaching 0x4000_0000 at all, which on the CM7 requires enabling the MPU (note the CM7 MPU configuration in daric_cfg_pkg.sv:117-127 is commented out) and on the Vex requires an MMU/PMP region that excludes 0x4000_0000 and 0x603D_C000-0x603D_FFFF. Additionally, boot code should re-run a full ACRAM integrity check (read back the CFG region and compare against the descriptors in use) before any key-slot access, and should set rrccr[15] so that access violations at least raise an NMI.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software execution on either CPU). No physical access required.

findings.title: ReRAM one-way (monotonic/anti-rollback) counters can be incremented by any bus master with no access-control check whatsoever
findings.cwe: CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection
findings.description: The RRC implements one-way counters at 0x603D_A000 and 0x603D_B000 as a read-modify-program sequence. A write to that region is detected by `oneway_counter_update_ahb` (rrc.sv:496-497) and is deliberately excluded from the normal write path: `ahb_array_write` masks it (rrc.sv:539) and, critically, `ahb_write_flag` is forced to 0 for such a transfer (rrc.sv:546). Since all five access-error terms (`key_access_error_pre` rrc.sv:712, `data_access_error_pre` rrc.sv:722, `code_access_error_*` rrc.sv:770-774, `info_access_error_pre` rrc.sv:781-782, `cfg_access_error_pre` rrc.sv:818-819) are qualified by `ahb_read_flag` and/or `ahb_write_flag`, they all evaluate identically to 0 for a counter update. Address decode confirms no region check applies either: `keysel`/`datasel` require 0x603F/0x603E, `codesel = (haddr_reg[31:12] < 20'h603D_A)` is false for 0x603DA/0x603DB, the CFG region requires haddr_reg[15:14]==2'b11, and `axi_info = haddr_reg[22]` is 0. Independently, the two-cycle sequencing explicitly bypasses `cmd_user_write_dis` for the counter branch while correctly applying it to the adjacent prog-only-data branch in the very same expression (rrc.sv:576-577). The result is that the increment reaches TRC_LOAD/TRC_WRITE unconditionally. Separately, the event-driven counter-burn path is disabled at reset: `oneway_counter_update_ev = |(evin_trigger[15:0] & rrccr[31:16])` (rrc.sv:513) and rrccr is `ahb_cr_ECO #(.A('h00), .DW(32))` whose IV defaults to 32'h0 (rrc.sv:274, 1144), on an SFR with `.sfrlock(1'b0)`.
findings.attack_scenario:
1. Unprivileged code on the CM7 or Vex (or the BDMA, whose AXI master reaches the ReRAM via nic400 .m0 per bmxcore.sv:199,292) performs a single store of any value to 0x603D_A000 (or any 32-byte-aligned offset up to 0x603D_BFFF).
2. `oneway_counter_update_ahb` asserts. `ahb_write_flag` and `ahb_read_flag` are both driven to 0 for this transfer, so key/data/code/info/cfg access-error logic is inert; `cmd_user_write_dis` is 0.
3. rrcfsm 0->1 reads the current 256-bit counter word into `ahb_rd_buf`; `two_cycle_load` (unqualified by cmd_user_write_dis) takes rrcfsm 1->3 with `axi_din = ahb_rd_buf + 'h1`; `two_cycle_write` takes rrcfsm 3->4 and programs the incremented value into ReRAM.
4. Repeat in a loop. Each iteration permanently advances a counter that is, by name and by construction (read-modify-increment, program-only, no decrement path — a direct write to the region is intercepted by step 2 and never reaches `ahb_wr_buf`), intended to be monotonic and therefore intended to be irreversible.
Impact depends on what the counters are used for, but the only sensible uses are anti-rollback / secure-version, provisioning-attempt limits, or tamper-event accounting. Advancing the secure-version counter past the version of the installed firmware permanently bricks the device (the installed image now fails its own anti-rollback check) — an unprivileged, one-instruction, unrecoverable DoS on a fabricated part. If a counter gates a provisioning or lifecycle transition, an attacker can burn through it to force a state change. Conversely, because `rrccr[31:16]` resets to 0 and lives in an unlocked SFR, an attacker can clear it to stop genuine security events (evc.sv:90 `rrc_ev[m] <= rrc_even[m] & evin[rrc_evsel[m]]`) from ever burning a counter — so the counters are simultaneously freely advanceable by an attacker and not advanced by real tamper events unless software opted in.
findings.preconditions: Write access to any address in 0x603D_A000-0x603D_BFFF on the ReRAM AXI slave. Available to the CM7 AXI master, both Vex AXI masters, both SCE DMA masters, and the BIO/BDMA AXI master. No privilege level, no coreuser value, and no AxPROT setting is required — the checks are structurally bypassed, not merely permissive. `brdone` must be set (boot read complete), which is always true in normal operation.
findings.mitigation:
RTL fix: evaluate the access-control checks for the one-way counter region instead of suppressing them. Concretely, (a) do not force `ahb_write_flag` to 0 for counter transfers at rrc.sv:546 — use a separate qualifier so the error logic still sees a write; (b) add a dedicated region term (e.g. `onewaysel = (haddr_reg[31:13] == {16'h603D,3'b101})`) to the access-error expressions, minimally requiring `coreuser_in[5]|coreuser_in[4]` (boot0/boot1) and `pri_op`/`vex_mm_reg` exactly as `cfg_prev_dis` does at rrc.sv:815; and (c) qualify the counter branch of rrc.sv:576-577 with `(!cmd_user_write_dis)` for symmetry with the prog_only_data branch on the same lines. Also give `rrccr[31:16]` a write-once lock so the event-driven burn cannot be disabled after boot, and give it a non-zero (fail-safe) reset value.
Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: none within the RRC. The only containment is to deny all non-boot code access to 0x603D_A000-0x603D_BFFF via the CM7 MPU / Vex PMP (the CM7 MPU config at daric_cfg_pkg.sv:117-127 is currently commented out and must be enabled), and to have boot0 set rrccr[31:16] before handing off. Systems relying on these counters for anti-rollback should treat them as untrusted against a compromised application core.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software on either CPU); also reachable from T3 if an external peripheral can drive the BIO/BDMA, whose whitelist registers at 0x5012_40E0+ are themselves unlocked.

findings.title: Per-slot key/data read-write-disable bits and the CPU privilege checks are only applied to four recognised master IDs; the BIO/BDMA AXI master (hauser 0x7) reaches ReRAM key slots with every disable bit and privilege term structurally nulled
findings.cwe: CWE-1259 Improper Restriction of Security Token Assignment (privilege tag not defined for all bus masters; check defaults to a permissive identity)
findings.description: `coreuser_mux` (rrc.sv:670-671) is a two-level conditional with no default arm: any transfer whose latched `hauser_reg` is not 0x2 (CM7A), 0x3/0x4 (VEXI/VEXD) or 0x5/0x6 (SCEA/SCES) silently inherits `coreuser_cm7`, the CM7's live execution-region identity. Worse, in that same case `cm7sel`, `vexsel` and `scesel` are all 0 (rrc.sv:666-668), which deletes almost the whole of the key- and data-slot check: in `key_access_error_pre` (rrc.sv:712-717) the terms `core_rd_dis_k & (cm7sel|vexsel)`, `core_wr_dis_k & (cm7sel|vexsel)`, `cm7sel&(!pri_op)`, `vexsel&(!vex_mm_reg)` and both `scesel` terms all evaluate to 0, leaving only the coreuser-overlap test and the trustkey test. The same holds for `data_access_error_pre` (rrc.sv:722-726), for `code_access_error_data` where `rrsub_code_dis` is ANDed with `(cm7sel|vexsel)` (rrc.sv:772), and for `cfg_access_error_pre` where both `cfg_rd_dis`/`cfg_wr_dis` are ANDed with `(cm7sel|vexsel)` and `cfg_prev_dis` requires cm7sel|vexsel|scesel (rrc.sv:815-819). The BIO/BDMA memory master is exactly such a master: bio_bdma.sv:122 defaults `parameter AHBMID4 = daric_cfg::AMBAID4_MDMA` (4'h7) and soc_ifsub.sv:344 instantiates it as `bio_bdma #() bio (` with no override, so bio_bdma.sv:1373 drives `axim.aruser = AHBMID4|'0` = 4'h7. Unlike the MDMA — which bmxcore.sv:164 deliberately address-excludes from ReRAM (`'{idx: 32'd0 , start_addr: 32'h6100_0000, end_addr: 32'ha000_0000}  // to nic_1, but no ReRAM`) — the BDMA's AXI master is routed through axi_mux_dma/axi_mux to nic_s2 and thence to nic400 .m0 = rrc_axi64, i.e. straight into the ReRAM slave.
findings.attack_scenario:
1. Unprivileged software programs the BIO/BDMA through its APB window at 0x5012_4000 (whose sfrlock is 0) with a memory descriptor pointing at a ReRAM key slot, e.g. 0x603F_0000. The BDMA's own address whitelist does not block this: bio_bdma.sv:2562/2576 redirect out-of-range transfers to a software-programmable `gutter` register rather than blocking them, and disable_filter is an unlocked CR bit.
2. The BDMA read arrives at the RRC with hauser_reg = 4'h7. `cm7sel = vexsel = scesel = 0`.
3. `key_access_error_pre` collapses to `(((coreuser_cm7[7:4] & userid_k[7:4])==0) & ahb_read_flag | (!trustkey[akeyid] & (haddr_reg[15:6] != 10'h0))) & data_op & keysel & (userid_k[7:4] != 4'h0)`. Every per-slot disable bit (`core_rd_dis_k`) and every privilege requirement (`pri_op`, `vex_mm_reg`) has vanished — the BDMA has no AxPROT-derived privilege requirement at all.
4. If the CM7 is at that moment executing anywhere outside boot0/boot1/fw0 — which cm7sys.sv:761 (`assign coreuserreg0pre[7] = ~|coreuserreg0pre[6:4];`) makes the default classification for SRAM, TCM, XIP and undefined PC — then coreuser_cm7[7] = 1 and any key slot owned by fw1 satisfies the overlap test. The attacker controls this, because the attacker IS the code running on the CM7.
5. The trustkey term is satisfied for key slots 0 and 1 (exempted by `(haddr_reg[15:6] != 10'h0)`), or for any slot whose ACRAM `akeyid` names an already-unlocked trust bit — note sce_sec.sv:123 (`assign ts = { 1'b1, tsreg };`) hardwires trustkey[127] permanently to 1.
6. The key word is returned in the clear to the BDMA, which writes it into BIO FIFO/RAM readable at 0x5012_4000-0x5012_8FFF.
Net effect: a key slot explicitly marked "CPU read disabled" (`core_rd_dis_k = 1`) and intended for SCE-only secure use is readable by unprivileged software through the BDMA, because the RRC never applies `core_rd_dis_k` to that master.
findings.preconditions: Ability to program the BIO/BDMA (APB 0x5012_4000, unlocked). Target key slot must have a non-zero owner nibble that overlaps coreuser_cm7[7:4] at the time of the transfer (attacker-controllable, since the attacker chooses where the CM7 is executing), and must either be slot 0/1 or have an akeyid whose trustkey bit is set. The same structural gap applies to the uDMA (0xA), the USB device controller (0xB) and the SDDC (0x0) should any routing change ever give them a path to the ReRAM slave, and to the BDMA's AHB peripheral master which drives `hauser = '0` (bio_bdma.sv:1580,1670).
findings.mitigation:
RTL fix: give `coreuser_mux` an explicit fail-closed default — `assign coreuser_mux = scesel ? sceuser : vexsel ? coreuser_vex : cm7sel ? coreuser_cm7 : 8'h00;` — so an unrecognised master matches no slot owner and is denied. Additionally, restructure rrc.sv:713-716 and rrc.sv:723-726 so the per-slot disable bits are applied unconditionally rather than being qualified by `(cm7sel|vexsel)`, and add an explicit `unknown_master = ~(cm7sel|vexsel|scesel)` term that forces every access error. Give the BDMA its own distinct AMBAID (the collision with AMBAID4_MDMA at bio_bdma.sv:122 is itself a defect) and apply the same ReRAM address exclusion to `bdma_axi32` that bmxcore.sv:164 applies to the MDMA.
Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: never leave the BIO/BDMA enabled while key material is resident in ReRAM key slots; hold the BIO in reset (its config resets on coreresetn) or gate its clock via `clkbiogate`. Provision key slots with an `akeyid` that requires a real HMAC trust unlock and never use akeyid 127 or key slots 0/1 for material that must be CPU-inaccessible. Where possible, set the slot owner nibble to a coreuser value the CM7 can never present.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software on either CPU, driving the BDMA).

findings.title: ReRAM mass-erase ("suicide") is triggered by a single unlocked, unprivileged 32-bit write to 0x4000_00F0
findings.cwe: CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection
findings.description: `sfr_rrcar` is an action register at RRC SFR offset 0xF0 (documented as RRC_SFR_RRCAR @ 0x400000f0 in rtl/scripts/headergen/output/doc/rrc.rst) instantiated with `.sfrlock(1'b0)` — hardwired unlocked. `ahb_ar` (rtl/modules/amba/rtl/ahb_sfr.sv:340-343) pulses `ar` on any write of the magic value; there is no key ladder, no two-phase arm/fire, no redundancy and, crucially, no reference to `coreuser`, `hauser`, `hprot` or any privilege input anywhere on the RRC's SFR AHB port. `rrcar_suicide` then starts the erase FSM at rrc.sv:307, which sweeps `suicide_adr_main` from 22'h3FFFFF down and then `suicide_adr_ifr` from 13'h1FFF down, programming `axi_din = 256'h0` (rrc.sv:867) into the entire main array and the entire INFO/IFR block. This destroys the secure-boot code, all key slots, all data slots, the ACRAM CFG backing store, the NVR config words (devena, coresel, region map) and the one-way counters. Every other security control in the RRC — the five access-error checks, the ACRAM descriptors, the trustkey linkage — is bypassed entirely by this path, since the suicide FSM feeds `axi_xadr`/`axi_yadr`/`axi_din` directly (rrc.sv:867-872) and never consults `cmd_user_write_dis`. This is the same primitive the CMS_SCDE lifecycle state uses (`(cmscode == CMS_SCDE) | rrcar_suicide`, rrc.sv:307), i.e. it is the chip's designated destroy-everything operation, exposed to software behind nothing.
findings.attack_scenario:
1. Any code able to issue one 32-bit store to 0x4000_00F0 writes 0x0000_2468.
2. `ahb_ar` compares `reg_wdata == 32'h2468` and pulses `rrcar_suicide` on the next hclk edge. There is no arm sequence, no second register, no lock bit, and no check of who issued the write — `ahb_ar` does not even receive `hauser`.
3. `suicide_start` sets `suicide_reg`; `ahbarray.hready` drops to 0 so the entire ReRAM slave stalls, and the FSM begins programming 256'h0 into every main-array word from 0x3FFFFF downward, then every IFR/INFO word.
4. On completion the device has no boot code, no keys, no lifecycle configuration and no ACRAM backing store. `nvrcfgdata` on the next sysresetn reads all zeros, which among other things makes `cmsdatareg == CMSDAT_USERMODE` (all four CMS patterns are 128'h0, cms.sv:34-39) and leaves every ACRAM descriptor with `userid_k[7:4] == 4'h0` — the fail-open case at rrc.sv:717.
The write is reachable from CM7 AHB-P (hauser 0x8), Vex AHB-P (0xD), the BIO/BDMA AHB master (0x0) and the MDMA (0x7), none of which are filtered on the 0x4000_0000 window (soc_coresub.sv:823-824 binds the RRC SFR port straight to coreahbmux[0]). It is also a single-point-of-failure comparison against a 16-bit constant on a 32-bit bus, so it is a plausible glitch/fault-injection target as well as a software one: a fault that forces `reg_wdata == AR` true during any unrelated write to offset 0xF0, or that forces `sfrsel`, destroys the part.
findings.preconditions: One 32-bit write to 0x4000_00F0 from any master on the core peripheral bus. No privilege level, no coreuser value, no lifecycle mode. `sysresetn` must be deasserted (normal operation).
findings.mitigation:
RTL fix: (a) drive a real `sfrlock` on `sfr_rrcar` — for example latch a write-once enable that boot0/boot1 must set, and clear it before handing off to application firmware; (b) require boot-stage coreuser (`coreuser_in[5]|coreuser_in[4]`) and `pri_op`/`vex_mm_reg` on the RRC SFR port generally, which today has no identity filter at all (every SFR at rrc.sv:274-286 is instantiated `.sfrlock(1'b0)`); (c) make the trigger redundant and non-glitchable — a two-register arm/fire sequence with distinct magic values written in order, and a counter that requires the arm to be recent. Note that rrc.sv:274-286 shows this is a systemic pattern in this module, not a one-off.
Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: none inside the RRC — the register cannot be locked. The only containment is to make 0x4000_0000-0x4000_0FFF unreachable to all non-boot code: enable the CM7 MPU (its configuration in daric_cfg_pkg.sv:117-127 is currently commented out) and configure Vex PMP regions to exclude it, and keep the BIO/BDMA and MDMA held in reset or clock-gated whenever untrusted code is running, since both can reach this address and neither presents a coreuser the RRC would check.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software on either CPU) for the software path; T2 (fault injection) for the glitch path against the single 16-bit magic compare.

findings.title: ReRAM ECC and controller error outputs are wired only to a status register — the boot read of all security configuration is consumed with no integrity check and no error path
findings.cwe: CWE-1261 Improper Handling of Single Event Upsets (uncorrectable NV error not acted upon)
findings.description: Both ReRAM macro wrappers export `ecc_err_o[2:0]` and `trc_err_o` (rrc.sv:999,1002,1085,1088). In the RRC these are OR-combined (rrc.sv:937,939) and then routed to exactly one place: bits of the read-only status register `rrcsr` (rrc.sv:289, `ahb_sr #(.A('h08), .DW(10)) sfr_rrcsr`). They are not sticky, they do not participate in `rrcint` (rrc.sv:291 `assign rrcint = |rrcfr;`, and `rrcfr` at rrc.sv:290 contains only the five access-error flags), they do not reach `rrcnmi` (rrc.sv:292), they do not gate `trc_dout_ready_done` (rrc.sv:491) and therefore do not prevent the faulted 256-bit word from being latched into `ahb_rd_buf` (rrc.sv:561) or into the boot-read image `brdatreg` (rrc.sv:156), and they do not stall or abort the boot FSM `brfsm` (rrc.sv:136-144), which advances purely on `trc_dout_ready_sdone`. Since the AHB response is hardwired OKAY (rrc.sv:583 `assign ahbarray.hresp = 2'h0;`), a faulted word is indistinguishable from a good one to the requesting master. This matters because `brdatreg` is not ordinary data — it is the entire security configuration, loaded once at boot and then used combinationally by the access-control logic for the rest of the power cycle: `brdatreg[20..23]` supply `user_code_cfg_boot0/boot1/fw0/fw1`, the code-region cross-stage read/write-disable matrix (rrc.sv:232-235, consumed at rrc.sv:731-757); `brdatreg[24..31]` supply the 256-bit `data_cfg_rd_dis`/`data_cfg_wr_dis`/`key_cfg_rd_dis`/`key_cfg_wr_dis` bitmaps (rrc.sv:616-619, consumed at rrc.sv:809-813); `brdatreg[axi_yadr][255:240]` supply the IFR write/read-disable bytes (rrc.sv:781-782). Every one of these is permissive-when-cleared. `brdatreg` is on `sysresetn`, so a corrupted image persists across every warm reset.
findings.attack_scenario:
Attacker has physical access and a laser/EM fault-injection setup (T2), or exploits natural ReRAM retention loss on an aged part.
1. During the power-on boot read (brfsm states 1-3, which fetch brdatreg[0..31] over a bounded and observable number of cycles at 0x603D_x), the attacker injects a fault targeting the sense/ECC path for word index 26 or 27 (`data_cfg_wr_dis`) or 30/31 (`key_cfg_wr_dis`), or word 20-23 (`user_code_cfg_*`).
2. The macro asserts `ecc_err_o` (and possibly `trc_err_o`) for that beat. Nothing in the RRC reacts: `trc_dout_ready_sdone` still fires, rrc.sv:156 still latches the corrupted 256 bits into `brdatreg`, and `brfsm` still advances. `brdone` is set normally, the CPU boots normally, and the only trace is a non-sticky bit in a status register that nothing polls.
3. Bits that were 1 ("disabled") in `key_cfg_wr_dis` / `data_cfg_wr_dis` are now 0, so `cfg_wr_dis` (rrc.sv:812-813) no longer blocks writes to those CFG slots; or bits cleared in `user_code_cfg_fw1` (rrc.sv:752-757) remove the boot0/boot1/fw0 code-region protections against fw1. The attacker's unprivileged code then writes the previously-protected CFG lines or the boot code region.
4. Because `brdatreg` is reset only by `sysresetn`, the corrupted policy survives every `coreresetn` (software reset, watchdog reset), so the attacker has the rest of the power cycle to work with, and only needs the fault to land once.
The same gap applies on the read path for ordinary array accesses: an ECC-uncorrectable key or code word is returned to the bus as valid data with hresp = OKAY, so a fault-injection attack that perturbs a signature or a key during a secure-boot verification is not distinguishable from a legitimate read by any software check.
findings.preconditions: Physical access and fault-injection capability (laser, EM, voltage/clock glitch) timed to the boot read, or a device with natural ReRAM retention degradation. Requires no software privilege. Exploitation requires the injected error to be uncorrectable-but-still-returned rather than silently corrected — I could not determine the macro's correction strength because the ECC decoder (encoder_new_h.v / decoder_invless.v) lives in asic_top/lib/, which is not in this repository; ecc_err_o being 3 bits wide strongly suggests it distinguishes corrected from uncorrectable, and the RTL ignores all three bits equally.
findings.mitigation:
RTL fix: (a) add `ecc_err`/`trc_err` to `rrcfr` so they contribute to `rrcint`, and make them sticky per-transaction rather than combinational status; (b) qualify `trc_dout_ready_done` and the `brdatreg`/`ahb_rd_buf` load enables with the absence of an uncorrectable ECC error, so a faulted word is never latched; (c) return `hresp = 2'b01` (ERROR) on the AHB for an uncorrectable read instead of the hardwired `2'h0` at rrc.sv:583; (d) hold `brdone` low and refuse to release the array if any beat of the boot read reports an uncorrectable error, so the device fails closed rather than booting with a corrupted policy; (e) add a CRC or hash over brdatreg[20..31] checked after the boot read completes, and consider storing the permissive-when-zero policy bitmaps in inverted or dual-rail form so a 1->0 fault is detectable.
Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: boot0 should read RRC_SFR_RRCSR at 0x40000008 immediately after boot and again after any array read of security-relevant data, and should independently re-read and cross-check the 0x603D_C000 CFG region against a firmware-held hash before trusting any access-control decision. This is only partial — rrcsr is not sticky, so an error that occurred during the boot read may already have cleared by the time firmware runs.
findings.threat_actor: T2 (physical access: laser/EM/glitch fault injection, or exploitation of retention loss).

findings.title: ReRAM code-region protection is disabled at reset: code_access_error is still gated by rrccr[12] (reset value 0) after the #eco16 ECO removed the equivalent gate from the other four checks
findings.cwe: CWE-1221 Incorrect Register Defaults or Module Parameters (security control defaults to disabled)
findings.description: An ECO annotated `#eco16` deliberately removed the `rrccr[n]` enable gate from four of the five RRC access checks: rrc.sv:719 (`//    assign key_access_error = key_access_error_pre & rrccr[10];`), rrc.sv:728 (`rrccr[11]`), rrc.sv:784 (`rrccr[14]`) and rrc.sv:824 (`rrccr[13]`) are all commented out and replaced with unconditional assignments. The code check was left gated: rrc.sv:778 still reads `assign code_access_error = code_access_error_pre & rrccr[12];` with the unconditional version commented out immediately below on line 779 — the exact inverse of the pattern applied to the other four. `rrccr` comes from `ahb_cr_ECO #(.A('h00), .DW(32))` (rrc.sv:274) whose IV parameter defaults to `32'h0` (rrc.sv:1144) and which resets on `coreresetn`. So from every reset until software writes 0x4000_0000, `code_access_error` is identically 0 and the entire code-region protection is off: the boot0/boot1/fw0/fw1 mutual read/write isolation matrix (`rrsub_code_dis`, rrc.sv:731-768) and the trustkey-linked code lock (`rrsub_code_dis_trustkey`, rrc.sv:761-763) — the only mechanisms in the design protecting the secure-boot code in ReRAM from being read or rewritten by a later boot stage — are both inert. The one mitigating factor is that `ahb_sfr2_ECO` force-sets bit 12 on every write (rrc.sv:1258 `? reg_wdata|32'h0000_1000 :`), so software cannot clear it once set without a reset; but `coreresetn` is assertable from software via the unlocked `sfr_rcurst1` at 0x4004_0084 (sysctrl.sv:872), and the RRC SFR window has no privilege filter, so nothing prevents a later stage from returning the chip to the unprotected state.
findings.attack_scenario:
1. On every reset (power-on, watchdog, or a software write of 0x55aa to sysctrl `sfr_rcurst1` at 0x4004_0084, which is unlocked and reachable from the same unfiltered peripheral bus), `rrccr` clears to 32'h0 and `rrccr[12]` = 0.
2. Until boot code performs its first write to 0x4000_0000, `code_access_error` cannot assert. Any read or write from the CM7 or Vex to the ReRAM code region (`codesel = ( haddr_reg[31:12] < PM_CODE_REGION_BORDER )`, i.e. all of 0x6000_0000-0x603D_9FFF) succeeds regardless of the boot0/boot1/fw0/fw1 policy in `user_code_cfg_*` and regardless of whether the required trustkey has been established.
3. This is a fail-open reset value on the root of the secure-boot chain: the window is bounded only by a software convention ("boot0 must write rrccr early") that the hardware does not enforce and that no lock bit backs. Any glitch, exception, or alternate entry point that reaches attacker-influenced code before that write — for example a fault-injected branch during the first instructions after reset, or any path where the reset vector `cm7cfg_iv` (soc_coresub.sv:263-266, an 8-bit ReRAM field) has been perturbed — executes with ReRAM code-region protection entirely absent and can rewrite the boot0 image.
4. The asymmetry with the four sibling checks is strong evidence this is an oversight in the ECO rather than an intended design choice: the ECO author clearly intended these enables to go away, and the code check was missed.
findings.preconditions: Any reset, plus a way to execute or influence execution before the first write to RRC_SFR_RRCCR. Also note the protection only ever applies to masters with `cm7sel|vexsel` (rrc.sv:772), so it is independently absent for the BDMA/MDMA/uDMA regardless of rrccr[12] — see the separate coreuser_mux finding.
findings.mitigation:
RTL fix (preferred): apply the same #eco16 treatment to line 778 as to lines 719/728/784/824 — `assign code_access_error = code_access_error_pre;` — removing the software-controlled enable entirely. If the enable must be retained, change the `sfr_rrccr` instantiation at rrc.sv:274 to pass a non-zero IV with bit 12 set (`ahb_cr_ECO #(.A('h00), .DW(32), .IV(32'h0000_1000))`) so the control comes up enabled, matching the force-set behaviour already present on the write path at rrc.sv:1258. Independently, remove the `(cm7sel|vexsel)` qualifier from `code_access_error_data` (rrc.sv:772) so the code region is protected against all masters.
Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: boot0 must write RRC_SFR_RRCCR at 0x4000_0000 as one of its very first instructions, before any branch that could be influenced by external data, and must verify the read-back shows bit 12 set. Because the write path ORs in 0x0000_1000, any write suffices. Boot code should also verify bit 12 is still set after every stage transition, and should treat a cleared bit 12 as a tamper indication. This does not close the reset-to-first-write window, which cannot be closed from software.
findings.threat_actor: T1 for the software-reset path; T2 (glitch during early boot) for the more serious variant.

finders.domain: BIO programmable I/O and BDMA memory/peripheral whitelist filters (rtl/modules/bio_bdma/)
finders.coverage_notes:
COVERED (read end-to-end or in full relevant extent):
- docs/src/ch02-00-bio-overview.md — the whitelist security claim (line 70), the SFR_CONFIG bit map (lines 796-806), the FILTER_BASE/FILTER_BOUNDS semantics (lines 1448-1550, which confirm `bounds` is a LENGTH in pages, matching the RTL — so I did NOT report the apparent base+length "off-by-semantics", it is correct), and the GUTTER descriptions (lines 1274-1300).
- rtl/modules/bio_bdma/rtl/bio_bdma.sv (2583 lines): full SFR bank (lines 457-654), both axil_cdc/axil_filter instantiations (1244-1479), AXI master tie-offs (1345-1378), AXIL->AHB bridge and hauser/hprot tie-offs (1481-1675), per-core imem/ext_addr decode (1735-1841), DMA owner FSM (1077-1138), and the axil_filter module itself (2466-2583).
- rtl/modules/bio_bdma/rtl/ram_1rw_s.sv (rbspmux BIST path), rtl/modules/bio_bdma/lib/cdc_level_to_pulse.sv, lib/axil_cdc*.v (clkmode synchronizer-depth selection), lib/axil_crossbar_addr.v (decode-error behaviour).
- Integration points grepped and read: rtl/modules/ifsub/rtl/soc_ifsub.sv (bio_bdma instantiation line 344, apbper map, bmxifm_map), rtl/modules/bmxcore/rtl/bmxcore.sv (BDMA AXI/AHB routing, MDMA ReRAM exclusion, nic400 slave map), rtl/modules/rrc/rtl/rrc.sv (master decode 660-672 and all five access-check expressions 712-828, ACRAM write path 352-435), rtl/modules/amba/rtl/aab_intf.sv and axitrans.sv (AxUSER propagation), rtl/modules/amba/rtl/apb_sfr.sv (apb_cr / sfrlock semantics, IV=0 reset), rtl/asic_top/rtl/daric_cfg_pkg.sv (AMBAID4_* values).

CHECKED AND FOUND CLEAN (deliberately NOT reported):
- Range comparison arithmetic in axil_filter: `bounds_unchecked` is 21 bits and saturates at 0xFFFFF (line 2549); base>=/bounds< is a correct half-open interval; length==0 correctly yields an empty window. No off-by-one, no wrap.
- Transfer-length coverage: the BDMA issues only single-beat, 4-byte AXI transfers (awlen='0, awsize=2, lines 1347-1348/1365-1366) and the peri byte-lane bodge (lines 1483-1521) can only add +3 to a word-aligned address, so no transfer can straddle the 4 KB filter granule.
- No check/use split inside axil_filter itself: `allow_write`/`allow_read` are computed from the same continuous wire that is muxed onto the master port, so there is no intra-module TOCTOU.
- axil_crossbar produces a proper DECERR for addresses outside 0x4000_0000-0x7FFF_FFFF, so a BIO program cannot reach ITCM/DTCM/QFC through the crossbar itself.
- Doc/RTL mismatch on CLOCKING_MODE default (doc says 0b11, apb_cr IV=0 gives 0b00): the RTL default is the SAFER one (2-stage sync), so not a finding.
- rrc.sv `data_access_error_pre` using `userid_k` instead of `userid_d` (a much-flagged pattern): benign — `keycfg` and `datacfg` are assigned identical expressions at rrc.sv:688-689, so `userid_k === userid_d`.

COULD NOT COVER / LIMITS:
- `nic400_1`, `ahb_bmx33_intf`, `ahb_bmxif_intf` and `CM7AAB` are black boxes not present in this repo. I verified AxUSER=0x7 is DRIVEN by the BDMA and is CONSUMED by rrc.sv, and that axitrans/aab_intf pass it through, but the propagation across the nic400 and the two AHB matrices is asserted by integration, not provable from open RTL. Finding 3 is stated at "high" confidence on that basis; if the nic400 rewrites AxUSER, the conclusion would change.
- I did not simulate. All exploit chains are derived by reading RTL, not by running the testbenches under testbench/.
- `picorv32.v` and `bio.sv` (the non-BDMA BIO variant, not instantiated in soc_ifsub) were only skimmed; I have not audited the PicoRV32 core itself for issues that would let a BIO program escape its own imem, beyond confirming the ext_addr decode (`mem_la_addr[31:28] >= 1`, line 1770).
- The exact reachability of 0x5012_4000 from a given software privilege level depends on the OS page tables / CM7 MPU configuration; `daric_cfg::CM7CFG` (which carries the MPU region count) appears inside a block-commented region at daric_cfg_pkg.sv:116-128 yet is referenced at soc_coresub.sv:321, which I could not resolve. I therefore did NOT rely on "the CM7 MPU is disabled" anywhere; Findings 1 and 2 are stated only in terms of hardware gates that provably do not exist (no sfrlock, no coreuser check, no pprot/hprot check).

findings.title: Peripheral whitelist filter is wired to DISABLE_FILTER_MEM; DISABLE_FILTER_PERI is a dead signal, so enabling memory DMA silently opens the entire peripheral space to the BIO
findings.cwe: CWE-1262 Improper Access Control for Register Interface
findings.description: bio_bdma declares two independent filter-disable control bits, `disable_filter_mem` and `disable_filter_peri` (lines 324-325), and packs both into SFR_CONFIG at 0x5012_4008 (lines 504-508, bit[7] and bit[6] respectively, exactly as documented). The memory-side `axil_filter` is correctly wired to `disable_filter_mem` (line 1342). The peripheral-side `axil_filter` is wired to `disable_filter_mem` as well (line 1478) — a copy-paste error. `disable_filter_peri` is consequently a dead net: a repo-wide grep for it returns only its declaration (line 325) and its packing into the SFR (line 506); it drives nothing. The result is that one control bit disables BOTH filters, and the documented peripheral-filter control bit does nothing at all. The two filters also share the same four `filter_base[]`/`filter_bounds[]` arrays (lines 1339-1340 vs 1475-1476), so there is no separate memory vs. peripheral policy either.
findings.evidence:
bio_bdma.sv:324-325
    logic disable_filter_mem;
    logic disable_filter_peri;

bio_bdma.sv:504-508 (SFR_CONFIG @ 0x5012_4008)
    apb_cr  #(.A('h08), .DW(10))     sfr_config           (.cr({
                                                            clocking_mode,
                                                            disable_filter_mem, disable_filter_peri,
                                                            snap_input_to_quantum, snap_input_to_which,
                                                            snap_output_to_quantum, snap_output_to_which}), .prdata32(),.*);

bio_bdma.sv:1341-1342 (mem_filter — correct)
        .gutter         (mem_gutter),
        .disable_filter (disable_filter_mem)

bio_bdma.sv:1477-1478 (peri_filter — WRONG SIGNAL)
        .gutter         (peri_gutter),
        .disable_filter (disable_filter_mem)

docs/src/ch02-00-bio-overview.md:804-805
| [6] | DISABLE_FILTER_PERI | When `1`, disables the host peripheral range whitelist filter. Setting this is strongly discouraged in secure applications. |
| [7] | DISABLE_FILTER_MEM | When `1`, disables the host memory range whitelist filter. Setting this is strongly discouraged in secure applications. |
findings.attack_scenario:
1. Firmware performs the documented, apparently memory-only operation of setting SFR_CONFIG bit[7] (DISABLE_FILTER_MEM) at 0x5012_4008 to let a BIO program stream freely through main memory, while deliberately leaving bit[6] (DISABLE_FILTER_PERI) clear and leaving the whitelist windows empty, believing peripheral access remains blocked.
2. Because of line 1478, `allow_write`/`allow_read` in the peripheral `axil_filter` are now unconditionally 1 (bio_bdma.sv:2556-2557).
3. The attacker's BIO program (loaded into the BIO instruction RAM at 0x5012_5000-0x5012_8FFF, an unlocked APB window) issues loads/stores to any address in 0x4000_0000-0x5FFF_FFFF. These are decoded by the internal axil_crossbar to the peripheral port (bio_bdma.sv:1198-1199, M_BASE_ADDR 0x4000_0000, 29-bit window), pass the now-disabled filter unmodified, and are emitted on `ahbm`, which soc_ifsub connects to `bdma_ahb32` -> bmxcore `ahb_mux_slave[0]` -> `bmx33s[1]` -> the bmx33 matrix -> `core_ahb32` and `bmxif_ahb32`, i.e. the entire peripheral map.
4. Concrete asset impact reachable in that window: the SCE unified crypto RAM at 0x4002_0000-0x4002_27FF (LKEY/KEY/SKEY/SCRT/AKEY/PKB), which is unconditionally open while `scemode==0` per sce_sec.sv:72 `assign ahben = mode_non ? 1'b1 : ...`; the ReRAM mass-erase action register (write 0x2468 to 0x4000_00F0, rrc.sv:286, `.sfrlock(1'b0)`); the sysctrl software resets at 0x4004_0080/84; the AO/PMU voltage trims at 0x4006_0000; the RAM timing trims at 0x4004_5000 (rbist_wrp.sv:161 `assign sfrlock = '0;`); and 0x5012_4000, the BIO's own configuration block, which lets the BIO program then rewrite its own whitelist and gutters (self-escalation).
5. Symmetrically, an operator who sets ONLY bit[6] expecting to relax the peripheral filter for a legitimate reason gets no effect at all and may conclude the filter is not enforcing anything.
findings.preconditions: Firmware sets SFR_CONFIG bit[7] at 0x5012_4008 — an operation the documentation describes as affecting only the memory range filter. Attacker (T1) must be able to place a program in the BIO instruction RAM and start the BIO, which requires only APB write access to 0x5012_4000/0x5012_5000-0x5012_8FFF (no lock bit, no privilege check — see the separate finding on sfrlock).
findings.mitigation: RTL fix: change bio_bdma.sv:1478 to `.disable_filter (disable_filter_peri)`. Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: never set SFR_CONFIG bit[7]. Grant memory access exclusively through the four whitelist windows (0x501240E0-0x501240FC), and treat DISABLE_FILTER_MEM as a bit that must remain 0 for the lifetime of the system. Note that DISABLE_FILTER_PERI (bit 6) can be set or cleared freely with no effect and must not be relied on for anything.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged/attacker-supplied code on either CPU able to load and start a BIO program, or an attacker-supplied BIO program running under otherwise-correct firmware)

findings.title: BDMA whitelist, DISABLE_FILTER bits and gutter registers have no lock bit and no privilege check — sfrlock is hardwired to zero, so the containment mechanism can be disabled by the code it is meant to contain
findings.cwe: CWE-1233 Security-Sensitive Hardware Controls with Missing Lock Bit Protection
findings.description: docs/src/ch02-00-bio-overview.md:70 states the whitelist "helps prevent abuse of the BDMA as a method for bypassing host CPU security features". For that guarantee to hold, the whitelist must be programmable by a strictly more privileged entity than the one it constrains. In the RTL there is no such asymmetry. Every configuration register in bio_bdma — SFR_CONFIG (which carries DISABLE_FILTER_MEM), the four FILTER_BASE/FILTER_BOUNDS pairs, both GUTTER registers, the instruction-RAM pages and SFR_CTRL (machine enable/restart) — is instantiated through `apb_cr`/`apb_ac2r` with `sfrlock` hardwired to zero at line 459. `apb_sfr2` gates writes solely on `~sfrlock & psel & penable & pwrite`; it does not examine `pprot`. No slave on the ifsub APB path consumes `pprot` or `hprot`, and there is no `coreuser` or `hauser` check anywhere between the AHB matrix and apbper[4] (soc_ifsub.sv:158-168, 361-362). There is therefore no write-once/lock-after-boot path in the RTL at all: the whitelist cannot be frozen after a secure boot stage configures it, and every register is re-writable for the lifetime of the reset domain. Reset value of all filter registers is 0 (apb_cr default IV=32'h0), which does make the whitelist empty at reset as documented — but an empty whitelist is worth nothing if the whitelist is freely rewritable.
findings.attack_scenario:
Path A (self-escalation by the BIO program, does not depend on the OS memory map): firmware whitelists any window that covers a page inside 0x5012_0000-0x5012_FFFF so the BIO can service a peripheral — the ifsub APB peripherals are packed at 4 KB stride inside that 64 KB region (soc_ifsub.sv:131 `'{idx: 32'd1 , start_addr: 32'h5012_0000, end_addr: 32'h5012_ffff}`), and with only four shared windows a coarse whole-block window is the natural configuration. The attacker's BIO program then stores to 0x5012_4008 setting DISABLE_FILTER_MEM, which by the companion defect at line 1478 disables both filters, and to 0x501240A0/A4 to repoint the gutters. From that point the BIO is an unfiltered read/write master over 0x4000_0000-0x7FFF_FFFF.
Path B (direct): any code on either CPU that has 0x5012_4000 mapped writes SFR_CONFIG bit[7] directly, loads a program into the BIO imem at 0x5012_5000, and writes SFR_CTRL at 0x5012_4000 to start it. It now owns a bus master whose ReRAM accesses carry `aruser=0x7` rather than its own identity (see the separate AMBAID finding), and which is not subject to the requesting core's MMU/MPU translation at all — precisely the "bypassing host CPU security features" the documentation claims is prevented.
In both paths there is no hardware event: the BIO block exposes no violation status bit or interrupt for a filtered access, and axil_filter returns the downstream OKAY response verbatim (bio_bdma.sv:2572 `assign s_axi_bresp = m_axi_bresp;`, 2582 `assign s_axi_rresp = m_axi_rresp;`), so neither the host nor an audit routine can observe that the whitelist was ever consulted or overridden.
findings.preconditions: APB write access to 0x5012_4000 (Path B), or a whitelist window that overlaps 0x5012_4000 (Path A). No debug mode, no lifecycle state, and no glitching is required.
findings.mitigation: RTL fix: drive `sfrlock` from a sticky write-once bit (e.g. `theregrn(sfrlock) <= sfrlock | cr_lock;`) covering SFR_CONFIG, the eight FILTER registers and both GUTTER registers, and additionally qualify writes to those specific SFRs on `coreuser`/`pprot[0]` so that only boot- or machine-mode code can program them. Firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: treat the whole 0x5012_4000-0x5012_8FFF range as a machine-mode-only resource, unmap it from every user/supervisor address space, never whitelist any window that overlaps 0x5012_0000-0x5012_FFFF (in particular do not use a single coarse window for the ifsub APB block — use 4 KB-granular windows on the specific peripheral pages the BIO needs), and program the whitelist only from the earliest boot stage.
findings.threat_actor: T1

findings.title: BDMA AXI master is tagged AMBAID4_MDMA (0x7), which matches no branch of the ReRAM controller's master decode — the BDMA inherits the CM7's coreuser while bypassing every per-slot and privileged-mode ReRAM access check
findings.cwe: CWE-1259 Improper Restriction of Security Identifier Assignment (hardware identity spoofing / mis-assignment)
findings.description: bio_bdma's AXI/AHB master identity parameter defaults to `daric_cfg::AMBAID4_MDMA` (0x7) and soc_ifsub instantiates the block with `bio_bdma #() bio (` — no parameter override — so the BDMA emits `awuser`/`aruser` = 0x7, colliding with the MDMA's `hauser` (mdma.sv:82). The ReRAM controller identifies its requester by exactly three comparisons (rrc.sv:666-668) covering 0x2 (CM7 AXI), 0x3/0x4 (Vex I/D AXI) and 0x5/0x6 (SCE), and then selects the coreuser bundle with a ternary chain that has NO default branch (rrc.sv:670-671): any unrecognised master falls through to `coreuser_cm7`. The BDMA therefore (a) borrows the CM7's live execution-region identity for the owner-nibble check, while (b) evaluating `cm7sel = vexsel = scesel = 0`, which annihilates every other term in all five RRC access-check expressions, because each of those terms is ANDed with `(cm7sel|vexsel)` or `scesel`. The MDMA — the master whose ID the BDMA re-uses — is deliberately barred from ReRAM by its own address demux (bmxcore.sv:162-165, comment `// to nic_1, but no ReRAM`), which is plausibly why rrc.sv has no case for 0x7; but the BDMA's AXI master has no such exclusion and reaches nic400 port m0 = `rrc_axi64` directly (bmxcore.sv:215-221 axi_mux_dma -> :254-260 axi_mux -> :292 `.s2(nic_s2)` -> `.m0(rrc_axi64)`).
findings.attack_scenario:
1. Attacker gets a BIO program running with a memory-side window covering ReRAM (either by whitelisting 0x6000_0000-0x603F_FFFF, or trivially by setting DISABLE_FILTER_MEM per the other findings). The BDMA memory path is decoded to 0x6000_0000-0x7FFF_FFFF by the internal crossbar (bio_bdma.sv:1198) and lands on nic400 m0 = the ReRAM controller.
2. BIO issues a data read of a ReRAM DATA slot at 0x603E_xxxx whose ACRAM descriptor has `core_rd_dis_d = 1` — the explicit "CPU cores may not read this slot, only the SCE may" control. Substituting hauser_reg = 0x7 into rrc.sv:722-726: `cm7sel=vexsel=scesel=0`, so the `core_rd_dis_d & (cm7sel|vexsel)` term is 0, the `cm7sel&(!pri_op)` privileged-mode term is 0, and the SCE terms are 0. The ONLY surviving condition is `(coreuser_cm7[7:4] & userid_k[7:4])==0` — the CM7's current execution-region nibble. Because the CM7 is running the firmware that set the BIO up, that nibble overlaps the slot owner, so the check passes and the secret is returned. The same read issued by the CM7 itself (hauser=0x2) would be denied by `core_rd_dis_d & cm7sel`. Note also that unlike the key-slot check, the data-slot check has no `trustkey[]` term at all, so no HMAC unlock is required.
3. Escalating to a full break: the BDMA reads and writes the ReRAM CFG/ACRAM region at 0x603D_C000-0x603D_FFFF, for which rrc.sv:815-821 evaluates to `cfg_access_error_pre = 0` identically when cm7sel/vexsel/scesel are all 0 — the boot0/boot1-coreuser requirement (`coreuser_in[5]|coreuser_in[4]`) and the privileged-mode requirement are both gated away. Writes to that region reprogram the ACRAM through rrc.sv:358-361 (`rramcfg_vld = (hwaddr_reg[31:14] == {16'h603D, 2'b11})`, `rram_write_run & rramcfg_vld ? ahb_wr_buf : acram_wrbuf`), i.e. the attacker can rewrite `userid_k`, `core_rd_dis_k` and `akeyid` for every key and data slot and then read the key material out.
4. The denial mechanism is silent regardless (rrc.sv:583 `assign ahbarray.hresp = 2'h0;` and rrc.sv:555-558 zero-fill), so probing costs nothing.
findings.preconditions: A BIO program with memory-path reach into 0x6000_0000-0x603F_FFFF (via a whitelist window or via DISABLE_FILTER_MEM). Step 2 additionally requires the CM7's live `coreuser_cm7[7:4]` to overlap the target slot's owner nibble at the moment the RRC evaluates the check — which is the normal case when the setup firmware and the target slot belong to the same region. AxUSER must propagate unmodified through axi_mux_dma/axi_mux and the nic400 (verified for the open-RTL portions at axitrans.sv:97/119 and aab_intf.sv:54/67/116, but the nic400 itself is a black box).
findings.mitigation: RTL fix (two parts, both needed): (1) allocate a distinct AMBAID for the BDMA and override it at instantiation, e.g. `bio_bdma #(.AHBMID4(daric_cfg::AMBAID4_BDMA)) bio (` at soc_ifsub.sv:344, so it no longer aliases the MDMA; (2) close rrc.sv:670-671 with an explicit default that denies — e.g. add `assign othersel = ~(cm7sel|vexsel|scesel);` and OR `othersel` into every access-error expression so an unrecognised master is denied rather than inheriting `coreuser_cm7`, and mirror the MDMA's ReRAM address exclusion onto `bdma_axi32` in bmxcore.sv. Software/firmware workaround on fabricated silicon: never grant the BDMA a whitelist window that overlaps 0x6000_0000-0x60FF_FFFF, never set DISABLE_FILTER_MEM, and lock down write access to 0x5012_4000 as described in the sfrlock finding — there is no way to make the RRC check correct from software, so the only mitigation is to prevent the BDMA from ever reaching ReRAM.
findings.threat_actor: T1

findings.title: Out-of-range BDMA accesses are re-addressed to a software-programmable, filter-exempt "gutter" address rather than blocked, and reads from it return real bus data — the filter has no deny primitive
findings.cwe: CWE-1220 Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
findings.description: The documentation describes the whitelist as blocking: "access to main memory is blocked by a whitelist" (ch02-00-bio-overview.md:70) and "By default, all base/bounds are set to 0, which effectively disables BIO DMA access to the rest of the system" (ch02-00-bio-overview.md, FILTER_BASE_0 section). The RTL never blocks anything. `axil_filter` passes AWVALID/ARVALID/WVALID and all data unconditionally to the master port and only substitutes the address: a non-matching transfer is issued to `gutter` instead of being suppressed or errored. `gutter` is `mem_gutter`/`peri_gutter`, two plain 32-bit read/write APB registers (lines 562-563) that are NOT themselves range-checked against the whitelist. The read data path is a straight wire (line 2581 `assign s_axi_rdata = m_axi_rdata;`), so a "blocked" read returns whatever the gutter address holds. The gutter is therefore not a bit-bucket, it is a filter-exempt one-word read/write aperture at an address of the programmer's choosing. There is also no violation status bit, interrupt or error response anywhere in the block — the response channels are passed through verbatim (lines 2572, 2582), so a filtered access is indistinguishable from a legitimate one to both the BIO and the host.
findings.attack_scenario: With the whitelist entirely empty (the documented "access disabled" configuration) an attacker writes 0x603F_0000 to SFR_MEM_GUTTER at 0x501240A0 — a single 32-bit APB store, no whitelist window and no DISABLE_FILTER bit touched. A BIO program then reads any address at all in 0x6000_0000-0x7FFF_FFFF; every such read fails the whitelist, is re-addressed to 0x603F_0000, and returns the ReRAM key-slot word to the BIO core, which forwards it to the host through the BIO output FIFO at 0x50124020. Sweeping the gutter register across a range of addresses gives word-by-word read-out of any region the BDMA master reaches; the same applies to writes. On the peripheral side, writing 0x4000_00F0 to SFR_PERI_GUTTER at 0x501240A4 and having the BIO store 0x2468 to any out-of-range peripheral address triggers the ReRAM mass-erase action register (rrc.sv:286, `.sfrlock(1'b0)`) — a permanent denial of service — even though the whitelist is empty and the peri filter is nominally enforcing. Because the gutter register is not part of the "whitelist" in the documentation's or an auditor's mental model, a firmware review that verifies the four base/bounds pairs and the two DISABLE_FILTER bits will not catch this. It also means a well-behaved system that sets a scratch gutter has to treat that scratch address as attacker-writable and attacker-readable, which the documentation does not say.
findings.preconditions: Write access to 0x501240A0/0x501240A4 (unlocked — see the sfrlock finding) and the ability to run a BIO program. No whitelist entry, no DISABLE_FILTER bit and no debug mode required. Reachability of a given gutter address is bounded by the downstream fabric decode: the memory gutter reaches ReRAM/SRAM/QFC via nic400, the peripheral gutter reaches all of 0x4000_0000-0x5FFF_FFFF via bmx33.
findings.mitigation: RTL fix: on a filter miss, suppress the transfer and synthesise a SLVERR response locally instead of re-addressing (i.e. deassert `m_axi_awvalid`/`m_axi_arvalid` and drive `s_axi_bresp`/`s_axi_rresp` = 2'b10 from a small local response FSM), and add a sticky violation status bit plus an interrupt so the host can observe attempts. If the gutter concept is retained, run the gutter address through the same `match_*` comparison so it cannot point outside the whitelist. Software workaround on fabricated silicon: at the earliest boot stage, program both SFR_MEM_GUTTER (0x501240A0) and SFR_PERI_GUTTER (0x501240A4) to a harmless dedicated scratch page that is inside a whitelist window and contains nothing sensitive, and then protect 0x5012_4000-0x5012_40FF from all non-boot code — but note this is only effective if the register cannot subsequently be rewritten, which the hardware does not enforce.
findings.threat_actor: T1

findings.title: Filter policy registers cross from pclk into the hclk/dmaclk filter with no synchronizer and no atomic commit, and in-flight transfers are never re-checked — narrowing a whitelist window can transiently open a wider one
findings.cwe: CWE-1037 Processor Optimization Removal or Modification of Security-critical Code (analogous: security decision made on data crossing a clock domain without synchronization)
findings.description: `filter_base[]`, `filter_bounds[]`, `mem_gutter`, `peri_gutter` and `disable_filter_mem` are `apb_cr` registers clocked on `pclk` (bio_bdma.sv:504-508, 562-563, 620-627; soc_ifsub.sv:341 `pclkbio` is gated from the system `pclk`). They are consumed purely combinationally inside `axil_filter`, which is instantiated on `hclk` for the memory path (line 1298 `.clk(hclk)`) and on `dmaclk` for the peripheral path (line 1434 `.clk(dmaclk)`, tied to `hclkbio` at soc_ifsub.sv:347). There is no synchronizer, no handshake and no shadow/commit register between the two domains: a 20-bit `filter_base` update is not atomic as seen by the comparator, so during the transition individual bits can be observed at their old and new values simultaneously, producing base/bounds pairs that were never programmed. The RTL itself acknowledges the hazard but only as a functional caveat, not a security one. Separately, the comparison is a pure combinational function of the live AW/AR address, so a transfer whose address phase is already outstanding downstream is never re-evaluated, and conversely the address presented on `m_axi_awaddr` can change from `gutter` to the real address (or vice versa) while `AWVALID` is held — an AXI address-stability violation whose outcome depends on when the slave samples.
findings.attack_scenario: Firmware wants to revoke a BIO window at runtime — the natural defensive action when handing the BIO from a trusted phase to an untrusted one, or when tearing down a DMA buffer. It writes SFR_FILTER_BASE_0 to move the window, for example from page 0x3FFFF to page 0x40000 (every one of the 20 bits toggles). Because `filter_base[0]` crosses pclk->hclk unsynchronized and is consumed bit-by-bit by the comparator at line 2550, the comparator can observe transitional values including 0x00000 for one or more hclk cycles, while `filter_bounds[0]` still holds its old, large value. For those cycles `match_read[0]`/`match_write[0]` is true for a far wider address range than either the old or the new policy allows. An attacker-supplied BIO program sitting in a tight load loop against a forbidden address (the BIO cores run free at fclk and can issue back-to-back DMA requests, bio_bdma.sv:1084-1096) has a direct chance of landing a transfer in that window, and can simply retry across many revocation events. A T4 attacker who can skew the pclk/hclk relationship (clock manipulation) widens the exposure. There is no interlock anywhere in the design that stalls or aborts BIO DMA while the filter registers are being updated, and no way for firmware to revoke a window safely — the block provides no "quiesce" bit and SFR_CTRL's enable is itself only cdc_level_to_pulse-synchronized (bio_bdma.sv:565).
findings.preconditions: Attacker-supplied BIO program running concurrently with a legitimate host update of the filter registers. Requires pclk and hclk to be sufficiently independent that a multi-bit update is not seen atomically; both are derived from the same clock tree via the sysctrl gearbox and ICGs (soc_ifsub.sv:340-341), so the exposure depends on the synthesized skew and on the pclk/hclk divider ratio — this is why confidence is medium rather than high.
findings.mitigation: RTL fix: register the whole policy set (base/bounds/gutter/disable_filter) into the filter's own clock domain behind a single-bit `commit` handshake synchronized with a 2-flop synchronizer, so the comparator only ever sees a complete, consistent policy; and add a quiesce/idle interlock so a policy change cannot take effect while a DMA transfer is outstanding. Software workaround on fabricated silicon: never change the filter registers while the BIO is enabled. Sequence every policy update as: clear SFR_CTRL enable at 0x5012_4000, poll until all four SFR_DBG registers show the machines halted, allow several hclk periods to drain, then rewrite the filter registers, then re-enable. Do not rely on window revocation as a security boundary against an already-running BIO program.
findings.threat_actor: T1 (with T4 amplifying the window)

finders.domain: CPU subsystems (CM7/Vex), TCM/SRAM, MDMA, QFC external-flash/XIP controller, bmxcore fabric
finders.coverage_notes:
READ END-TO-END: rtl/modules/core/rtl/{cm7sys.sv, cm7sys_tcm.sv, tcmram.sv, itcm16kx18x2.sv, core_srambank.try8k.sv, coresub_sramtrm.sv, vexram.sv, vexsys.sv, mdma.sv, qfc.sv, qfc_aes.sv, duart.sv}, rtl/modules/bmxcore/rtl/bmxcore.sv, rtl/modules/common/rtl/gnrl_sramc.sv. READ IN PART (for integration tracing): rtl/modules/soc_coresub/rtl/soc_coresub.sv (lines 195-700, 830-930), rtl/modules/rrc/rtl/rrc.sv (lines 230-440, 540-860), rtl/asic_top/rtl/daric_cfg_pkg.sv, rtl/asic_top/rtl/soc_top.sv (APB/duart/pad sections), rtl/asic_top/rtl/pad_frame_arm.sv (pad section), rtl/modules/amba/rtl/apb_sfr.sv (apb_sfr2 lock semantics).

VERIFICATION METHOD: every claim below was re-derived from the RTL, not taken from the shared recon. In particular the coreuser index inversion (finding 1) was derived independently by expanding the generate loop against the `idx:` self-documenting fields of `code_mem_map` and `coreusermap_cm7`, and cross-checked against the RRC's own per-bit comments (`//master boot0 read` etc.) and against the Vex's opposite convention in cram_axi.sv.

COULD NOT COVER / LIMITATIONS:
- `cm7top` / `CORTEXM7INTEGRATIONCS`, `CM7DAP`, `pl230_udma`, `sdvt_spi_master_core`, `ahb_bmx33_intf`, `nic1_intf`'s `nic400_1`, and all SRAM/ReRAM macro models are encrypted/absent black boxes. I could not audit the MDMA engine's own address/length handling, the QFC SPI FSM's response to a malicious/hostile flash device (overrun, stall, DQS glitching, opcode-phase abuse), or the exact address decode inside `ahb_bmx33`. Finding 2's "reaches the CM7 TCMs" therefore rests on the open-RTL demux map plus the port wiring, not on the bmx33 decoder itself.
- `cm7sys_cfg.svh` is NOT present in this repo (`find` returns nothing), so I could not confirm the CM7 `MPU`/`ICACHE`/`DCACHE`/`CACHEECC` parameter values that `daric_cfg::CM7CFG` supplies. I deliberately did not report anything about the MPU because I cannot read its configuration.
- The QFC XIP decryption itself lives inside `sdvt_spi_master_core` (the in-repo `qfc_aes` is a verified pure pass-through, qfc_aes.sv:24-74), so I can state that the key and enable are software-writable but cannot state what the cipher/mode/integrity behaviour is.
- I did not audit the BIO/BDMA, SCE, TRNG, tamper, AO or ReRAM-macro domains (other teams' scope); I only traced into rrc.sv far enough to establish the consumer side of the CM7 coreuser signal.
- Timing/power side channels in the CM7 or Vex datapaths are not assessable from this RTL (cores are black boxes).
- docs/src/ contains no specification of coreuser, TCM protection, MDMA or XIP, so no doc-vs-RTL comparison was possible in this domain beyond clock-generation.md.

findings.title: CM7 coreuser bits are generated in reversed index order: rrc.sv reads the memory-region bits where it expects the boot0/boot1/fw0/fw1 identity, collapsing the ReRAM privilege ladder
findings.cwe: CWE-1220 Insufficient Granularity of Access Control (privilege tag mis-encoded between producer and consumer)
findings.threat_actor: T1 (privileged-mode application firmware on the CM7, i.e. any code that is not boot0/boot1); amplified by T3 for the XIP variant
findings.preconditions: CM7 selected as the active core (default: soc_coresub.sv:283 `cm7cfg_en = ~vexcfg_enreg | cm7cfg_enreg`). Attacker executes CM7 code from anywhere in the ReRAM window 0x6000_0000-0x603F_FFFF or the SRAM window 0x6100_0000-0x611F_FFFF with AxPROT[0]=1 (CM7 privileged mode). No boot-stage privilege is needed.
findings.description:
`coreuser` is an 8-bit sideband identity produced by cm7sys and consumed by rrc.sv (and sce_sec.sv). soc_coresub.sv builds the region table so that array index 7 = fw1, 6 = fw0, 5 = boot1, 4 = boot0 and indices 3..0 = `daric_cfg::code_mem_map` = {3:sram, 2:reram, 1:dtcm, 0:itcm} (the `idx:` fields in both literals confirm the positional mapping). cm7sys then assigns bit `PM_COREUSERCNT-gvi-1` = `7-gvi` from map entry `gvi`, i.e. it writes the map hits into the coreuser vector in REVERSED index order. With PM_COREUSERCNT=8 (soc_coresub.sv:234-235, passed at soc_coresub.sv:312) the produced vector is:
  coreuser[6] = PC in DTCM (0x2000_0000-0x3FFF_FFFF)
  coreuser[5] = PC in ReRAM (0x6000_0000-0x603F_FFFF)  <- the WHOLE 4 MB, not boot1
  coreuser[4] = PC in SRAM  (0x6100_0000-0x611F_FFFF)  <- the WHOLE SRAM, not boot0
  coreuser[7] = ~|coreuser[6:4]  = PC in ITCM / XIP flash / anywhere unmapped
  coreuser[3:0] = {boot0, boot1, fw0, fw1} hits  <- the real identity, parked where nobody reads it
rrc.sv consumes ONLY coreuser_in[7:4] and documents them as {fw1, fw0, boot1, boot0} (rrc.sv:642 and the per-line comments at rrc.sv:731-757). The Vex takes the opposite convention (cram_axi.sv:20921 puts its 4-bit identity in [7:4] and the reversed copy in [3:0]), and vexsys.sv:221 carries an unresolved designer note about exactly this: `// bunnie: @[name redacted] need to check MSB vs LSB bit ordering`. So the CM7 and the Vex disagree with each other, and the CM7 disagrees with its consumer.
The most damaging consequence is at rrc.sv:815: the ReRAM CFG region (0x603D_C000-0x603D_FFFF), which IS the live ACRAM access-control descriptor array (rrc.sv:358-361 `rramcfg_vld` -> `acram_wrbuf` -> `acram2kx64`) and the NVR config words (devena/coreselcm7/coreselvex/tkey_en/cfgsce), is gated by `!(coreuser_in[5] | coreuser_in[4])`, intended to mean 'must be boot1 or boot0'. In the shipped RTL that expression means 'PC is anywhere in ReRAM, or anywhere in SRAM' - which is true for essentially all firmware, including fw1 application code and any code the attacker copies into SRAM.
Secondary consequences: key-slot ownership `coreuser_in[7:4] & userid_k[7:4]` (rrc.sv:712) now matches on memory region rather than boot stage - a slot provisioned to owner nibble 4'b1000 ('fw1') is unlocked by any code fetching from ITCM or from the external XIP flash at 0x8000_0000 (T3-controlled), while genuine ReRAM fw1 code never asserts bit 7 at all; and the whole boot0/boot1/fw0/fw1 code-region matrix at rrc.sv:731-757 is evaluated against the wrong four bits.
findings.attack_scenario:
1. Attacker gains code execution in ordinary CM7 application firmware (fw1 region of ReRAM) in privileged mode - e.g. an RTOS kernel task, or by exploiting any memory-safety bug in fw1. This is explicitly NOT boot0/boot1 code, so the design intends it to have no access to the ReRAM CFG region.
2. Because the PC is in 0x6000_0000-0x603F_FFFF, cm7sys sets coreuser[5]=1 (the 'reram' code_mem_map hit landing in the bit rrc.sv calls 'boot1'). coreuser[7]=~|coreuser[6:4]=0, and the true fw1 hit sits unread in coreuser[0].
3. The CM7 issues a privileged (AxPROT[0]=1) write to 0x603D_C000+N*32, the ACRAM descriptor for a target ReRAM key slot. rrc.sv:815 evaluates `!(coreuser_in[5]|coreuser_in[4])` = `!(1|0)` = 0, so `cfg_prev_dis`=0, so `cfg_access_error`=0 and the write is allowed. rrc.sv:358-361 latches it into `acram_wrbuf` and it is committed into the live `acram2kx64` descriptor array.
4. The attacker writes a descriptor with `userid_k[7:4] = 4'h0`. Every term of `key_access_error_pre` is ANDed with `(userid_k[7:4] != 4'h0)` (rrc.sv:717), so the entire key-slot access check - owner match, core_rd_dis, privilege, keytype, and the trustkey gate - is switched off for that slot.
5. The attacker reads 0x603F_0000+N*32 and receives the raw ReRAM key material; rrc.sv:555-558 returns it because `cmd_user_read_dis` is 0. The denial path is silent anyway (rrc.sv:583 `assign ahbarray.hresp = 2'h0;`), and `rrccr[15]` (NMI on access error) resets to 0, so even a failed probe raises nothing.
6. Variant with T3: the attacker instead arranges CM7 execution from the external XIP flash at 0x8000_0000 (which he controls). Then coreuser[6:4]=000 and coreuser[7]=1, i.e. the attacker's off-chip code presents the identity that rrc.sv treats as 'fw1' for every key slot and code-region check - an identity that no on-chip ReRAM firmware can ever assert.
findings.mitigation:
RTL fix: index the coreuser vector consistently with the map, i.e. `assign coreuserreg0pre[gvi] = (corecm7pc >= coreusermap[gvi].start_addr) & (corecm7pc < coreusermap[gvi].end_addr);` for gvi = 0..PM_COREUSERCNT-1, and set the catch-all as `coreuserreg0pre[7] = ~|coreuserreg0pre[6:4]` only after that reindexing (so [6:4] really are fw0/boot1/boot0). Align vexsys/cram_axi to the same convention and delete the reversed [3:0] shadow copy. Add an assertion that coreuser[7:4] is one-hot and that coreuser[7:4] and coreuser[3:0] are bit-reverses of the same value.
Silicon workaround (this part is unpatchable in hardware, so it must be done in firmware and provisioning): (a) provision the ACRAM `userid_k`/`userid_d` nibbles against the ACTUAL encoding {bit7=ITCM/XIP, bit6=DTCM, bit5=ReRAM, bit4=SRAM}, never against the documented {fw1,fw0,boot1,boot0}; in particular never use nibble 4'b1000 for any slot, since that nibble is unlockable from attacker-controlled XIP flash. (b) Since the CFG region cannot be restricted to boot code, boot0/boot1 must, before handing off to fw0/fw1, set `key_cfg_wr_dis`/`data_cfg_wr_dis` (rrc.sv:616-619, sourced from the boot-read ReRAM image) for every ACRAM descriptor line that protects a live key, so that `cfg_wr_dis` blocks the rewrite independently of `cfg_prev_dis`. (c) Set `qfc_disable` in the ReRAM core config so the XIP window is never a fetchable code source in the field. (d) Keep all post-boot firmware in unprivileged (AxPROT[0]=0) mode wherever possible, since `cm7sel & !pri_op` is the only remaining independent term in the CFG and key checks.

findings.title: MDMA (pl230) is a fully unauthenticated bus master: its control registers have no lock and no privilege check, and its address map reaches the CM7's ITCM and DTCM
findings.cwe: CWE-1189 Improper Isolation of Shared Resources on System-on-a-Chip (DMA master with no address whitelist or requester authentication)
findings.threat_actor: T1 (unprivileged software on either CPU that can reach the coresub APB window), and any other AHB master that reaches core_ahb32 - including the BIO/BDMA AHB port whose hauser is hardwired 0
findings.preconditions: Attacker can issue APB writes to 0x4001_1000-0x4001_1FFF (pl230 channel control) and 0x4001_2000-0x4001_2FFF (mdmareq event select). Reachable from the CM7 AHB-P port, the Vex AHB-P port (soc_coresub.sv:613 -> coreahbpmux -> bmxcore .cm7_ahbp), the BDMA AHB master and the SCE AHB path - none of which is filtered by hprot/pprot anywhere in the design.
findings.description:
The MDMA wrapper hardwires its SFR lock to zero (`assign sfrlock = '0;`) and passes the pl230's own APB port straight through with no lock at all (`.psel(apbs_dma.psel)` etc., mdma.sv:71-76). No consumer of `hprot`/`pprot` exists anywhere on this path, so there is no privileged-vs-unprivileged distinction on the MDMA control interface. The MDMA then emits a constant, non-authenticating master tag `assign ahbm.hauser = AHBMID4 |'0;` = 4'h7, identical for every requester and identical to the value the BIO's BDMA AXI master emits (bio_bdma.sv:1360/1373 with the un-overridden default `AHBMID4 = daric_cfg::AMBAID4_MDMA`), so a downstream checker cannot tell who programmed the transfer. In rrc.sv the value 4'h7 matches none of `cm7sel`/`vexsel`/`scesel` (rrc.sv:666-668) and therefore falls through the defaultless mux at rrc.sv:670-671 to `coreuser_cm7`.
The MDMA's only containment is the address map in bmxcore. That map deliberately carves ReRAM out of the nic400 path with the comment `// to nic_1, but no ReRAM`, but the other rule sends the ENTIRE 0x0000_0000-0x5FFF_FFFF space to `ahb_bmx33`, whose master port 0 is the CM7's AHB slave port (`ahb_thru bmx33m0 ( .ahbslave(bmx33m[0]), .ahbmaster(cm7_ahbs ));`). 0x0000_0000-0x1FFF_FFFF is the CM7 ITCM and 0x2000_0000-0x3FFF_FFFF is the CM7 DTCM (daric_cfg_pkg.sv:65-66). The CM7's AHBS port is instantiated with `.AHBSPRI(1'b0)` (cm7sys.sv:530) and the CM7 MPU does not apply to AHBS traffic, so nothing in the design gates DMA access to the TCMs. The same map also delivers the MDMA to the SCE window, sysctrl (including the software-reset action registers), secsub/tamper and the AO/PMU bridge.
findings.attack_scenario:
1. Attacker runs unprivileged code on the Vex (or unprivileged CM7 code, or drives the BIO/BDMA AHB master, whose hauser is 0 and matches no check anywhere). All of these reach core_ahb32 and therefore 0x4001_1000.
2. He writes a pl230 channel control-structure base pointer into the pl230 register block at 0x4001_1000, pointing at a scratch buffer in SRAM he owns, and programs a channel descriptor with source = 0x2000_0000 (the CM7's D0/D1TCM) and destination = that SRAM buffer. There is no sfrlock (mdma.sv:100), no privilege qualification, and no requester check, so the write succeeds.
3. He arms the request path by writing `cr_en`/`cr_reqen` in `sfr_cr` and selecting a trigger event with `cr_evsel` at 0x4001_2000 (mdma.sv:105-106, 111), or uses the pl230's own software-request register.
4. The MDMA issues AHB reads at 0x2000_xxxx. The bmxcore demux (bmxcore.sv:163) routes 0x0000_0000-0x5FFF_FFFF to ahb_bmx33, whose master 0 is `cm7_ahbs` (bmxcore.sv:271). The CM7 AHBS port services the read from the DTCM with no privilege or coreuser check. The CM7's stack, heap and any key material it has loaded into DTCM are copied into the attacker's buffer.
5. Reversing source and destination writes attacker-chosen bytes into the CM7's ITCM at 0x0000_xxxx - direct code injection into the other CPU, at a moment of the attacker's choosing (e.g. while the CM7 is halted in WFI, cm7sys.sv:331).
6. The same primitive also reaches sysctrl at 0x4004_0080/0084 (the `sfr_rcurst0/1` software-reset action registers) and the AO/PMU bridge, so it doubles as a fault/reset primitive.
findings.mitigation:
RTL fix: (a) give the MDMA the same base/bounds whitelist the BIO/BDMA has, applied to `ahbm.haddr` before the demux, with the whitelist and the pl230 control registers behind a real `sfrlock` that boot code sets and only a full reset clears; (b) drive `sfrlock` on both `apbs_dma` and `apbx` from a lockable register rather than `'0`, and gate the MDMA APB on `hprot[1]`/`pprot[0]` so unprivileged code cannot program it; (c) remove 0x0000_0000-0x3FFF_FFFF (ITCM/DTCM) from `mdma_ahb_demux_map` unless DMA-to-TCM is a required feature, or assert `AHBSPRI` and add an AHBS-side filter; (d) give the MDMA a distinct AMBAID (it currently collides with the BDMA's 4'h7) and add a `default:` deny arm to `coreuser_mux` in rrc.sv:670-671.
Silicon workaround: boot0/boot1 must, before handing control to application firmware, permanently gate the MDMA - the only lever available is the clock/reset: hold the MDMA in reset or disable its clock enable via the sysctrl clock-gate registers, and then set the sysctrl SFR lock. Note that `soc_top.sv:217` declares `logic sfrlock;` with no driver anywhere in the file, so the sysctrl write-protect that would normally hold that configuration is itself inert - firmware must verify empirically whether the clock gate can be re-enabled by an attacker before relying on it. Additionally, never leave key material in DTCM across a call into untrusted code.

findings.title: A single unlocked APB bit permanently disables ITCM/DTCM parity and read/write verification, removing the CM7's only fault-injection detector on its instruction memory
findings.cwe: CWE-1256 Improper Restriction of Software Interfaces to Hardware Features (software-controlled disable of a hardware integrity check)
findings.threat_actor: T1 to set the bit; T2 (laser / EM / voltage fault injection on the TCM macros) to exploit the resulting blind spot
findings.preconditions: Attacker can perform one APB write to 0x4001_4004 (ITCM trim) or 0x4001_4008 (DTCM trim) with bit 0 set. `coresub_sramtrm` is `coresubapbs[4]` (soc_coresub.sv:477) inside the 0x4001_0000 window, reachable from the CM7 AHB-P port, the Vex AHB-P port, the MDMA, the BDMA AHB master and the SCE AHB path. No privilege or coreuser check exists on that path.
findings.description: `cm7sys_tcm` selects between two TCM datapaths with a bit derived from the SRAM trim register: `fastmode <= fastmode | sramtrm[0]`. This is a set-only sticky flop - once set it cannot be cleared until `resetn` (= `sysresetn_cm7`) de-asserts. In the non-fast path the TCM traffic goes through `gnrl_sramc`, which generates a per-byte parity bit on write and recomputes and compares it on read (`gnrl_sramc.sv:328-336`, `assign prerr0[gvi] = prbit0[gvi] ^ prbitreg[gvi];`) and additionally performs a read-back verify of every write and every read (`gnrl_sramc.sv:136-144`). In fast mode the whole `gnrl_sramc` instance is clock-gated off (`ICG ramc0_icg ( .CK (clk), .EN ( ~fastmode ), ...)`) and traffic is routed through `tcmramc_thru`, which writes a CONSTANT parity bit of 0 and discards the stored parity bit on read. Crucially, `verifyerr` and `prerr` are also explicitly forced to 0 in fast mode. `err_o = verifyerr | prerr` (cm7sys_tcm.sv:75) is the CM7's `ITCMERR`/`D0TCMERR`/`D1TCMERR` input (cm7sys.sv:432, 446, 459, 1003), i.e. the only mechanism by which a corrupted TCM word raises a fault instead of being silently executed or consumed. The controlling register is a plain APB CR with `assign sfrlock = '0;` and no lock bit of any kind (coresub_sramtrm.sv:41, 57-58); the same block also exposes `sfr_ramsec` (coresub_sramtrm.sv:63, IV 4'h0) which gates the background scrub/verify engine (`gnrl_sramc.sv:163 assign evenable = ipdone & even;`) and is likewise unlocked and OFF at reset.
findings.attack_scenario:
1. The CM7 has been running secure-boot-verified code out of ITCM (INITTCMEN is hardwired to 2'b11, cm7sys.sv:417, so the TCMs are enabled from reset).
