This is unique among the SFR primitives in this library - `ahb_cr`, `ahb_sr` and `ahb_fr` all pass sfrlock down to `ahb_sfr2`, which applies it at line 256 (`assign reg_write_en = ~sfrlock & reg_write_en0;`), and the APB twin `apb_ar` (apb_sfr.sv:234-262) applies it via `apb_sfrop2` (apb_sfr.sv:378). `ahb_ar` is the only one that drops it. Consequently there is no way, ever, to write-protect an ahb_ar action register: the input exists and is silently discarded. The design's only instance of ahb_ar is the ReRAM mass-erase (`suicide`) trigger in the ReRAM controller, rrc.sv:286, which also passes `sfrlock(1'b0)` - so today the behaviour is identical, but the RTL removes the ability to fix it with a lock bit, and it removes the one write-protect hook that a firmware or ECO could have used to gate the single most destructive register in the SoC.
missed.evidence:
rtl/modules/amba/rtl/ahb_sfr.sv:286-345 (sfrlock is a port, never used)
```
module ahb_ar #(
        parameter AW=12,
        parameter A=0,
        parameter AR=32'h5a
     )(
        input  logic  hclk,
        input  logic  resetn,
        ahbif.slavein                       ahbs        ,
        input  bit                          sfrlock     ,
...
    assign sfrsel = ( reg_addr[AW-1:0] == A[AW-1:0] );
    assign reg_write_en = reg_write_en0 & sfrsel;

    `theregfull(hclk, resetn, ar, '0) <= reg_write_en & ( reg_wdata == AR );
```
Contrast, the same library's ahb_sfr2 which does honour it - rtl/modules/amba/rtl/ahb_sfr.sv:256
```
    assign reg_write_en = ~sfrlock & reg_write_en0;
```
and the APB twin which does honour it - rtl/modules/amba/rtl/apb_sfr.sv:378
```
    assign apbwr = ~sfrlock & apbslave.psel & apbslave.penable & apbslave.pwrite & sfrsel;
```
The sole instantiation in the design - rtl/modules/rrc/rtl/rrc.sv:256 and :286
```
    localparam PM_RRAM_SUICIDE = 16'h2468;
...
    ahb_ar #(.A('hF0), .AR(PM_RRAM_SUICIDE))    sfr_rrcar       (.ar(rrcar_suicide), .resetn(coreresetn), .sfrlock(1'b0), .*);
```
and what that pulse does - rtl/modules/rrc/rtl/rrc.sv:307
```
    `theregfull(clktop, sysresetn, suicide_start, '0) <= ((cmscode == CMS_SCDE) | rrcar_suicide) & (!suicide_reg) & (!suicide_start) & (suicide_adr_main == 'h0) ? 1'b1 :
```
missed.attack_scenario: A single 32-bit store of 0x2468 to the RRC action register at 0x4000_00F0 (RRC is coreahb_demux_map idx 0, daric_cfg_pkg.sv:55, base 0x4000_0000) asserts rrcar_suicide, which starts the ReRAM erase walk over the whole main array and then the IFR (rrc.sv:307-322). There is no lock bit, no coreuser qualifier on this register, no magic-sequence beyond the single 0x2468 value, and - because ahb_ar discards sfrlock - no way to add one without an RTL change. Any AHB master that can reach 0x4000_00F0 (CM7 AHB-P, Vex AHB-P via the same core_ahbp mux, the SCE DMA's AHB path, or the BDMA/MDMA peripheral master) permanently bricks the device. The absent sfrlock also means that even if firmware wanted to lock the register down after boot - the pattern used everywhere else in this library - the hardware would ignore it.

missed.title: APB and AHB SFR banks ignore write byte strobes, so any sub-word write clobbers all 32 bits of the register
missed.description: `apb_sfr2` and `ahb_sfr2` are the register-bank primitives behind every apb_cr/apb_acr/apb_fr and ahb_cr/ahb_fr instance in the SoC. Neither consumes the write strobes. In `apb_sfr2` the register update at apb_sfr.sv:339 writes the full `apbslave.pwdata` whenever the address matches and `apbwr` is asserted; `pstrb` is never referenced anywhere in apb_sfr.sv (I grepped the whole file - the only pstrb hit is `assign apbmaster.pstrb = 0` in the null-master stub at line 269). `ahb_sfr2` is the same: ahbs_trans is instantiated with `.byte_strobe(reg_byte_strobe)` and the resulting net is never read, while the update at ahb_sfr.sv:262 stores the whole `reg_wdata`. On AHB and APB, the byte lanes not selected by the transfer size / strobe carry undefined data, so a byte or halfword store to any control register in this SoC overwrites the other lanes with whatever the master happened to leave on the bus. Security-relevant control registers routinely pack a lock/enable bit next to a data field in the same 32-bit word (e.g. sysctrl CGUSEC, the SCE global control registers, the RRC control register at rrc.sv:274), so a driver performing a byte-granular field update silently rewrites the neighbouring security bits to an attacker-irrelevant but unpredictable value - and a compiler is entitled to narrow a volatile field access to a byte store.
missed.attack_scenario: This is a latent-corruption defect rather than a direct attacker primitive - an attacker who can write the register at all can already write the whole word. The realistic failure is a confused-deputy one: privileged firmware updates one byte-wide field of a packed security register (for example a trim or mode byte) with a byte store; the hardware writes all four bytes, and the adjacent lock/enable bits in the same word are set to the undefined content of the unselected byte lanes. If those bits control a write-protect or a mode gate, the register silently ends up in a permissive state that the firmware believes it never touched, with no bus error and no way to detect it other than reading the register back. The same mechanism means any sub-word write anywhere in the SoC's SFR space is a latent corruption of three neighbouring bytes.

missed.title: Mailbox APB slave returns PREADY=1 unconditionally, so gating the mailbox clock silently discards inter-CPU messages with an OKAY response
missed.description: `mbox_apb` expands the `apbs_common` macro (apb_sfr.sv:19-23), which hard-ties `apbx.pready = 1'b1` and `apbx.pslverr = 1'b0` as pure constants - they do not depend on pclk and are not qualified by the peripheral's clock gate. Meanwhile both of the mailbox's clocks are software-gateable: soc_coresub.sv:438-439 gates aclk and hclk into the mailbox with `clkmboxgate`, which is soc_top.sv:576 `aclksubgate[5]`, which is a plain read/write control register in the CGU (sysctrl.sv:864, `apb_cr #(.A('h60), .DW(ACKCNT), .IV('hff)) sfr_aclkgr (.cr(aclksubgate),...)`, documented as CGUACLKGR at 0x4004_0060), whose sfrlock is the undriven net at soc_top.sv:217. Clearing bit 5 stops both mailbox clocks. Because PREADY is a constant, every subsequent AHB/APB access to 0x4001_3000-0x4001_301C still completes with an OKAY response and no bus fault, but nothing is clocked: apb_sfr2's register update (apb_sfr.sv:339) is a pclk flop and never fires, and the apb_acr/apb_asr action pulses (mbox.sv:177, :237) are pclk flops and never fire, so no word is pushed and no word is popped. The status register read path is combinational, so it keeps returning the frozen pre-gate values - typically tx_free=1, rx_avail=0, tx_err=0, rx_err=0. The sender therefore polls a status register that permanently says 'ready, no error' while every message it writes is discarded.
missed.evidence:
rtl/modules/amba/rtl/apb_sfr.sv:19-23 (the macro used by mbox.sv:105)
```
    `define apbs_common \
    assign apbx.pready = 1'b1; \
    assign apbx.pslverr = 1'b0; \
    assign apbrd = apbs.psel & apbs.penable & ~apbs.pwrite; \
    assign apbwr = apbs.psel & apbs.penable & apbs.pwrite
```
rtl/modules/soc_coresub/rtl/soc_coresub.sv:438-439 (both mailbox clocks gated by one software bit)
```
    logic aclkmbox; ICG icg_mbox_aclk ( .CK (aclk), .EN ( clkmboxgate ), .SE(cmsatpg), .CKG ( aclkmbox ));
    logic hclkmbox; ICG icg_mbox_hclk ( .CK (hclk), .EN ( clkmboxgate ), .SE(cmsatpg), .CKG ( hclkmbox ));
```
rtl/asic_top/rtl/soc_top.sv:576 (the gate source)
```
                               .clkmboxgate ( aclksubgate[5] ),
```
rtl/modules/sysctrl/rtl/sysctrl.sv:864 (a plain software control register)
```
    apb_cr #(.A('h60), .DW(ACKCNT),   .IV('hff)) sfr_aclkgr     (.cr(aclksubgate),.prdata32(),.*);
```
and the write-protect that would have covered it is an undriven net - rtl/asic_top/rtl/soc_top.sv:217 and :361
```
    logic               sfrlock;
...
    /*        input logic      */   .sfrlock     (sfrlock|'0     ),
```
missed.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker code writes 0x4004_0060 clearing bit 5. There is no lock bit protecting this register (sysctrl's sfrlock is never driven), and the CGU clock-gate register is not covered by any coreuser or hauser check. 2. Both mailbox clocks stop. 3. The CM7's secure firmware continues its normal send loop: it reads 0x4001_3008, sees the frozen tx_free=1 and tx_err=0, writes a word to 0x4001_3000, and gets an OKAY response - the AHB-to-APB bridge completes because PREADY is a constant 1. The word is never registered and never reaches the Vex. 4. The Vex's secure task never receives the command; the CM7 never receives a reply and never sees an error bit, because the status register is frozen at 'idle, no error'. The result is a stealthy, unattributable cut of the inter-CPU trust channel: neither endpoint can distinguish it from a peer that is simply slow, and any firmware protocol that relies on the mailbox status register for liveness or error detection is defeated. Restoring the gate bit does not recover the lost words, so an attacker can also use it to delete a specific message from a sequence and desynchronise a positional protocol.

verdicts.title: Vex fabric identity tag (coreuser) is selected by a software-written satp.ASID, is not bound to the executing code region, and ignores satp.MODE entirely
verdicts.reasoning: Every quoted line reproduces. cram_axi.sv:212-213 declares `wire cramsoc_satp_mode; wire [8:0] cramsoc_satp_asid;`. An exhaustive grep of cram_axi.sv for `cramsoc_satp_mode` returns exactly two hits (212 declaration, 23106 `.MmuPlugin_satp_mode(cramsoc_satp_mode)`) — it is genuinely a dangling net, so satp.MODE never qualifies the tag. The LUT at cram_axi.sv:5814-5849 is an 8-way priority compare of `cramsoc_satp_asid` against `coreuser_lut01..71`, falling through to `coreuser_user_default` at 5840. cram_axi.sv:20921-20922 registers the result into `coreuser_vex[7:4]`. VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:8288-8292 writes `MmuPlugin_satp_asid <= CsrPlugin_csrMapping_writeDataSignal[30:22]` with no MODE qualification; satp is CSR 0x180 whose [9:8]==2'b01, so the gate at VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:7466 (`CsrPlugin_privilege < csrAddress[9:8]`) admits S-mode and M-mode. Consumers verified: rrc.sv:670-671 `coreuser_mux = scesel ? sceuser : vexsel ? coreuser_vex : coreuser_cm7;` and rrc.sv:712 `(((coreuser_in[7:4] & userid_k[7:4])==0) & ...)`, rrc.sv:815 `cfg_prev_dis` requiring `coreuser_in[5]|coreuser_in[4]`; soc_coresub.sv:839 wires it in. The contrast with the CM7 is real: cm7sys.sv:754-761 derives `coreuserreg0pre[gvi]` from `(corecm7pc >= coreusermap[gvi].start_addr) & (corecm7pc < ...end_addr)` — a PC comparator, plus a debounce filter (`coreuser_keep`/`coreuser_filtercyc`) that the Vex path does not have at all. I looked for compensating controls and found none: (a) `coreuser_protect` (cram_axi.sv:20878-20918) only holds the shadow copies; it does not constrain which ASID software installs; (b) the LUT is still readable after protect — the read mux at cram_axi.sv:21108-21128 returns `coreuser_map_lo_storage`/`map_hi_storage`/`uservalue_storage` unconditionally; (c) mstatus.TVM is not implemented anywhere in VexRiscv_CramSoC.v, so satp access cannot be trapped. One scoping correction below.
verdicts.correction: The attack requires `coreuser_enable1 == 1`. cram_axi.sv:5851-5883 shows `coreuser_coreuser_4bit` is derived from `coreuser_coreuser_2bit` (the ASID LUT result) ONLY when `coreuser_enable1` is set; otherwise it comes from the ReRAM `default_user`. So ASID-spoofing applies once firmware has enabled the coreuser block — which is the intended operating state, but the finding should say so. Also, the mitigation text's suggestion to gate on `cramsoc_satp_mode` is correct in spirit but note the CM7's own comparator is on the *fetch* PC while the Vex tag would have to be derived per-transaction; and the 'secondary note' about in-flight re-tagging is independently confirmed (rrc.sv:660-664 latches axid_reg, axprot_reg and vex_mm_reg at the AXI handshake, but rrc.sv:670-672 consumes `coreuser_vex` live and un-latched) — though it adds no capability beyond simply writing the ASID first.

verdicts.title: vex_mm, the 'CPU is privileged' signal the ReRAM controller trusts, is not the hardware privilege level: it is a static ReRAM constant in the reset state and is invertible by an unprotected software bit
verdicts.reasoning: cram_axi.sv:20923-20927 reads exactly as quoted: `if (coreuser_enable1) vex_mm <= ((cramsoc_privilege[0] | cramsoc_privilege[1]) ^ coreuser_invert_priv1); else vex_mm <= default_mm;`. `coreuser_invert_priv0 = coreuser_control_storage[1]` (cram_axi.sv:13178) is an ordinary R/W CSR bit in a bank with no privilege qualification (see finding #3), shadowed to `coreuser_invert_priv1` at 20900. Reset values are at 22400-22401 (`coreuser_enable1 <= 1'd0; coreuser_invert_priv1 <= 1'd0;`), not 22399-22400. `default_mm` traces cleanly: cram_axi.sv:165 port -> vexsys.sv:46/390 -> soc_coresub.sv:424 `.default_mm(vexcfg_def_mm)` -> soc_coresub.sv:276 `assign vexcfg_def_mm = nvrcfgdata.cfgrrsub.rv_def_mm;`. nvrcfgs.sv:69 does contain `rv_def_mm : '1,`. Consumers verified: `vex_mm_reg` is the sole Vex privilege deny term in the key check (rrc.sv:713-714), the data check (rrc.sv:723-724), the INFO check (rrc.sv:781-782) and the CFG check (rrc.sv:815); there is no second, redundant or independent privilege input on the Vex path anywhere (grep of the whole rtl/ tree shows `vex_mm` is consumed only by rrc.sv). The design defect — a security-critical privilege signal with a software-controlled polarity XOR and a non-CPU-derived constant fallback — is real and Path B is exploitable exactly as described.
verdicts.correction: Path A is overstated on one point. In the ASIC path `nvrcfgdata` is NOT the `defcfgrrsub` literal: brc.sv:120 (`assign nvrcfgdata = nvrcfg_pkg::defnvrcfg;`) is inside `\`ifdef FPGA`, while the silicon path is brc.sv:131 `assign nvrcfgdata = syscfgdata;`, where `syscfgdata` is a `\`theregrn` register bank (brc.sv:84-89) loaded from the ReRAM boot record and reset to 0. So the *hardware reset* value of `default_mm` on silicon is 0 (deny), not 1. Path A therefore reduces to: if the shipped ReRAM boot record carries the reference `rv_def_mm='1` (nvrcfgs.sv:69) and firmware never sets `coreuser_enable1`, `vex_mm` is stuck at 1 and U-mode Vex transfers are presented to the RRC as privileged. That is still a real and important defect, but it is a configuration-image exposure, not a reset-state exposure. Second minor point: `(privilege[0]|privilege[1])` maps S-mode (2'b01) to `vex_mm==1` as well as M-mode — this is consistent with the CM7's `pri_op = axprot_reg[0]` ('not user'), so it is by design, not an additional bug.

verdicts.title: The coreuser identity/privilege configuration block is a plain memory-mapped register bank on the CPU's own data bus with no privilege qualification; AxPROT is carried but never examined, and the only lock is cleared by a software-reachable warm reset
verdicts.reasoning: Address decode reproduces end to end: cram_axi.sv:5675 `socbushandler_slave_sel_dec0 = (slice_proxy0[29:16] == 14'd14336);` with cram_axi.sv:16499 `slice_proxy0 = cramsoc_corecsr_aw_payload_addr[31:2]`, i.e. addr[31:18]==0x3800 -> 0xE000_0000; cram_axi.sv:4001/4100/5007 confirm the CSR address bus is 16 bits (= addr[17:2]), so cram_axi.sv:13121 `csrbank0_sel = (interface0_bank_bus_adr[15:10] == 2'd2)` places the bank at 0xE000_2000 with the six registers at +0x00..+0x14, and the reads at 21108-21128 confirm the offsets. I independently decoded the crossbar constant: M_BASE_ADDR = 96'd29710560958990027663148580864 -> {0x6000_0000, 0xE000_0000, 0x4000_0000}, so 0xE000_xxxx is on the ordinary dbus. I grepped every occurrence of `payload_prot` in cram_axi.sv (44 hits) and confirmed each is a pass-through assignment or a port connection — AxPROT is never compared anywhere, so there is no M/S/U qualification on writes to this bank. cram_axi.sv:13168-13175 and 21147-21149 are quoted correctly (note the LiteX naming inversion: `_re` is the write strobe). The FDRE at 22889-22895 with `.R(sys_rst)` and `assign sys_rst = rst` (5095) fed by `~resetn_vex` (vexsys.sv:233) with `resetn_vex = cmsatpg ? 1'b1 : resetn & vexcfg_en` (vexsys.sv:126) is exact. sysctrl.sv:872 `apb_ar #(.A('h84), .AR('h55aa)) sfr_rcurst1 (.ar(corereset_sw), .*)` is exact. The core claim — the entire fabric identity of the Vex is set by an unqualified store on the CPU's own load/store path — is confirmed and is the root enabler for findings #1 and #2. As a bonus corroboration, the same unqualified bank contains `irqarray0..N_soft_storage` (cram_axi.sv:616 et seq.), so the same primitive lets unprivileged code inject arbitrary interrupts.
verdicts.correction: Two corrections. (1) The crossbar evidence is attributed to the wrong file: M_ADDR_WIDTH/M_BASE_ADDR are at rtl/modules/vexriscv/rtl/cram_axi.sv:22958-22961, not VexRiscv/VexRiscv_CramSoC.v. (2) Attack step 3 — 'pre-load the storage registers, then trigger a warm reset; protect clears and the shadows reload from attacker-written storage' — is REFUTED. `sys_rst` clears the storage registers too, in the same reset block that clears the lock: cram_axi.sv:22387 `coreuser_control_storage <= 2'd0;`, 22392 `coreuser_map_lo_storage <= 32'd0;`, 22396 `coreuser_uservalue_storage <= 18'd0;`, 22398 `coreuser_protect_storage <= 1'd0;`, 22418 `coreuser_user_default <= 2'd0;`. The warm reset also resets the Vex itself, so the attacker's code stops running. What the warm reset actually does is return the block to `coreuser_enable1==0`, i.e. the `default_mm`/`default_user` state of finding #2 — a real concern, but a different one than described. Also, the bank is behind the Vex's own dbus crossbar inside cram_axi, so it is reachable only from the Vex, not from 'any bus master'.

verdicts.title: The RISC-V core has no PMP of any kind; with satp.MODE=Bare every privilege level, including U-mode, has unrestricted physical access to the entire SoC
verdicts.reasoning: `grep -ci pmp VexRiscv/VexRiscv_CramSoC.v` returns 0, and I enumerated every CSR literal in the netlist (`grep -o "12'h[0-9a-f]*" | sort -u`): 0x0,100,104,105,140,141,142,143,144,180,300,301,302,303,304,305,340,341,342,343,344,9c0,b00,b02,b80,b82,bc0,c00,c02,c80,c82,cc0,dc0,f11,f12,f13,f14,fc0 — no pmpcfg (0x3A0-3A3) and no pmpaddr (0x3B0-3BF). GenCramSoC.scala:87-193 contains no PmpPlugin. The MMU fail-open behaviour reproduces verbatim at VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:6564 and 6691 (`requireMmuLockupCalc = (...) && MmuPlugin_satp_mode`), 6753/6761/6769 (allowRead/allowWrite/allowExecute forced 1'b1), 6777-6783 (exception forced 1'b0), 6745-6750 (physical = virtual pass-through), and 7701 (`MmuPlugin_satp_mode <= 1'b0` at reset). So with satp.MODE==0 there is no gate of any kind on the Vex's data path, and there is no mechanism by which M-mode can sandbox itself from S-mode. This is a genuine and material weakness in this specific SoC because the fabric-side coreuser bank sits at 0xE000_2000 on that same unchecked path (finding #3).
verdicts.correction: Two calibrations. (1) This is an architectural omission, not an RTL defect: PMP is optional in the RISC-V privileged spec, and a core with no PMP and satp.MODE=0 permitting all accesses is spec-conformant behaviour, so it should be reported as a design weakness rather than a bug. (2) The 'U-mode has unrestricted physical access' framing overstates the realistic case — U-mode only sees flat physical memory if the supervisor runs it with satp.MODE==0, which no real OS does. The substantive, always-true consequence is narrower: S-mode has unrestricted physical read/write of the whole map at any time (one `csrw satp, 0` away), so M-mode firmware cannot be isolated from a compromised kernel, and the four coreuser identities sharing this core have no CPU-level isolation. Minor evidence error carried in the attack scenario: rrc.sv:286 is `ahb_ar #(.A('hF0), .AR(PM_RRAM_SUICIDE)) sfr_rrcar (.ar(rrcar_suicide), .resetn(coreresetn), .sfrlock(1'b0), .*);` — an `ahb_ar`, not an `apb_ar`, and PM_RRAM_SUICIDE is 16'h2468 per rrc.sv:256.

verdicts.title: sstatus (CSR 0x100) exposes and permits writing mstatus.MPRV, an M-mode-only field, letting Supervisor mode redirect Machine-mode data accesses through Supervisor-controlled page tables
verdicts.reasoning: The RTL defect is real and every citation reproduces (with two one-line offsets). VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:8264-8272 is the `execute_CsrPlugin_csr_256` (sstatus) write block and it does contain `MmuPlugin_status_mprv <= CsrPlugin_csrMapping_writeDataSignal[17];` at line 8271; the identical assignment for mstatus is at 8195, confirming MPRV is registered against both CSRs. The read-back leak is at 7362 `_zz_CsrPlugin_csrMapping_readDataInit_25[17:17] = MmuPlugin_status_mprv;`. csr_256 is 12'h100 (line 9017) and the privilege gate is at 7466 (not 7467), `CsrPlugin_privilege < csrAddress[9:8]`, which for 0x100 is `priv < 2'b01` — S-mode passes. I traced the MMU consumption by hand: with MPRV=1 and MPP!=2'b11, `when_MmuPlugin_l131_1` (6702) is false and `when_MmuPlugin_l134` (6704) is false, so neither clear at 6693-6699 fires and `MmuPlugin_ports_1_requireMmuLockupCalc` stays equal to `MmuPlugin_satp_mode` while `CsrPlugin_privilege == 2'b11`. The permission check at 6777 does use `CsrPlugin_privilege` rather than MPP, so no U/S bit constrains the redirected access. MPRV is cleared only at 7948-7950 on `CsrPlugin_xretAwayFromMachine`. This is a genuine deviation from the RISC-V privileged spec (sstatus is defined to contain only SIE/SPIE/UBE/SPP/VS/FS/XS/SUM/MXR/SD) and it is an upstream VexRiscv MmuPlugin issue worth reporting to the vendor.
verdicts.correction: Severity is overstated in this SoC's context. Because there is no PMP and satp.MODE resets to Bare (finding #4, verified), an S-mode attacker already has unrestricted physical read/write over the entire address map, including all M-mode code and data, with a single `csrw satp, x0`. MPRV therefore adds only a redirection primitive against M-mode's own virtual accesses; it does not unlock anything the attacker cannot already reach directly. It is a real spec-conformance defect that would be critical on a core with PMP, but here it is incremental. Downgrading high -> medium.

verdicts.title: mcounteren and scounteren are not implemented, so User mode has unrestricted access to the cycle-accurate cycle and instret counters
verdicts.reasoning: Verified directly. VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:6266-6285 contains the four blocks `if(execute_CsrPlugin_csr_3072/3200/3074/3202) if(execute_CSR_READ_OPCODE) execute_CsrPlugin_illegalAccess = 1'b0;` exactly as quoted, and 9005-9014 confirms those are 12'hc00/c80/c02/c82. My independent enumeration of every `12'h...` literal in the netlist contains neither 12'h306 (mcounteren) nor 12'h106 (scounteren), and `grep -c "12'h306\|12'h106"` returns 0. The gate at 7466 is a no-op for the 0xC00 block since `2'b00 < 2'b00` is false. I also confirmed the supporting claim about cacheability: VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:6801 shows `DBusCachedPlugin_mmuBus_rsp_isIoAccess` matches only physical addr[31:28] in {4,5,A,B,C,D,E,F}, so ReRAM at 0x6xxx_xxxx — including the key window 0x603F_xxxx — is cacheable in the 16 KB D-cache and therefore observable by cache timing. The AesZkn constant-time note also checks out (VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:2839-2847, ROM `en` tied 1'b1, fixed latency).
verdicts.correction: Severity is overstated. Absent counter-enable CSRs is common in embedded RISC-V cores and, per the spec, when mcounteren is not implemented the *machine-mode* view is simply that the counters are always enabled — this is a hardening gap, not a defect. More importantly it is largely subsumed: on this core untrusted code sharing the CPU with key-handling code already has unrestricted physical access with no PMP (finding #4), so `rdcycle` is not the marginal primitive that makes attacks practical. Downgrading medium -> low. The finding is still worth reporting as a hardening recommendation for a respin.

missed.title: Every RRC key/data/CFG/INFO access-control check is qualified by `data_op` (!AxPROT[2]), and the Vex instruction bus hardwires AxPROT[2]=1 — so an instruction fetch reads ReRAM key slots with no access control at all
missed.description: The Vex's instruction-fetch AXI port drives a constant AxPROT: `assign iBusAxi_ar_payload_prot = 3'b110;` (VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:7484), i.e. AxPROT[2]=1 = instruction fetch. That value is passed through cram_axi.sv:5132 (`assign ibus_axi_arprot = cramsoc_ibus_axi_ar_payload_prot;`) to vexsys.sv:269 (`.ibus_axi_arprot(iaxim.arprot)`) with `iaxim.aruser = AXIIID4` = daric_cfg::AMBAID4_VEXI = 4'h3 (daric_cfg_pkg.sv:73), so the RRC classifies it as `vexsel` (rrc.sv:667). Inside the RRC, rrc.sv:678-679 define `inst_op = axprot_reg[2]` and `data_op = !axprot_reg[2]`, and EVERY one of the five access-control terms is ANDed with `data_op`: `key_access_error_pre ... & data_op & keysel` (rrc.sv:712-717), `data_access_error_pre ... & data_op & datasel` (723-727), `code_access_error_data ... & data_op & codesel` (772-774), `info_access_error_pre ... & data_op` (781-782), `cfg_access_error_pre ... & data_op` (818-819). The only instruction-fetch check, `code_access_error_inst` (rrc.sv:770), is additionally qualified by `codesel`, and rrc.sv:686 defines `codesel = (haddr_reg[31:12] < PM_CODE_REGION_BORDER)` with PM_CODE_REGION_BORDER = 20'h603D_A (rrc.sv:644). The key region is PM_KEY_REGION = 16'h603F and the data region 16'h603E (rrc.sv:355-356) — both ABOVE the code border, so `codesel` is 0 there. Consequently, for an instruction fetch targeting 0x603F_xxxx or 0x603E_xxxx, all five error terms evaluate to 0, `cmd_user_read_dis` (rrc.sv:828) is 0, and the RRC returns the raw key/data-slot contents. The coreuser owner check, the `vex_mm` privilege check, the `core_rd_dis` bit and the `trustkey` check are all bypassed simultaneously. This is a complete access-control bypass of the ReRAM key store, independent of findings #1-#3 (it does not require the attacker to control the coreuser tag at all).
missed.attack_scenario: 1. Attacker has code execution on the Vex at any level that can set the PC to an arbitrary physical address — trivially M-mode or S-mode, and U-mode too whenever satp.MODE==0 (no PMP, finding #4). 2. Attacker installs a trap handler and jumps to 0x603F_0000 (the ReRAM key window). The fetch is issued on the iBus with AxPROT=3'b110, so `data_op`==0 and `codesel`==0, every RRC error term is 0, and the RRC returns the 32-byte key-slot line into the 16 KB I-cache and into the decode stage — with no coreuser, no vex_mm, no core_rd_dis and no trustkey check performed. 3. The fetched word is decoded. Because `catchIllegalInstruction = true` (GenCramSoC.scala:141) and VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:5420 sets `decodeExceptionPort_payload_badAddr = decode_INSTRUCTION`, which lands in mtval/stval at 8465/8473, an illegal encoding hands the attacker's trap handler the fetched 32-bit word verbatim. Iterating the PC across the key window reads out key material a word at a time; legal encodings are recovered from their architectural side effects and from mepc deltas. 4. The same bypass applies to the ReRAM DATA region 0x603E_xxxx and to any INFO/CFG word reached by fetch.

missed.title: ReRAM key and data regions are cacheable in the Vex's 16 KB write-back D-cache and 16 KB I-cache, and nothing invalidates them on an ASID / coreuser / privilege change, so RRC access control is enforced only on the first fill
missed.description: The MmuPlugin's ioRange — the only thing that marks an address non-cacheable — covers physical addr[31:28] in {0x4,0x5,0xA,0xB,0xC,0xD,0xE,0xF} only (GenCramSoC.scala:172-181, synthesized at VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:6671 for the iBus and 6801 for the dBus). ReRAM at 0x6xxx_xxxx is absent, so the ReRAM key window 0x603F_xxxx, the data window 0x603E_xxxx and the CFG/ACRAM window 0x603D_Cxxx are all CACHEABLE, in both the 16 KB 4-way instruction cache and the 16 KB 4-way write-back data cache (GenCramSoC.scala:95-121). Note that `isIoAccess` is computed from the *physical* address unconditionally, so this holds even with satp.MODE==0. The RRC performs its coreuser/vex_mm/ACRAM check per AXI transaction (rrc.sv:660-664, 712-727) — that is, only on a cache fill or a dirty writeback. A subsequent load that HITS in the D-cache never reaches the AXI bus and is therefore never checked. There is no invalidation of the data cache on any security-relevant event: the only flush source in the whole design is `dataCache_1_io_cpu_flush_valid = (execute_arbitration_isValid && execute_MEMORY_MANAGMENT)` (VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:5179), i.e. an explicit cache-management instruction. A satp write invalidates only the MmuPlugin TLB entries (`MmuPlugin_ports_0_cache_N_valid <= 1'b0` at VexRiscv_CramSoC.v:8293-8301) — not the data or instruction caches. `withInvalidate = false` in the DataCacheConfig. Nothing observes `coreuser_vex` or `vex_mm` changing. The CM7 path shows the designers were aware that identity transitions need handling (cm7sys.sv:768-773 implements a `coreuser_keep`/`coreuser_filtercyc` debounce on identity change); the Vex path has no equivalent and, critically, no cache action.
missed.attack_scenario: 1. Privileged Vex firmware running under the boot0 identity (coreuser_vex[4]=1, vex_mm=1) reads a ReRAM key slot at 0x603F_xxxx. The RRC permits the fill; the 32-byte line lands in the D-cache. 2. Control transfers to lower-privilege or different-identity code — an S-mode kernel, a U-mode task, or simply another ASID (`csrw satp` with a different ASID, which the coreuser LUT then maps to fw1). No cache maintenance is performed, because none is architecturally required and the RTL provides no automatic invalidation. 3. The attacker executes an ordinary load from 0x603F_xxxx. With satp.MODE==0 there is no page permission (no PMP, finding #4); the access hits in the physically-tagged D-cache and returns the key bytes without ever generating an AXI transaction, so the RRC's coreuser/vex_mm/core_rd_dis/trustkey checks are never evaluated. 4. The dual also holds for writes: a store that hits an already-resident dirty line is never seen by the RRC, and the eventual writeback carries `vex_mm` sampled at eviction time rather than at store time.

missed.title: The Vex coreuser encoder has no 'no identity' value — every possible ASID maps one-hot onto one of the four privileged ReRAM identities, and both the reset and unmatched-ASID defaults select boot0, the most privileged
missed.description: `coreuser_coreuser_4bit` is produced by a full 2-to-4 one-hot case at cram_axi.sv:5851-5883 whose four arms emit 4'd1, 4'd2, 4'd4 and 4'd8 and which covers all four values of the 2-bit selector, so the initial `coreuser_coreuser_4bit <= 4'd0;` is always overridden and the output can never be 4'b0000. That value becomes `coreuser_vex[7:4]` (cram_axi.sv:20921). Per the RRC's own map (rrc.sv:642 `coreuser [7]:fw1, [6]:fw0, [5]:boot1, [4]:boot0`) and the bit ordering at cram_axi.sv:20921, selector 0 -> coreuser_vex[4] = boot0, 1 -> boot1, 2 -> fw0, 3 -> fw1. There is therefore no way for firmware to express 'this context has no ReRAM identity': every ASID the CPU can install owns exactly one of the four identities and passes the RRC's owner test `(coreuser_in[7:4] & userid_k[7:4])==0` for every slot assigned to it. Worse, the encoding is fail-open in the least-privileged direction: selector 0 — the value every relevant register resets to — is boot0, the identity that also satisfies the CFG/ACRAM gate `coreuser_in[5] | coreuser_in[4]` at rrc.sv:815. The relevant resets are cram_axi.sv:22396 `coreuser_uservalue_storage <= 18'd0;` (all eight LUT uservalues and the default, cram_axi.sv:13194-13205) and cram_axi.sv:22418 `coreuser_user_default <= 2'd0;`. So if firmware sets `coreuser_control.enable` before programming `coreuser_uservalue` (0xE000_2010), or if any ASID fails to match a LUT entry and falls through to `coreuser_user_default` at cram_axi.sv:5840, the resulting identity is boot0 with full access to the boot0-owned key slots and to the 0x603D_Cxxx CFG/ACRAM region. A safe design would reserve one encoding for 'deny' (coreuser == 4'b0000) so that unconfigured and unmatched contexts fail closed.
missed.attack_scenario: 1. Boot firmware writes `coreuser_control = 0x1` at 0xE000_2000 to enable the coreuser block but has not yet (or does not fully) program `coreuser_map_lo`/`map_hi`/`uservalue` at 0xE000_2008/0x200C/0x2010 — the storage registers are still at their reset value of zero. 2. Any code running with any ASID now resolves through the LUT to selector 0 (either by matching a zero-valued LUT entry or by falling through to `coreuser_user_default`, cram_axi.sv:5840), which encodes to 4'd1 = coreuser_vex[4] = boot0. 3. Because boot0 is the identity that satisfies both the key-slot owner test at rrc.sv:712 for every boot0-owned slot and the `coreuser_in[5] | coreuser_in[4]` gate at rrc.sv:815, that code reads the boot0 key slots and the 0x603D_Cxxx CFG/ACRAM region — which contains the ACRAM ownership descriptors themselves. 4. Even with a fully programmed LUT, firmware has no way to give an untrusted context a null identity; the best available choice is fw1, which still owns whatever slots are tagged fw1, so a compromised fw1 process cannot be demoted below fw1 without reprogramming the ACRAM.
missed.line_note: Reset values at cram_axi.sv:22396 and 22418; LUT uservalue field map at cram_axi.sv:13194-13205

refuters.reasoning:
I independently reproduced the whole chain from the RTL rather than trusting the write-up.

Confirmed facts:
- bio_bdma.sv:122 `parameter AHBMID4 = daric_cfg::AMBAID4_MDMA` (=4'h7 per daric_cfg_pkg.sv:77), emitted on the memory AXI master at :1360 `assign axim.awuser = AHBMID4|'0;` and :1373 `assign axim.aruser = AHBMID4|'0;`.
- soc_ifsub.sv:344 instantiates `bio_bdma #() bio (` with no override; :370 `.axim (bdma_axi32_local)`; :100 `axi_thru bdma_thru (bdma_axi32_local, bdma_axi32);` — no AxUSER rewrite anywhere.
- Routing: bmxcore.sv:199 `axitrans_axi2pulp at5(.axis(bdma_axi32),.axim(aximux_dma_pulp[1]));` -> axi_mux_dma (:215) -> axi_mux (:254) -> at3 -> nic `.s2` (:292) -> `.m0(rrc_axi64)`; nic1_intf.sv:362/157 carry ARUSER_s2->ARUSER_m0. Widths are consistent (axiif default UW=8, bmxcore XUDW=8), so the 4-bit ID survives.
- rrc.sv:473 `bit [3:0] hauser_reg;` loaded at :545 from `ahbarray.hauser`, which aab_intf.sv:116 drives from ARUSER. rrc.sv:666-668 compares only against CM7A/VEXI/VEXD/SCEA/SCES; :670-671 `assign coreuser_mux = scesel ? sceuser : vexsel ? coreuser_vex : coreuser_cm7;` has no deny default, so 0x7 silently inherits the CM7's live coreuser.
- Substituting cm7sel=vexsel=scesel=0 into rrc.sv:815-821 makes `cfg_prev_dis`=0 and both `cfg_rd_dis&(cm7sel|vexsel)` / `cfg_wr_dis&(cm7sel|vexsel)`=0, so `cfg_access_error_pre` is identically 0. The boot0/boot1 (`coreuser_in[5]|coreuser_in[4]`) and privileged-mode gates on the ReRAM CFG/ACRAM region disappear entirely for this master.
- rrc.sv:722-726 (data slots) collapses to only the `((coreuser_in[7:4] & userid_k[7:4])==0)` owner-nibble term evaluated against the CM7's live tag; `core_rd_dis_d`/`core_wr_dis_d` and the privileged-mode terms are annihilated.
- bmxcore.sv:162-165 confirms the MDMA — whose ID the BDMA re-uses — is address-excluded from ReRAM (`// to nic_1, but no ReRAM`), which is exactly why rrc.sv never needed a case for 0x7. The BDMA's AXI port has no equivalent exclusion.

Refutation attempts that failed: AxUSER width truncation (none, UW=8 end to end); a compensating address filter on bdma_axi32 (none); a deny-by-default or assertion in rrc (none); an override at a second instantiation site (bio_bdma_wrapper.sv:477 is also unparameterized).

Escalation I verified beyond the original claim: `key_access_error_pre` (rrc.sv:715-717) is gated by `& (userid_k[7:4] != 4'h0)`, so a key slot with a zero owner nibble is open to every master. Because the CFG/ACRAM region is unconditionally writable by hauser 0x7, the attacker rewrites `userid_k[7:4]` to 0 (or repoints `akeyid` at a trusted key id) and then reads the key material out with no `trustkey` requirement. The write-enable register itself is unprotected: rrc.sv:274 `sfr_rrccr (.cr(rrccr), ..., .sfrlock(1'b0), .*)`, and rrc.sv:579-580 gate `rram_write_run` only on `rrccr[1]` plus a magic data word. So this is a path to full ReRAM key extraction, not just a data-slot read.

Exploitability walk-through: attacker needs software execution with MMIO write access to the BIO/BDMA APB pages (soc_ifsub.sv:361-368, apbper[4] config and apbper[5:8] imem) — i.e. driver/kernel-level code, not an arbitrary MPU-confined userspace task. They load a BIO program, set the memory-filter window (or disable_filter_mem) to cover 0x6000_0000, and issue reads/writes; the internal axil_crossbar at bio_bdma.sv:1195-1199 decodes 0x6000_0000/29 bits onto the memory master. No physical access, no glitching, no decapsulation, no probing. Observation is direct read data returned to the BIO program.

Honest caveats that lower it slightly from the write-up's framing: (a) it is not reachable from fully unprivileged userspace under a correct MPU/MMU configuration — it needs peripheral MMIO; (b) for a boot0-owned data slot the owner-nibble term still needs the CM7 to be in that region at the moment the read lands, which is a (very winnable) race since BIO can spam the read in a loop. Neither caveat matters for the decisive part: cfg_access_error_pre is a hard constant 0 for this master, with no coreuser dependence at all, and cm7sys.sv:761 `coreuserreg0pre[7] = ~|coreuserreg0pre[6:4]` means code executing from SRAM already carries the [7] tag, so fw1-owned slots need no race either.

The controls defeated — per-slot core_rd_dis/core_wr_dis (SCE-only slots) and the boot0/boot1-only ACRAM config region — are exactly the ones designed to hold against privileged CPU firmware, so this is a genuine boundary crossing and not a capability the attacker already had. Silicon is taped out and unpatchable. I could not refute it.

I attempted to refute this and could not; I independently re-derived every step from the RTL rather than accepting the prior reviewers' trace.

Verified facts (all read directly):
1. sce.sv:414-418 instantiates the one and only SCERAM with `.clrend (scedma_pkg::SEGADDR_RNGA-1)`. I checked every other cryptoram instantiation in the repo (alu.sv:580, alu.sv:598, pke.sv:1511, pke.sv:1529, aes.sv:512, combohasha.sv:854) — none overrides clrend, so all other crypto RAMs get the full `thecfg.WCNT-1` wipe. The truncation is unique and deliberate.
2. Segment map recomputed from scedma_pkg.sv:211-230 gives SEGADDR_RNGA=1984, SEGADDR_RNGB=2240, WCNT=2560 (scedma_pkg.sv:319). Independent cross-check: daric_defs.sv:271 `SCE_SEG_RNGA (SCEMEMBASE + 32'h1F00)` and bao1x_peri.h:27751 `SEG_RNGA_BASE 0x40021f00` → 0x1F00/4 = 1984. Exact match.
3. cryptoram.sv:61-64: `ramclrdone = (ramclrfsm == clrend)` with the write asserted while ramclren — addresses 0..1983 are zeroed, 1984..2559 are never written. Confirmed.
4. sce_sec.sv:87 `assign sceramclr = ( initregs == 4'h7 ) | ar_clrram ;` is the ONLY driver of the wipe; grep for ramclr/sceramclr across rtl/ shows no other sanitisation path, no tamper-triggered wipe. cryptoram.sv:112-113 ties `.scmben('0), .scmbkey('0)` so there is no scrambling either.
5. Readability: sce_sec.sv:72 `ahben = mode_non ? 1'b1 : ...` opens the SCE AHB gate unconditionally in mode_non; sce.sv:370 `acenable = mode_sec` plus scedma_ac.sv:47 `chnlac[i] = acenable ? chnlacrule : '1` (I read scedma_ac.sv end-to-end) bypasses the entire rule table in mode_non for every channel. Even with rules enabled, RNGA's 8'b10_11_10_10 in the `bit[0:CHNLACCNT-1]` field yields ahb-read = 1.
6. Raw-word addressing: scedma_amba.sv:103 `segaddr: ( SEGCFGS[...].isfifo & segfifoen[...] ) ? SEGCFGS[...].segaddr : ahbshaddr_dp`. sfr_ffen (sce_glbsfra.sv:93) is an apb_cr with IV=0; and even if a previous owner left it set, the attacker reaches the same SCE APB space through the open ahben gate and can clear it first.
7. No auto-overwrite compensating control: trng.sv:280-282 shows `rngcore_en` is a software-started bounded batch (`ar_start` ... `rngcnt == opt_rngcnt-1 & chnlo_done`), not free-running, so consumed words are not promptly refreshed. sce_memc is on the system reset (sce.sv:397), so the FIFO pointers also survive an SCE reset.
8. Asset relevance: `grep -rl trng rtl/modules --include=*.sv` returns only crypto_top/trng.sv (plus a VexRiscv FPGA soft block). RNGA/RNGB at 0x40021F00/0x40022300 is the chip's sole RNG delivery path, exported in the SoC memory map and headers. Residue there is by construction the random values firmware used for nonces/ephemeral scalars/session keys.

Exploitability walk-through I validated step by step: trusted session takes the SCE (scemode!=0, which then self-locks via sce_glbsfra.sv:78 `sfrlock(~devmode & (|cr_scemode))`), draws randomness from the pool, then relinquishes via ar_reset (0x5a at SCE+0x1c) or a warm/system reset. sceresetn drops, cr_scemode returns to 0 (glbsfr is on sceresetn, sce.sv:224), initregs reaches 4'h7, the wipe runs and stops at word 1983. The SCE is now mode_non: ahben=1, acenable=0, everything open. Attacker — unprivileged code on either CPU, or BIO/BDMA/MDMA as an AHB master, no physical access, no glitching, no equipment — clears sfr_ffen and issues 512 word loads from 0x40021F00-0x400226FF, recovering the prior session's randomness verbatim. scedma_ac raises acerr only on denials, so nothing is logged.

Aggravator the original finding understates: in mode_sec the RNGA/RNGB rule has ahb-write = 0, so the owning secure firmware cannot even zero the pool over AHB. The only self-help is a SCEDMA AXI write channel (axi-write bit = 1) DMAing zeros in with the FIFO disabled — non-obvious and undocumented. So the hardware provides no practical sanitisation for exactly the region its sanitisation primitive skips.

Why not critical: the leak is conditional on the previous owner having drawn secret-bearing randomness and not having manually flushed the pool, and a firmware-level mitigation (DMA zeros in, or drain 512 words) does exist. It is not an unconditional key-read primitive. Why not lower than high: the precondition is the ordinary case for any chip that signs or does key agreement, the only entropy path on the die goes through this pool, the attack needs nothing beyond ordinary code execution, the values recovered (ECDSA/EdDSA nonces, ephemeral scalars, session keys) collapse directly to long-term private keys, and the part is fabricated and unpatchable in hardware.

Not refuted. Severity high, exploitability practical.

I could not refute this. Every mechanical claim reproduces from the RTL independently.

VERIFIED CHAIN:
1. rtl/modules/crypto_top/rtl/sce.sv:414-418 overrides the wipe end address on the single SCERAM instance: `.clrend (scedma_pkg::SEGADDR_RNGA-1)`. RAMCNT=1 (scedma_pkg.sv), so the generate loop covers the one and only SCERAM.
2. rtl/modules/crypto_top/rtl/cryptoram.sv:61-64: `assign ramclrdone = ( ramclrfsm == clrend ); theregrn(ramclrfsm) <= ramclr ? clrstart : ramclrdone ? '0 : ramclrfsm + ramclren; theregrn(ramclren) <= ramclr ? 1'b1 : ramclrdone ? 1'b0 : ramclren;` with ramaddr_clr=ramclrfsm, ramwr_clr='1, ramwdat_clr='0. Address 1983 IS written (ramclren still 1 that cycle), so coverage is words 0..1983 and words 1984..2559 are never zeroed.
3. I re-derived the segment map from scedma_pkg.sv rather than trusting the report: LKEY0/KEY64/SKEY128/SCRT192/MSG256/HOUT384/SOB448/PCON512(sz0)/PKB512/PIB768/PSIB1280(sz0)/POB1280/PSOB1536/AKEY1792/AIB1856/AOB1920/RNGA1984(256)/RNGB2240(256). Every segment has ramsel:'0, so RNGA/RNGB are in the same SCERAM. rtl/verif/utility/daric_defs.sv:271-272 independently corroborates (`SCE_SEG_RNGA = SCEMEMBASE + 32'h1F00`, RNGB +0x2300).
4. sceramclr is the ONLY sanitisation trigger in the whole tree (grep ramclr): sce_sec.sv:87 `assign sceramclr = ( initregs == 4'h7 ) | ar_clrram ;`, initregs from sce_sec.sv:85 on sceresetn release. cryptoram gets .ramclr(sceramclr) at sce.sv:424.
5. TRNG destination confirmed: trng.sv:366 `assign chnlo_cfg.wpsegcfg = ~opt_segsel ? scedma_pkg::SEG_RNGA : scedma_pkg::SEG_RNGB;` with chnlo_start = rngcore_en & rngcore_dataout_vld & ~chnlo_busy (trng.sv:357). There is no alternative software-visible TRNG output path -- the apb_buf buf_* port is an INPUT path (personalization/additional input), not an output.

COMPENSATING CONTROLS I SPECIFICALLY HUNTED FOR AND DID NOT FIND:
- No second wipe primitive anywhere (grep ramclr/clrend across rtl/ returns only the per-engine ramclr fanout of the same sceramclr, all inside the wiped range or in separate RAMs).
- ar_ffclr only clears scedma_simplefifo pointers, not memory.
- No SRAM scrambling: cryptoram.sv:112-113 `.scmben('0), .scmbkey('0)`.
- sce_memc is on the SYSTEM reset (sce.sv:397 `.resetn(resetn)`), so an SCE-level reset does not even reset the FIFO pointers.
- The NVR access-rule override (scedma_ac.sv:66-68, nvracrules[29]==8'h5a) cannot mitigate: it feeds chnlacrules which are bypassed entirely when acenable=0.
- sfr_scemode self-locks once nonzero (sce_glbsfra.sv:79 `.sfrlock(~devmode & (|cr_scemode))`), so the ONLY way to leave a secure session is a reset -- exactly the path that runs the truncated wipe. This makes the exposure the normal, unavoidable end-of-session state rather than a corner case.
- No upstream coreuser filter on the SCE AHB slave: soc_coresub.sv routes coreahbmux[2] straight into sce.ahbs; the only gate is sce_sec's ahb_gate, which is wide open in mode_non. (sce_sec's ahbs_lock output is dangling in sce.sv -- declared at sce.sv:109, connected at 287, consumed nowhere.)

EVIDENCE THE PRIOR REVIEWERS MISSED THAT STRENGTHENS THE FINDING: RNGA's rule 8'b10_11_10_10 has index 6 (internal-channel read) = 1, so the SCE's internal DMA is permitted to copy RNGA into the key segments SKEY(128)/AKEY(1792)/PKB(512). Those destinations lie below word 1983 and ARE wiped, while the byte-identical source copy in the RNG pool is not. The hardware thus demonstrably erases generated key material from one location while leaving an exact copy in another -- turning this from a speculative firmware-dependent issue into a concrete intent-vs-implementation mismatch.

MINOR CORRECTIONS (do not affect the verdict): a full system reset also asserts sceramclr and produces the same truncated wipe, so the report's parenthetical about the SRAM macro having no reset is beside the point but harmless; and the uncleared range is words 1984..2559 (2496..2559 unallocated), not 1984..2495.

CAVEATS ON MAGNITUDE (why I did not raise it to critical): the residue only contains secrets if the prior owner actually pulled randoms through the pool with segfifoen set for that FIFO (with segfifoen=0 the TRNG channel repeatedly rewrites only words 1984..1987, since chnlo_cfg.wpptr_start='0 and transsize=4), and the ultimate impact depends on what firmware does with those randoms. But the pool is the sole hardware path from the TRNG to software and to the key segments, so any on-chip key/nonce generation goes through it, and firmware is given no hardware means to sanitise it.

Exploitability is practical and software-only: an unprivileged AHB master reaches 0x4002_0000 in mode_non, writes 0 to sfr_ffen at 0x4002_8030 if needed, and issues 512 word loads from 0x4002_1F00..0x4002_26FF. No error is raised because the access is permitted, not denied. The chip is taped out, so this is unpatchable in hardware; the only mitigation is firmware explicitly overwriting RNGA/RNGB before releasing the SCE, which is worth telling the vendor.

CONFIRMED MECHANISM (all in rtl/modules/rrc/rtl/rrc.sv):

- rrc.sv:853 shows the NV path IS gated: `( rrcfsm == 0 ) & rram_write_run & (!cmd_user_write_dis) ? 4`. The asymmetry is genuine; cmd_user_write_dis (rrc.sv:827) is consumed only at rrc.sv:576/577/850/853.
- The SRAM really commits: rrc.sv:390 `acram_cs = (!acram_wrbusy) & (!acram_rdbusy_pre)` (low-active cen), rrc.sv:391 `acram_wr = !acram_wrbusy` (low-active gwen), rrc.sv:396 clock enable, rrc.sv:380 idx increment — four 64-bit writes at {haddr_reg[13:5],acram_idx}.

ADDRESS MAP CORROBORATED INDEPENDENTLY: the testbench image loader daric_rv32_tb.sv:717 loads 512 CFG lines from 0x3DC000, 2048 key lines from 0x3F0000, 2048 data lines from 0x3E0000. That matches the 11-bit write index {haddr_reg[13:5],idx} covering the whole 2048-entry acram2kx64 and the read index ahbarray.haddr[16:6], with write-side haddr[13] aliasing read-side haddr[16] (key vs data half). A CFG write at 0x603D_E000+n*32 lands exactly on key descriptors.

ENFORCEMENT IS NULLED: rrc.sv:688-697 show keycfg/datacfg come only from acram_rdata; rrc.sv:717 and 726 terminate both error expressions with `& (userid_k[7:4] != 4'h0)` / `& (userid_d[7:4] != 4'h0)`. A forged zero-owner descriptor zeroes key_access_error, so cmd_user_read_dis is 0 and rrc.sv:555-558 return raw key data instead of 64'h0. The trustkey term sits inside that AND and never needs defeating, so the report's akeyid/trustkey[127] argument is superfluous but not load-bearing.

REFUTATIONS I TRIED AND FAILED:
1. "The RRC SFR is privileged" — it is not. rrc.sv:274 `.sfrlock(1'b0)`; ahb_cr_ECO/ahb_sfr2_ECO (rrc.sv:1139-1185) have no user/privilege port. soc_coresub.sv:823-824 binds ahbs/ahbx to coreahbmux[0] from ahb_demux_map (soc_coresub.sv:626-637); ahb_demux.sv:114 `assign ahbmaster[i].hauser = ahbslave.hauser;` is pure pass-through; bmxcore.sv has zero hauser/coreuser/filter logic. Nothing gates rrccr[1].
2. "The attacker already has this privilege" — no. cm7sys.sv:744-776 derives coreuser from corecm7pc against coreusermap, with coreuserreg0pre[7] = ~|coreuserreg0pre[6:4], so code outside boot regions (including from SRAM) gets the fw1 catch-all with coreuser[5:4]==0. Such code is denied by cfg_prev_dis (rrc.sv:815) and by the (coreuser_in[7:4] & userid_k[7:4])==0 term, so it provably cannot read a boot0-owned or core_rd_dis key without the forge. Genuine cross-privilege escalation.
3. "Unreliable burst" — partly true: because the write is denied rrcfsm stays 0, so ahbarray.hready (rrc.sv:582) stays high and haddr_reg is not frozen during the 4-cycle ACRAM burst; an intervening RRC transaction would retarget it. But the attacker avoids that by running the sequence from SRAM/cache, and it is freely retryable. Does not refute; only a sequencing nuance.
4. "Something re-syncs ACRAM" — the only other load is trc_dout_ready_sdone & (brfsm==4) at rrc.sv:360, i.e. the boot read. grep for acram outside rrc.sv returns only SRAM-macro plumbing and testbench. Corruption persists until sysresetn.
5. "Detectable" — rrc.sv:583 `ahbarray.hresp = 2'h0` (silent denial); rrc.sv:292 rrcnmi = rrcint & rrccr[15] with rrccr IV 32'h0 (rrc.sv:1144), and the attacker owns rrccr and can clear rrcfr.

Also checked ahb_array_write is not suppressed for the CFG region: the oneway-counter exclusion is haddr[23:16]==8'h3D & haddr[15:13]==3'b101 (rrc.sv:497) and prog_only_data_write requires haddr[23:16]==8'h3E (rrc.sv:535); CFG at 0x603D_C000+ hits neither. And ahb_wr_buf load (rrc.sv:568-571) is qualified only by `ahb_array_write_reg & !rrccr[1]` — no access check at all.

Side observation that strengthens rather than weakens the report: cfg_prev_dis (rrc.sv:815) and cfg_rd_dis/cfg_wr_dis (rrc.sv:809-813) are all qualified by (cm7sel|vexsel) or scesel, so a master whose hauser is MDMA/BDMA matches none and cfg_access_error is identically 0 — and bmxcore.sv:186-198,287-295 do route mdma_axi/bdma_axi32 to rrc_axi64. That is a separate potential issue, not a reason to discount this one.

EXPLOITABILITY: software-only, deterministic, no glitching/probing/decap. ~10 stores (clear rrccr[1], fill the 256-bit buffer with a forged zero-owner descriptor line, set rrccr[1], write 0x9528 to the CFG address) then read the key slot. Yields plaintext ReRAM key material owned by earlier boot stages and keys marked SCE-only, plus write access to them, from unprivileged fw0/fw1-stage code. Silent, no NMI, persists until reset. This is a direct compromise of the primary asset on an unpatchable taped-out part.

That is a genuine, RTL-anchored privilege escalation across a boundary the RRC explicitly implements.

SEVERITY CALIBRATION: I downgrade critical to high. The break is total once reached (ACRAM rewrite of userid_k/core_rd_dis_k/akeyid, then key readout) and unpatchable, but it is not reachable from a bare unprivileged context — it requires write access to the BIO SFR block plus either a whitelist window over ReRAM or DISABLE_FILTER_MEM, and step 2 additionally requires the CM7's live coreuser nibble to overlap the target slot owner. For a firmware-level attacker (or any T1 attacker whose MPU/MMU does not block 0x5012_4000, which nothing in the RTL enforces) it is straightforwardly practical.

MECHANISM (verified myself, not taken from the prior review):

At t+1 the flop loads rpptr <= thecfg.rpptr_start (the clamp term tests the PREVIOUS rpptr, which is in range after any normal transfer) and simultaneously rprdvld <= 1, and rprd = rprdvld (line 140). DOES THE ATTACKER GAIN ANYTHING REAL? Yes. Reading them back escalates from "may use the key" to "may clone the key," defeating device binding and the sce_ts attestation built on hmac_pass/hmac_kid (sce_sec.sv:120). No cheaper path exists for the same actor: alu.sv:512-517 implements the ST_KI guard the hash engine lacks, and ACRULEs deny external reads of LKEY/KEY/SKEY/SCRT/PKB/AKEY (scedma_pkg.sv:290-299); AES/PKE consume keys but never emit them.

WHERE I NARROWED THE CLAIM: the attack_scenario overstates the attacker. sce_sec.sv:72-74 `assign ahben = mode_non ? 1'b1 : ((sceusersel == 0) ? (ahbs.hauser == AMBAID4_CM7P) : ...) & ((sceusersel == 0) ? In mode_non, acenable=0 makes every key segment directly AHB-readable anyway, so the bug gains nothing there. The real attacker is the SCE-owning crypto client in secure mode — exactly the actor the write-only AHB ACRULEs exist to contain, so the boundary is real, but narrower than "any unprivileged code."

With an idle SCE the rr_arb_tree grant is combinational and arbm_gnt=1 (sce_memc.sv:211), so ready is asserted. Under contention the attempt degrades harmlessly to reading MSG[0] and the attacker simply retries. Retry-based, not single-shot.

CONFIRMED RTL FACTS: daric_cfg_pkg.sv:74/81 (AMBAID4_VEXD=4'h4, AMBAID4_VEXP=4'hD); sce_sec.sv:62 and :73 both test AMBAID4_VEXD; bmxcore.sv:268-272 and :287-299 show vex_daxi reaches only nic1_intf .s4 -> rrc/sram0/sram1/qfc, never the SCE at coreahbmux[2] (soc_coresub.sv:549); the Vex's only route is vex_ahbp -> core_ahbp3[1] (soc_coresub.sv:613) -> ahb_mux3 (amba_components.sv:275 forwards hauser) carrying 4'hD (vexsys.sv:166,178 + soc_coresub.sv:402 + aab_intf.sv:116); cm7sys.sv:761 `assign coreuserreg0pre[7] = ~|coreuserreg0pre[6:4];` means coreuser_cm7 is never 8'h00 for running code; ahbs_lock is genuinely dead (sce.sv:109, sce_sec.sv:77). So yes, the VEXD branch is unreachable.

WHY THE ATTACK YIELDS NOTHING:

(1) Self-contradictory oracle. sceuserlock fires on the same 0->nonzero scemode transition that installs the CM7 identity, and from that instant ahben is 0 for hauser==4'hD. The Vex can therefore never load a key into the session the CM7 inherits, and SCE RAM was cleared by sceramclr (sce_sec.sv:87) after the preceding reset. The CM7 inherits an EMPTY engine. The finding's own attack_scenario step 3 concedes this mid-sentence ("no: every one of those accesses also goes through the same AHB slave").

(2) Zero incremental capability for the CM7. sce_sec.sv:72 `assign ahben = mode_non ? 1'b1 :` and sce.sv:150-175/270-288 show the whole SCE register space INCLUDING the glbsfr scemode register sits behind ahbsgate. In scemode==0 (the state after every reset) any master has unrestricted access, so the CM7 can write scemode=2 itself at any moment and become the legitimate owner with exactly the same coreuser. coreuserreg is loaded from coreuser_cm7 on the CM7's own access, so the bug never lets the CM7 acquire a coreuser it does not already hold. The delta versus correct RTL is nil for the CM7.

(3) The sceuser==8'h00 residual is maximally restrictive, not permissive. rrc.sv:712/717: `key_access_error_pre = (((coreuser_in[7:4] & userid_k[7:4])==0) & (ahb_write_flag|ahb_read_flag) | ...) & ... & (userid_k[7:4] != 4'h0)`. With coreuser_in==0 every owned key slot denies; userid_k[7:4]==0 slots are NO_OWNER and already open to all. An SCE DMA carrying sceuser=0 gets strictly LESS than an ordinary CPU access.

(4) Not silently shippable. ahb_gate (amba_components.sv:1037-1039) forces hsel/htrans to 0 with no error response, so a Vex secure session reads zeros for every status and result register. RV firmware entering scemode 1 or 2 fails on its first crypto operation at bring-up, and there is no bypass (ahbs_lock dead, devmode_sce[0] therefore inert). The exploit scenario requires a deployment that provably does not function.

(5) No threat-model capability changes this. It is a static parameter mismatch, not a glitchable or racy comparison; T2/T3/T4 add nothing over T1.

WHAT REMAINS (worth vendor disclosure at low severity, not high): the SCE's owner-exclusive modes (scemode 1 and 2) are structurally unusable from the VexRiscv, so any RV-hosted SCE use is confined to scemode==0 where ahben is unconditionally 1 and the CM7 has unrestricted access to SCE RAM and engines. That is a real design limitation with a latent security consequence, but it is "the isolation feature was never available," not an attack, and it is contingent on firmware we cannot inspect. The claimed high-severity cross-core key-oracle escalation is refuted.

CONFIRMED. I independently reproduced every link in the chain from the RTL and found no compensating control.

(1) sce_memc.sv:212 `assign ramm_addr[gvk] = arbm_dat[gvk].segaddr + arbm_dat[gvk].segptr;` is a bare add into an `adr_t` (12 bits, scedma_pkg.sv:23,29), so it truncates mod 4096. There is no comparison against `segcfg.segsize`, no mask, and no clamp anywhere between scedma_ac and the RAM. cryptoram.sv adds no bound either (`ramaddr0 = ramclren ? ramaddr_clr : ramaddr` straight into wire2ramm/gnrl_sramc), and `scmben('0)` means no address-dependent scrambling that would garble a cross-segment read.

(2) The bounds term really is one cycle late. sce_dmachnl.sv:123-125:
    `theregrn( rpptr ) <= ( rpptr > therpsegcfg.segsize ) ? 0 :
                          chnlstart ? thecfg.rpptr_start :
                          transdone ? (( rpptr == therpsegcfg.segsize - 1 ) ? 0 : rpptr + 1 ) : rpptr;
`theregrn` expands (rtl/modules/common/rtl/template.sv:90-91) to a plain posedge flop with async reset to '0. The clamp is evaluated on the CURRENT rpptr. rpptr is 0 after reset and 0 after every previously-clamped run, so `0 > segsize` is false and the unbounded software value loads.

(3) The read strobe is armed on the same edge: sce_dmachnl.sv:114 `assign transstart = ~busy ? start : ...`, :134 `theregrn( rprdvld ) <= transstart ? 1'b1 : ...`, :139 `assign rprd = rprdvld;`, :70 `assign rpreq.segptr = rpptr;`. Cycle N (start, busy==0): rpptr<=rpptr_start and rprdvld<=1. Cycle N+1: rprd==1 while rpptr==rpptr_start (out of range). End of N+1: clamp forces rpptr to 0. Exactly one out-of-range read is issued. It is captured at N+2 via rprdpl1vld into thedatreg (:158-168) and pushed out by `wpwr0 = ( rprdpl1vld | rprdpl2 )` (:192) to the AXI write port. sce_memc.sv:211 ties `arbm_gnt[gvk] = 1'b1`, so the arbiter grant is immediate and the read lands.

(4) scedma_ac.sv:45-47 keys only on `chnlinreq[i].segcfg.segid` and forwards `segptr` untouched (:51). scedma_amba.sv:426 bounds-checks only cr_segid; :447 `assign chnlo_thecfg.rpptr_start = cr_segptrstart;` passes the raw 12-bit SFR (scedma.sv:102/109, DW(AW)=12) through. scedma.sv:91 `assign sfrlock = 0;` — the pointer SFRs are never write-protected or locked.

(5) Live in silicon: rtl/modules/soc_coresub/rtl/soc_coresub.sv:511-553 instantiates `sce`, and rtl/asic_top/rtl/soc_top.sv:555 instantiates `soc_coresub`. Not dead or emulation-only.

Compensating controls checked and ruled out: SCERAM IS cleared on scemode transitions (sce_sec.sv:83-87, initregs/sceramclr re-armed by sceresetn via modequit), but that is irrelevant because the attack is entirely intra-session inside mode_sec. `acenable = mode_sec` (sce.sv:370) and the ahb_gate (sce_sec.sv:72-76) admits only the latched SCE owner in mode_sec, which means ACRULEs exist solely to constrain the SCE owner — so bypassing them defeats the entire purpose of the mechanism rather than being a no-op. rrc.sv:674 (`keytype_in = axid_reg[6:2]`, driven by `axim.arid = cr_segid` at scedma_amba.sv:385) plus the `keytype_in != keytype_k` term in key_access_error binds a ReRAM key slot to a specific SCERAM segment; SKEY's rule 8'b01_01_01_01 grants axi-s write (bit[5]=1) but denies axi-s read (bit[4]=0). That is an explicit "SCE may use this ReRAM key but may not read it back" guarantee, and this defect breaks it.

One correction to the reported attack path, which makes exploitation EASIER rather than refuting it: the finding uses SEGID_AOB, but AOB has isfifo:'1, fifoid:'d3 (scedma_pkg.sv:251), and sce_memc.sv:90 `assign ramptr0[gvi] = ffen[thesegid[gvi]] ? fframptr[thesegid[gvi]] : ramsreq[gvi].segptr;` substitutes the FIFO pointer for segptr whenever ffen is set — so that specific path first requires clearing cr_ffen[3] (a plain SFR in sce_glbsfr, sce.sv:239). Cleaner non-FIFO instances exist: SEGID_SOB (6, base 448) and SEGID_PSOB (12, base 1536) are both isfifo:'0 with accessrule 8'b10_00_10_00, whose bit[4] (axi-s read, chnlreq[4] per sce.sv:344 and the CHNLACCNT index comment at scedma_pkg.sv:279-282) is 1. So: sfr_sch_segid=6, sfr_sch_func=1, sfr_sch_segstart=3776, sfr_sch_transize=1, sfr_sch_axstart=<attacker buffer>, then write 0xaa to offset 0x00 -> 448+3776 = 4224 wraps to 128 = SKEY word 0, exfiltrated over axim[1]. Repeat 64 times (rpptr is left clamped at 0/1 between runs, so the primitive re-arms cleanly).

Caveat on scope, stated honestly: the attacker must be the entity that owns the SCE in mode_sec (the ahb_gate restricts mode_sec SCE access to the coreuser latched at mode entry, sce_sec.sv:58-64,72-77), and SCERAM is zeroed on mode entry, so the attacker can only read back secrets loaded during their own session. That is still a complete defeat of the only control that separates "use a ReRAM key / engine intermediate" from "read it out", and it also exposes PKB (PKE private scalars), AKEY (AES key schedule), LKEY/KEY and SCRT to any mode_sec DMA. No glitching, no timing, no physical access — pure APB register writes, fully deterministic.

CONFIRMED — I could not refute it; every load-bearing line reproduces in the RTL and the attack closes end to end with software-only access.

Mechanism verified independently, cycle by cycle:
- sce_memc.sv:212 `assign ramm_addr[gvk] = arbm_dat[gvk].segaddr + arbm_dat[gvk].segptr;` — no segsize compare, no clamp anywhere in sce_memc (lines 82-90 forward `ramsreq[gvi].segptr` untouched whenever the segment FIFO is off). adr_t is 12 bits (scedma_pkg.sv:23,29) so the add wraps mod 4096 and any of the 2560 SCERAM words is reachable from any segment base.
- sce_dmachnl.sv:123-125: the out-of-range term `( rpptr > therpsegcfg.segsize ) ? 0 :` is a branch of the SAME flop that loads `chnlstart ? thecfg.rpptr_start`. `theregrn` (ips/incdir/template.sv:82-91) is a plain async-reset flop. At the chnlstart edge rpptr still holds its in-range prior value (0 from reset, 1 after a completed 1-word transfer), so the clamp does not fire and the unbounded software value is loaded. rprdvld is armed on the same edge (:134 with transstart = ~busy ? start, :114) and `assign rprd = rprdvld` (:139). Cycle T+0: rpptr = rpptr_start, rprd=1, arbiter grants (sce_memc.sv:211 arbm_gnt=1), RAM read issued at the wrapped address; end of T+0 the clamp forces rpptr<=0 and rprdvld<=0, so exactly one out-of-range word is fetched per start. T+1: rprdpl1vld latches it into thedatreg (:158-168), wpwr (:192,195) pushes it to the write port and out as axim.wdata (scedma_amba.sv:418). Repeatable indefinitely — not a one-shot race.
- Access control is segment-ID-only, no address term: scedma_ac.sv:45-47. sce.sv:370 acenable = mode_sec; sce.sv:340-341 maps xchrpreq to chnlreq[2] = the "axi R" rule bit (scedma_pkg.sv:278-282). AOB's 8'b10_10_10_10 (scedma_pkg.sv:307, packed [0:7], index 2 = 1) permits the read; SKEY/SCRT/AKEY/PKB are 8'b01_01_01_01 (read denied on every channel). acerr never fires because the segid was legitimately permitted.
- Registers unlocked and directly software-writable: scedma.sv:91 `assign sfrlock = 0;`, scedma.sv:101-103 (segid @0x1c, segstart @0x20), scedma_amba.sv:447 `assign chnlo_thecfg.rpptr_start = cr_segptrstart;` with :445 rpsegcfg = axim_segcfgreg = SEGCFGS[cr_segid] (:426). The design bounds-checks cr_segid at :426 and never the pointer.

The asset is real, which I verified beyond the original finding: rrc.sv:620-634 documents and :712-717 implements a per-keyslot split where core_rd_dis_k = keycfg[0] (CPU read denied) is independent of sce_rd_dis_k = keycfg[2] (SCE read allowed), qualified by sce_sec_op = axprot_reg[0] & mode_sec with coreuser_in = sceuser (:670). So a ReRAM key slot can be provisioned "this coreuser may have the SCE USE this key but may never READ it." The secure AXI channel (axim[1]; the general channel gets scemode&2'h1 at scedma.sv:251, so only the secure one asserts sce_sec_op) may WRITE SKEY/AKEY/PKB (rule index 5 = 1) but not READ them (index 4 = 0). The ACRULEs are the sole enforcement of that use-but-don't-extract boundary, and this defect voids it entirely.

Concrete attack, unprivileged software only (T1), no probing/glitching/decap: take SCE ownership by writing sfr_scemode=2 while it reads 0 (sce_glbsfra.sv:78, sfrlock = ~devmode & (|cr_scemode) only latches AFTER the first write; sce_sec.sv:58-64 latches the writer's coreuser as sceuser); have the secure channel load the entitled keyslot into SKEY; clear cr_ffen for AOB's FIFO id (sce.sv:239 — required so sce_memc.sv:90 selects segptr instead of the FIFO pointer); then per word write segid=0x0f, segstart=(target-1920) mod 4096, transize=1, func=1, axstart=attacker buffer, and 0xa5 to the start AR. 64 iterations recover a 256-bit key; the same primitive reaches SCRT, AKEY, PKB, KEY, LKEY.

Refutations I attempted and that failed: (a) no downstream clamp exists in sce_memc; (b) the FIFO-pointer override does not save it because segfifoen is a plain software register; (c) segid aliasing is not an easier pre-existing route — cr_segid >= SEGCNT falls back to SEGCFG_DEF with segid:0 (LKEY), which is read-denied, so the pointer wrap is genuinely the unique bypass and this is a real escalation, not something the attacker already had; (d) rpptr is reliably in range at every chnlstart, so the window is deterministic and repeatable.

Severity high rather than critical: it requires the attacker to already hold SCE ownership in mode_sec while the target key is live in SCERAM (SCERAM is cleared on mode exit via sce_sec.sv:81-87 modequit -> sceresetnin -> sceramclr), so it does not cross to another coreuser's keys. But within that scope it fully defeats a deliberately implemented, documented hardware guarantee with a handful of APB writes, and the part is taped out and unpatchable.

The SCE is at 0x4002_0000 (daric_cfg_pkg.sv:53), i.e. exclusively in the peripheral window. CONFIRMED RTL FACTS
- sce_dmachnl.sv:123-125 is verbatim as quoted. `theregrn` (rtl/modules/common/rtl/template.sv:90) is a plain synchronous-reset non-blocking flop, so ternary priority holds: `( rpptr > therpsegcfg.segsize ) ? 0 : chnlstart ? thecfg.rpptr_start : ...` tests the RESIDENT rpptr, which is 0 after reset and wraps to 0 at the end of every completed transfer (the `transdone` branch). Therefore an out-of-range `rpptr_start` is loaded unconditionally on `chnlstart`.
- Cycle trace re-derived: `chnlstart = start & ~busy` (:104); `transstart = ~busy ? start : ~lasttrans & transdone` (:114) so `rprdvld <= 1` at the same edge (:134); `busy` only sets one edge later (:102). At cycle 1, `rprd = rprdvld` (:139) is asserted while `rpreq.segptr = rpptr` (:70) still carries the raw software value. `transdone` requires `wpwr` (:112, :192) which cannot be true at cycle 1, so exactly one out-of-range read is issued before the clamp fires. The finder's claim that the write pointer is NOT exploitable is also correct for the same reason.
- No bound downstream: scedma_ac.sv:45-46 authorises on `segcfg.segid` only; :50-51 forwards `segaddr`/`segptr` verbatim. sce_memc.sv:212 `ramm_addr[gvk] = arbm_dat[gvk].segaddr + arbm_dat[gvk].segptr;` is a 12-bit `adr_t` add (scedma_pkg.sv:23,29) into a 2560-word RAM (scedma_pkg.sv:319). `segtype` is never consulted in sce_memc.sv.
- Pointer SFRs are unlocked and full-width: scedma.sv:91 `assign sfrlock = 0;`, scedma.sv:102/109 `.DW(AW)` = 12 bits. scedma_amba.sv `chnlo_thecfg.rpptr_start = cr_segptrstart`.
- Segment map arithmetic checks out: LKEY 0, KEY 64, SKEY 128, SCRT 192, MSG 256, HOUT 384, SOB 448, PKB 512, PIB 768, POB 1280, PSOB 1536, AKEY 1792, AIB 1856, AOB 1920, RNGA 1984, RNGB 2240.
- Exfiltration path is real: soc_coresub.sv:550/599 wires `sce_axi32` into `bmxcore`, which fans out to sram0/sram1/rrc/qfc, so the fetched word lands in attacker-readable SRAM.

WHERE THE REPORT IS WRONG / OVERSTATED
1. Preconditions understate the gate. sce.sv:370 `assign acenable = mode_sec;` — the ACL is only live when scemode[1]=1. In mode_non and mode_xls the ACL is disabled outright, so the bug yields nothing there (everything is already readable). In secure mode the whole SCE APB block sits behind sce_sec's ahb_gate (sce.sv:145-181 derives apbs[1] from the gated `ahbs0`), and sce_sec.sv:72-74 requires both the latched owning CPU's `hauser` and `coreuser == sceuser`. So this is NOT reachable by arbitrary unprivileged software on either CPU, as the threat-model framing implies. The attacker must be the coreuser context that owns the SCE in secure mode.
2. The chosen vehicle is unnecessarily exotic. The general (non-secure) AXI channel suffices: AOB rule 8'b10_10_10_10 gives accessrule[2]=1 (axi read permitted), AOB segaddr=1920, so sfr_xch_segstart=1344 hits AKEY (1792) with no modular wrap at all; 2304 wraps to SKEY (128).

WHY IT SURVIVES REFUTATION
I tried to kill it on the "yields nothing the attacker did not already have" axis and could not. rrc.sv:684 and :713-717 show the ReRAM KEY_REGION is readable only by `scesel` under `sce_sec_op`, with `core_rd_dis_k` denying the CPUs outright, and rrc.sv:674 `keytype_in = {3'h0,axid_reg[6:2]}` derives the permitted keytype from the AXI ID, which scedma_amba drives from `cr_segid`. That binds keytype-0 ReRAM keys to SCERAM segids 0..3 — exactly LKEY/KEY/SKEY/SCRT, all 8'b01_01_01_01 (write permitted on every channel, read denied on every channel). So the SCERAM ACL is genuinely load-bearing: a hardware-only ReRAM key can only be DMA'd into a write-only SCERAM segment, and this defect reads it straight back out. The same applies to AKEY (live AES key/IV) and PKB (PKE private key buffer).

EXPLOITABILITY WALK-THROUGH
Software-only, no glitching, no probing, no decap. Write sfr_xch_segid=15 (AOB), sfr_xch_segstart=1344, sfr_xch_axstart=attacker SRAM buffer, sfr_xch_func=1 (SCERAM->AXI), sfr_xch_transize=1, then 0xa5 to the start SFR; poll sr_sdma; read the SRAM buffer. One word per start, ~2-3 register writes plus one load per word, so the full 2560-word SCERAM dumps in milliseconds. Deterministic, no race, no timing sensitivity.

SEVERITY
High. The bypass is trivial, deterministic, and unpatchable in fabricated silicon, and the asset is the crown jewel (ReRAM hardware-only keys, SKEY/SCRT/AKEY/PKB). It is held below critical only because the attacker must already be the SCE-owning coreuser context in secure mode rather than arbitrary unprivileged software — but that is precisely the boundary ACRULEs exists to enforce, so it is a genuine access-control bypass, not a no-op. The vendor should be told the corrected precondition plainly, and the fix is to clamp the loaded value (`(chnlstart ? thecfg.rpptr_start : rpptr) > segsize ? 0 : ...`) or to bound `segaddr + segptr` in sce_memc.

RULE TABLE RE-DERIVED: bit [0:CHNLACCNT-1] accessrule is ascending so index 0 is the leftmost literal bit, and index 0 is the AHB read channel per the comment at scedma_pkg.sv:278-282 and the wiring at sce.sv:203 (rpreq -> chnlreq[0]). THE CHECK THE PRIOR REVIEWS MISSED, WHICH STRENGTHENS IT: the mask is a live, unconditional countermeasure, not vestigial logic. rtl/modules/crypto_aes/rtl/AesDataPath.v:101 `assign DataIn_tmp = DataIn ^ MaskIn;` feeds all four AesSbox instances (lines 103-133), each also taking MaskIn[7:0]..[31:24], and the round-output mux at lines 171-176 XORs MaskOut/MixMaskOut back out. There is no security-enable gate on this path — contrast pke.sv:800 which passes `.sen(optsec)`. So every AES operation on this chip runs its S-box under a mask the attacker can compute offline.

EXPLOITABILITY, STEP BY STEP (my assigned lens)

Access needed: physical possession plus a power or EM probe (ChipWhisperer-class, ~$1k; no decapsulation, no laser, no glitching, no JTAG). Plus the ability to invoke AES under the victim key — either T1 software or any firmware-exposed encrypt/decrypt service. This is squarely T2, explicitly in the stated threat model, and at the cheap end of it.

Why the mask is recoverable in practice, not just in theory: the LFSR is reset to a literal constant, `sen` is tied to '1, and the only clock is clksub[3], ICG-gated by cr_suben[3] (sce.sv:256). So the state is a pure function of the count of AES-subblock-enabled cycles since sysresetn. That count is deterministic for a fixed firmware boot flow, identical on every power-up, and — because the IV is a compile-time constant with no per-device diversification — identical on every device. The attacker profiles the mask sequence once on a sacrificial sample and it is valid for all units. Even if they misjudge the phase, the offset is a small integer they brute-force with one CPA pass per candidate; it is not a 229-bit search.

What they get: with MaskIn known, DataIn_tmp = DataIn ^ MaskIn lets the attacker un-mask their own hypothesis — for key-byte guess k they predict (P^k)^MaskIn[byte] and correlate. That is textbook first-order CPA on an effectively unmasked S-box: order 10^3-10^4 traces, full 128/192/256-bit key recovery from the AKEY segment. Unpatchable silicon.

DOES IT YIELD ANYTHING THE ATTACKER DIDN'T ALREADY HAVE? Yes, but only for a T2 attacker. The AES key is sourced from the SCE RAM AKEY segment (aes.sv:43,47,323-324), which software loads. A T1-only attacker who can already read that RAM gains nothing from DPA. So this is strictly a physical-attacker capability: it breaks key confidentiality against someone holding a locked device whose trusted firmware uses root keys. For a chip in the Betrusted/Precursor secure-element lineage that is exactly the scenario the part exists to survive. This is also why I hold it at high rather than critical: it does not cross the T1 privilege boundary and it needs lab work.

REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT FAILED, AND THE ONE CORRECTION I OWE THE VENDOR

1. "Firmware can seed it." Partly true, and the finding overstates the limit. Because swr only blocks the shift for that one cycle, firmware CAN inject N bits with N separate writes to sfr_maskseedar (0x24) interleaved with normal shifting — roughly 229 writes would randomize the whole state. So "at most one bit" is wrong as a total; it is one bit per write. But this does not rescue the design: I grepped the entire repo (`grep -rn 'MASKSEED|maskseed'` across all file types) and the register appears in no documentation and no firmware — docs/src/ contains no SCE register map at all. There is no hardware autoseed. The post-reset default is a known constant, so any AES executed before firmware performs ~229 undocumented action-register writes runs fully predictable. And even a correctly seeded 229-bit LFSR is linear, so masks at cycles t and t+k are related by a known linear map — weak against algebraic and second-order analysis.
2. "The maskin port was never intended for TRNG." Possibly — that part is inference about intent. Irrelevant to substance: the mask still has exactly one source and it is the fixed-IV LFSR.
3. "The countermeasure was never load-bearing anyway." I checked whether the design is already broken independent of mask quality: AesDataPath.v:135 `assign SboxDataOut = SboxDataOut_tmp;` and the mux at 171-176 remove the mask combinationally, so the round-state register holds unmasked data and leaks by Hamming distance regardless. That is a reason the chip was never going to be DPA-hard — but it is an additional weakness, not an exculpation. The masking hardware is instantiated, consumes area, and delivers approximately zero first-order protection.

Minor citation fix for the report: the sysresetn connection is sce.sv:513, not 512 (512 is `.resetn(sceresetn)`). The finder's own prior-verification note already caught this.
