Exploitability — the angle I most expected to kill the finding, and could not:
The question is whether DPA yields a secret the attacker could not already read. It does. scedma_pkg.sv:305 sets the AES key segment rule to `'{ segid:SEGID_AKEY , accessrule: 8'b01_01_01_01 }`, where accessrule[0]=AHB-read=0 and accessrule[1]=AHB-write=1 per the comment at scedma_pkg.sv:279-280. This is enforced in scedma_ac.sv:47 (`assign chnlac[i] = acenable ? chnlacrule : '1;`) with acenable = mode_sec (sce.sv:370). Companion rules are consistent (AIB write-only 8'b01_01_01_01, AOB read-only 8'b10_10_10_10). The expanded round-key schedule lives in the AES-private ARAM at addresses reachable only through the hardcoded AESSEG_* localparams (aes.sv:67-71), so software cannot address it. The hardware thus deliberately implements a use-but-never-read key oracle, and this defect converts that oracle into a readable key. That is a real escalation across a boundary the RTL itself enforces — not a capability the attacker already had.

Concrete attack: unprivileged software (T1) writes plaintext to AIB, kicks sfr_ar (aes.sv:145), reads ciphertext from AOB — a free, unlimited chosen-plaintext oracle under the resident secret key. Attacker with physical possession (T2) records power/EM. Because every DataOut arm strips the mask, both endpoints of the round-boundary register transition are plain AES state, so textbook CPA on HD(SReg_r, SReg_r+1) with a K0 hypothesis applies unmodified. Equipment is commodity (ChipWhisperer class, low hundreds of dollars); the 32-bit serialized datapath separates key words in time, giving strong SNR; order 1e3-1e4 traces for full key recovery. Chip is taped out and unpatchable.

Two honest caveats that do not refute:
(1) Attack step 2 is slightly overstated. The SReg transition in EN_ROUND0 is P -> P^K0, whose Hamming DISTANCE is HW(K0), constant across traces, so that particular flop toggle is not per-trace data-dependent. The exploitable leakage is the combinational XOR/mux cone and output bus settling to P^K0, plus the step-4 round-boundary HD, which is the robust target and is valid precisely because lines 171-176 unmask both endpoints. Conclusion unchanged.
(2) Remediation overlaps with the sibling mask/TRNG finding: sce.sv:508-509 ties aesmask='0 and the aes module's maskin port is dead; the mask actually comes from the internal drng_lfsr (aes.sv:282-283) seeded by the software-writable sfr_maskseed. Both findings collapse to one statement and one silicon fix. This finding remains independently valid because fixing the mask source would restore nothing: no masked value ever reaches a register, and FirstRound has no mask at all.

Severity high is honest: the vendor evidently intended a first-order countermeasure (masked Sbox, mask MixCol path), the compromised asset is the top-listed one (secret keys in the SCE), the confidentiality boundary is hardware-enforced in RTL, and the part cannot be patched. It requires physical presence plus measurement gear, so it is not remotely exploitable — but physical possession is the canonical adversary for this product class.

The RTL observations are all accurate (qfc.sv:176 sfrlock tied '0; qfc.sv:202-203 cr_aeskey/cr_aesena; apb_sfr.sv:333 write gate; qfc_aes.sv pass-through; coresubapbs[0] unfiltered), but the security consequence does not survive an exploitability walk.

(1) Not a QFC-specific defect: sfrlock is hardwired '0 in ~20 blocks including every tamper/security block (mesh.sv:46, sensorc.sv:57, gluechain.sv:42, trng.sv:52, dkpc.sv:182, ao_sysctrl.sv:362, mdma.sv:100, bio.sv:219, mbox.sv:104, scedma.sv:91, ahb_sfr.sv:31). The only non-zero drivers are the SCE mid-operation interlock (aes.sv:135, pke.sv:287, alu.sv:131 `optlock ? 1'b1 : mfsm_done ? '0 : sfrlock`). coreuser is consumed only by rrc (ReRAM key slots) and the SCE. Peripheral register protection is delegated to the CPU MPU/PMP by design. No doc, SVD, or register description anywhere in the repo mentions aeskey/aesena, so there is no documented guarantee to contradict.

(2) The key is not a hardware-protected secret: the only source of aeskeyin is the APB write at qfc.sv:202 — no ReRAM/SCE key-ladder path exists. Software must hold the plaintext key in CPU registers/SRAM to program it, so anyone who can write 0x4001_0040 can also read it from SRAM. The read-back omission is not a protection being defeated.

(3) The "permissive default" claim is factually wrong: apb_cr with no IV parameter defaults IV=0 (apb_sfr.sv:339 `theregfull(pclk, resetn, sfrdatarr[i], IV)`), so out of reset aeskeyin=0 and aesena=0 — decryption OFF, the safe state. All cr_xip_* config (opcode/width/dummy/prescaler, qfc.sv:194-199) also resets to 0, so the XIP path returns nothing usable until software configures it, and the CPUs boot from ReRAM. qfc_en='1' at soc_coresub.sv:287 only ungates clock/reset (soc_coresub.sv:866-868); it does not make XIP live.

(4) The attack yields nothing new: writing 0x4001_0050 requires an attacker who can already execute an arbitrary store to any peripheral, i.e. arbitrary code execution. The payoff of the scenario (execute payload at 0x8000_0000) is code execution he already has. The only claimed increment is the coreuserreg0pre[7] = ~|coreuserreg0pre[6:4] identity at cm7sys.sv:761, which is a separate finding that stands or falls on its own.

(5) The bypassed mechanism is not an integrity boundary: XIP AES without a MAC is anti-clone confidentiality. An attacker with T3 flash control faces no authentication gate either way; even with a locked key he can cut-and-paste ciphertext and use the chip as a decryption oracle by placing chosen ciphertext in flash and reading 0x8000_0000, requiring zero register writes. Nothing places XIP content in the secure-boot chain. The qfc_aes.sv pass-through cited as "no second integrity gate" is a vestigial unused wrapper (qfc.sv:244); the real cipher is in the absent closed IP (qfc_socbus_aes.sv, referenced at rtl/asic_top/include/qfc_inc.sv:35 but not present), so the claim that aesena/aeskeyin are "the only security inputs" is unverifiable in-repo.

Residual value: a product using encrypted XIP, with a firmware arbitrary-write primitive but not code execution, whose attacker also has physical flash-rewrite access, could turn one 32-bit store into code execution. That justifies a sticky lock bit as hardening, but it is contingent on a separate firmware bug plus physical flash access and has an equivalent chosen-ciphertext fallback. Low severity hardening note, not a high-severity vulnerability.

I confirm the RTL mechanism but refute the finding as a security finding: there is no attacker in the stated threat model who gains anything from it.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (the mechanism is real)

- scedma_amba.sv:99-109 mixes the two: `segid: ahbs_segid` (live) with `segaddr: ... ahbshaddr_dp` (held).
- scedma_amba.sv:111 `` `theregrn( ahbs_segcfgreg ) <= ahbs_segcfg;`` has no enable term, so it is a plain 1-cycle delay of the mixed descriptor, not an address-phase capture. The finder's contrast at line 133 is therefore not a "correct" path.
- The cycle walk holds: chnli_start (line 116) fires in the address phase; transstart→rprdvld at cycle 1; rprdpl1vld→wpwr at cycle 2 (sce_dmachnl.sv:134-138, 192, 195); wpptr is pinned at 0 (wpptr_start='0, segsize forced to 'd4 at scedma_amba.sv:105); wpseg = thewpsegcfg.segaddr (sce_dmachnl.sv:121). So scedma_ac.sv:45-46 authorises on `chnlinreq[1].segcfg.segid` = the NEXT address's segid, while sce_memc.sv:212 `ramm_addr = segaddr + segptr` drives the PREVIOUS address's word. sce.sv:190-200 confirms chnlreq[1] is the AHB write port; scedma_pkg.sv:279-282 confirms index 1 = "ahb W". ramsel is '0 for every segment so there is no RAM-select divergence.
So yes, in principle a write aimed at an AHB-write-denied segment can be authorised against the following transfer's segid.

WHY IT DOES NOT HOLD UP AS AN ATTACK

1. Only the SCE owner can reach this port, and only in a mode where being the owner already means owning the crypto engine. sce.sv:370 `assign acenable = mode_sec;` — the ACRULE table is enforced ONLY in mode_sec. In mode_non/mode_xls chnlac is forced to '1 (scedma_ac.sv:47), i.e. every segment is already freely writable from AHB with no bug at all. And in mode_sec, sce_sec.sv:72-77 gates the whole AHB slave: `ahben = mode_non ? 1'b1 : (hauser match) & (coreuser == sceuser)`. So the only actor who can exercise this primitive is the latched SCE owner — the trusted crypto client that already writes all key segments (LKEY/KEY/SKEY/SCRT/AKEY/PKB, all accessrule[1]=1), supplies all engine inputs, and programs the DMA SFRs. T1 (unprivileged software) is locked out by ahben; T2/T3/T4 are irrelevant to this path. There is no cross-domain victim: sceuser is latched once on the 0→nonzero mode transition (sce_sec.sv:58,64) and any exit from a nonzero mode asserts modequit → SCE reset + RAM clear (sce_sec.sv:81-87, sce.sv:414 `clrend(SEGADDR_RNGA-1)`), so two mutually distrusting contexts never share a live SCE.

2. The flagship impact — TRNG substitution in RNGA/RNGB — needs no bug. scedma_pkg.sv:308-309 `accessrule: 8'b10_11_10_10` on a `bit [0:7]` field gives [0]=1 (ahb R), [1]=0 (ahb W), [2]=1 (axi R), **[3]=1 (axi W)**. chnlreq[3] is xchwpreq (sce.sv:342-343), the SCE-RAM write port of the general AXI DMA channel (scedma.sv:252-254), whose cr_segid, cr_segptrstart and axstart are plain SFRs (scedma.sv:263-265) reachable through the same ahb_gate. The same actor can therefore DMA arbitrary bytes from system memory straight into RNGA/RNGB through a fully sanctioned path. The claim that RNGA/RNGB "are specifically write-protected" is only true of the AHB port, not of the attacker.

3. The residual capability is empty. Subtracting RNGA/RNGB, the AHB-write-denied set is SOB, PSOB, AOB (8'b10_00_10_00 / 8'b10_10_10_10) and POB (8'b00_00_00_10). SOB/PSOB/AOB are already AHB-*readable* by the same owner, and their contents are entirely determined by inputs the owner already chooses; forging them buys nothing that loading a chosen key into AKEY/SKEY does not. POB is unreadable by every AC'd channel except ich[6], and ich can only write into segments that are themselves AHB-read-denied, so a substituted POB value cannot even be observed. The one hardware trust decision in the block — sce_ts truststate — is driven by combohasha.sv:479-490, which XOR-compares the SCRT segment against a key-store word fetched over AXI from PM_KS_BA; it does not read SOB/POB/AOB, and SCRT is already AHB-writable, so this primitive does not move truststate.

4. One premise is unverifiable in-repo. The whole thing needs HADDR at the slave port to advance to the next transfer's address during the stalled data phase. All in-repo glue (ahb_gate amba_components.sv:1037-1047, ahb_demux.sv:105-107) is combinational pass-through, but the two elements that actually decide this — `cmsdk_ahb_to_ahb_sync` (instantiated at amba_components.sv:820) and the `ahb_bmx33` matrix (bmxcore_inc.sv:20-32) — are not present in the repository. AHB permits the overlap, so it is likely, but I could not demonstrate it. Notably, if it did occur the *read* path (scedma_amba.sv:144, combinational `rpsegcfg = ahbs_segcfg`) would mis-address every FIFO-mode AHB read that crosses a segment boundary, which would be a gross functional failure — weak evidence that the overlap may not materialise here.

NET: the RTL defect is real and worth reporting to the vendor as a robustness/defence-in-depth item (the read-side sibling at line 144 is the one with actual secret-disclosure potential). But as stated — "high", write into RNGA, "firmware receives attacker-chosen values in place of TRNG output" — it is circular: the attacker IS that firmware, it already owns the engine, and it already has a sanctioned AXI path to the same bytes. It crosses no privilege boundary and yields no asset.

CONFIRMED — I could not refute this, and my independent trace strengthened it.

WHAT I VERIFIED MYSELF (not taken on trust):
1. mimm.sv:338-342 FSM. mfsm_sub1cyc is held at 0 while mfsm != MFSM_SUB1 (line 356), so on the first SUB1 cycle mfsm_sub1cycpl2 == 0 != dblen-1; with sub1skip set, line 341 fires and the FSM reaches MFSM_DONE in ONE cycle. The timing delta is therefore an UNCONFOUNDED one-bit "did the extra reduction happen" oracle — cleaner than the finder described.
3. mimm.sv:116 confirms MFSM_SUB is entered once per Montgomery multiply (gated on lastrnd), not once per exponentiation.

REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT FAILED:
a) Operand blinding? None. grep for "mask" in PkeCtrl.sv returns ZERO hits. sfr_maskseed/pkemaskdat (pke.sv:793) only drives mimm_dbrnd into mac_cell.sv:51 (`~ME & (opt_pl>=i) ? (opt_sec ? DB_rnd : '0)`) — a POWER-SCA countermeasure filling idle multiplier lanes. It cannot influence final-reduction cycle count.
b) Is variable-time final reduction an accepted tradeoff here? NO — and this is the decisive corroboration. The sibling multiplier does the same conditional subtraction in CONSTANT time: mgmr_mul.v:464 `mgmr_mul_comalg_mode = is_M_bigeer_N ? UINT_BA_SUB_A : UINT_B_MOV_A`, and com_alg.v:153-168 walks write_counter to comalg_wlen-1 for EVERY mode, so both the subtract and the move take identical cycles. The design team deliberately implemented a constant-time conditional reduction in mgmr_mul. mimm_sub regresses against the team's own in-repo pattern. This converts a generic side-channel class into a demonstrable design-intent violation.
c) Observability without prior compromise? Two independent channels. sfr_tickcnt @ 0x4002_C054 is an apb_sr (pke.sv:314) fed by a 32-bit counter latched at pcore_done (pke.sv:813-824) with programmable granularity via tickcyc — set tickcyc=0 for a CYCLE-EXACT, ZERO-NOISE duration of the whole hardware exponentiation. Even if sce_sec.sv coreuser gating blocks SCE APB reads under scemode!=0, the ~1-2% total-time swing is well within the Brumley-Boneh (2003) remote-measurement bar demonstrated against noisier hardware.
d) Does the attack imply full compromise? No. Minimum capability is: submit chosen messages to a firmware signing service and time responses. Strictly weaker than reading the key.

CONCRETE ATTACK PATH: victim firmware performs RSA-CRT sign or ECDSA scalar-mult with mimmcr[8]=1. Attacker submits chosen ciphertexts and reads the exact operation duration from sfr_tickcnt (or times the call from its own CPU cycle counter, or remotely). Total exponentiation time = base + (number of extra reductions) x ~36 cycles. Schindler (CHES 2000) / Brumley-Boneh: the extra-reduction count is a monotone function of input vs. modulus proximity with a sharp discontinuity at multiples of the secret CRT prime p; binary search on chosen inputs recovers p, factoring N. Thousands of queries suffice, and with a noiseless on-chip counter far fewer than the network case.

HONEST LIMITATION (weighed, does not refute): mmsel = mimmcr[8] (pke.sv:767) is a plain apb_cr resetting to 0, so the leaky multiplier is opt-in. If production firmware never sets it, the leak is unreachable. But mimm is the PL=4 parallel datapath — the only performance-viable choice for RSA-2048/4096 — and there is no lock bit, no documentation warning, and no firmware in the repo to settle usage. This is why I hold at high rather than critical.

SEVERITY: high. Unpatchable taped-out silicon; outcome is direct RSA private-key / ECC scalar recovery; zero hardware countermeasure; regression against the team's own constant-time pattern in mgmr_mul; amplified by an on-chip cycle-exact timer register. Not critical only because it is contingent on a non-default configuration bit and is mitigable in firmware via standard base/scalar blinding.

EXPLOITABILITY: practical. Requires only a chosen-input signing oracle plus timing observation — no glitching, no decapsulation, no probing. Conditioned on mimmcr[8]=1.

RECOMMENDATION TO VENDOR: mimm_sub should always execute the full dblen-word pass and conditionally select between (areg-breg) and areg on the write, exactly as com_alg.v already does for mgmr_mul; and firmware must apply base/exponent blinding (and scalar blinding for ECC) whenever mimmcr[8] is set on this silicon.

I attempted to refute this and could not. Independent verification:

CODE TRUTH CONFIRMED
- PkeCtrl.sv:1932-2117 is verbatim as quoted: a binary extended-Euclidean FSM with fully data-dependent control flow. MI_JUDGE1 (1932-1943) branches 3 ways on Y3IsEven/X3IsEven; MI_JUDGE2 (1951-1957) and MI_JUDGE3 (1990-1996) insert MI_X1ADDU+MI_X2SUBV / MI_Y1ADDU+MI_Y2SUBV only when a low bit is set; MI_X3CMPY3 (2028-2038) branches 3 ways on compare sign/zero; MI_Y2ADDP/MI_Y2SUBP (2090-2117) loop an unbounded, sign-dependent number of times.
- The branch predicates are genuinely secret-derived, not from a public parameter: PkeCtrl.sv:2164-2211 shows every *IsEven / Y2IsNeg flag is loaded from LongAlgSR[2] / LongAlgSR[1], the LSB and sign status of the preceding com_alg pass over the live working values.
- Each step is constant-cycle, so step count == cycle count: com_alg.v:135-180 is a fixed comalg_wlen-word loop; CMALG_STATE4/5/6 all exit only on write_counter == comalg_wlen-1, no data-dependent early exit. Total ModInv time is therefore a linear function of the number of EEA steps.

REAL SILICON, NOT DEAD/EMULATION CODE
soc_top.sv:573 -> soc_coresub.sv:511 (sce #( ) -> sce.sv:478 (pke #() pke( ) -> pke.sv:755 (PkeCore pcore( ) -> PkeCore.sv:167 (PkeCtrl uPkeCtrl( ). sce_inc.sv:63,65 includes the real PkeCtrl.sv/PkeCore.sv; the PkeCore_dummy.sv include at sce_inc.sv:58 is commented out. No parameter override at any instantiation site touches the ModInv FSM.

REACHABILITY (stronger than the original claim)
- Directly dispatchable microcode opcodes: pke.sv:76 PIR_ECINV = 8'h08, pke.sv:92 PIR_MODINV = 8'h18, matching PkeCtrl.sv:960/968 and the dispatch at PkeCtrl.sv:1213-1215.
- Also invoked involuntarily: PkeCtrl.sv:1875 "assign StartModInv = EccStartModInv | StartModInv_M2I | StartModInv_EDM2I | RsaStartModInv;" with PkeCtrl.sv:1858 "assign StartModInv_M2I = (EccM2IState == ECCM2I_MOVUT2U) & LongAlgDone;". So PIR_ECM2I (0x07) and PIR_EDM2I (0x27) -- the standard projective-to-affine conversion after a scalar multiply -- run this same non-constant-time inverter on Z internally. Firmware using the built-in M2I cannot opt out.

COMPENSATING CONTROLS SEARCHED FOR AND NOT FOUND
- optsec / pkemaskdat / mimm_dbrnd (pke.sv:753, 788-793, 800-805) is Montgomery-multiplier randomization wired only into the mgmr_mul datapath. It has no path into com_alg or any MI_* state and does not blind the inversion.
- ErrorDetect (ModInvCnt >= 16'd32768) is a runaway watchdog, not a timing balancer.
- Grep for blind|constant.?time|mask|dummy|random across PkeCtrl.sv / PkeCore.sv / pke.sv returns only the Montgomery masking and unrelated EDPA_* state parameters. No dummy-op insertion, no input blinding, no constant-time mode bit.

EVIDENCE THAT STRENGTHENS THE FINDING BEYOND THE ORIGINAL WRITEUP
The timing channel is not merely inferrable -- the PKE contains a purpose-built cycle counter that latches the exact duration of the completed operation, removing measurement noise from the T1-only (software-only) variant. pke.sv:818-824:
  assign tickclr = ~pcore_busy;
  assign ticklock = pcore_done_sync;
  `theregfull(clkpke, resetn, tickcnt, '0 ) <= tickclr ? '0 : tickcnt + tickhit ;
  `theregfull(clkpke, resetn, tickcntsr, '0 ) <= ticklock ? tickcnt : tickcntsr;
read back at pke.sv:314 via "apb_sr #(.A('h54), .DW(32)) sfr_tickcnt (.sr(tickcntsr), ...)".

MINOR CORRECTION (does not change the conclusion)
The finding's prose says "Each of those states waits on LongAlgDone". MI_JUDGE1/2/3 are actually single-cycle combinational branch states with no LongAlgDone wait (1932-1943, 1951-1957, 1990-1996). The states they branch into (MI_X1ADDU, MI_X2SUBV, MI_*DIV2) are the ones costing a full N-word RAM pass, so the substantive claim -- extra full-width passes occur only when the low bit is set -- is correct as written.

SEVERITY / EXPLOITABILITY
This is squarely in the in-scope class "timing/power side-channel leakage in crypto datapaths where the data or key controls the number of cycles". Under T2 (EM/power), the halving-vs-subtract pass sequence is directly readable from a single trace, giving essentially the whole branch sequence of the inversion input -- full nonce recovery from one or a few ECDSA signatures. Under T1 alone, sfr_tickcnt gives a noise-free aggregate step count, which is the classical BEEA leak (a few bits of nonce per signature) and is exploitable via the hidden-number-problem lattice attack over a modest number of signatures. The one honest caveat is that the T1-only attack depends on firmware actually calling ModInv on secret material (k^-1 mod n); the hardware does offer a randomized ModExp that firmware could use for Fermat inversion instead. But the M2I path makes ModInv unavoidable in the normal ECC flow, and shipping an unblinded BEEA as the SCE's only inversion primitive is a real design weakness in a taped-out, unpatchable secure element. High / practical stands.

I verified the raw RTL claims: scedma_amba.sv:111 is indeed an unenabled free-running register, and the descriptor at lines 99-109 genuinely mixes ahbs_segid (combinational, from the live HADDR via addr2seg on ahbshaddr_local at line 94/97) with segaddr = ahbshaddr_dp (the address-phase-latched address, line 95). scedma_ac.sv:45 authorises on segcfg.segid while sce_memc.sv:84/212 addresses on segaddr+segptr, and I confirmed there is no compensating redirect: all 18 segments have ramsel '0 with RAMCNT=1 (scedma_pkg.sv:25,236-253), segsize is forced to 'd4 so the wpptr clamp is inert, and nothing bounds-checks segaddr against segid. The block is real silicon (sce.sv:189 -> soc_coresub.sv:518 -> soc_top.sv:555 -> daric_top.sv:362).

However, the exploit requires the AHB master to present a different address during the slave's data phase, and two in-repo facts say that cannot be happening.

(1) This slave physically cannot accept a pipelined AHB stream. transsize is 'd1 (scedma_amba.sv:137) so lasttrans is permanently 1, meaning `done`/HREADY-high always coincide with a pipelined master's next address-phase completion. On that cycle sce_dmachnl.sv:102 (`busy <= start ? 1 : busy & done ? 0 : busy`) holds busy=1, while chnlstart = start & ~busy (line 104) and transstart = ~busy ? start : ~lasttrans & transdone (line 114) are both zero. The second transfer is dropped, busy never clears, and ahbs.hready (scedma_amba.sv:90) is stuck low - a permanent hang. This is latency-independent. A shipped chip whose firmware does back-to-back stores into the SCE therefore is not seeing pipelined address phases at this slave.

(2) The de-pipeliser is present and is what drives HADDR: sce.sv:151 instantiates ahb_sync #(.SYNCDOWN(0),.SYNCUP(0)) = ARM cmsdk_ahb_to_ahb_sync (amba_components.sv:819-861) between coreahbmux[2] and the entire SCE interior, and amba_components.sv:865 assigns ahbmaster.haddr = uahbcore_HADDRM, i.e. the SCE's internal HADDR is the bridge's registered output, not the fabric's live HADDR. Held across the data phase, ahbs_segid = seg(A0) and the descriptor is self-consistent. The bundled BFM (sce_tb_v0.2_hash.sv:1393-1421) drives exactly that regime: haddr held, wait on hready before changing.

Caveat: cmsdk_ahb_to_ahb_sync.v is external (referenced via rtl/asic_top/include/common_cell_inc.sv:41) and not readable here, so point 2 relies on standard registered-bridge behaviour; point 1 is derived entirely from in-repo RTL and is by itself decisive about what the fabric must be delivering.

Additionally, even granting the premise the preconditions are much narrower than "high": acenable = mode_sec only (sce.sv:370), and in mode_sec sce_sec.sv:72-77 admits only the SCE owner (matching hauser AMBAID4_CM7P/VEXD and matching coreuser) to the SCE AHB at all, so the bypassed rules are an intra-owner compartment. And the finding's own scenario (RNGA store followed by an MSG address phase) is precisely the start&done coincidence that hangs the slave, so it would give one corrupted word followed by a permanent AHB deadlock rather than a usable primitive.

Net: the segid/segaddr stage mismatch is a real latent fragility worth reporting as a robustness/defence-in-depth item (segid should be latched with ahbs_cpvld alongside ahbshaddr_dp), together with the separate back-to-back hang, but the claimed access-control bypass as written does not hold up.

I attempted to refute this and could not. Every quoted line is verbatim correct, and I independently re-derived the load-bearing details rather than trusting the report.

Key independent checks:
1. Access-rule bit order. The whole attack hinges on SEG_SCRT/SEG_KEY being AHB-writable. `scedma_pkg.sv:286` declares `bit [0:CHNLACCNT-1] accessrule`, comment says 0/1 = ahb R/W. I validated the index-0-is-read reading against unambiguous entries: SEGID_AOB `8'b10_10_10_10` (AES output buffer -> read allowed, write denied) and SEGID_RNGA `8'b10_11_10_10` (RNG output -> readable, not writable). Under the opposite ordering these become write-only, which is nonsense. So for SEGID_KEY/SEGID_SKEY/SEGID_SCRT (`scedma_pkg.sv:293-295`, all `8'b01_01_01_01`) AHB read = 0, AHB write = 1. The attacker CAN plant both the HMAC key and the expected digest from the bus.
2. The AHB channels are the AC-checked ones: `sce.sv:203/205` wire `scedmachnl_ahbs` to `chnlreq[0]` (read) and `chnlreq[1]` (write), which pass through `scedma_ac.sv:47`. `acenable = mode_sec` (`sce.sv:370`), so the rules are enforced during the attack and still permit the writes.
3. The binding really is broken only on the tsmode=0 path. In tsmode=1 the compare source is the ReRAM key store at `PM_KS_BA + kid*32` (`combohasha.sv:462`, PM_KS_BA=32'h603f0000 per `sce.sv:443`), so kid does bind to the expected digest there and that path is NOT forgeable. `combohasha.sv:477` swaps in SEG_SCRT when tsmode=0 while `hmac_kid` (`:490`) remains the raw software `sfr_keyidx`. `sce_ts` has no tsmode/ifskey port at all (`sce_sec.sv:91-105`), so it cannot distinguish the two.
4. The compare mechanics work as claimed: `chnli_cfg.opt_xor = (mfsm == MFSM_LD_SECRET)` (`:684`), so segwdat = SCRT ^ computed_ST; planting the correct tag gives all-zero and `chkprepass` stays 1. `chnli_start` includes `(mfsm==MFSM_LD_SECRET)&~tsmode` (`:699`) and `chkdone <= mfsmcheckscrt & (schdonex|chnli_done)` (`:484`), so the tsmode=0 path completes and asserts hmac_pass.
5. The consumer is armed unconditionally. `rrc.sv:719-720` shows the `rrccr[10]` enable was removed by ECO: `assign key_access_error = key_access_error_pre;`. So `!trustkey[akeyid] & (haddr_reg[15:6] != 10'h0)` at `:717` is always in force for key slots >= 2. `soc_coresub.sv:836` feeds `truststate` in, `.TSC(256)` matches akeyid's 8-bit range.
6. I looked for an easier pre-existing bypass that would make this finding moot. `ts[255]` is hardwired 1 (`sce_sec.sv:123`), so an attacker who could rewrite an ACRAM descriptor's akeyid to 255 would not need the HMAC forge at all. But ACRAM is written only from the BIST/ReRAM config load or `rram_write_run & rramcfg_vld` (`rrc.sv:360-365`), i.e. it mirrors the access-controlled ReRAM config region. So the HMAC path genuinely is the gate, and forging it is the attack.
7. Persistence claim verified: `sce.sv:298` connects sce_ts with `.resetn,` (the sce module's main resetn) while `sce_sec` and the other blocks use `.resetn(sceresetn)`. A forged bit survives sfr_arrst / sfr_arclr / mode-quit, so it outlives the attacker's ownership of the SCE.

Where I DO correct the report: the attacker profile is overstated. `sfr_scemode` is sfrlocked once non-zero (`sce_glbsfra.sv:78`) and `ahben` (`sce_sec.sv:72-77`) blocks every master whose hauser/coreuser does not match the latched owner, so arbitrary unprivileged software cannot reach the SFRs when secure firmware claims the SCE at boot. The attacker needs code execution in the SCE-owning coreuser domain (or must claim a released/unclaimed SCE). Forging also does not cross the userid partition: `rrc.sv:712-717` still requires `(coreuser_in[7:4] & userid_k[7:4]) != 0`, `!core_rd_dis_k`, and `cm7sel & pri_op` / `vexsel & vex_mm_reg`. So this is not a coreuser-boundary escape.

That bound does not refute the finding. What it defeats is the second factor: the documented-by-construction property "a ReRAM key slot only unlocks after hardware verifies an HMAC against a secret the CPU cannot forge" is fully bypassed with attacker-chosen key, message and expected tag, no secret knowledge, software only, no fault injection. This is exactly the passphrase/attestation-gated key unlock in the Betrusted lineage, so bypassing it converts "keys require an authentication event" into "keys are usable by any code already in the domain," and the forged bit persists past the SCE reset that is supposed to scrub SCE state. The single non-redundant `chkprepass` bit seeded to PASS is a real secondary glitch target but is not needed for the software attack.

Concrete attack, step by step, software only: (1) claim/own SCE, write scemode=2; (2) AHB-write chosen K to SEG_KEY at RAM offset 0x100 and chosen tag T to SEG_SCRT at 0x300 (both permitted by ACRULE index 1); (3) write SFR_OPT2 offset 0x14 with ifskey=0, tsmode=0, scrtchk=1; (4) write SFR_KEYIDX offset 0x60 = N, the akeyid of the target slot; (5) run HF_HMAC256_PASS1 then PASS2; PASS2 enters MFSM_LD_SECRET, XOR yields zero, chkpass asserts; (6) tsreg[N]=1, observable via sfr_ts at glbsfr offset 0xe0; (7) rrc.sv:717 no longer blocks key slots with akeyid==N. The asset obtained is authenticated-only ReRAM key material loaded into SCE key segments and usable as a crypto oracle (SEG_SKEY/SEG_AKEY are not AHB-readable, but use of the key is equivalent to possession for signing/decryption).

Severity high, exploitability practical, with the caveat that the attacker must hold SCE ownership in mode_sec rather than being arbitrary unprivileged code.

The RTL claim is fully confirmed by independent reading. PkeCtrl.sv:1933-1943, 1951-1957, 2028-2038, 2099-2116 are verbatim as quoted: ModInvState is a binary extended-Euclidean FSM whose next-state is selected by Y3IsEven/X3IsEven, by (~X1IsEven | ~X2IsEven) / (~Y1IsEven | ~Y2IsEven), and by ResultIsZero/ResultIsNeg (= LongAlgSR[1:0], PkeCtrl.sv:2130-2131), with an unbounded sign-driven MI_Y2ADDP/MI_Y2SUBP correction loop. I verified the per-step cost is constant: com_alg.v:135-180 is a fixed comalg_wlen-word walk whose only terminator is (write_counter == comalg_wlen-1), no data-dependent exit. So elapsed time is a linear function of the number of EEA steps, i.e. of the operand's bit pattern. I confirmed there is no balancer: PkeCtrl.sv:2475-2481 (`assign ErrorDetect = (ModInvCnt >= 16'd32768);` with ModInvCnt incrementing only in MI_JUDGE1) is a watchdog ceiling. I confirmed no blinding of the ModInv operand: the only randomization in the block is mimm_dbrnd (pke.sv:788-805, `assign mimm_dbrnd = optsec ? pkemaskdat : '0;`), an LFSR dummy-randomizer routed to the Montgomery multiplier under mimmcr[3]; it never touches the EEA operands. Corroborating context that strengthens the report: the designers DID make the scalar multiply constant-time — ECCPM (PkeCtrl.sv:4715+) and X25519 (5175+) are ladders with fixed state sequences and only key-bit-dependent address swapping — so ModInv is the single variable-time path in an otherwise timing-hardened ECC flow.

Where the finding does not survive scrutiny, and why I downgrade it from high to medium/difficult rather than refute:

(1) The stated observation mechanism is blocked. Step 2 claims unprivileged software reads sfr_tickcnt at PKE+0x54 (pke.sv:314). But the entire SCE AHB slave is coreuser-gated at sce_sec.sv:72-77: `assign ahben = mode_non ? 1'b1 : ((sceusersel == 0 ) ? ( ahbs.hauser == daric_cfg::AMBAID4_CM7P ) : ( ahbs.hauser == daric_cfg::AMBAID4_VEXD )) & ((sceusersel == 0 ) ? ( coreuser_cm7 == sceuser ) : ( coreuser_vex == sceuser ));`. In secure/exclusive mode a non-owning core cannot read the tick counter during the victim's session. In mode_non it can — but then it can equally read the PKE operand RAM directly, so the timing channel yields nothing the attacker did not already have. The realistic software attacker is reduced to end-to-end latency of a signing service call.

(2) The software-only leak is far smaller than claimed. From total elapsed time the attacker recovers one scalar (the total EEA step count), which is an aggregate constraint, not known nonce bits, so it does not feed an HNP lattice directly as step 4 asserts — it is a bias usable only in Bleichenbacher-style aggregation over very many signatures. The published BEEA breaks that recover the full input need the branch SEQUENCE, which here requires an EM/power trace (T2), not a software timer. The 'tens of bits per signature' claim is overstated.

(3) The precondition is firmware-dependent and unverifiable in this repo. There is no hardware ECDSA sequencer anywhere in crypto_pke/rtl or pke.sv. The two hardware-internal invocations are ECCM2I_MODINVZ (PkeCtrl.sv:1750-1758) and EDM2I_MODINVZ, both inverting a projective Z — leaking Z's bit pattern does not invert the ladder to recover the scalar, so the internal uses are not exploitable. The dangerous case (k^-1 mod n, or q^-1 mod p) only arises if firmware calls EccModInv/RsaModInv (IR 0x08/0x18, PkeCtrl.sv:960/968, dispatched 1213-1215) on unblinded secret material. Ed25519 and X25519 — both first-class hardware paths here — need no nonce inversion at all.

(4) It is cheaply firmware-mitigable on a taped-out part: multiplicative blinding (invert k*r, then multiply by r) uses ModMul primitives the engine already exposes. That makes this 'firmware must blind' rather than 'silicon is unfixably broken', which is materially different from the report's framing.

Net: a real, correctly-anchored RTL weakness worth disclosing, but the honest framing is 'EM/power SPA on the BEEA branch sequence recovers the full ModInv input in one trace, if firmware ever feeds it an unblinded secret'. That requires physical access plus measurement equipment (T2) and a firmware precondition, and the software-only path's stated observation mechanism is gated off by sce_sec. Medium severity, difficult exploitability.

RTL claims independently verified line by line. qfc.sv:176 `theregrn(sfrlock) <= '0;` expands via template.sv:90 to a flop reset to 0 with '0 as its only assignment — sfrlock is a hard constant. apb_cr (apb_sfr.sv:74-124) forwards it into apb_sfr2 whose write strobe is `assign apbwr = ~sfrlock & apbslave.psel & apbslave.penable & apbslave.pwrite;` (apb_sfr.sv:333), so cr_aeskey (qfc.sv:202) and cr_aesena (qfc.sv:203) are freely writable. Key read-back is genuinely blocked (cr_aeskey.prdata32 omitted from the OR-list at qfc.sv:183-189; apbx_prdata1 only covers paddr[11:9]=='h1 per qfc.sv:257). The block is in real silicon: soc_coresub.sv:870 instantiates qfc on coresubapbs[0]; soc_coresub is in soc_top.sv (qfc pads at soc_top.sv:76-92, 608-625). Reachability confirmed with no filter: cm7_ahbp/vex_ahbp -> ahb_mux3 coreahbpmux -> bmxcore -> core_ahb32 -> ahb_demux_map idx 1 (daric_cfg_pkg.sv:54, 0x4001_0000-0x4002_0000) -> apb_bdg u1 (soc_coresub.sv:643) -> apb_mux -> coresubapbs[0]; grep of bmxcore.sv for coreuser|hauser|auser|filter|firewall returns zero hits, and the `// apb security` section at soc_coresub.sv:930 is empty. qfc_aes.sv:24-74 is a verified pure pass-through. soc_coresub.sv:287 qfc_en resets to '1.

However the finding is materially overstated on three points. (1) sfrlock tied to 0 is the design-wide convention, not a QFC-specific omission: evc.sv:140, duart.sv:30, mdma.sv:100, bio.sv:219, bio_bdma.sv:459, sddc.sv:103, coresub_sramtrm.sv:41, ahb_sfr.sv:31/503 and every rrc.sv:274-286 SFR pass sfrlock=0; the only live lock in the design is soc_ifsub.sv:580 `.sfrlock(ioxlock)`. No peripheral APB register anywhere in this SoC is hardware-lockable or coreuser-filtered, so there is no access control being bypassed — peripheral protection is delegated to the CM7 MPU/firmware. The SCE's .coreuser_cm7/.coreuser_vex (soc_coresub.sv:541-542) are data-path key-slot identity inputs, not an APB write filter, so they are not the counter-example the finding presents. (2) The 'no second, independent integrity gate' claim is unverifiable, not verified: the actual cipher is qfc_socbus_aes.sv inside ips/smartdv/spi_flash_controller_iip/ (qfc_inc.sv:35) and that directory is entirely absent from the repo — sdvt_spi_master_core has no definition anywhere in the tree. qfc_aes.sv is a leftover renamed pass-through that was never the decryptor. Also, an unauthenticated cipher provides no integrity regardless, so aesena was never an integrity control that clearing it could bypass. (3) No asset is disclosed and no privilege is gained standalone: the provisioned key stays unreadable, the attacker must already hold bus-master code execution to write 0x4001_0050, and confidentiality of the XIP image versus on-chip software is already nil since the CPU reads it decrypted through the same window. The escalation in scenario steps 5-6 rests entirely on a separate unproven coreuser finding. The registers appear in no SVD, header or doc in the repo (grep for aeskey|aesena across *.svd/*.py/*.rs/*.h/*.md hits only qfc.sv), so there is no documented guarantee the RTL contradicts.

Residual real defect, worth vendor disclosure: a 128-bit external-flash decryption key and its enable have no hardware lock, in a design that provides the sfrlock mechanism and uses it elsewhere (iox), so firmware cannot make them immutable after boot. With T1 + T3 an attacker can clear aesena or install his own key and run chosen plaintext from the XIP window. That is a missing-lock / defense-in-depth weakness, not a high-severity access-control bypass.

I re-derived the defect from the RTL myself rather than accepting the finding's chain.

CONFIRMED MECHANICS:
1. sce_dmachnl.sv:123-125 — the range guard `( rpptr > therpsegcfg.segsize ) ? 0 : chnlstart ? thecfg.rpptr_start : ...` tests the CURRENT register with priority over the load, so the software-supplied start pointer is committed unchecked and only zeroed one clock later. Real bug, not a misreading.
2. The first read is issued in that unclamped cycle. Cycle-by-cycle: chnlstart=1 and transstart=~busy?start (line 114) at cycle 0 → posedge loads rpptr<=rpptr_start and rprdvld<=1 (line 134); cycle 1 rprd=rprdvld (139) with rpreq.segptr=rpptr (70) = raw SFR value; clamp fires only at the cycle-1→2 edge. Transfer reads {X, AKEY[1..3]}.
3. No downstream masking: sce_memc.sv:212 `ramm_addr = segaddr + segptr`; arbm_gnt=1'b1 (211); rr_arb_tree is a combinational grant tree, so a sole requester is granted in the presented cycle and segready is high at cycle 1. The finding's own arbitration caveat is a retry cost, not a blocker.
4. Address space checks out: AW=12 (scedma_pkg.sv:23), every SEGCFGS entry has ramsel:'0 (236-253), one flat RAM. Computed map: LKEY 0, KEY 64, SKEY 128, SCRT 192, PKB 512, AKEY 1792, top 2496. 1792+2304 wraps mod 4096 to 0; all 2496 words reachable.
5. The AES port genuinely bypasses scedma_ac: sce.sv:377-380 wires the AC over chnlreq[0:7] only; AES is ramreq[12]/[13] (520-522) straight into sce_memc. The bypassed rule is meaningful: ACRULEs gives LKEY/KEY/SKEY/SCRT/PKB/AKEY 8'b01_01_01_01 (scedma_pkg.sv:292-305) — with [0:7] ordering the four read channels are 0, the four write channels are 1, i.e. these segments are deliberately write-only to every bus master.
6. Observability confirmed: chnli_cfg.wpptr_start='0 (aes.sv:359) so the leaked word lands at ARAM word 0 (AESSEG_I / AESSEG_IV). In CBC (ld_d_to_iv=0, aes.sv:292) it is the IV XORed into attacker-known plaintext; in CTR it is the counter block. Either way the result reaches SEG_AOB, whose rule 8'b10_10_10_10 permits AHB reads. With a self-chosen key the attacker inverts and recovers the 32-bit word. One word per run, sweepable over the whole RAM.
7. Write side correctly excluded: wpwr0=(rprdpl1vld|rprdpl2) (line 192) cannot assert before cycle 2, by which time wpptr is clamped.

WHERE THE FINDING OVERSTATES: the attack scenario says "unprivileged software". That is wrong. All SCE register access including the AES APB block passes through ahb_gate in sce_sec.sv:72-76, and since acenable = mode_sec (sce.sv:370) and mode_sec = scemode[1] (sce_sec.sv:56), the AC rules only exist in the one mode where the SCE is simultaneously coreuser-locked to the domain that set the mode. Arbitrary unprivileged code on either CPU cannot reach the AES SFRs in mode_sec. In mode_non/mode_xls acenable=0 and the RAM is directly readable anyway, so the bug adds nothing there.

That correction does NOT refute the finding. The boundary broken is exactly the one intended to hold against the SCE owner: ACRULEs denies key-segment reads on all eight channels, including the secure AXI channel, so key material DMA'd from the ReRAM key store and HMAC-verified (combohash PM_KS_BA / hmac_kid / truststate, sce.sv:442-473) is meant to be unextractable by the very software that uses it. This bug gives that software a repeatable, software-only, 32-bit-at-a-time dump of the entire 2496-word crypto RAM including SKEY, SCRT, LKEY, KEY and PKB. No glitching, probing, or decapsulation. The chip is taped out and unpatchable.

Additional confirmed instances beyond the finding as written: the same stale-value clamp on wpptr (sce_dmachnl.sv:127-129), the same raw-SFR pointer in MFSM_LD_K and MFSM_LD_D (aes.sv:323, 332), and software-programmed segstart SFRs feeding the same scedma_chnl in scedma.sv:102/109/218/264 — giving the same one-word out-of-segment read on the sdma channels with output straight to AXI, i.e. through the nominally access-controlled path.

Severity high is justified against the asset (raw private key material) and the fact that this defeats the SCE's central write-only-key guarantee via software alone. Exploitability practical, with the honest qualifier that the attacker needs execution in the SCE-owning coreuser domain rather than any unprivileged context, and that each attempt depends on winning the memc arbiter in the presented cycle (retryable, and free when the attacker keeps other masters idle).

I attempted to refute this and could not. Every load-bearing claim reproduces from the RTL.

CONFIRMED MECHANICS:
1. sce_dmachnl.sv:123-125 — the range guard `( rpptr > therpsegcfg.segsize ) ? 0 : chnlstart ? thecfg.rpptr_start : ...` is inside a `theregrn` flop (template.sv:82-91, a real async-reset FF), so the guard's operand is the OLD rpptr. At the chnlstart edge the old value is in range, so rpptr_start is loaded unchecked and the clamp only fires one clock later.
2. The read is issued in exactly that cycle: transstart = ~busy ? start (line 114) is 1 at the same edge, rprdvld <= 1 (line 134), rprd = rprdvld (139), rpreq.segptr = rpptr (70).
3. The request is accepted that cycle: SEG_AKEY.isfifo='0 (scedma_pkg.sv:249) so sce_memc.sv:90 passes segptr through verbatim (no FIFO ptr substitution); arbm_gnt tied 1'b1 (sce_memc.sv:211); rr_arb_tree gnt_o is combinational (rr_arb_tree.sv:281-289); segrdatvld hardwired 1'b1 (sce_memc.sv:98). With AES the sole requester the grant is immediate, so the "caveat" in the finding resolves in the attacker's favour.
4. No masking anywhere: sce_memc.sv:212 `ramm_addr = segaddr + segptr` in 12-bit adr_t (scedma_pkg.sv:23,29); cryptoram.sv:71 passes ramaddr through unbounded. I recomputed the segment map from scedma_pkg.sv:211-230: LKEY 0, KEY 64, SKEY 128, SCRT 192, PKB 512, AKEY 1792 — matches the finding exactly. 1792+2304 wraps to 0; SKEY reachable at segptr 2432, PKB at 2816, all inside the 12-bit SFR.
5. The SFR is fully writable 12 bits (aes.sv:157 apb_cr .DW(scedma_pkg::AW) .SFRCNT(4); apb_sfr.sv:74-124). sfrlock (aes.sv:135) only blocks writes while the op runs, so setting the pointer before start is unimpeded.
6. scedma_ac really is limited to 8 channels (scedma_ac.sv:21 CHNLCNT = CHNLACCNT = 8; sce.sv:377-380 drives only ramreq[0:7]); the AES engine drives ramreq[12]/[13] straight into sce_memc (sce.sv:520-523, 402). sce_memc conditions segready only on FIFO state, never on segsize or porttype for non-FIFO segments. No compensating gate on that path.
7. Exfiltration verified in the AES core itself, not assumed: AesCtrl.v:936-944 encrypts ARAM 0..3 (AESSEG_I, aes.sv:68) into 68..71 (AESSEG_O at 'h44, aes.sv:69); AesMode=opt_mode+1=3'b011 for CTR enables Mode1 (AesCtrl.v:483) which XORs O with AESSEG_IV and rewrites O (AesCtrl.v:555-577). ld_iv_to_i=1 for CTR (aes.sv:291-292) puts the leaked word in AESSEG_I[0]. AOB is read-allowed (ACRULEs 8'b10_10_10_10) while every ST_KI key segment is read-denied (8'b01_01_01_01). Known key + known plaintext inverts to the secret word.
8. Live silicon: aes is inside `ifdef FULL_CHIP (sce.sv:475), the only occurrence of that macro in the tree, explicitly annotated as present in the full chip and excluded only from verilator. sce -> soc_coresub.sv:511 -> soc_top.sv:555.

COMPENSATING CONTROLS I LOOKED FOR AND DID NOT FIND: no segsize mask in sce_memc or cryptoram; no bound on the SFR; no lock on cr_segptrstart at boot; no parameter override at the aes instantiation; no redundant check in the arbiter; the FIFO path (which would have substituted fframptr) is disabled for AKEY because isfifo='0.

WHAT I DID FIND THAT ADJUSTS THE FINDING (does not refute it):
- The attacker is not generic unprivileged software. In mode_sec the SCE APB sits behind sce_sec's ahb_gate (sce_sec.sv:61-76), so only the coreuser that latched sceuser can program the AES SFRs; in mode_non/mode_xls acenable=mode_sec is 0 (sce.sv:370) and the AC table is off anyway. The correct framing is that the AES engine lets the SCE-owning software defeat the write-only property of the ST_KI key segments — the exact guarantee ACRULEs exists to provide, including against the ich channel that injects keys from ReRAM.
- Minor: words 1..3 come from AKEY[1..3], not AKEY[0..2].
- The defect is broader than aes.sv: scedma's ich channel takes a software segid AND a software rpptr_start (scedma.sv:277-287), so the same stale-clamp bug lets an AC-covered channel declare segid=SEGID_AOB (read-allowed) while segptr wraps into SKEY/SCRT/PKB, since scedma_ac.sv:45-46 keys the decision off segcfg.segid only and never off the resulting address. The fix belongs at sce_dmachnl.sv:123 and :127 (clamp the value being loaded, and use >= not >), not in aes.sv.
- The > vs >= off-by-one is real but minor standalone: it permits segptr == segsize, a one-word read of the adjacent segment.

Severity high, exploitability practical: software-only, deterministic, no glitching or physical access required, and it converts read-denied key segments into recoverable ciphertext in a read-allowed segment. Unpatchable silicon.

The RTL facts in the finding are all verbatim correct and I reproduced them independently: INITSIZE=428 (hash_pkg.sv:90-104), SEG_INIT reads SCERAM word 0 for 428 words (combohasha.sv:78-87), MFSM_LD_INIT DMAs it into HRAM 0..427 (combohasha.sv:580-588), and cryptoram's clear FSM starts at clrstart=INITSIZE so HRAM 0..427 is never wiped (combohasha.sv:854-858, cryptoram.sv:59-63). HF_INIT is an unconditioned SFR command (combohasha.sv:251-266). What does not survive is the security impact.

(1) The decisive point: HRAM 0..427 has NO hardware initial value whatsoever - no ROM, no reset value, no NVM load, and the clear FSM deliberately starts at 428. At cold boot those words are raw SRAM power-up state. Therefore every software stack MUST issue HF_INIT before its first hash or it computes garbage on a clean part. HF_INIT is a mandatory element of the programming model, not an optional one. The attack's steps 4-5 require a victim that hashes using constants it did not itself load; such a victim would fail bring-up on an unattacked chip. Any victim that does call HF_INIT overwrites the poisoning with its own table.

(2) The capability required already implies control of the hash. sce.sv:150-176 shows ahbs -> ahb_sync -> sce_sec(ahb_gate) -> ahb_demux_map -> {SFR page, SCERAM, PKERAM}: both the COMBOHASH SFR page and SCERAM are behind the single ahben in sce_sec.sv:72-76. And sce.sv:370 'assign acenable = mode_sec;' means the per-segment ACRULEs are BYPASSED entirely in mode_non (scedma_ac.sv:47 'chnlac[i] = acenable ? chnlacrule : 1'). So in the only window in which an unprivileged master can reach the SCE (mode_non, the state the finding relies on), that master can already read and write every segment including SEG_SKEY/SEG_SCRT, overwrite SEG_MSG mid-operation, write SEG_HOUT and run arbitrary hash/HMAC commands. Constant poisoning gains nothing over that.

(3) No window exists where the boundary tightens while the attacker keeps a foothold. sce_glbsfra.sv:78 'apb_cr #(.A(h00),.DW(2)) sfr_scemode (.sfrlock(~devmode & (|cr_scemode)))' makes the mode a one-shot claim; once a trusted stage claims it, sceuser latches (sce_sec.sv:58-63) and a non-matching master is gated off from the SFR page too, so it can never issue HF_INIT. An attacker that does match sceuser in mode_sec IS the trusted crypto agent and can already write SEG_KEY/SEG_MSG and choose what is measured. sfr_arclr does not change the ownership gate, so surviving it crosses no privilege boundary; sfr_arrst resets scemode to 0 but that re-opens the whole SCE to everyone, which subsumes the issue.

(4) The 'excluded from the wipe' framing is misleading about the asset. HRAM 0..427 holds only public constants. The wipe covers 428..767, which is exactly RAMSEG_ST (0x200=512) and RAMSEG_MSG (544) - the chaining state and message block, i.e. the key-derived material. Excluding the constants so software does not have to re-run HF_INIT after every arclr is a defensible design choice, not secret retention.

Residual real-but-minor issue worth passing to the vendor: there is no integrity check, lock bit or one-shot on HF_INIT, and the 428-word source region overlaps SEG_SKEY/SEG_SCRT, so HF_INIT will copy the bus-write-only secret segments into HRAM 88..247 where they become the SHA-512 round constants (combohasha uses ramreq[8]/[9] at sce.sv:454-457, outside the AC-checked range chnlreq[0:7], so no acerr is raised). That is a hygiene/defense-in-depth gap exercisable only by an entity that already owns the SCE, and it yields a nonlinear oracle no stronger than the HMAC oracle that entity already possesses. It is not a secure-boot bypass by an unprivileged attacker, and it is not the finding as written.

CONFIRMED — I could not refute it. I re-derived mimm_sub's FSM cycle-by-cycle rather than trusting the narrative.

Code truth:
- rtl/modules/crypto_pke/rtl/mimm.sv:338-342: the ONLY transition to MFSM_DONE is `((mfsm == MFSM_SUB1) && sub1skip)`. mfsm_sub1done (line 340) has higher priority and sends the FSM back to MFSM_SUB0.
- Pipeline alignment checked: areg/breg (383-384) are 2-cycle-delayed RAM reads, matched by mfsm_sub0pl2 / mfsm_sub0cycpl2 (362-363). sub0cmpdone (348-349) therefore fires at the first differing word walking MSW->LSW (daptr = dblen - mfsm_sub0cyc - 1, line 369), and sub1skip (352-354) is registered in that same cycle. So on entry to SUB1, sub1skip is already valid, and mfsm_sub1cycpl2 is 0 (reset while not in SUB1, line 356) so mfsm_sub1done is false on cycle 1.
- Net: da < db => SUB0(k) -> SUB1(1 cycle) -> DONE. da >= db => SUB0(k) -> SUB1(dblen+2) -> SUB0 (second full compare) -> SUB1(1) -> DONE. dblen = nlen+1 (line 266) => ~+35 cycles for RSA-2048, ~+67 for RSA-4096 per Montgomery multiply, plus the leading-match-length leak from the SUB0 early exit even when no reduction happens.

Instantiation in real silicon (not dead / not emulation-only):
- PkeCore.sv:362-401 instantiates mimm unconditionally; grep for ifdef/ifndef/endif in PkeCore.sv returns NOTHING, so there is no guard.
- Chain: soc_top.sv:555 soc_coresub -> soc_coresub.sv:511 sce -> sce.sv:478 pke -> pke.sv:754 PkeCore -> mimm. rtl/asic_top/include/sce_inc.sv:72 includes mimm.sv into the ASIC build.

Propagation to the exploitable signal:
- PkeCore.sv:373 .done(ModMulDone_s1); PkeCore.sv:343 assign ModMulDone = ModMulDone_s0 | ModMulDone_s1 -> MpcDone.
- PkeCtrl.sv:1280-1310 MODEXP is a regular R0/R1 Montgomery ladder (MMR0R1/MMR1R0 then MMR0R0/MMR1R1 for every exponent bit), i.e. deliberately operation-count-invariant. That makes mimm_sub's variance the residual, clean Walter/Schindler extra-reduction signal rather than noise inside a larger leak — it strengthens the finding.

Compensating controls searched for and NOT found:
- opt_sec / db_rnd (pke.sv:788-793, mimm.sv:88,248) terminate in mac_cell.sv:49-53 (`pb[i] = ... ~ME & (opt_pl >= i) ? (opt_sec ? DB_rnd : '0) : '0`) — a power/EM dummy-activity measure inside the multiplier array. mimm_sub's port list (mimm.sv:299-317) has no db_rnd/opt_sec input at all, so it cannot affect the reduction timing.
- opt_mask decodes to opt_inithcal/opt_inithnt/opt_wbpsob/opt_edpcomp (pke.sv:347-349, 1317) — HCal/init options, not base or exponent blinding. No blinding exists anywhere in PkeCtrl/PkeCore.
- No dummy subtraction, no constant-time padding, no top-level tie-off of mimm_opt or mmsel.

Contrast claim verified (shows the constant-time discipline was understood elsewhere in the same block): mgmr_mul.v:464 `assign mgmr_mul_comalg_mode = is_M_bigeer_N ? UINT_BA_SUB_A : UINT_B_MOV_A;` always launches a com_alg operation, and com_alg.v:143-172 advances solely on `write_counter == comalg_wlen - 1` with no value-dependent exit. So the default multiplier's final reduction IS constant time; only the mimm path is not.

Timing oracle is on-chip and noise-free: pke.sv:814-824 (`tickclr = ~pcore_busy`, `ticklock = pcore_done_sync`, `tickcntsr <= ticklock ? tickcnt : tickcntsr`), exposed read-only via apb_sr sfr_tickcnt at offset 0x54 (pke.sv:314). With sfr_tickcyc (0x50) = 0, tickhit asserts every clkpke cycle, giving a cycle-exact per-operation duration.

The one genuine narrowing factor (already disclosed as a precondition, so not a refutation): mmsel = mimmcr[8] (pke.sv:767) comes from `apb_cr #(.A('h24), .DW(9)) sfr_mimmcr` (pke.sv:310), and apb_cr's IV parameter defaults to 32'h0 (rtl/modules/amba/rtl/apb_sfr.sv:81), so the reset default selects the constant-time mgmr_mul. Firmware must opt into the mimm path. PkeCtrl.sv:1539-1542 special-cases HLen for the mimm 1/2/4-MAC modes, so mimm is a supported production configuration rather than vestigial, and sfr_mimmcr has no dedicated lock bit (the shared sfrlock at pke.sv:287 only blocks writes while the core is busy). But no firmware is present in this repo, so I cannot demonstrate that shipped code enables mimmcr[8].

Severity: high — unpatchable silicon, private-key recovery on RSA/ECC via a well-established attack, with a noise-free on-chip cycle counter as the oracle. Exploitability: difficult rather than practical, solely because the vulnerable multiplier is not the reset default and the attacker generally does not choose that bit; conditional on firmware selecting mimm, the attack is pure software with thousands of chosen-input queries and no measurement noise.

RTL claims verified as literally accurate but the security impact is refuted. healthtest.v:38 genuinely omits the healthtest_en term that line 34 has, and cr_postproc resets to '0 (trng.sv:110 + apb_sfr.sv:81), so with len=0 the predicate (cnt 0 >= len 0) is true and healthtest_err toggles on healthy data. That much is a real RTL defect. It is not exploitable, for five independent reasons.

(1) No consumer, no gate. trng.sv:357 `assign chnlo_start = rngcore_en & rngcore_dataout_vld & ~chnlo_busy ;` has no health term, and trng.sv:283-284 `theregrn( intr ) <= '0;` / `theregrn( err ) <= '0;` hardwire the module's interrupt and error outputs to zero. fr[2] (trng.sv:124) reaches only an apb_fr read/W1C register (trng.sv:118); apb_fr (apb_sfr.sv:180-202) has no interrupt port. A correctly-gated health test in this design would stop exactly zero bits of degraded entropy from reaching SEG_RNGA/B, so the attacker's outcome in the scenario's step 4 is bit-identical with or without the bug. The finding's own harm chain therefore adds nothing.

(2) No firmware or documented guarantee to degrade. grep -rin "hlthtest|healthtest" over the whole repo (excluding healthtest.v, rng_top.v, trng.sv) returns zero hits: no firmware, no register-map export, no doc under docs/src/, no testbench reads this bit. The "firmware validation sees it fire on good parts and learns to mask it" step is pure speculation with no code exhibiting it, and there is no documented behavior for the RTL to contradict.

(3) No attacker action. The only lever is cr_postproc (APB 0x08). trng.sv:52 ties sfrlock to '0, so any agent that can write cr_healthtest_len can also write cr_ana (trng.sv:132) — and digitalization.v:76 `ana_vld_sys[i]= clk_ana_pos[i] & ana_en[i] & ana_vld[i]` means clearing cr_anaen stops the source outright — or write rngchainen. An attacker with that access already owns the entropy source directly; the health-flag noise yields nothing new. An attacker without that access cannot influence the configuration at all, since it is set by legitimate firmware.

(4) The reset-configuration framing overstates reach. cr_ana also resets to 0, so on a genuinely untouched TRNG digi_data_vld never asserts (digitalization.v:83-86, :126) and healthtest_err never fires. The chatter requires firmware that configured cr_src/cr_ana but deliberately left the health test off — firmware that opted out of the feature and has no reason to consult its status bit.

(5) The "no hardware minimum on healthtest_length" sub-claim inverts the risk: len=0 is the strictest possible repetition-count cutoff (any repeat flags), not a bypass; len=63 is loose but is a normal point in a configurable SP 800-90B RCT range chosen by software that could equally just not use the TRNG.

Net: a real functional asymmetry worth a non-security note to the vendor, but no asset read or influenced, no access control bypassed, no guarantee the hardware actually provides degraded. The substantive weakness nearby — health result is advisory-only and gates neither chnlo_start nor err[] — is a separate finding, and it is precisely what renders this one impact-free. Severity "high" is not sustainable.

I could not refute this. Every RTL claim reproduces verbatim and I independently re-derived the arithmetic and the access-control chain.

CONFIRMED FACTS:
1. INITSIZE = 428. Re-derived hash_pkg.sv:88-104: SHA256_H=0, SHA256_K=8, SHA512_H=72, SHA512_K=88, BLK2s_H=248, BLK2b_H=256, BLK2_X=272, BLK3_H=292, BLK3_X=300, RIPMD_H=314, RIPMD_K=320, RIPMD_X=330, SHA3_P0=370, SHA3_P1=380, CHACHA20_H=428.
2. combohasha.sv:78-87 SEG_INIT {segaddr:'0, segsize:INITSIZE} and combohasha.sv:580-588 MFSM_LD_INIT {rpsegcfg=SEG_INIT, rpptr_start='0, transsize=INITSIZE} — HF_INIT DMAs SCERAM words 0..427 into HRAM 0..427.
3. combohasha.sv:854-858 .clrstart(INITSIZE); cryptoram.sv:24-25 clrend defaults to thecfg.WCNT-1 (combohasha.sv:836 WCNT=256*3=768); cryptoram.sv:61-63 clear FSM runs clrstart..clrend. HRAM 0..427 is never wiped by sceramclr. Notably the genuinely secret regions (RAMSEG_ST=512, RAMSEG_MSG=544) ARE inside 428..767 and are wiped — so the exclusion is deliberate and the poison survives every mode-quit / sfr_arclr / sfr_arrst.
4. Access control independently re-derived, not taken on faith: sce.sv:203-206 shows chnlreq[0]/[1] are the AHB slave read/write channels; scedma_ac.sv:46 indexes chnlacrules[segid][i] with [0:CHNLACCNT-1] MSB-first ordering, so bit index 1 == AHB write; scedma_pkg.sv:292-297 gives LKEY/KEY/SKEY/SCRT/MSG = 8'b01_01_01_01 and HOUT = 8'b01_00_00_10, all with index 1 = 1. SCERAM 0..427 is AHB-writable in every mode.
5. sce_sec.sv:72 "assign ahben = mode_non ? 1'b1 : ..." — in scemode==0 there is no hauser/coreuser check whatsoever, and sce_glbsfra.sv:78 sfr_scemode has default IV 0, so mode_non is the reset state.
6. NO hardcoded constants exist anywhere in the design. grep -ri "428a2f98|6a09e667|71374491|bb67ae85" across the entire tree returns only comments in hashcore_blk.sv:159-161 and testbench literals. There is no ROM fallback, no second copy.
7. Instantiated in real silicon: soc_top.sv -> soc_coresub.sv:511-552 (sce, .ahbs(coreahbmux[2])) -> sce.sv:442 combohash(.ramclr(sceramclr), .resetn(sceresetn)). combohasha.sv is pulled in by rtl/asic_top/include/sce_inc.sv:49. Not dead, not emulation-only, no parameter override at instantiation that changes clrstart.
8. Intended usage confirmed by the vendor's own testbench (sce_tb_v0.2_hash.sv:143-150): $readmemh("hashram.dua"); memwr('0,512); sfrwr(HASH_crfunc,32'hff); sfrwr(HASH_ar,32'h5a). Software supplies the constant image from SCERAM word 0 — exactly the claimed mechanism.

COMPENSATING CONTROLS SEARCHED FOR AND NOT FOUND: no lock/one-shot bit on HF_INIT (combohasha.sv:203 sfrlock is only asserted for the duration of an operation); no integrity or known-answer check; no ROM copy; nothing in docs/src/*.md that documents or protects hash constants; nvracrules (scedma_ac.sv:40,66) can only replace the access rules and the compiled-in default already permits AHB write.

THE ONE CONTROL THAT DOES TEMPER IT (understated by the prior reviewers): sce_glbsfra.sv:78 apb_cr sfr_scemode has .sfrlock(~devmode & (|cr_scemode)), so scemode is write-locked once non-zero. Returning to mode_non requires sfr_arrst (sce_glbsfra.sv:85), which sits behind the same ahb_gate and is therefore reachable only by the CURRENT SCE owner. So an unprivileged runtime attacker cannot unilaterally force mode_non. The attack requires either (a) the cold-reset window before any code claims the SCE — in which state the SCE has literally zero access control — or (b) an owner that voluntarily releases the engine, or (c) the attacker sharing the owner's coreuser tag. Additionally, a victim that always issues its own HF_INIT at the start of its session is immune, and since HRAM is undefined at cold power-up any correct first user must do so.

OVERSTATEMENT IN THE WRITE-UP (should be corrected before disclosure, but does not refute the defect): malicious-constant attacks yield attacker-chosen colliding pairs, not second preimages against a pre-existing reference digest. "Supplies a rogue image whose doctored-SHA-256 digest equals the reference digest" does not follow. Sound impact is loss of collision resistance and of the standard-IV assumption wherever the attacker influences both sides of a measurement, degenerate SHA-3 (rho/pi indices at HRAM 370..379 are used as rotation/permutation amounts) and BLAKE sigma, and silent-wrong-crypto DoS. Also, sce_ts truststate (sce_sec.sv:117) is driven by hmac_pass, whose comparison (combohasha.sv:481-489, chnlscrt_wpreq.segwdat == '0 against a keystore value fetched over AXI) still requires knowledge of the secret reference, so constant poisoning alone does not forge truststate.

VERDICT: the core defect is real and unpatchable in silicon — the sole copy of every hash constant in the chip lives in a bus-loadable RAM region that the SCE's own ownership-change wipe deliberately skips, with no lock and no integrity check. High severity because the payoff is total compromise of every hash primitive and because it punches a hole in the chip's own tenant-isolation primitive; exploitability difficult rather than practical because the attacker must hold the SCE (cold-reset window or owner release) and the victim must skip its own HF_INIT.

PARTIALLY REFUTED - mechanism confirmed, headline impact refuted, severity overstated.

CONFIRMED FROM RTL:
- combohasha.sv:740 `assign chnlo_cfg.wpptr_start = cr_segptrstart[SEGID_HOUT2];` with SEGID_HOUT2 = SEGID_SOB+1 = 7 (line 68). sfr_segptr (line 223) is A=0x20, DW=scedma_pkg::AW=12, SFRCNT=SEGCNT+1=8 (SEGCNT param = 7, line 23), so index 7 at offset 0x3C is a real, fully software-writable, range-unchecked 12-bit CR.
- The guard at combohasha.sv:230 is real, and MFSM_LD_KEY really selects SEG_SKEY when opt_ifskey (line 645). HF_HMAC256_PASS2 with opt_check=0 really reaches MFSM_WB_HOUT.
- Access-rule polarity verified in scedma_ac.sv:47-53 (chnlac = acenable ? rule : '1, then segrd/segwr & chnlac) => 1 = ALLOW. With `bit [0:7]`, index 0 is the MSB. So SEG_HOUT (8'b01_00_00_10) is AHB-read DENIED and SEG_SOB (8'b10_00_10_00) is AHB-read ALLOWED. The ifsob/ifskey guard is therefore load-bearing, exactly as the finding claims.
- sce.sv:456 does route the hash write port to ramreq[9], outside the scedma_ac [0:CHNLACCNT-1] window, and sce_memc.sv:212 does no bounds check.

REFUTED - THE ARBITRARY-WRITE CLAIM. I traced sce_dmachnl.sv cycle-accurately (theregrn expands to a plain sync FF, rtl/modules/common/rtl/template.sv:82-90):
  cycle 0: chnlstart=1 -> busy<=1, rprdvld<=1, wpptr <= wpptr_start (previous wpptr is in range, so the clamp does not block the load).
  cycle 1: wpptr = wpptr_start. wpwr = rprdpl1vld | rprdpl2 (sce_dmachnl.sv:189-191) is still 0 because rprdpl1 cannot be set before cycle 2 (rprdpl1 <= rprdvld & rpready). NO write is issued.
  end of cycle 1: the clamp `(wpptr > thewpsegcfg.segsize) ? 0` fires and forces wpptr(2) = 0 for ANY wpptr_start > segsize.
  cycle >=3: the first actual write beat occurs, by which time wpptr is already 0.
So an out-of-range wpptr_start is neutralized before any write beat exists. The ONLY out-of-segment value that survives is wpptr_start == segsize exactly (64 > 64 is false), i.e. exactly ONE word past the segment end. There is no arbitrary-address write.

That kills the entire second half of the attack scenario: setting the pointer to 1472 to hit SEG_AOB does nothing (and 1856 is SEGADDR_AIB anyway - SEGADDR_AOB is 1920). SEG_AOB, SEG_POB and SEG_PSOB are unreachable. There is no chosen-32-bit-word planting into engine output buffers, so the 2^32 offline-grinding forgery story does not exist. Note the read/write asymmetry the finder missed: rprd IS asserted in cycle 1, so the read-side pointer genuinely yields one arbitrary-address read - but the write side does not.

WHAT SURVIVES: steps 1-4 of the scenario work. cr_segptrstart[7] = 64 during MFSM_WB_HOUT writes digest word 0 to SCERAM word 384+64 = 448 = SEG_SOB[0], which ACRULEs make AHB-readable, while combohasha.sv:230 has forced opt_ifsob=0 precisely to stop an SKEY-derived digest from reaching SOB. That is a genuine, software-only bypass of an explicit anti-exfiltration control, reachable with two APB register writes and no physical access.

WHY SEVERITY IS MEDIUM, NOT HIGH:
- The leak is 32 bits (digest word 0) per invocation. Words 1..7 are unreachable: wpptr advances to 65 and is clamped to 0 before the second beat's write is issued, so beats 1..7 land back in HOUT. This is not key recovery; the attacker cannot forge a full HMAC.
- Secondary variants are weak: MFSM_WB_KEY at ptr 64 writes one word to SKEY[0] (a corrupt-not-read primitive), MFSM_WB_SOB at ptr 64 writes to PKB[0] - both AHB-read-denied.
- Preconditions: mode_sec (sce.sv:369 acenable = mode_sec; with mode_sec=0 the AC is fully disabled and SKEY is directly readable anyway) and an attacker who already owns the SCE APB. That is the right boundary to attack (the design intends SCE-driving software to USE but not EXTRACT a keystore-loaded SKEY), so it is a legitimate finding - but the same attacker also holds the far stronger read-side rpptr_start primitive, so the marginal capability gained here is small.

BOTTOM LINE: report the defect (unchecked wpptr_start at combohasha.sv:740 combined with the mis-prioritized clamp at sce_dmachnl.sv:127-129), but rewrite the impact as "one-word overflow past the end of the hash output segment into SEG_SOB[0], defeating the ifsob/ifskey guard and leaking 32 bits of SKEY-derived digest per run." Drop the arbitrary-address / chosen-value / AOB-POB-PSOB claims entirely - they are not achievable in this RTL.

RTL CLAIM: CONFIRMED, verbatim, from my own read.

healthtest.v:34-39 is exactly as quoted. Line 34 gates the counter with `(~healthtest_en) ? 6'h0 :`; line 38 has no healthtest_en term. With en=0 the counter is pinned at 0, so with healthtest_length=6'h0 the assert predicate `healthtest_cnt>=healthtest_length` is 0>=0 = true and healthtest_err asserts on every pair of equal consecutive digitized bits (~50% of samples on a healthy source), clearing on the next differing bit.

Reset value CONFIRMED: trng.sv:110 `apb_cr #(.A('h08), .DW(17) ) sfr_pp (.cr(cr_postproc), ...)` has no IV override; apb_cr's default is `parameter IV=32'h0` (apb_sfr.sv:81), so out of reset cr_hlthtest_en=0 AND cr_healthtest_len=6'h0. trng.sv:257-264 confirms both fields live in cr_postproc.

INSTANTIATED IN REAL SILICON: CONFIRMED. sce.sv:531 `trng trng(` sits inside `ifdef FULL_CHIP (sce.sv:475 ... 571) — i.e. present in the chip build, excluded only from the verilator sim. sce is instantiated at soc_coresub.sv:518. healthtest.v is pulled into the build by rtl/asic_top/include/sce_inc.sv:40. The second `module trng` at sce.sv:603 that I checked as a possible stub override is inside a /* */ comment block, so it is not a competing definition. rng_top.v:79-87 wires healthtest with only healthtest_err out, and rng_top.v:89-140 passes digi_data_out/digi_data_vld to data_buf and postprocess with no qualification.

NO COMPENSATING CONTROL FOUND: trng.sv:52 `theregrn( sfrlock ) <= '0;` means the SFRs are never locked. Grep for healthtest|hlthtest across the entire repo returns hits only in healthtest.v, rng_top.v, trng.sv and sce_inc.sv — zero hits in docs/, firmware, headers, SVD or any register-map artifact. No boot gate, no lock bit, no redundant check, no parameter override.

TWO MATERIAL ERRORS IN THE FINDING that force a severity downgrade from "high":

(1) The attack scenario's step 4 is mechanically WRONG. If the attacker freezes the noise source (e.g. rngchainen=0: trng.sv:228 `assign rngclkhfxor = ^( {...} & rngchainen[CHAINW-1:0] )` goes to constant 0, so t_rngsrc_dat and hence digi_data_out are constant), then digi_data_out==digi_data_save holds forever and the clear term at healthtest.v:39 `(digi_data_vld&(digi_data_out!=digi_data_save))? 1'b0` never fires. sr_hlthtest_err latches HIGH and stays high, producing exactly ONE rising edge at trng.sv:269, so sr_hlthtest_errcnt reaches 1 — not '1. A stuck source therefore yields a LOW count, not "the identical health indication" the finding claims. The finding's causal story is inverted. (The real weakness this exposes — that the rising-edge counter at trng.sv:268-271 structurally cannot saturate on a stuck source even when the test IS correctly configured — is a different defect than the one reported.)

(2) The impact chain is much weaker than described. trng.sv:283-284 ties both block outputs off unconditionally: `theregrn( intr ) <= '0;` and `theregrn( err ) <= '0;`. fr[2] (trng.sv:124) feeds only sfr_fr (trng.sv:118), an apb_fr (apb_sfr.sv:180-231) which is a plain write-1-to-clear APB read register with NO interrupt or error output. So the "cry wolf" signal generates no interrupt, no SCE-level error, no event — it is a bit software must deliberately poll. Furthermore cr_hlthtest_en and cr_healthtest_len are fields of the SAME register cr_postproc, so any firmware that enables the test necessarily writes a length in the same store; the false-positive case only afflicts firmware that left the test disabled and therefore has no reason to read sr_hlthtest_errcnt (trng.sv:266). "Trains firmware to ignore it" is a firmware-behaviour hypothesis, not an RTL consequence.

(3) The sub-claim about no hardware minimum on healthtest_length crosses no privilege boundary: any agent that can write cr_postproc can already write cr_hlthtest_en=0 outright, or stop the generator via ar_stop (trng.sv:114).

CONCLUSION: I do not refute the RTL observation — the enable/error asymmetry at healthtest.v:34 vs :38 is a genuine, correctly-quoted defect present in taped-out silicon, and the degenerate length=0 reset default is real. But it exposes no asset, bypasses no access control, drives no interrupt, and the reported exploit mechanism is incorrect. It is a status-signal quality bug, not a high-severity vulnerability. Report it to the vendor at low severity, with the correction that the more serious sibling issue is the rising-edge counter's blindness to a permanently stuck source.

NOT REFUTED. I re-derived the entire chain from the RTL myself and found no compensating control.

Instantiation is real silicon: combohash at sce.sv:442 (outside the `ifdef FULL_CHIP` guard that begins ~line 476), sce at soc_coresub.sv:511 with .TSC(256), soc_coresub at rtl/asic_top/rtl/soc_top.sv:555, soc_top at daric_top.sv:362. truststate flows soc_coresub.sv:546 -> soc_coresub.sv:836 (.trustkey(truststate)) -> rrc.sv:717 unmasked.

The three forgeable inputs are all confirmed unlocked and unbound:
- combohasha.sv:218 sfr_opt2 carries tsmode and ifskey as a plain apb_cr with no sfrlock argument (contrast sce_glbsfra.sv:78, which does pass .sfrlock(~devmode & (|cr_scemode)) - the designers used write-once elsewhere and did not here).
- combohasha.sv:221 sfr_keyidx -> combohasha.sv:490 assign hmac_kid = kid, with nothing correlating kid to the key or digest actually processed.
- combohasha.sv:645 chnli_cfg.rpsegcfg = opt_ifskey ? SEG_SKEY : SEG_KEY, and combohasha.sv:477/660-668 select SEG_SCRT vs the ReRAM key store at PM_KS_BA + kid*32 (line 462). chnli_start for MFSM_LD_SECRET is gated &~tsmode (line 699) and schstartx is gated &tsmode (line 457), so tsmode=0 genuinely substitutes the bus-writable SEG_SCRT.

The plant is achievable: I read scedma_ac.sv in full - chnlac[i] = acenable ? chnlacrules[segid][i] : '1 (line 47), chnloutreq[i].segwr = chnlinreq[i].segwr & chnlac[i] (line 53), channels 0/1 = AHB R/W per the comment at scedma_pkg.sv:279-282. With bit [0:CHNLACCNT-1] accessrule and 8'b01_01_01_01, index 0 = 0 (AHB read denied) and index 1 = 1 (AHB write allowed) for both SEGID_KEY and SEGID_SCRT. scedma_amba.sv:94-97/116/133 decodes an AHB write address directly to that segid. SEGADDR_KEY = word 64 (byte 0x100) and SEGADDR_SCRT = word 192 (byte 0x300) per scedma_pkg.sv:212-214, matching the claimed addresses.

No gate exists between hmac_pass and the trust bit: sce.sv:466-468 forwards hmac_pass/hmac_fail/hmac_kid raw, and I read sce_sec.sv lines 91-126 in full - sce_ts has no tsmode/ifskey input at all. A repo-wide grep shows tsmode and kid appear nowhere outside combohasha.sv.

The reset asymmetry is real: sce.sv:298 is a bare `.resetn,` while combohash (sce.sv:445) and sce_glbsfr (sce.sv:224) both use `.resetn(sceresetn)`, and soc_coresub.sv:225 says `assign resetn = sysresetn;`. So a forged tsreg bit outlives sfr_arrst, ar_clrram and mode-quit.

The only thing resembling a mitigation is scedma_ac.sv:40/66 - nvrrule_enable = (nvracrules[29] == 8'h5a) lets ReRAM config replace ACRULEs. That is not the default, is a soft configuration rather than an RTL control, and nothing in RTL enforces it.

Two framing corrections that narrow impact without refuting: (1) at rrc.sv:717 the !trustkey[akeyid] term is one disjunct among several in key_access_error_pre - the coreuser/ownership terms ((coreuser_in[7:4] & userid_k[7:4])==0, core_rd_dis_k, pri_op/vex_mm_reg) still apply, so the forged bit removes the cryptographic-attestation precondition rather than the ownership check. (2) Conversely the finding understates one consumer: rrc.sv:761-763/770 gates all ReRAM access including instruction fetch for boot1/fw0/fw1 on trustkey[3]/[5]/[7] when tkey_en is set, so forging those indices defeats an attest-before-execute control.

The ownership precondition is weaker, not stronger, than the finding states: sce_glbsfra.sv:78 locks cr_scemode once non-zero, but sce_glbsfr is reset by sceresetn and sfr_arrst (sce_glbsfra.sv:86) drives ar_reset -> sceresetnin (sce_sec.sv:83) -> sceresetn, clearing scemode to 0 and re-opening the claim. With ahben = mode_non ? 1'b1 : ... (sce_sec.sv:72), any software context that is a legitimate SCE user can mount this; it is not a one-shot boot race.

Exploitability is practical: pure software, no fault injection, no knowledge of any secret - the attacker computes HMAC over a key it chose itself and plants the expected tag. Severity high rather than critical because the forged trust bit clears one gate and the rrc coreuser/ownership checks still stand.

Independently re-derived the whole chain from RTL; the finding survives.

CONFIRMED MECHANICS:
1. combohasha.sv:740 `assign chnlo_cfg.wpptr_start = cr_segptrstart[SEGID_HOUT2];` is the sole driver of the output DMA write pointer for all three writeback states (the in-FSM assignments at 712/719/726 are commented out). chnlcfg_t is a packed struct (scedma_pkg.sv:70-82) and the always_comb at 707-736 drives only rpsegcfg/wpsegcfg/transsize, so there is no override.
2. cr_segptrstart is declared [0:SEGCNT] with SEGCNT=7 (combohasha.sv:185), so index 7 is in range (not an out-of-bounds tie-off). apb_cr #(.A('h20), .SFRCNT(8), .DW(AW=12)) at combohasha.sv:223 with apb_sfr2 decode `sfrsel[i] = (paddr == sfrpaddr + 4*i)` (apb_sfr.sv:342) gives 8 real writable 12-bit words at 0x20..0x3C, IV=0. sfrlock only blocks writes during an operation; the attacker writes before start.
3. sce_dmachnl.sv:127-129 clamp priority is genuinely wrong: `theregrn` (template.sv:82-91) is a plain flop, so `(wpptr > thewpsegcfg.segsize)` is tested against the PREVIOUS wpptr and `chnlstart ? thecfg.wpptr_start` loads verbatim.
4. No downstream bounds check: sce_memc.sv:212 `ramm_addr = segaddr + segptr`. I checked the FIFO path as a candidate compensating control (sce_memc.sv:88-90, ramptr0 = ffen ? fframptr : segptr) — SEG_HOUT has isfifo:'0 (scedma_pkg.sv:241) so the raw attacker pointer is used. RAMCNT=1 and all segments ramsel '0, so it is one flat space and the escape lands in neighbouring segments. SEGADDR_HOUT=384, SEGSIZE_HOUT=64, SEGADDR_SOB=448 — the arithmetic in the scenario is right.
5. AC bypass is real: scedma_ac only loops over CHNLCNT = CHNLACCNT = 8 (scedma_ac.sv:43, scedma_pkg.sv:278) and sce.sv:377-380 wires only chnlreq[0:7] through it; combohash's write port sce.sv:456 `.chnl_wpreq(ramreq[9])` goes straight into sce_memc (sce.sv:402).
6. The guard it defeats is real and is the only one: combohasha.sv:230 `opt_ifsob <= optlock ? cr_opt.ifsob & ~cr_opt.ifskey : opt_ifsob`, and opt_ifsob is the sole selector of MFSM_WB_SOB (FSM lines 319/365/424). Decoding the packed bit[0:7] accessrule: SEG_HOUT 8'b01_00_00_10 => AHB read DENIED / write allowed; SEG_SOB 8'b10_00_10_00 => AHB read ALLOWED / write denied; SEG_SKEY 8'b01_01_01_01 => read denied on all buses. So HOUT is deliberately non-readable and SOB is the only readable digest sink, which is exactly why the ifsob&~ifskey guard exists. FSM path verified: HF_HMAC256_PASS2 with opt_check=0 goes MFSM_HF -> MFSM_WB_HOUT (combohasha.sv:412-416), and MFSM_LD_KEY sources SEG_SKEY when opt_ifskey (combohasha.sv:645).
7. Live silicon, not dead/emulation code: combohash is instantiated only at sce.sv:442 (only .PM_KS_BA overridden, so SEGCNT=7 stands); sce at soc_coresub.sv:511-518 (only AXID/COREUSERCNT/INTC/ERRC/TSC overridden); soc_coresub at asic_top/rtl/soc_top.sv:554.

CORRECTIONS (do not change the verdict):
- Not the whole 8-beat transfer escapes. Because the clamp fires exactly one cycle late, wpptr_start > 64 yields exactly ONE out-of-range beat (digest word 0) at 384+P before wpptr snaps to 0; wpptr_start == 64 yields TWO beats, landing at SOB[0] and SOB[1]. Remaining beats wrap back into SEG_HOUT.
